chapters.title: 证人席上的哑巴
chapters.content:
Fishermen stood along the bar of the court with their caps in their hands, and the gallery filled by nine. Every chair in the well of the court was taken but one. A dozen of them had come down from the fleet before four, and the room held the smell of wet wool, wax and cold tea. "We can start," Judge Hollis said.

"Is the witness ready?" "He has been ready since six," replied Brann. Croft stood, old and slow. "Your Honor, before the witness is sworn, I would like to put one matter on the record." "Objection," said Brann, like a door shut. "Overruled. Then proceed," said Hollis, looking across at Sam.

"Mr. Samuels, do you have anything to say before I swear you?" Sam never had anything to say in rooms like that. Six pencils in a tin cup, a blank pad, and a sister three towns inland whom he had not named to anyone in eleven days. He wrote on the pad instead. I am ready. Hollis read the page twice.

"Very well. The witness will be sworn." The clerk then raised his hand. "Do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?" Sam unhooked the cap of his pencil. Nineteen days earlier the town had called him Dumb Sam, and thirty years had not worn the name off him.

Sam was a bachelor of fifty-three, thin as a brush handle. He chose the sign trade at nineteen and never learned another. Above the shop on Harbor Lane he kept a paint closet, a leaning ladder, and a canary kept only to amuse his sister Martha on Sundays.

The town's attitude toward him was cordial at a distance and amiable contempt up close. Everybody liked him. Nobody listened, and it is possible to be a whole town's servant in that way, useful and invisible, which is all Sam would have stayed if Mr. Ash had kept his feet.

He had painted the ballet school a soft rose, the chess club a deep green, the cricket ground an honest white, cabbages for the grocer, cherries for the bakery, cattle on the stockyard wall, a cone of cream for the parlor, a gold spoon for the chef, and the cabin numbers of the fishing fleet.

Sam worked from habit and never from a blueprint, and he believed in the beauty of a well-cut letter the way other men believed in weather. Six pencils, sharpened every Monday, and discipline was the whole of it.

Ash kept the antique shop by the water. A Turkish carpet gone dim, a green velvet couch, ship models under glass, and clocks that disagreed with one another on principle. His prize was the Meridian, an alloy gold pocket watch the tourists called the watch that keeps harbor time.

The brochure printed that line beside a photograph of the bay, and the watch was worth more than three fishing boats. On the last Friday of September, at half past eleven at night, Ash fell down the cement stairs at the shipyard gate and did not get up.

Two cracked ribs. A bruised bowel. A brutal fall for a man of seventy. The doctor wrote the cause as a fall. The town wrote a crisis. "How is he?" Sam asked at the door the next morning.

"Ribs, stitched. The old man keeps asking for his watch," the nurse said. Sam had seen it. He was walking home along the dock with a pot of green paint, as he did every Friday, past a coil of harbor rope where a claw worked in and out, under October fog that lay like a blanket. Fog was a bonus that night for anyone hoping not to be seen.

He was ten paces from the shipyard stairs when a figure came out of the dark. A dark cloak with a high collar. Gloves. No warning and no word, then two hands and a shove, and an old man went down on wet stone with a crush Sam would hear for the rest of his life.

The thief bent and clutched something from Ash's waistcoat, then dashed for the gate. He ran wrong-armed, the way a left-handed man runs, and did not slow at the curb or come to an abrupt stop.

He was gone, swallowed by the fog and the dazzle of the dock lamps. Sam did not chase. He could not shout, which was the whole difficulty of him: even his terror stayed private. The harbor office kept a security camera, an old machine that wrote the night onto a cassette hissing with interference, and nobody had watched the tape in a year.

Inspector Dawe came with lamps and questions, a cop in a labeled coat, the chief at his shoulder surveying the stairs for the photographers, and a dozen constables walking the tide line. "Say it," Dawe said. "Just say it." "I cannot." "You can write." Dawe put a blank notebook in front of him.

"Start with what you saw." Sam wrote four concrete sentences: a man in a dark cloak, gloves, he pushed Mr. Ash down the stairs, he ran toward the shipyard gate, the man was left-handed. Dawe read the page twice and put it in his bureau pocket. "You did your deed," he said.

"Leave the rest to men who can talk." It was said kindly, which made it worse.

Dawe took that statement the way a clerk inventories furniture, quickly, by category, without looking up at the man who was telling him nothing. "Did you see a face?" Dawe asked at the dock an hour later. "No." "Hands?" "Gloves." "Left or right?"

"Wrong arm."

Three days later the police arrested Tomas Reed, a twenty-six-year-old deckhand whose ferry commute the whole harbor could set its clocks by, and charged him with robbery. The Meridian had turned up in a pawnshop two streets up, and Reed told anyone who would listen that the watch had been his father's, pawned in August, a bargain struck to cover a debt when the boats stopped running.

Found later, the pawnbroker's cheque stubs proved it. The dates did not coincide with the theft, and it was no coincidence that the ledger entry had surfaced two streets from Dawe's own route home, where a bribe here and a sorry tale there had made up the town's mind for it. "Was it yours?" Sam asked in the cafe. "It was my father's," said Reed.

"Ask the clerk anyhow." The crime assembled itself so neatly that nobody asked why a criminal would pawn, for a fraction of its worth, the one object that could convict him. Nobody asked what kind of thief keeps a souvenir, and nobody asked what a town that had discriminated against Sam for thirty years had done to a stranger.

The police had apprehended the wrong man and had no choice but to call him guilty, because anything else was a scandal. In Sam's chest a small thing happened, which he later called the hour his fear converted itself into patience. He spent the three weeks before the trial the way he spent everything. Quietly, with a brush within reach.

He went back to the dock at half past eleven and stood where he had stood, contemplating the stairs, until the fog and the warm fireplace of the cafe taught him a second patience. "You come here a great deal," the cook said.

"I like the fire," said Sam. He walked the boundary between his shop and the pawnshop every evening. The gossip gave him nothing definite, and the harbor told two accounts of that night that conflicted in every detail except the ones that mattered.

"What does the clerk say?" Sam asked one night.

"Nothing. The frightened kind."

"Who does he owe?"

"One policeman." In the cafe, beside the fire, he collected every anecdote about the pawn clerk: a young man with pinhole pupils and the trembling hands of a cocaine addict. It was not intuition. It was attention, laid out page by page.

He studied his own torn statement from memory and determined that he could deduce the truth of a page the way he judged a sign, by edges. A line is defined by its pressure. Even an ant on the dock rail had a better view of that night than the police had, and the ant simply had no motive to improve on it.

His criterion was simple, set out in a second notebook as a full breakdown of that night, minute by minute. He began to classify handwriting the way he judged weather, by weight and edge, until he could name the letters of this town that had been painted by a drinking hand. Classification was only reading made patient.

The pawnshop visit came last. He surveyed the ledger, found the Meridian's entry, and understood the whole construction at once. It was not a trail. It was a device for ending a dispute. Someone had devised a closing, not a theft, a lie that contradicted nothing and was consequently hard to check, because it agreed so neatly with the truth.

That was the cunning of it. In conjunction with the cheque stubs sitting unexamined in a drawer, it was also, for anyone willing to look, a confusion that dissolved the moment the two documents came together. The county appointed Reed a lawyer and gave Sam none, for a witness needs none.

Croft was sixty, appointed by the court, working to a bill and a budget fit for a fish net. His advice to his client was short: keep your head down. He did not advise hope, and hope was a bonus he could not bill. Croft, chewing the end of a thin cigaret, read the second notebook twice. "This is it?"

"This is it."

"Then understand what you are doing. If this is right, the man who framed your testimony sits in the well of that court with a badge on."

"What happens to witnesses who contend with policemen?" Sam wrote back one line. My sister is in the county home. That is their choice of hostage, and they have already made it. Croft approved the plan with a nod and added one condition: answer nothing except in writing, in court, before everyone. Then they would all bite the bullet together.

The station buffet catered the wake and, grudgingly, the first morning of the trial, while the town arrived hungry and lingered past dessert. Fog had lifted into a hard clean cold. Croft's cigarette climbed the ceiling. The bar of the court was packed with fishermen in their boots, the courthouse carpet was gray with harbor grit, and the proceedings commenced at ten sharp.

Hollis took the bench with a cup of tea, a dry old man with a constitution of iron, famous for hearing motions in his chambers before anybody could make them theatrical. Brann led for the Crown, the youngest attorney in the office, young, arrogant, compelling, in a gray blouse whose collar sat exact as a verdict. Croft came second, cordial the way tired men are.

"He is probably guilty," Croft had told the newspaper's court critic,

"but every man deserves a defence." The press had run article after article for a week, and in some superficial corner of every column the town was told that a silent witness is a suspicious witness. Nobody closed the page.

Brann, the advocate who had never lost a morning, rose and called her first witness. "The prosecution calls Samuel Samuels," she said, and she opened like a tide.

"The accused owns a dark coat. The witness describes a dark cloak. The accused handled the stolen watch, the witness saw it taken, and the stolen watch was in his possession by his own admission."

"Members of the jury, the conclusion is not a mystery. It is arithmetic, and I conclude my opening with it. In addition to the pawn record we hold an array of facts written by a man with nothing to gain."

"In advance of any influence from either side?" the clerk suggested.

"What does the law allow a jury to do?" asked Brann.

"To weigh what a man writes as what he is," said Hollis.

"The court knows character when it sees it." She called her star witness, and the room went quiet in the particular way rooms go quiet around Sam. He walked up the aisle with six pencils in a tin cup, and thirty years of interference parted around him like water.

"Mr. Samuels, you keep a notebook. Is this your hand?" She held the pages up, pinned in a wire bracket as Exhibit A. Four sentences. And at the foot of page two, one line more. It was at this point that the trial, which had been a parade, became a duel. Croft rose, his pencil still between his teeth.

"Your Honor, before we hang a man on paper, on what basis does this court accept a page no one saw written?"

"A claim with no voice behind it is ambiguous. I do not challenge the mute man, I challenge the page. To cast doubt on nothing but one mute man's honesty would be arbitrary, and I anticipate the prosecution will produce a certificate, because a certificate certifies nothing except that someone with a pen said so. Justice is blind. We ask only that she not be blindfolded."

Hollis adjusted his glasses. "Can you assert authorship, Mr. Samuels? In your own hand, before this court?" Sam uncapped a pencil. The click of the tin lid was the loudest thing in the room. He wrote in a hand so even it looked printed. I wrote it. I saw it. I have been writing all my life. Ask me anything.

He turned the pad and held it up, and the neatness of it amazed the room. The contrast between the nickname and that handwriting collapsed the concept of Dumb Sam on the spot, and the critic wrote that evening it was like finding a swan in the barrel of herring.

The clerk assessed the pages and committed them to the record without comment. The judge deemed them conclusive as to authorship, notwithstanding the witness's silence. Brann pressed on, walking Sam through the statement line by line. He nodded to each. Coherent. Cautious. Certain. The jury leaned in as one animal.

No one disputed the pages. No one could discount them. Even the cross-examination, when Croft finally made it, arrived wrapped in cordial apology, questions about light and about distance, about a mute man who had not spoken since boyhood and might therefore confuse what he saw with what he had been told. Sam answered in writing, and every answer landed with the weight of a definition.

Then Brann asked the question she had saved. Her aim had been true all morning, and it had achieved everything except the truth. "Mr. Samuels. Did you see the accused, Tomas Reed, push Mr. Ash down the stairs?" Sam looked at the accused. Not at the dark coat. At the hands, the right-handed hands of a boatman, unburned. And he wrote one word.

No. The word went around the room like cold water.

"Your own notebook," Brann said slowly. Sam was already writing, fast, six sharpened points and nothing between his belief and the page.

I wrote that a man in a dark cloak pushed Mr. Ash. I wrote it because it was true. I never wrote that the man was Tomas Reed.

That sentence was added after Inspector Dawe took my page. Compare the two and you will see it. The ink is the same. The difference is the pressure.

My hand settles harder at the end of a sentence, like a boat coming to rest. That line floats. A comparative study will show a cultivated hand imitating mine, superficially perfect, and wrong at every edge.

I have classified this town's hands for thirty years. I know what a copied line resembles. It takes my shape the way a gull resembles an albatross, from a distance, and only if you want it to. The truth, once it is written, is not hard to comprehend. The courtroom did not so much gasp as inhale together.

There it was: three sentences sitting like boats at anchor, and the added line riding higher, lighter, brittle where Sam's letters were rooted. A blunder made by a man in a hurry with a steady hand and a guilty one. The decay of the ink told its own story, and the forged line lay at the page's lower border, where a forger's thumb had steadied the sheet.

Under the critical eye of a sign painter, the width of that thumb was something every man in the well of the court had seen before. Dawe contrived to look surprised. He contrived it badly.

"Whose hand is that line, Mr. Samuels?" the judge asked. Sam did not write. He pointed. He pointed at Inspector Dawe. What followed took eleven minutes and rearranged the town. Brann did not defend her own investigator. She conferred with her assistant in a cordial whisper with frost in it, then sat down pale.

"Why should this court believe you over an officer?" Hollis asked. Sam filled the page and turned it around.

Because he chose the wrong hostage and the wrong trade. I paint letters, and letters are evidence that keeps. Whoever set down that fifth sentence conceived it without my consent.

Three weeks ago he came to my shop and told me that if I opened my mouth, even on paper, he would have my sister Martha confined to a ward two days inland, with paperwork so correct that no one could complain.

He told me a mute man is a convenient witness, because you cannot allege what you cannot say. He gave me a choice: my sister, or the truth.

That man knows how to dispose of a witness, and he has done it before, with the pawn clerk, a young man with trembling hands who owed him money and who found the watch in his ledger on his order.

And because the man he framed rides the ferry every day of the year, and the watch he stole sits in his coat this minute, the theft was the bizarre mercy of a thief who steals for keeps. There is harbor sand in his watch chain, Your Honor.

Check the seams of his sailing gloves. Brown wool, left thumb worn through. I painted the harbor office sign fourteen years ago, and I have seen those gloves every winter since. The gloves were found in Dawe's bureau with harbor sand in the stitching. The clerk confessed before lunch, weeping about the interest.

The cassette, played that afternoon in chambers with the court and both counsel present, demonstrated the minute to the second: a man in brown wool gloves on the stairs as Ash climbed.

A side-by-side comparison of the two inks left nothing comparable. The true contradiction was not between truth and lie but between two pressures of one pen. By the time the tape ran out, not an atom of doubt remained in the building. The charge against Tomas Reed was dismissed before the clock struck one, a morning that would defy any dramatist the town could have hired.

Reed sat captive between two officers until the clerk called the order, while his mother clinging to the rail was watched by the whole gallery. The brass buttons of his only coat had been polished by her every Sunday for nine years.

The accused rose out of his dark coat like a man coming up from deep water. His mother crossed the floor, threw caution to the tide, and hugged the mute man with everything she had. Sam held the tin cup out of the way and stayed perfectly calm.

In the crush at the doors, with reporters, fishermen and the crew of every boat in the harbor, Dawe was walked out to a waiting car at the curb. It was a breach of every trust the harbor had ever extended to a uniform, and the town took it personally. Hollis asked the last question before he adjourned. It was not about the watch.

"You knew from the night of the arrest that the line had been added. You could have come forward weeks earlier. Why wait until a man stood one afternoon from doom?"

My silence was an act of cowardice, Your Honor. I told myself a man with a record would survive a suspended sentence.

I told myself that until I saw his mother's face in your gallery. Conversely, I will tell you what I know now: fear does not cope with itself, and it must be converted daily into work.

That is all courage is. I am not the quiet one. I have been talking for thirty years. This town has simply been reading too slowly. The conviction of Inspector Dawe came at the winter circuit, on robbery, on tampering with evidence, on suborning a witness, and, because the clerk had helped forge the page, on the lesser charge of accessory. His appeal failed in the spring.

In his instructions to the winter jury the circuit judge cited the painter's second notebook almost word for word, and the court record was amended at last to say what it should have said on the first night.

The county home kept Martha where she was. The harbor clergy called on her with cakes. The management, embarrassed, sent Sam a framed certificate of thanks, which he used, practically, to wedge the shelf under his leaning ladder. Ash brought a civil action against the harbor corporation for the state of the stair lamps and won, and the award paid for new lights along the whole pier.

A letter from the pier conservation society arrived with money to restore the harbor office sign Sam had painted fourteen years before, because, the letter said, some things should be retained exactly as a town first heard them. Brann came to Harbor Lane with the approach of winter, cordial, no frost in her this time, and asked in writing how a sign painter had learned to read hands so well.

Sam wrote: when you cannot speak you have nothing to do but look. You should try it. Anyhow, you have the face for it. She laughed until she had to sit on his paint stool, and then she hired him, of all things, to letter the doors of the new chambers.

Criticism from the press was one thing. To criticize a mute man in the street was another, and the sharpest criticism of the whole affair came from the fishwives. The town abolished the nickname by spring, not by decision but by disuse. People said the Witness the way they said the Judge, a title earned once and worn for life.

A consensus formed, unspoken, that justice was a public affair and that everyone's assistance was wanted. The largest public assembly the county had seen since the regatta had changed its mind in one morning. The harbor had learned that powerful men can be wrong in company while one quiet man can be right alone.

There was champagne, of all things, at the cafe the night the verdict came. Reed paid, and everyone pretended that was normal.

The cafe put the six pencils in a frame by the till, next to the first dollar Sam ever earned lettering a cherry pie sign, and the complement of regulars grew by one. The harbor code held a single clause about found property, and the harbor had learned that a kept word is an asset no ledger holds.

Reed had been rehired by the pier corporation to run the morning ferry. He repainted Sam's shop front himself, top to bottom, free, the trim done in the deep green of the chess club, and Sam painted the last letter of his own name in the window. "Defends you at his own risk," Sam wrote under it.

"Deserves a color you can defend." One subsidiary mystery was never solved: who fed the canary during the trial. Martha had arranged it in advance, of course. She is, after all, a carrier of the same quiet.

The real page, four sentences, three true and one never written, hangs now behind glass in the harbor office, where the light off the water moves across it all day like a reader's finger. Under it the town had a small plate made, and there is no copyright on what it says, because it belongs to everyone who was ever handed the wrong name.

I am not the quiet one. I am the one who was listening.
chapters.translation:
渔民们捏着帽子站在法庭的围栏边，旁听席九点就坐满了。法庭当中那一圈座位，除了一把，全坐满了。他们里有十二个天没亮就从船队赶来，满屋子是湿羊毛、蜡烛和冷茶的气味。"可以开始了，"霍利斯法官说。

"证人准备好了吗？""他六点就准备好了，"布兰恩答道。克罗夫特站了起来，又老又慢。"法官大人，在证人宣誓之前，我想往案卷里记一件事。""反对，"布兰恩说，声音像一扇关上的门。"驳回。继续，"霍利斯说完，目光越过众人看向萨姆。

"萨缪尔斯先生，在我给你宣誓之前，你有什么要说的吗？"萨姆在这种屋子里从来没什么可说。铁罐里六支铅笔，一本空白的本子，还有一个住在内陆三镇之外的妹妹，十一天里他没对任何人提过她的名字。他往本子上写。我准备好了。霍利斯把那一页看了两遍。

"很好。现在给证人宣誓。"书记员举起手。"你愿意说真话，说全部的真话，只说真话吗？"萨姆把铅笔帽勾下来。十九天前，这座镇还管他叫哑巴萨姆；三十年过去，这名字没从他身上磨掉。

萨姆五十三岁，单身汉，瘦得像根笔杆。他十九岁选了画招牌这行，此后再没学过别的。港湾街他铺子楼上有一间颜料间、一架斜靠着的梯子，还有一只金丝雀，养它只为星期天逗他妹妹玛莎开心。

镇上人对他的态度是：离得远了亲切，凑近了是和气的轻蔑。人人都喜欢他。没人听他说话。一个人完全可以这样当上一整座镇的仆人，有用，隐形；如果不是阿什先生没站稳脚跟，萨姆大概就会这么当一辈子。

他给芭蕾学校刷过柔和的玫瑰色，给象棋俱乐部刷过深沉的墨绿，给板球场刷过本分的白；给杂货铺写过卷心菜，给面包房写过樱桃，在牲口圈的墙上画过牛，给客厅画过一只奶油甜筒，给主厨画过一把金勺子，还给整个渔船队编过舱号。

萨姆凭习惯干活，从不照图纸；他信一笔刻得好的字的漂亮，别的男人信天气。六支铅笔，每星期一削，纪律就是全部。

阿什在水边开着一家古董店。一块褪了色的土耳其地毯，一张绿丝绒长沙发，玻璃罩下的船模，还有几只按道理彼此不肯对时的钟。他的镇店之宝是"子午线"，一块合金金怀表，游客管它叫替海港守时的表。

宣传册把那句话印在海湾照片旁边。这块表比三条渔船还值钱。九月最后一个星期五，夜里十一点半，阿什从船厂大门的水泥台阶上摔了下去，没能再站起来。

两根肋骨裂了，肠子挫了伤。对一个七十岁的老人，这一跤摔得太狠。医生把原因写成跌倒，镇上人把它写成了一场危机。"他怎么样？"第二天清早，萨姆站在门口问。

"肋骨缝了几针。那老头一直要他的表，"护士说。萨姆看见了。他提着一罐绿漆沿码头往家走，跟每个星期五一样，路过一卷缆绳，一只蟹钳在里面进进出出；头顶是十月的海雾，铺得像一条毯子。那一夜，对任何不想被人看见的人来说，雾是件白捡的便宜。

离船厂台阶还有十步，一个人影从黑暗里走出来。一件深色斗篷，高高竖起的领子，手套。没有警告，没有一句话，接着是两只手，一推，一个老人倒在湿石头上，那一声闷响萨姆往后半辈子都忘不掉。

那贼弯下腰，从阿什的马甲里抓走一件东西，撒腿奔向大门。他甩臂的姿势别扭，是左撇子的跑法；到了路边既没放慢，也没有猛地停住。

人没了，被海雾和码头灯的炫光一口吞掉。萨姆没有追。他喊不出声，这就是他全部的要紧处：连害怕也是他自己的事。海港办公室有台监控摄像机，一台老机器，把那一夜录进一盘满是干扰嘶声的磁带，一年没人看过。

道尔警督提着灯、带着问题来了，一个别着名牌的警察，局长在他身后正为摄影师勘察台阶，还有十几个警员沿着潮线走。"说出来，"道尔说，"就把它说出来。""我说不了。""你可以写。"道尔在他面前放下一本空白笔记本。

"从你看见的开始写。"萨姆写下四个确凿的句子：一个穿深色斗篷的男人，戴手套，他把阿什先生推下台阶，他朝船厂大门跑，那人是个左撇子。道尔把那页看了两遍，塞进自己上衣口袋。"你算是办了事，"他说。

"剩下的交给会说话的人吧。"话说得很客气，这反而更糟。

道尔收下那份陈述，像个店员清点家具，飞快，分门别类，头都不抬地对着一个什么都没告诉他的男人。一小时后在码头，道尔问："你看清楚脸了吗？""没有。""手呢？""手套。""左手右手？"

"用错了那条胳膊。"

三天后，警察逮捕了汤姆斯·里德，二十六岁的水手，全港都拿他每天的渡轮班次对表，并指控他抢劫。"子午线"在往北两条街上一家当铺里冒了出来。里德逢人就讲：这是他父亲的表，八月当掉的；船停航那年，为了抵一笔债做的买卖。

后来查出来的当票存根证明了这点。日期跟案发那天根本对不上；而那条账目偏偏从离道尔回家路线两条街的地方冒出来，绝不是巧合。这边塞一笔钱，那边讲一段可怜的故事，镇上人的主意早就被他们替定好了。"那是你的吗？"萨姆在咖啡馆问。"是我父亲的，"里德说。

"去问店员，问了也白问。"这桩罪案拼得太齐整了，以至于没人问：一个犯人为啥要把唯一能给他定罪的那样东西贱价当掉？没人问，什么样的贼会留个念想；也没人问，一座歧视了萨姆三十年的镇子，对外乡人做过什么。

警察抓错了人，却只剩下认定他有罪这一条路，因为反过来说就是丑闻。萨姆胸口发生了一件小事，他后来管那一刻叫：恐惧自己变成了耐心。开庭前那三个星期，他怎么过日子还怎么过，安安静静，手边放一把刷子。

他回到码头，十一点半，站在原来那个位置，盯着那截台阶，直到海雾和咖啡馆里暖烘烘的壁炉教会了他第二种耐心。"您常来这儿，"厨子说。

"我喜欢这团火，"萨姆说。每天傍晚他都沿着自家铺子和当铺之间的界走一个来回。流言没给他一句准话，海港把那一夜讲成两个版本，除了要紧的那几条，处处打架。

"店员说什么？"有天晚上萨姆问。

"没说什么。吓得哆哆嗦嗦的那种。"

"他欠谁的钱？"

"一个警察。"在咖啡馆，在火边，他把关于那个当铺店员的每一桩轶事都收拢起来：一个瞳孔缩成针尖的年轻人，一双可卡因瘾君子的发抖的手。那不是直觉。那是把注意力一页一页摊开。

他凭记忆研究自己那张被撕走的陈述，断定他能像判断一块招牌那样，凭笔锋推断一页字的真假。一笔字是被它的压力定义的。那天夜里，连码头上栏杆的一只蚂蚁都比警察看得清楚，蚂蚁只不过没有动机去改动它。

他的标准简单得很，写进第二个笔记本，是那一夜一分钟一分钟的全程拆解。他开始像看天气那样给笔迹分类，按轻重，按锋边，最后他能点名这镇上哪些字是喝醉的手写下去的。所谓分类，不过是把读放慢。

最后才是当铺那一趟。他把账本从头翻到尾，找到子午线那一行，一眼看穿了整个布局。这不是一条线索，这是一件用来了结纠纷的工具。有人设计的是一个收尾，不是一桩偷窃。一句什么都不抵触的谎话，正因如此才查不动，它跟真相贴合得太齐整了。

这就是它狡猾的地方。配上抽屉里那叠没人翻过的支票存根，在任何一个肯看的人眼里，它还是一个迷雾，两份文件一对上就当场化开。县里给里德派了律师，没给萨姆派，因为证人用不着。

克罗夫特六十岁，法院指派的，拿着一份渔网似的账单和预算。他给当事人的建议很短：低头，别出声。他不劝人抱希望，希望是他开不出账单的外快。克罗夫特点着一支细烟，末梢咬在嘴里，把第二个笔记本读了两遍。"就这个？"

"就这个。"

"那你得明白自己在做什么。如果这管用，那构陷你证词的那个人，此刻就别着警徽坐在法庭正中那圈椅子里。"

"跟警察作对的证人会落什么下场？"萨姆回写成一行字：我妹妹在县疗养院。那就是他们挑的人质，而且他们已经挑定了。克罗夫特点头认可了这个计划，只加一个条件：除了书面，什么也不答，在庭上，当着所有人。然后他们就一起咬下这颗子弹。

车站餐室承办了守灵酒席，也勉勉强强承办了开庭头一天早上的茶点，小镇的人饿着肚子来，吃完甜点还赖着不走。雾散成一种又硬又干净的冷。克罗夫特的烟一截截爬向天花板。法庭围栏边挤满穿硬底靴的渔民，法院的地毯被海港的沙砾扑成灰色。十点整，开庭。

霍利斯端着一杯茶坐上法官席。干瘦的老头，一副铁打的身子，出名的是谁都还没把动议演成戏，他就在内庭里听完了。布兰恩代表王室出庭，是办公室里最年轻的律师，年轻，傲慢，有逼人的劲，穿一件灰衬衫，领口挺得像判决书上的判定。克罗夫特排在第二位，是累坏了的人那种客气。

克罗夫特早就跟报社那位法庭评论员说过："他八成有罪，"

"可人人都有权受一场辩护。"报纸连着一周一篇接一篇地发，每一篇都成功地在某个浮浅的角落里告诉小镇：沉默的证人，就是可疑的证人。没有谁把那页纸合上。

布兰恩这个从没输过一个上午的辩手站起来，传她的第一个证人。"请传证人塞缪尔·萨缪尔斯出庭，"她说，开口像涨潮。

"被告有一件深色外套，证人描述的是一件深色斗篷。被告经手过那块失窃的表，证人看见它被夺走；而按被告自己的说法，那块表曾在他手里。"

"陪审团的各位，这个结论不是谜。这是算术，我的开场白就以它收尾。除了当铺记录，我们手上还有整整齐齐一长列事实，写这些字的人一无所图。"

"在这之前，没有受任何一方的影响吧？"书记员提示道。

"法律允许陪审团做什么？"布兰恩问。

"把一个人写下的字，当作他这个人来掂量，"霍利斯说。

"这庭上的人好歹认得人品。"她传唤她的王牌证人，屋子以一种特别的方式安静下来，人在萨姆身边就是这么安静的。他提着装六支铅笔的铁皮杯走过过道，三十年的干扰像水一样在他两边分开。

"萨缪尔斯先生，你有个笔记本。这是你的笔迹吗？"她把那几页举起来，用铁丝夹别着，作为物证甲。四个句子。第二页底下还多出一行。就在这一刻，这场本来像游行的审判变成了决斗。克罗夫特站起来，嘴里还咬着铅笔。

"法官大人，在把一个人吊在几页纸上之前，本庭凭什么接受一页谁也没看见写下的纸？"

"一句话背后没有声音，它就是含混的。我不是要质疑那个哑巴，我质疑的是那页纸。若除了一个哑巴的诚实之外别无凭依就投下怀疑，那是武断；我料想控方会拿出一份证明书，因为一份证明书能证明的，不过是某个拿笔的人这么说过。正义是盲的，我们只求别再给她蒙上眼罩。"

霍利斯扶了扶眼镜。"你能断言这是你写的吗，萨缪尔斯先生？用你自己的手，就在这个庭上？"萨姆拔开一支铅笔。铁皮杯盖一响，是全屋最响的东西。他写下的字整齐得像印刷体。是我写的。我看见了。我写了一辈子字。尽管问我。

他把本子转过去举起来，那工整让满屋人都愣了。绰号和这笔迹之间的反差，当场把哑巴萨姆这个概念压塌了。那天晚上评论员写道，这就像在腌鱼桶里翻出一只天鹅。

书记员验过那几页，一言不发地收进案卷。法官认定笔迹归属已有定论，尽管证人不能出声。布兰恩继续推进，带着萨姆把陈述逐行过一遍。他一行一抬头。连贯，谨慎，笃定。陪审团像一头兽那样齐齐俯身。

没人质疑那几页，也没人能折价它们。就连克罗夫特终于开口的交叉盘问，也是裹着客气的歉意来的：问光线，问距离，问一个从少年起就没开过口的人，会不会把亲眼所见跟听来的话弄混。萨姆以笔作答，每个回答都带着一个定义的分量落下来。

接着布兰恩问出了她一直留着的那一个。她一上午瞄得很准，除了真相，什么都办成了。"萨缪尔斯先生，你看见被告汤姆斯·里德把阿什先生推下台阶了吗？"萨姆看被告，不是看那件深色外套，是看那双手，那双水手般的、右利的、没被烫过的手。然后他写下一个词。

没有。那个词像冷水一样在屋里漫过。

"是你自己笔记上的字，"布兰恩慢慢地说。萨姆已经在写了，笔尖飞快，六支削好的铅笔，他的信念和纸面之间空无一物。

我写的是一个穿深色斗篷的男人推了阿什先生。我写它，是因为那是真的。我从来没写过那个人是汤姆斯·里德。

那句话是在道尔警督拿走我那页之后添上去的。把两页摆在一起比，你就能看出来。墨水一样。差别在压力。

我的手在一句的末尾会沉得更重，像船靠了岸。那一行是浮的。一份对比研究会告诉你，那是一只有教养的手在模仿我，表面上天衣无缝，每一处笔锋都是错的。

我为这座镇的手分类做了三十年。我知道仿出来的一行长什么样。它长得像我，就像海鸥像信天翁，隔着一段距离，还非得你愿意。真话一旦落到纸上，并不难看懂。满庭与其说是倒抽冷气，不如说是齐齐吸了一口气。

就在那儿：三个句子像泊稳的船安坐在纸上，添上去的那一行浮得更高、更轻，萨姆的字根扎在纸上，它却发脆。一个败笔，出自一只急着赶事情的手，稳，而且有罪。墨迹的褪色自己会说话，伪造的那一行趴在纸页下缘，造假者的拇指在那里按稳过纸面。

在一个招牌画师审视般的目光下，那个拇指的宽度，法庭里人人都见过。道尔费劲想装出惊讶。他装得很失败。

"那一行是谁的手，萨缪尔斯先生？"法官问。萨姆没有写。他抬起手，指向道尔警督。接下来的事花了十一分钟，把整座镇重排了一遍。布兰恩没有替自家的调查员说话。她跟助手低声商量了几句，客气，字字带霜，然后脸色发白地坐下。

"本庭凭什么信你胜过信一名警官？"霍利斯问。萨姆写满一页，转了过来。

因为他选错了人质，也选错了行当。我是画字的，字是留得住的证据。写下那第五句的人，动那个念头时没经我同意。

三个星期前他来我铺子，跟我说，只要我开口，哪怕只是在纸上，他就把我妹妹玛莎送进内陆两天路程外的一间病房，手续办得挑不出错，谁也埋怨不了。

他说，哑巴是最省事的证人，因为你说不出口的，就没法指控。他给了我一个选择：要妹妹，还是要真相。

那人知道怎么打发一个证人，而且干过，就干在当铺店员身上：一个手抖的年轻人，欠着他钱，那块表是他吩咐下在账本里找出来的。

还有，他构陷的那个人一年到头天天坐渡轮，而他偷的那块表此刻就在他外套口袋里，这桩偷窃是贼里面一种古怪的心软，为的是留着。他的表链里有海港的沙，法官大人。

去翻他那副航海手套的缝。棕色羊毛，左手拇指磨穿了。海港办公室的招牌是我十四年前画的，从那以后，每年冬天我都见过那副手套。手套在道尔的上衣口袋里被搜出来，缝里嵌着海港的沙。午饭前那个店员就招了，哭着说利息的事。

那盘磁带当天下午在内庭放过，法庭和双方律师都在场，把那一分钟演示到了秒：阿什往台阶上走的时候，台阶上有个戴棕色羊毛手套的人。

两种墨迹并排一比，找不到一处可比的地方。真正的矛盾不在真话和谎话之间，而在同一支笔的两种压力之间。带子放完时，这栋楼里连一粒怀疑都不剩。汤姆斯·里德所受的指控在一点钟敲响前撤销了，那个上午足以难倒镇上能请到的任何一个编剧。

里德被两名法警一左一右夹着坐住，直到书记员宣读判决，他母亲死死抓着栏杆，被整个旁听席看着。他那件唯一的外套上，黄铜纽扣她擦了九年，每个星期天都擦。

被告从那件深色外套里站起来，像一个人从深水里浮上来。他母亲穿过整间法庭，把顾忌一股脑扔进潮水里，用尽所有的力气抱住了那个不会说话的人。萨姆把铁皮杯挪开一点，稳稳地，一动不动。

门口乱成一团，记者、渔民、全港每条船的水手都在。道尔被架到路边那辆等着的小车旁。这是对海港给过一身制服的所有信任的背弃，镇上人当成自己的事来记。休庭前霍利斯问了最后一个问题，跟那块表无关。

"从逮捕那天夜里起你就知道那行字是添的。你早几个星期就能站出来。为什么非要等到一个人离毁灭只剩一个下午？"

我的沉默是懦夫的行径，法官大人。我对自己说，一个有前科的人，判个缓刑也熬得过去。

这话我说到在您的旁听席上看见他母亲的脸为止。反过来，我把如今懂的讲给您听：恐惧自己料理不了自己，它必须每天被转化成活儿。

勇气就这么多。我不是那个安静的人。我说了三十年的话。是这座镇读得太慢了。道尔警督的定罪在冬季巡回法庭落下，因抢劫，因毁损证据，因教唆证人，还因为那个店员帮着伪造了那页纸，加了从犯这条轻罪。他的春天上诉被驳回。

巡回法官给冬季陪审团的指示里，几乎逐字援引了那位画师的第二个笔记本。法院的卷宗终于补上了它第一晚就该写的那句话。

县疗养院让玛莎留在原处。海港的神职人员拎着糕饼去看她。院方有些难堪，给萨姆送了一张裱好的感谢状，他物尽其用，拿它塞了塞那架斜梯子底下的横撑。阿什为台阶灯的年久失修，把海港公司告上了民事法庭，并且赢了，那笔赔款给整条栈桥换了新的灯。

栈桥保护协会来了封信，夹着钱，要修复萨姆十四年前画的那块海港办公室招牌，信里说，有些东西就该原样留着，留成小镇第一次听见它们时的样子。冬天快到的时候布兰恩来了港湾街，客气，这回她身上没霜，还用书面问：一个画招牌的人，是怎么学会这样读笔迹的。

萨姆写道：不能开口的人，除了看没有别的事可做。你也试试。反正，你这张脸就是干这个的。她笑得坐倒在他的油漆凳上；然后，你猜怎么着，她雇了他给新内庭的门上写字。

报纸上批评是一回事，在路上当面议论一个哑巴是另一回事；整件事最狠的批评来自那些卖鱼的女人。到开春，镇上把那个外号废了，不是谁下的决定，是没人再叫。人们说那位证人，就像说那位法官，一个挣来一次、戴一辈子的头衔。

一种不用挑明的共识慢慢长成：公道是公众的事，人人得搭一把手。自从划船赛以来全县最大的一次公众集会，在一个上午改了主意。海港学会了，有权的人会在一群人里一起错，一个安静的人却能独自对。

判决下来的那天晚上，咖啡馆里居然开了香槟。里德付的钱，人人都装作这是件平常事。

咖啡馆把那六支铅笔装进框，挂在收银机旁，紧挨着萨姆画樱桃派招牌挣到的第一块钱，熟客的行列添了一个。海港的规矩里只有一条关于拾得物的条款，海港还学会了，一句守住的诺言，是任何账本都记不下的家当。

栈桥公司重新雇了里德跑早班渡轮。他分文不取，自己把萨姆的铺面从上到下重刷了一遍，收边用的是象棋俱乐部那种深绿；最后一笔，是萨姆在橱窗里写下自己名字的末一个字。他底下写了一行："护着你，是他自己担风险。"

"配得上一抹你也守得住的颜色。"还有一桩次要的悬案始终没破：开庭那阵子，是谁在喂那只金丝雀。当然是玛莎提前安排好的。她身上毕竟传着的是同一种安静。

真的那一页，四个句子，三句为真，一句从未写下，如今装在玻璃框里，挂在海港办公室，水面上反上来的光整日在其上移动，像一个读书人的手指。底下压着一块小镇定做的小牌子，牌子上写的话没有版权，因为它属于每一个被叫错过名字的人。

我不是那个安静的人。我是那个一直在听的人。

chapters.title: 凌晨三点的急诊室
chapters.content:
At ten past three a woman in a green coat was groaning in the corridor, and the automatic doors kept sliding open behind her, as if the building could not make up its mind. "She's hysterical," Dr. Fane said. Then, seeing Delia's face: "I mean, she has every right to be."

"My mother," the woman said. "She isn't breathing." "Then we will make her breathe," Delia said. "Sit down. Breathe with me. In. Out. In. Out."

The incident book lay open on the desk. Delia wrote in it with a biro and no capital letter. "What is your complaint?" "My throat," the woman said. "Then my chest. Then nothing." She could not stop biting her lip.

Errol came out with gloves on. "Her mother is on the floor of the front room. A neighbour called it in." "Send someone. And go and wash your hands properly."

Dr. Fane went, and diagnosed in her head as she walked: a germ, or anemia, or a nerve that had finally given way. Delia put a blanket over the woman's shoulders. "We will wait for your mother. Nobody touches her before you have seen her."

"Nobody has touched her. I came first. I was frightened, and I came first." The county had its own slow epidemic that winter, and very little of it was medical in the way the board used the word.

Old people who had stopped eating. Men who had stopped talking. A chronic shortage of anybody to sit with them. Delia had given first aid to four thousand people in her life and remembered perhaps ninety of them.

She had long ago stopped deciding which of these things was an illness and which was simply a life. A chronic cough in chair six. A woman arrived hysterical and left calm. A cut that never infected.

An old injury that ached when the weather turned. Some of that winter did harm and some of it did not, and infectious laughter crossed the room faster than any infection grown in that dish.

Nobody in her experience was immune to three in the morning, and she had looked once through the lens at the bacterium in its dish and thought: a cell is only a room with a rule about who may come in. Fenrow stood on Linden Avenue, forty kilometres by road from the metropolitan hospital the county had been told to prefer.

It was raised in 1902 by an empire that wanted its soldiers alive. Red brick, an imperial crest over the door, a king nobody in Fenrow could name, and in the board room a portrait of a monarch in a kingdom's worth of gold braid.

The old colonial block had an ancient boiler that howled every February, an antique clock that lost four minutes a week, and doors that sat flush with the wall only if you shouldered them. The advent of a regional board, twenty years earlier, had changed the signage and very little else.

A century of nights had worn the floor to the colour of weak tea. In twenty-six years Delia had decided that the hour between three and four was the cardinal hour of the whole establishment, the hour when the building stopped pretending to be a business.

There was no aesthetic to the waiting room. The chairs had been chosen by somebody who disliked comfort, the walls were the green of a government corridor, and the only decoration was a notice about handwashing and a stack of magazines.

Nobody had ever complained about the chairs, and nobody had ever sat in one on purpose, which is the difference between furniture and a place. The night smelled of floor polish and bitter tea, and of the sour breath of whoever had been sick into a kidney bowl.

Delia was fifty-four and had worked nights for twenty-six of those years. She had begun upstairs in the nursery, where a day shift never teaches what the night does. A baby breathes loudest just before it stops frightening you, and a mother will forgive a nurse anything except hurry.

On the quiet nights she knitted. Eleven scarves a year, all given away by December. In her locker she kept a row of glass jars she had never been able to throw out. She had been born two streets from the hospital, and in her childhood had watched the ambulances climb the hill with the interest other children give to trains.

Errol was the orderly: muscular, an athlete at school, with the torn muscle to prove it. One hand could manoeuvre a trolley through a door. By post he was training to be a genealogist. He was apt to be right about people and wrong about dates.

"You will never finish it," Delia said. "I will. I have started at Adam." Dr. Fane was twenty-eight, aspired to neurology, and therefore diagnosed everything twice. "Say it once," Delia said. "Once," Fane said. "Fine."

On the ground floor a chemist kept a culture of a bacterium in a dish and looked at it once a week out of curiosity. Croy and Dita drove the ambulance and brought in whatever the motor roads of the county had left on them. Between three and four the incidence of genuine casualty cases was low, according to the board.

What arrived instead was everything else. A magistrate with a headache who had been awake since Tuesday. "Doctor, I have a headache." "Where?" "Behind my eyes. And in my jaw." "Which day?" "Tuesday. I have been awake since Tuesday."

An adolescent boy with a bruise on his abdomen and a story that did not fit it. "How did it happen?" "A bike." "Where is the bike?" "It hurts." A man of sixty had eaten a raw mushroom on a dare and wanted, above all, not to be told he was stupid.

November. A millionaire whose name was on the new scanner sat in chair four, and an hour later a young man found cold in the bus shelter sat in chair four as well. He was nineteen, and therefore an adult, and therefore allowed to be frightened alone.

"Heroin," Dita said quietly. "I won't ask how he came by it," Delia said. "You gave them the same blanket," Fane said. "I gave them the same blanket."

Then there was Amos Pell. He walked in at three on Thursdays, bald as a cucumber, lame on the left, where an old fracture of the bone above the knee had never healed. "Evening, Pell." "Evening. It is the same ache." "Show me."

His finger pressed one point low in his abdomen. "A stone wrapped in cloth." "Eleven months. Eleven tests. Every one mild. One was invalid." "There is no organ," the young doctor said. "No organic cause. Nothing an organism could be blamed for."

"That is the most miserable sentence in the language," Delia said, "because it means the pain is real and there is nothing to show for it." Fifty-one years he had been the butcher on Quarry Lane, the fourth of a Pell dynasty to cut meat there.

As a boy he had grazed his uncle's cattle on the hill above the town. He boasted for fifty years that the knife had never injured him, a boast his hands did not support. You would have endured worse from him and forgiven it.

He was beloved by exactly one person, and he had adored her back with the obstinate affection of a quiet man. Her name was Ines. She had kept doves in a shed at the back, and knitted him six scarves, of which he could find five.

"Pell's mother kept doves," Delia said one night. "That explains the shed." "There is a reason for everything," Pell said, which was not true. She had died in this hospital at three in the morning, eleven months earlier, of cancer of the lung.

Amos had not grieved so much as stopped. His liver, which had survived half a century of sausage, was sound; his nerves were not. What he had left was his independence, a cold house, and an obedience to a rule nobody had ever said out loud.

A man must be ill before he is allowed to be looked at. That was the rule, and sitting in a chair at three was how he kept it. His blood was thin. A bypass eleven years earlier had left him on a drug for life, a small dose every morning, and a standing order repeated by every doctor who met him.

"Never miss it. Never on an empty stomach." "I have never missed it. Then you have eaten. I have eaten." He also brought a jar. A pound of pickled cucumbers from the corner shop, a white label attached to the lid in his own hand.

"For the lady who gave me hers," he said. Delia had eleven of them in the locker, every one unopened. "You have never told him," Fane said. "Pickled cucumber makes my throat close. Then tell him. Not at three. Not ever, apparently."

On the night Ines died Delia had sat with him in a plastic chair for four hours and, at five, gone to the staff room and come back with her own jar and a spoon. "He has not eaten since Tuesday," she said.

A hungry old man will take food from a stranger. He ate six. Afterwards he said it was the best thing anyone had done for him in forty years. The anniversary of that night fell in January, and every other Thursday of the year belonged to it as well.

"He is the three o'clock man," said the day staff. They meant it kindly. "He is lonely," Fane said. "He is a nuisance," Errol said once, within Delia's hearing. "In the corridor," Delia said. "Now." Errol apologized to Pell, who found it absurd and rather moving.

The four of them conspired, most weeks, to find him a bed instead of a chair. It was less a conspiracy than a convention, and the victim was the only person who gained.

November. The board sent a man whose brief was one page. "Efficient," Corin Slake said. "That is the word in my brief. My emphasis is always on that one word." "Every time you open your mouth I hear it," Delia said. "It is about money. It is about money. It is about the distance between a door and a chair."

He quoted the cost of a night, the average wait, the distance an ambulance must drive, and the incidence of real casualty cases. "I have governed two trusts through the same winter," he said. "I have a mania for closing things."

"They will close the night service and allocate my two nurses and my one doctor forty kilometres away," Fane said. The board would administer it from a desk in the city. The publication of the report was set for the second week of December.

The governor of the trust, a retired dentist from the northwest, was expected to sign without reading past page two. The government's regional office had already sent the paperwork, and the organization that employed Slake had a hierarchy of people who would be appalled by an empty return.

He knew, having written the annual report himself for six years, that nothing in the nation was harder to defend than a small thing that worked. The staff argued at half past two, in the room with the kettle. Errol wanted to petition. Fane wanted data, and spent three nights making a series of charts proving that the night service saw eleven people a night, which Slake had already counted.

"Do these charts mean anything?" Errol asked. "They mean eleven." "Eleven what?" "Eleven people. Somebody count the chairs, then." "Delia," Fane said at last, "what does he actually have?" "Not a disease," Delia said. "A sorrow."

Delia said nothing for a week, and then said: "They are not counting the chairs." They took a democratic vote on whether to keep sitting with Pell, which was absurd, since there were only four of them and she would have done it anyway.

Democracy at three in the morning is a slow business. After four, the dominant fact of any night is tiredness, and it dominated them alike. Even Errol was anxious in the way big men are anxious: quietly, and always about somebody else.

The dynamic of a night shift, Delia had decided, is set by whoever makes the tea. Slake did not know this, and it agitated her to think that he might never need to.

She had a dry humor and used it the way other people use a hazard light: rarely, and only when something was already wrong. What she could not joke about was how the closure would affect Pell, who had no car, no independence left to speak of, and no intention of asking anyone for a lift.

"You will have no transport," Delia said. "I have two legs. They are slow." "Forty kilometres is slow." One night Slake walked the building with a clipboard and a torch.

The architect of the new wing had made a corridor two trolleys could not pass. There was mould in the basement. The faulty valve on the boiler was a hazard nobody had logged. The fire certificate for the dispensary had expired in 2019, and a formation of boxes behind it had stood so long that moving them would have required an orderly, a form and a short argument.

He descended the stone steps at the back, and the descent took him into a room that smelled of herb tea and old wool, where Delia kept her locker and, amid the coats, her eleven jars. "What is this?" he said. "A room, sir." "Whose?" "Mine. Mine and three others, and the jars are not mine either."

They looked back at him for a long moment. He did not ask. Questions arise at three that do not arise at noon, and a man with a clipboard knows better than to write one down. He did, however, watch.

On the second Thursday of December, at half past two, Errol said: "He is late." At three, nothing. At ten past three the aural alarm over the automatic doors gave a small explosive chirp, and Croy and Dita came through with Amos Pell on a trolley: bloody at the mouth, grey as ash, his flesh gone, his hands cold.

"Active bleeding," Fane said, and then, having diagnosed twice as usual, said the word that stops a room. "Malign. A growth pressing on an artery." "Dita wrote down the time," Dita said. "Three forty-three. Do write it down or you will say three tomorrow."

Delia had gone to the locker, and came back with eleven jars, set out in a row on the desk, the way you set out evidence. "He has not eaten a meal since his wife died," she said.

"Every Thursday he eats six pickled cucumbers on an empty stomach and drinks the vinegar, because I gave him mine and he is too proud to bring me anything else. This drug he takes for his heart every morning, and the acid aggravates what the acid has already done."

She stood there. "Eleven months of that is not a malignant growth. Eleven months of that is a man bleeding into his own abdomen because he has forgotten how to eat." It was curiosity, not pity, that made Fane open one and smell it.

The smell made her check the dates on the lids against the incident book, where every one of Pell's Thursday visits had been recorded in six words. What she found was not a carrier of anything contagious. It was a carrier of a habit, and the habit was grief, which is not catching but very good at imitation. Fane did not argue, which surprised Delia and, later, surprised Fane.

She put an oxygen mask on him, injected what needed injecting, called the theatre, and accompanied him to its door. The operation took ninety minutes. "Benign," the surgeon said, coming out at six. "No cancer. A bleeding ulcer the size of a coin, and a stomach as empty as a church."

"How long?" "Ninety minutes," Errol said. "And he was laughing in the corridor at four." Slake had been in the building all night. He stood at the end of the corridor with his hands in his pockets and did not bypass the moment by looking at his phone.

What he had seen heightened something in him for which he had no word, and the silence in that corridor impressed him more than any figure in his folder. He was aware, standing there, that he was watching the only part of his job that had never fitted into a publication.

It appalled him, and he wrote it down in a sentence his deputy crossed out and then put back. Pell came round at noon on Friday, ashamed, and blushed so hard that Fane checked his temperature again.

"Sorry for the trouble. I knew the pain was real and did not want to be a nuisance about it. I also did not want to be operated on." "That too," Delia said. "You did not. A direct question is kinder than a gentle one."

His masculine pride did what masculine pride always does, which is arrive late and useless. "When did you last eat a meal?" He could not remember, which was the answer she had expected.

"You may come at three," she said. "You may come on Thursday. You may come with a complaint or without one. But you will bring nothing in a jar, and you will eat what we give you." She paused. "It is imperative, and I do not say that word to many people."

He started to protest, and then did something he had not done in eleven months. He laughed. It erupted out of him like water through a door, and it was infectious, and Fane, nervous about him for weeks, laughed too.

Even Errol, carrying a box of swabs, had to put the box down. Later, sitting up, he told her about Ines the way people tell things at three, which is sideways. She had kept doves in a shed at the back.

She had blessed the shop on the day they opened it, a thing he had thought silly at twenty-four and missed at seventy. He had not been back to the tomb since August, because the walk hurt his leg and because a tomb is a place you visit with an appetite for grief, and he had none.

He had come every Thursday because Thursday was the day and three was the hour, and because if he sat in his own kitchen at that time he could hear the house waiting. His hands, which had never once betrayed him at the block, betrayed him now, shaking round the cup.

Never once had he cursed the wait, which is more than can be said for most of us. Delia had mourned her own mother at the same hour, two streets away, and understood him perfectly. She could not cure a house that is too quiet, and she said so.

What she could do was nourish him, slower than curing and, in her experience, the more useful trade. She had inherited a compassion she had never applied for and would never have mentioned to a soul. It had been her inspiration at nineteen, when a night sister had done the same for her, and she had spent thirty-five years inspired by a woman whose name she could not remember.

The hearing was on the eighteenth, in the board room under the monarch's portrait, where Slake read his report aloud. He had evolved, in six weeks, into somebody who did not enjoy the sound of his own numbers.

Then he said what his brief required: that the night service be integrated into the big unit and the clinic at Fenrow keep daylight hours only. The room asked Delia to speak. She came forward with a cardboard box and set eleven jars on the table, each with a date on the lid.

"The floor will have a vote on this," someone said. It was not intended as a joke. "These constitute a series of Thursdays between the second of January and the eleventh of December. The first is the night his wife died. The last is the night he nearly died."

"Between them sits somebody who was fed, warmed and watched over by people who were not treating anything. If this service had closed in March, he would have died in his kitchen at three in the morning with a jar in his hand."

"Nobody would have counted it, because the dead at home are not relevant to any budget," she said. "Dr. Fane will tell you about patient autonomy, which is the right of a man to refuse the thing that would heal him. I will tell you about the opposite."

"Somebody has to be there when he changes his mind. That is not efficient. That is the whole job." Slake looked at the row for a long time. "I cannot put that in a spreadsheet." "Then write it in the margin."

He did, and administrated the change himself, a bold thing for a man whose whole trade was accuracy, and attached one handwritten page. Costed separately: the hour between three and four.

The governor read the page twice and signed the report with the night service still in it. The regional office wrote back to ask whether the margin note was relevant to the formation of next year's budget. Slake wrote back one word: Yes.

Under the heading THE THREE O'CLOCK MAN, the county paper printed a photograph of the eleven jars, after denouncing the closure in a leader the week before. A magazine in the city sent a reporter, who sat in chair four for a night, was given a blanket, and wrote two thousand words that blurred badly at the edges.

Nobody in Fenrow minded. A small movement began, of the sort that has no name and no chairman: the nursery school sent a drawing, the chemist sent a box of plasters, the auxiliary staff signed a sheet, and the millionaire wrote a letter saying he had never been asked beforehand and would have said no.

Slake did not condemn the place he had come to close. He was awed, he said, by a climate in which four people could do the work of a department for the cost of a dose of nothing. What he had not expected was the complication of being wrong in public and relieved about it.

His anger at the bureaucracy he served, carried for twelve years like a muscle, went quiet overnight. There is no fixing that either. There is only tea at half past two, and somebody else's chair.

By Christmas the waiting room had a small tree with a china angel on it, and an amateur band from the school came in on the twenty-third. "Four carols badly and one well," Errol said. "I counted. I counted every one of them."

The flu had arrived, and the chairs were full of people groaning in misery and surprised by how quickly a blanket helps. The bats had gone from the car park for the winter; an owl had taken the chimney and hunted the field at dusk. Errol finished his course and, as a qualified genealogist, traced the Pell family back five generations and found four butchers and one blacksmith.

Amos Pell had been born in the room above the shop and had not left the town for more than a fortnight since 1963. Errol considered that the most innocent thing he had ever uncovered, and he mentioned it at half past two, every night, for eleven years.

On the last Thursday of the year, at three in the morning, Amos Pell walked in on his own two feet: lame, bald, obstinate, carrying nothing. Delia looked at his empty hands and then at his face.

"I was bound to forget something," he said. "Sit down," she said. "I will find you something." "Tea?" Delia asked. "Yes, please. It has been a long month." He had two slices of toast, a boiled egg and a banana.

He took one bite, stopped, and looked at the plate as though it had insulted him. Then he inhaled the steam off a cup of tea before he drank it, and groaned with something that was not agony, not anguish, not distress, but the ordinary ease of somebody who has just been fed.

Later he said it was the best thing anyone had done for him in forty years, and then corrected himself. "Forty-one." He asked whether he might come on a Tuesday instead, because Thursday had begun to arouse an anxiety he could not explain. She said Tuesday would do very well.

"What do you want me to bring?" he asked. "Nothing," Delia said. "That is the whole of it." Finally he asked what he should bring. Delia, who had eleven of them on a shelf above the kettle and no use for a twelfth, told him the truth for the first time in eleven months.

Come at three. Bring nothing.
chapters.translation:
三点十分，一个穿绿外套的女人在走廊里呻吟，自动门在她身后一次次滑开，好像这栋楼拿不定主意。"她歇斯底里，"费恩医生说。看见迪莉娅的脸，他又补一句："我的意思是，她完全有理由这样。"

"我妈，"那女人说，"她不呼吸了。""那我们就让她呼吸，"迪莉娅说，"坐下。跟我一起呼吸。吸气。呼气。吸气。呼气。"

登记簿摊在桌上。迪莉娅用圆珠笔在上面写字，名字连大写都不用。"你的主诉是什么？""我喉咙，"那女人说，"然后是胸口。然后什么都没有。"她停不下来，一个劲儿咬自己的嘴唇。

埃罗尔戴着手套从治疗室出来。"她妈躺在客厅地板上。是邻居报的信。""叫人去。还有，把手洗干净再出来。"费恩医生走了。

她一边走一边在脑子里下诊断：病菌，或者贫血，或者一根终于撑不住的神经。迪莉娅往那女人肩上搭了条毯子。"等您妈妈。您没看清她之前，谁也不许碰她。""没人碰过她。我先来的。

我害怕过，可我先来的。"那个冬天，这个郡流行着一场慢性的瘟疫，而它里面几乎没有一件事是董事会嘴上那个"医学"的意思。不再吃饭的老人。不再说话的男人。

慢性的、没人陪着坐坐的短缺。迪莉娅这辈子给人做过四千次急救，记住的也许有九十个。她早就不再去分辨这些事里哪一样算病、哪一样只是日子。

六号椅上一阵慢性咳嗽。一个女人来的时候歇斯底里，走的时候平静了。一道从来没被感染过的伤口。一处天一变就隐痛的旧伤。

那年冬天，有些事造成了伤害，有些没有；而那些有传染性的笑声，比这只培养皿里养出来的任何感染都更快地穿过了整个房间。

在她的经验里，没有人对凌晨三点免疫。她曾经透过镜片看过一次那只培养皿里的细菌，当时想：一个细胞不过是一间规定了谁能进来的屋子。芬罗在林登大道上，离郡里被人劝着"优先选择"的那家大都市医院有四十公里车程。

它是一九〇二年由一个想让士兵活下来的帝国盖起来的。红砖，门楣上一枚帝国纹章，一位芬罗没人叫得出名字的国王，董事会会议室里挂着一幅君主的画像，配着够撑起一个王国的金色绶带。

老殖民时代的病区里有一台每年二月都要嚎叫的旧锅炉，一座每周慢四分钟的古董钟，还有几扇只有用肩膀顶才肯和墙齐平的门。二十年前一个地区理事会的到来，只换了指示牌，别的什么也没换。

一个世纪的夜晚把地板磨成了淡茶的颜色。上了二十六年夜班，迪莉娅认定，三点到四点之间是整栋楼最要紧的钟头——这会儿它不再假装自己是一门生意。

候诊室毫无美感可言。椅子是一个不喜欢舒服的人挑的，墙是政府走廊那种绿，唯一的装饰是一张洗手须知和一摞杂志。

没有人对椅子抱怨过，也没有人是特意坐上去的——这就是家具和一个地方的区别。夜里的空气里有地板蜡和发苦的茶的味道，还有今早吐进腰形盘里那个人嘴里带酸味的呼气。

迪莉娅五十四岁，其中二十六年在值夜班。她从楼上的婴儿室做起，那地方白班永远教不了夜里要用的东西。婴儿在不再吓着你之前，呼吸声最响；一位母亲能原谅护士做一切事，除了慌张。

安静的夜里她织毛线。一年十一条围巾，十二月之前全送出去。她的储物柜里留着一排玻璃罐，从来舍不得扔。她出生在离医院两条街的地方，小时候看救护车上坡，怀着别的孩子看火车时才有的那种兴趣。

埃罗尔是护工：肌肉结实，上学时是运动员，身上那块拉伤的肌肉就是证明。一只手就能把推车挪过一道门。他还在函授家谱学。"你永远学不完，"迪莉娅说，"我会的。

我从亚当开始查。"费恩医生二十八岁，有志于神经内科，因此什么都要诊断两遍。"说一遍，"迪莉娅说。"一遍，"费恩医生说，"行。"

一楼的药剂师在培养皿里养着一株细菌，每周出于好奇看它一次。克罗伊和迪塔开救护车，把郡里公路上剩下的一切都送进来。三点到四点之间，真正急症的发生率很低，这是董事会说的话。送进来的反而是其他一切。

一位从星期二起就没合过眼的地方法官，头痛。"医生，我头痛。""哪儿？""眼睛后面。还有下巴。""哪一天？""星期二。我从星期二起就没合过眼。"

一个少年，腹部有一块淤青，还有一个跟淤青对不上的说法。"怎么碰的？""骑单车。""单车呢？""它疼。"一个六十岁的男人打赌生吃了一只蘑菇，最要紧的是别让人说他蠢。十一月。

一台新扫描仪上刻着名字的百万富翁坐在四号椅上；一小时后，一个在公交候车亭里被发现冻僵的年轻人也坐在四号椅上。他十九岁，因此是个成年人，因此被允许一个人受惊。

"海洛因，"迪塔轻声说。"我不问他是哪儿弄来的，"迪莉娅说。"你们给他们同一条毯子，"费恩医生说，"我给了他们同一条毯子。"

然后是阿莫斯·佩尔。他每周四三点走进来，秃着，左边瘸着——膝盖上方那根骨头的旧骨折从来没有长好。"晚上好，佩尔。""晚上好。还是那阵疼。""给我看。"他的手指按在腹部下方一个点上。"

一块裹在布里的石头。""十一个多月了。十一次检查。每次都是轻微。有一次算无效。""没有哪个器官，"那个年轻医生说，"也没有器质性的原因。没有任何生物体可以归咎。"

"这是这门语言里最让人难受的一句话，"迪莉娅说，"它等于在说：疼是真的，可拿不出任何东西来证明。"五十一年来他一直是采石巷上的屠夫，佩尔家第四个在那里切肉的人。

他小时候在镇子后面的山上放过叔叔的牛。五十年来他一直吹嘘刀子从来没有伤过他一次——这个吹牛他自己的双手并不支持。换作是你，从他手里受过的气比这还多，也一样会原谅他。

这辈子只有一个人真心喜欢过他，而他以那种沉默寡言的人特有的固执的深情爱着她。她叫伊内丝。她在后院的棚子里养过鸽子，给他织过六条围巾，他只找得到五条。

"佩尔他妈养过鸽子，"有一天夜里迪莉娅说，"这就说明那个棚子。""什么事都有一个缘故，"佩尔说——这话并不真。她十一个月前凌晨三点死在这家医院，死于肺癌。

阿莫斯与其说是在悲伤，不如说是停了下来。他的肝脏——熬过了半个世纪的香肠——是好的；他的神经不是。他剩下的东西只有独立、一座冷房子，以及对一条从没人说出口的规矩的服从。

一个人得先病了，才被允许被人看一看。这就是那条规矩；凌晨三点坐在一把椅子上，是他守住规矩的方式。他的血很稀。十一年前的一次搭桥让他终身离不开一种药：每天早上小小一剂，还有一条每个见他的医生都会重复的医嘱。"绝不能漏。

绝不能空腹。""我从没漏过。这么说来你吃过饭了。我吃过饭了。"他还会带一只罐子来。一磅街角小店里买来的腌黄瓜，盖子贴着一张小小的白标签，上面是他亲手写的日期。

"给那位把自己的给我的女士，"他说。迪莉娅的储物柜里有十一只，每一只都没开封。"你一直没告诉他，"费恩医生说，"腌黄瓜会让我喉咙发紧。那你就告诉他。别在三点说。

反正也永远是别说。"伊内丝死的那夜，迪莉娅陪他在一张塑料椅上坐了四个小时；五点上下，她去值班室，回来时手里是自己的那只罐子和一把勺子。"他从星期二起就没吃过东西，"她说。

一个饿着的老头会从一个陌生人手里接过饭。他吃了六条。事后他说，那是四十年来别人为他做过的最好的一件事。那天夜的纪念日在一月，一年里其余每个星期四也都属于它。

"他是三点钟的男人，"白班的人说。他们是好意。"他孤单，"费恩说。"他是个麻烦，"埃罗尔有一次当着迪莉娅的面说。""在走廊里，"迪莉娅说，"现在。"埃罗尔向佩尔道了歉，佩尔觉得这很荒唐，又相当动人。

他们四个人大多数星期都合谋给他找一张床，而不是一把椅子。与其说这是阴谋，不如说这是惯例，而唯一的受益者就是那个"受害者"。

十一月，董事会派来一个人，任务书只有一页。"高效，"科林·斯莱克说，"我任务书里就这一个词。我的重点永远落在那一个词上。""你每张嘴我都听见了，"迪莉娅说，"这跟钱有关。""这跟钱有关。这说的是一扇门和一把椅子之间的距离。"

他报出一夜的成本、平均等待时间、救护车必须开到的距离、真实急症的发生率。"同一个冬天我治理过两家信托机构，"他说，"我对关停有一种狂热。"

"他们要把夜间服务关了，把我这两个护士和我一个医生调去四十公里外，"费恩说。董事会会在城里的办公桌后面管这件事。报告的发布日期定在十二月第二周。

信托机构的主管——一位来自郡西北部的退休牙医——预计不会读完第二页就会签字。政府的地区办公室已经把文件寄来了；而雇用斯莱克的那个机构有一整层等级，要是空手回去，他们会震惊。

他知道——因为年度报告他自己写了六年——在这个国家，没什么比一件确实有用的小东西更难辩护。职工们两点半在水壶那间屋里吵。埃罗尔想请愿。费恩想要数据，花了三个晚上做了一串图表，证明夜间服务每晚接诊十一个人——而斯莱克早就数过了。"这些图有啥用？"埃罗尔问。"数字是十一。""十一什么？""十一个人。

那你们去数数椅子。""迪莉娅，"费恩医生最后说，"他到底得的是什么病？""不是病，"迪莉娅说，"是难过。"迪莉娅一个星期没说话，然后说了一句："他们没有在数椅子。"

他们就"要不要继续陪佩尔坐着"进行了一次民主表决，这很荒唐，因为他们一共只有四个人，而她不管怎样都会这么做。凌晨三点的民主是一件慢吞吞的事。

四点以后，任何一夜的主导事实都是疲倦，它一视同仁地支配着所有人，连埃罗尔也不例外——他焦虑的方式是大个子男人的方式：安静，而且总是替别人焦虑。

一个夜班的动力机制，迪莉娅早就认定了，是由煮茶的那个人决定的。斯莱克不知道这一点，一想到他也许永远用不上，就让她心里发烦。

她有一种干巴巴的幽默，用起来像别人用危险报警灯：很少用，而且只在已经出了岔子的时候用。她笑不出来的，是关停会怎么影响佩尔——他没有车，没剩下多少独立可言，也根本不打算开口求谁搭一程。

"你没车了，"迪莉娅说。"我有两条腿。腿是慢。""四十公里才算慢。"有一夜，斯莱克拿着写字板和手电筒把楼走了一遍。

新翼的建筑师造了一条两辆推车都过不去的走廊。地下室长了霉。锅炉上那个有缺陷的阀门是个没人登记过的隐患。配药室的消防合格证二〇一九年就到期了，它后面那堆箱子摆得太久，要挪动它们得要一个护工、一张表格，外加一场关于这是谁的分内事的简短争吵。

他从后面的石阶走下去，这一下降把他带进一间闻着草药茶和旧羊毛味的屋子，迪莉娅的储物柜就在那里，她的十一只罐子就在那些外套中间。"这是什么？"他说。"一间屋，先生。""谁的？""我的。还有另外三个人的，罐子也不是我的。"

它们久久地看着他。他没有问。有些问题在三点才会冒出来，在正午不会；而一个拿着写字板的人懂得，最好不要把它写下来。不过，他确实在看。

十二月第二个星期四，两点半，埃罗尔说："他迟到了。"三点，没人。三点十分，自动门上方那个听觉报警器发出一声小小的爆裂似的鸣叫；克罗伊和迪塔推着阿莫斯·佩尔进来：嘴上是血，脸色灰得像灰烬，身上的肉没了，手是凉的。

"活动性出血，"费恩说。她像往常一样诊断了第二遍，然后说出了那个能让一间屋子安静下来的词。"恶性。一个东西压着动脉。""迪塔把时间记下来，"迪塔说，"三点四十三分。

你得记下来，不然明天你自己都说是三点。"迪莉娅去了储物柜，抱着十一只罐子回来，在桌上一排摆开，像摆出证物。"自从他老婆死后，他一顿饭都没吃过，"她说。

"每个星期四，他空着肚子吃六条腌黄瓜，还把醋喝下去，因为我给了他我的那条，而他太骄傲，不肯给我带别的。这药是他为心脏吃的，每天早上一次，那酸只会加重酸已经做过的事。"

她站在那儿。"十一个月这样，不是恶性肿块。十一个月这样，是一个男人忘了怎么吃饭，正在往自己肚子里流血。"让费恩打开一只闻一闻的是好奇，不是怜悯。

那股气味让她去核对盖子上的日期和登记簿——佩尔每一次周四来诊，都在那上面被用六个词记下来。她发现的不是什么传染病的携带者。它携带的是一种习惯，而那种习惯是悲伤；悲伤不会传染，但它非常擅长模仿。

费恩没有争辩，这让迪莉娅意外，后来也让费恩自己意外。她给他戴上氧气面罩，把该注射的注射了，打电话给手术室，还亲自陪他到手术室门口。手术做了九十分钟。"良性，"外科医生六点出来，"不是癌。

一个硬币大小的出血性溃疡，还有一个空得像教堂的胃。""多久？""九十分钟，"埃罗尔说，"四点的时候他在走廊上笑。"斯莱克整夜都在楼里。他双手插在口袋里站在走廊尽头，没有靠看手机来绕过这一刻。

他看到的东西在他心里催长了某样叫不出名字的东西；那条走廊里的寂静，比他文件夹里的任何数字都更让他震动。他清楚地意识到，自己正在看着这份工作里唯一从来塞不进一份出版物的部分。

他对此感到震惊，并且把它写了下来，用一句话写进报告——他的副手把那句划掉了，他又给加了回去。佩尔星期五中午醒过来，很害臊，脸红得让费恩医生又给他量了一次体温。

"对不起，麻烦你们了。我早知道那疼是真的，只是不想拿它当个麻烦。我也不想被拉去开刀。""也算，"迪莉娅说，"你是不想。一个直接的问题比一个温和的问题更仁慈。"

他的男性自尊做了男性自尊一贯做的事：迟到，而且没用。"你上一次吃饭是什么时候？"他想不起来，这正是她预料的答案。

"你可以三点来，"她说，"可以星期四来。可以带着主诉来，也可以不带着。但什么都不能装在罐子里带来，我们给你什么你就吃什么。"她顿了一下，"这是非做不可的，而这个词我不常对人说。"

他刚要开口抗议，然后做了十一个月来没做过的一件事：他笑了。那笑声像水冲开门一样从他身上喷出来，而且是有传染性的；几星期来一直为他提心吊胆的费恩也笑了。

连端着一箱棉签的埃罗尔都不得不把箱子放下。后来，他坐起来，给她讲伊内丝——用的是人们在凌晨三点讲事情的方式，从侧面讲。她在后院的棚子里养过鸽子。

他们开张那天，她给铺子祈过福；一件他二十四岁时觉得很蠢、七十岁时很想念的事。他从八月起没再回过墓地，因为那段路伤他的腿，也因为墓地是一个你得带着对悲伤的胃口才去得了的地方，而他什么胃口都没有。

他每个星期四都来，因为星期四是那个日子，三点钟是那个钟点；也因为如果那个时辰他坐在自家厨房里，他能听见那座房子在等他。他那双手在肉案前从来没有背叛过他，此刻却背叛了他，端着杯子发抖。

他从来没有咒骂过一次等待，这一点我们大多数人做不到。迪莉娅曾在同一个钟点、离医院两条街的一座房子里为母亲服过丧，完全懂得他。她治不好一座太安静的房子，她就这么说了。

她能做的是滋养他，这比治愈慢，而且在她的经验里更有用。她继承了一种自己从未申请、也绝不会向任何人提起的同情心。那是她十九岁那年、一位夜班护士对她做过同样的事时给她的灵感；此后三十五年，她一直被一个已经记不住名字的女人激励着。

听证会在十八号，在董事会会议室里、那幅君主画像底下，斯莱克把报告念了出来。六个星期里，他已经变成了一个不喜欢听自己念数字的人。

然后他说了任务书里要求的话：夜间服务并入那个大科室，芬罗的门诊只保留白天的时段。会议室请迪莉娅发言。她抱着一个纸箱走上前，把十一只罐子摆到桌上，每一只盖子上都有一个日期。

"这事议会要投票的，"有人这么说——并不是一句玩笑。"这些罐子构成了一串星期四，从一月二号到十二月十一号。第一只是他妻子去世的那一夜。最后一只是他差点死掉的那一夜。"

"中间是一个被人喂饱、焐暖、看着的人，而看着他的人并没有在治疗什么。这项服务要是三月就关了，他会在凌晨三点死在自己家的厨房里，手里还攥着一只罐子。"

"没有人会把它算进去，因为死在家里的人跟任何预算都不相干，"她说，"费恩医生会跟你们讲病人的自主权，那是一个人拒绝那个能治愈他的东西的权利。我来讲相反的一面。"

"他改主意的时候，得有人在。那不高效。那就是全部的工作。"斯莱克盯着那一排看了很久。"这个我塞不进电子表格。""那就写在页边空白处。"他写了。

他亲自把这件事办了——对一个毕生以精确为业的人来说，这是一件大胆的事——还附上了一页手写的纸：成本另计：三点到四点这一个钟头。

那位主管把那页纸读了两遍，然后在报告上签了字，夜间服务还在里面。地区办公室回信问，那条页边备注跟明年预算的构成是否相关。斯莱克回了一个词：是。

一周前还在社论里痛斥关停的郡报，此刻在"凌晨三点的男人"这个大标题下登出了那十一只罐子的照片。城里一家杂志派来一位记者，在四号椅上坐了一夜，拿到一条毯子，写了两千字，边角糊得厉害。芬罗没有人介意。

一场小小的运动开始了，就是那种没有名字也没有主席的运动：幼儿园送来一幅画，药剂师送来一盒创可贴，辅助人员在一份表格上签了名，而那位百万富翁写信说，从来没人事先问过他，否则他会说不行。

斯莱克没有谴责他来关停的这个地方。他说，他被一种氛围震住了：四个人能以"一剂什么都没有"的代价，干下一个科室的活。他没有料到的是，当众认错却如释重负，这其中的复杂滋味。

他对他所服务的那套官僚体制的愤怒——他像带着一块肌肉一样带了十二年——一夜之间安静下来。这也没有别的办法可以修补。

有的只是两点半的茶，和别人的一把椅子。到了圣诞节，候诊室里有一棵小树，树上立着一只瓷天使；二十三日，学校的一支业余乐队进来，唱了四首糟糕的颂歌和一首唱得好的。"

四首糟糕的，一首好的，"埃罗尔说，"我数了。每一首都数了。"流感来了，椅子上坐满了在痛苦里呻吟的人，并且惊讶地发现一条毯子竟然这么快就有用。蝙蝠冬天从停车场走了；一只猫头鹰占了烟囱，黄昏时在那片田里捕猎。埃罗尔读完了课程，作为一名合格的家谱学者，他把佩尔家往上追了五代，查出四个屠夫和一个铁匠。

阿莫斯·佩尔出生在铺子楼上的那间屋里，一九六三年以来离开镇子的时间从未超过两周。埃罗尔认为这是他查出来的最无害的一件事，而且十一年里，他每晚两点半都要讲一遍。

那年最后一个星期四，凌晨三点，阿莫斯·佩尔自己走进来了：瘸着，秃着，硬邦邦的，什么也没带。迪莉娅看看他空着的双手，又看看他的脸。

"我准是忘了点什么，"他说。"坐下，"她说，"我去给你找点东西。""喝茶？"迪莉娅问。"好，麻烦了。这个月真长。"他吃了两片吐司、一只煮鸡蛋和一根香蕉。

他咬了一口，停住，看着盘子，好像盘子侮辱了他。接着他把杯子里的茶凑近吸了口热气才喝下去，然后发出一声呻吟——那不是剧痛，不是极度痛苦，也不是危难，而是一个刚被人喂饱了的人那种寻常的舒坦。

过了一会儿他说，这是四十年来别人为他做过的最好的一件事，然后自己纠正道："四十一年。"他问能不能改在星期二来，因为星期四开始在他心里唤起一种他解释不了的焦虑。

她说星期二很好。"你想让我带点什么来？"他问。"什么都不用，"迪莉娅说，"就这些。"最后他问，他到底该带什么来。迪莉娅——水壶上方的架子上已经摆着十一只，她用不上第十二只——十一个月来第一次对他讲了实话。

三点来。什么都别带。
