chapters.title: 第七次爆炸
chapters.content:
Lab 7 of the Kell Building had exploded six times in nineteen years, and Nell Carrow had swept up after every one of them.

She was forty-one, a senior technician who had never graduated, and the only human being in the building who had been present for all six. She could tell you, without looking anything up, that the fourth one smelled of burnt sugar and rain, that the second one put the window out into the courtyard, and that on the morning after the fifth somebody had come down from the floor above to complain about their teeth. The Thackmoor Academy of Sciences called the room the Cinder Room in its paperwork and the basement in a panic. The dental school upstairs called it the ceiling problem.

Each of the six bangs had been given a letter, in the tidy alphabet of official failure: Incident A, the Business with the Zinc; Incident B, the Sulfur Morning; Incident C, Hydrogen and Good Intentions; Incident D, which nobody discussed; Incident E, which cost Thackmoor a filter and a window; and Incident F, known throughout the coffee houses on the pavement opposite as the Terror of 2019. Six letters. Six figures on a chart pinned up in the corridor for eleven years. Six young people who had gone away with their confidence crippled and their fellowships quietly not renewed. Nell had stayed. Somebody had to know where the broom was kept.

The seventh, everyone said, was only a matter of time, and Professor Aldous Kemble had already decided what to do with the room afterwards.

Kemble was chairman of the Department of Physical Sciences, a man whose intellectual vanity had the symmetry of a well-made box: nothing wasted, nothing openable. He wanted a podcast studio. The Academy needed content, he told the council, and a studio in the basement would cost minus nothing, less than the annual allowance for paper and less even than the glue. In the formulation he had constructed for the occasion, and he had a formulation for every occasion, this was called "translating research into the vernacular."

The agenda item was number three. Under it, in smaller type, sat Nell's assignment: certify Lab 7 as safe within nineteen days, or be assigned to a desk in Estates.

"You could be very comfortable in Estates," Kemble told her afterwards, in the corridor, with a smile rehearsed for this conversation. "There is a window. There is tea. Nobody's life ends in Estates."

"Mine would," said Nell.

He had a verbal formula for this, which he delivered with no kindness in it at all: redundant with warmth. He gave her until the nineteenth and an appointment to see him at four in the afternoon of the nineteenth day.

Nell had come to Thackmoor at twenty-two, straight out of a household in a town with one street, to work one summer in the glasshouse and, she had thought, to leave in September. The glasshouse closed. The Cinder Room did not. She had stayed for the reason people stay in rooms like that one: somebody had to know where the broom was kept, and after the second bang she was the only one left who did.

Into this walked Dr. Heston Pike.

Pike was twenty-nine, energetic, a theoretical physicist with a grant, a machine arm and a projector he had bought with his own money. He had come to Thackmoor to reproduce the experiment the building had been built for: Bramwell Kell's demonstration of 1908, in which a rotary cylinder of hydrogen was let go against a nickel rod, and the velocity of the burning front was measured with a mirror, a clock and an unusual quantity of patience. Pike had rebuilt it as the Pike Rig, and the Pike Rig was sophisticated, experimental and nine-tenths hardware. It had one laser, one turbine pump, three heat gauges, a detector the size of a suitcase, a keyboard bolted to the bench, a compressed-air line running along the ceiling from the last century, and a robot arm that could manipulate a needle with what he called "metric precision." It had an interface of forty-one parameters and a screen the colour of a swimming pool. It was geared, Nell decided on the first morning, entirely for the camera.

Pike was not a bad man. He was simply a man who had never lubricated anything.

He called her "the cleaner" for four days and then, as though stamping a name on a fresh specimen, "Nell." He had browsed the literature on basement ventilation for perhaps nine minutes. He did not subscribe to her view that a building is an instrument like any other and must be read before it is used. On the contrary, he said, a building is a setting, and that is a matter of taste; what mattered was the quality of the science and the momentum of the programme. He believed, and put it in a memorandum, that laboratory safety was nine-tenths psychology and one-tenth signage.

"Fear is a habit," he told her on the Thursday. "People blow things up because they expect to."

"People do not blow things up," said Nell. "Things blow people up, as a rule, at four in the morning."

He said that relativity was the premise upon which all modern physics stood. Nell, who had read three books and remembered two, said that relativity was also what a physicist quotes when he is losing an argument. He was thrilled by this and wrote it down, which was, in fairness, exceptional behaviour in a man of twenty-nine. He declined to collaborate with Estates, on the grounds that Estates had no input worth having, and he presumed — this was his assumption about everything — that whatever had not happened to him personally had not happened at all. He could not grasp why a woman who kept animals in a jar should be allowed an opinion about his apparatus. He had the energy of a man who has never once been wrong in public, and the invention he had invented under a silly name of its own did nothing but divide the bench in half. He had, in short, everything a young man needs in order to be blamed for something he had not done.

Nell ran the Cinder Room the way other people run a parish: by knowing everybody in it.

There was the mouse, called Bram, who lived behind the cabinets and who had, on the evidence of six previous incidents, a detector of his own: he left the room roughly forty minutes before every bang and came back an hour after it, a fact which the sociology department had once tried to publish under the title Rodent Anticipation of Industrial Mishap. There was the spider in the shutter rail, whose web was the oldest fixture in the room and whose habit, on the mornings that mattered, was to take it down to a single thread and drop out of sight.

And there were the worms.

For nineteen years Nell had kept, in a shallow enamel basin on the window ledge, a species of worm from the stream at the bottom of the grounds. She had isolated a clone line in 2007. She had raised four hundred generations of descendants from a single specimen. She was, in the strictest sense, the world's leading authority on one gene and one chromosome of an animal nobody had ever wanted. She fed them on oat and apple, and they went on multiplying with an enthusiasm she privately called unusual. Their tissue regenerated, a trick of biology she had never stopped finding odd. A parasite had once taken the whole population down for a summer, and she had counted them back one by one under the microscope, which is how she had learned that patience is only arithmetic applied to creatures. The ecology of that jar was the only system in the building never to have gone wrong, she used to say.

What Kemble had given her was, on paper, an insult. In practice it was three weeks of access she would not otherwise have had, and she used all of it.

She began with her diary: a black ruled book kept since Incident A, in which every datum about every bang had been written down in the order it happened, because a thing written down cannot be deleted by anybody with a password. The institute's maintenance database, as it happened, had a retention policy of seven years, which meant that four of the six incidents had been erased by automation rather than by malice, which was the worse way to lose it, since nobody had meant it. She had sent feedback to Estates in writing, monthly, for six years, and Estates had filed every page of it. So she dived into the places where paper survives: the Estates archive, the boiler house log, and the room on the roof belonging to the Astronomy Society, whose telescope sat directly above the Cinder Room and whose members had logged, in eleven years of observing, six unexplained shudders which they had blamed, every single time, on poor seeing.

She gathered everything into one file: the traces from the plant room, the power log, the outdoor temperature readings for eleven winters, and a bundle of complaints from upstairs. She analysed it. The analysis was analytic to the point of boredom. She drew a graph. It was not mathematical in any clever sense; it was maths of a kind a child could do, and the statistics said one thing. Every bang had happened at four-twelve in the morning, within a fraction of a minute, when the outdoor thermometer stood below four degrees. Every bang was preceded on the recorder by a voltage dip of a few volts, far too small to trip a breaker and far too regular to be weather. Nobody had ever thought to look at the time of day, which was the one dimension on which all six agreed.

Her hypothesis was not about chemistry at all, and there was no chemical reason for any of it.

She wrote it in the diary in one line: Nothing in the lab explodes. Something in it is exploded. Under it she set out the outline of the mechanism as four things: hot air, a rusted bar, a stuck shutter and a spark. Somewhere in the middle of the page she wrote a sentence she did not show anybody for a long time: In all six reports the operator was blamed, and the operator is the one element here that never goes off.

Getting down to see it cost her a favour.

Access to the sub-basement was controlled by Mrs. Verna Adane, the stores clerk, who assumed, correctly, that Nell had no business down there, and, incorrectly, that this was a reason to refuse. Nell owed Verna a favour from Incident E and called it in, and Verna, who had been waiting eleven years to be asked, produced a key the size of a hand. Mick Tallow, the estate carpenter, came along with a crowbar, a torch and an axe he had taken out of a glass case in 1994 and had never managed to put back. Roy Hoyt, the mechanic who had serviced the building's boiler since the last century, came because Mick had promised him entertainment.

Before they went down, Nell went up.

Professor Halvard Snell, historian of science, kept the history of the place in a room the size of a cupboard and was delighted, for the first time in a decade, to be asked a question. Yes, he said: Kell's notebooks survived, eleven volumes of them, in the safe. Yes: the apparatus had come from Hamburg by steamer in 1908, carried up the hill by six men and one horse, and the formula for the whole business had been scribbled on the back of a bill. And yes, said Snell, and he went slightly pink saying it: there was one telegraph. March 1908. Filed, for reasons nobody could now explain, under "Boiler House": EAST SHAFT NOT TO BE SEALED UNTIL STEAM TRAP REMOVED STOP KELL STOP. It had never been translated into the catalogue, because catalogues are made by people who are not told about wires.

They went down on the Tuesday, in boots.

The elevator in the Kell Building stopped at the basement and had been held together since 1998 by wire and a prayer, so they took the stairs. The sub-basement was a basin of black water two centimetres deep, cold enough to hurt through rubber. In the beam of Mick's torch: the old coal chute; a turbine half dismantled; forty metres of lagged pipe with a white calcium crust inside it; a hot-water cylinder the size of a wardrobe; a condensate pot, still warm. And across the mouth of the east shaft there was a sheet of composite board, saturated, eaten away at every edge and held on with six nails and a bit of wire, which somebody in 1974 had signed off as a wall.

The shaft behind it was a tube of brick, eighty centimetres in diameter, rising eleven metres on an axis that ended at the back of the Cinder Room's fume cupboard, where a sash and its rod sat in the airflow like a throat. Beyond it lay a network of old shafts, most of them bricked, one of them not, and the whole arrangement had, Nell thought, an inherent flaw which could be described in four words: somebody had been in a hurry.

The wall was warm. The warmth radiated up the shaft in a slow radiant column, and somewhere behind the brick the modern boiler roared and went quiet again. On the wall at shoulder height, in a brass case with a cracked front, hung one of those old gauges that keeps its highest reading: a maximum thermometer, installed in 1908, whose column had frozen at sixty-one degrees. Someone had used a fossil as a doorstop in 1961 and left it there. On a sill beside it, under a single forty-watt bulb, stood a toy locomotive in brass, dropped down the coal chute by a caretaker's son and never retrieved; Roy Hoyt picked it up, turned it over, and put it in his pocket, as though he had wanted one since he was nine. In a lead box on the same sill sat the only radioactive specimen in the building, which had been there since 1952 and had never, in seventy years, hurt anybody at all.

"Well," said Mick, after a while. "It's hot down here."

"It is hot," said Nell. "It has been hot twice a day for twenty-six years, and every single time it got hot at the wrong moment, somebody upstairs lost their job."

Nell clipped a probe to the pipe, measured it, computed, and stood a long time with her hand flat on the brick. Then she wrote it out in the diary, in the neat hand she kept for facts. At four-twelve the automation box opens the rotary valve for the nightly programme. The pulse goes up the east shaft, because the west shaft was bricked properly in 1974 and the east shaft was closed with a board and a lie. The hot air penetrates the back of the fume cupboard and gives the air inside it a boost of about two metres a second. The rod, corroded since 1974 and saturated with sulfur and old nickel dust, sticks for ninety seconds. The shutter has no brake; it falls by its own weight. Flow reverses, and the cupboard, which normally refreshes its air twenty times an hour, stops doing it at all. Hydrogen and oxygen meet in the ratio they prefer. The electrical relay in the sash motor throws one electron it was not asked to throw at one molecule it was not asked to meet. She turned the page. Every element of this is a fixture. Not one of them is a scientist.

The bug, when she found it, was four characters wide.

In 1998 somebody had typed the set-point into the control box as 04:12, in a field that wanted a twenty-four-hour clock, and the loop, being a generous thing, had read it twice: once as four in the morning and once as four in the afternoon. It had taken Nell six days to link the two times of day to each other, and most of a seventh to accept that the link was real, because the scope of what it meant was larger than her brief and larger than her nerve, such as it was. It was a virtual certainty, she wrote, that the next bang would come at sixteen-twelve on the nineteenth, because that was when Pike had booked the arm, the projector and the men with money. The building had been trying to explode at four-twelve twice a day for twenty-six years, and the rooms above it had been polite enough to oblige only on the days when somebody had left the gas on.

And then, in a file marked Basement, Miscellaneous, Do Not Destroy, she found the thing that made her sit down.

Four pages, typed, dated 1998: On the Bearing of Building Services upon Combustion in Basement Laboratories, by A. Kemble, research fellow. It said, in substance, exactly what she had just worked out, and it said it with data. It was rational. It was systematic. It was exceptional. At the foot of the last page, in a hand Nell had seen on eleven years of agendas, somebody had written: Too abstract. Not academic. Resubmit as engineering. Kemble's fellowship had not been renewed that summer. He had gone into administration instead, and had spent twenty-six years becoming the man who says that people are the problem.

Nell sat with it for a long time, the way she sat with a jar of them. Then a messenger came up from the chairman's office with a tentative knock and a note asking whether she had made any progress, and she wrote back one word: No.

The night before, Nell sat in the coffee house opposite the gates with a cup of tea and a plate of something grey, and Junie, who had been watching the windows of the Kell Building for eleven years and knew the look of the sixth one by heart, asked whether tomorrow would be the day. Nell said it would. Junie asked whether anybody would be hurt. Nell said no, and then, because she had thought about it for six years, she said: Nobody has ever been hurt in that room. That is the one thing nobody believes.

The demonstration was scheduled for the nineteenth day, at four in the afternoon, in front of the founders and a camera. Pike had asked for four because four photographs well. Pike had asked, in writing, that the output of the room be described to the founders as "a new generation of technology". Nell, who held that hot-air technology was older than chemistry itself, crossed it out and wrote "Kell's experiment, again" instead. The institute had a procedure for asking to be left alone with another person's rig, four pages of it, and Nell went round it by asking Pike at half past four on a Friday, when he was tired. He would not cooperate about the schedule, or about the fume cupboard either, and in the end Nell stopped asking him about both. What she did ask for, quietly and in writing, was one hour alone with the rig on the morning of the nineteenth, and Pike granted it on impulse, because nothing is cheaper to a man than a favour he has been asked for.

She did four things with that hour.

She swapped the gas bottle for nitrogen and checked the ratio twice. She set a packet of flour on the shelf inside the cupboard, where the pulse would find it, because every particle of flour in the world is waiting for exactly one afternoon like that one. She erected around the whole rig a tent of transparent plastic sheeting. She told Pike it was a draught guard. Pike, delighted, described it on camera as "a clean-room aesthetic." And she left the sash exactly as it was: rusty, dry, and idle in the wrong position, with her good sleeve rolled up and her hands shaking slightly, because she was forty-one and had never once broken a rule on purpose.

Then she wrote one line in the black book, went upstairs, and made tea.

At four sharp the founders sat down. Pike, glowing, introduced the premise of Kell's 1908 work and invited everyone to observe the performance of the arm. At twelve minutes past four, exactly as the diary said it would, the wall behind the cupboard threw out one long column of hot air, the thermometer in the shaft climbed past sixty, the shutter dropped, the needle on the pressure gauge jumped, and the flour went off inside the plastic with a thrilling and entirely harmless bang, like a very expensive party favour. It billowed white. Nobody was hurt. Pike's hair was white for a week, and the founders, who had come for a laser, stood out in the rain for twenty minutes afterwards, describing to one another what they had seen. Two of them asked for their money back, and one of them asked, rather loudly, for Pike. The fourth, an old woman who had given the institute money every year since 1974 and who had never once been inside a laboratory, sat down on the wet step outside, laughed until she had to hold the rail, and asked whether they might do it again at six, for her husband.

The video was on the internet by six and half of cyberspace had seen it by seven. For one afternoon the Cinder Room was not off the radar but at the very centre of it, and the institute's telephone rang for three days.

Kemble arrived at twenty past four, late from a dental appointment, with one side of his face still numb.

Nell did not shout. She laid things out on the bench the way she laid out jars of worms: the old gauge in its cracked case; the trace with its daily voltage dip at sixteen-twelve; the 1908 wire; Kell's notebooks, open at March; her own black book, open at the line about the shaft; and, last of all, the four pages from 1998.

Kemble read his own report twice. Then he said the only thing he could say, and half of his mouth would not cooperate: "I was twenty-eight."

"Twenty-six years," said Nell. "Twice a day. The building has been saying it since before I was born."

"What do you want?"

Nell had given this some thought. "The east shaft bricked. The control box replaced before the installation of anything else in this room. A new filter, a new hoist, and a stop on the sash." She paused. "And six letters, one to each of the six people who were blamed. Written by you. Sent by the Academy."

"Six letters," said Kemble.

"Six of them," said Nell. "One appliance." She tapped the kettle, which was the only appliance in the room and the only thing in it that had ever been properly oiled.

He wrote them. It took him a week, and, by his own account, most of a bottle of something pleasant; he quoted the 1998 report in each of them, and in the sixth he copied out her line about the shaft, which she had not expected and did not forget. A woman in Estates was assigned to coordinate the replies, and four of the six wrote back, and two of the four came to Thackmoor to see the shaft with their own eyes. Of the four who answered, one had become a teacher, one worked in a shop, and one had spent six years driving a van and did not want to talk about Thackmoor at all. The fourth was the woman from Incident A, who had been twenty-six and had cried in the corridor for an hour, and who wrote back a single page to say that she had never understood what had happened to her, and had spent eleven years believing it was her fault. The east shaft was bricked in November by a contractor who specialized in chimneys and who, on seeing the toy engine, asked whether he might keep it; Roy Hoyt said no, and the contractor, who had not expected to be refused by a mechanic, said that this was only fair. The parameter was corrected by an engineer from Estates who read the manual twice and found the bug in nine minutes, which he considered slow. Pike lubricated the shutter himself on a Saturday, with a grease gun and his cuffs rolled up, and he and Nell collaborated on a paper, On the Bearing of Building Services upon Combustion in Basement Laboratories, with a Retrospective Analysis of Six Events, which was published in a journal nobody in Thackmoor subscribed to, and which, in the abstract, credited "N. Carrow, technician" first.

The fellowship that had been idle since 1998 was renewed, and Kemble offered it to her.

She refused it, which amused him for a year, and asked instead for the retention of Verna Adane's job, a proper lift, and a key of her own. She got all three. What she could not refuse, and did not, was the notebooks of Bramwell Kell, which the institute gave her on the condition that she would keep writing in it, and which she keeps to this day on the shelf above the jars.

The spider came back and rebuilt it in the new rail within a week. Bram retired to the cupboard under the bench and has not predicted anything since. They went on as they always had, feeding and regenerating, entirely indifferent to the story of the room they live in, and entirely indifferent as well to the proposition that anybody had ever been at fault. Pike's machine was renamed Bram as well, which confused everybody, and Pike, who had come to Thackmoor to reproduce one experiment, stayed to do it properly, which took him another year and made him, in the end, a scientist.

There is a card on the wall of the Cinder Room now, in a frame, and on it Nell wrote the line she had wanted to write since Incident A. The card is a scrap of the bag the flour came in, which she thought was funny, and which Junie, the waitress at the coffee house on the pavement, said was the best thing anybody had done on that street in eleven years. Junie had run a book on the seventh explosion for years and had lost it in one afternoon; she owed Nell eleven pounds, and paid it in coffee, which Nell considered perfectly fair.

The card says:

Nothing in this lab ever wanted to explode. It was only ever warm, and it was only ever four-twelve.

凯尔楼七号实验室在十九年里爆炸过六次，每一次都是内尔·卡罗收拾的残局。

她四十一岁，是个没念完学位的高级技术员，也是这栋楼里唯一一个六次事故全都在场的人。她不用查任何资料就能告诉你：第四次那回闻起来像烧焦的糖和雨水；第二次把窗户崩到了院子里；第五次过后的第二天早上，楼上有人下来抱怨自己的牙。萨克穆尔科学院在文件里管这间屋子叫煤渣室，慌起来的时候管它叫地下室。楼上牙科学院管它叫天花板问题。

六声巨响各有一个编号，用的是官方失败记录里那套整齐的字母表：事故甲，锌那桩事；事故乙，硫磺的早晨；事故丙，氢气与好意；事故丁，没人提起过；事故戊，让萨克穆尔赔了一个过滤器和一扇窗；事故己，对面人行道上的咖啡馆里人人都叫它"二〇一九年的恐怖"。六个编号。六组数字，贴在一张图表上，在走廊里挂了十一年。六个年轻人，走的时候信心尽毁，研究奖学金也悄无声息地没有续。内尔留了下来。总得有人知道扫帚放在哪儿。

第七次，大家都说，只是时间问题；而奥尔德斯·肯布尔教授已经想好了那之后要拿这间屋子干什么。

肯布尔是物理科学系的主任，他那点知识分子的虚荣心精致得像一只做工考究的盒子：一点都没浪费，也一点都打不开。他想要一间播客录音棚。他对理事会说，学院需要内容，而地下室里的一间录音棚几乎不用花钱，比每年的纸张津贴还便宜，甚至比胶水还便宜。用他专门为这种场合炮制的说法——他每种场合都有一套说法——这叫作"把研究翻译成老百姓的话"。

议程上的第三项就是这件事。下面用小一号的字体写着内尔的任务：在十九天之内证明七号实验室是安全的，否则就调去房产处坐办公桌。

"你在房产处会很舒服的，"事后肯布尔在走廊里对她说，脸上挂着一副为这场谈话排练过的笑，"那里有窗户。有茶。在房产处，谁的日子也不会完。"

"我的会完。"内尔说。

他对这种事有一套口头说法，说出来时没有半点善意：带着温情地冗余。他给了她期限到十九号，又约她十九号下午四点来见他。

内尔二十二岁来到萨克穆尔，从只有一条街的小镇上的一个家里出来，本想在温室干一个夏天，然后——她当时是这么想的——九月就走。温室关了。煤渣室没有。她留了下来，理由和所有留在那种屋子里的人一样：总得有人知道扫帚放在哪儿；而第二次爆炸之后，只剩下她一个人知道。

就在这时候，赫斯顿·派克博士走了进来。

派克二十九岁，精力充沛，是个拿着研究基金的理论物理学家，带着一只机械臂和一台自己掏钱买的投影仪。他来萨克穆尔，是要重现这栋楼当年为它而建的那个实验：布兰韦尔·凯尔一九〇八年的演示——让一筒旋转的氢气顶着一根镍棒释放出来，再用一面镜子、一只钟和非同寻常的耐心去测量燃烧锋面的速度。派克把它重建成"派克装置"，这台装置复杂精密、带有实验性质，而且九成是硬件。它有一台激光器、一台涡轮泵、三个测温计、一只行李箱大小的探测器、一个用螺栓固定在实验台上的键盘、一根从上个世纪沿天花板拉过来的压缩空气管，还有一只能以他所谓的"公制精度"操控一根针的机械臂。它有四十一个参数的界面，还有一块游泳池那种颜色的屏幕。内尔第一天早上就断定，这东西整个儿就是为了上镜而造的。

派克不是坏人。他只是个从没给任何东西上过润滑油的人。

他叫了她四天"打扫卫生的"，然后，像给新鲜标本贴一个标签那样，改口叫"内尔"。关于地下室通风的文献，他大概浏览了九分钟。他不认同她的看法：一栋楼和别的仪器没什么两样，在用之前得先读懂。相反，他说，一栋楼只是背景，而背景关乎品味；真正要紧的是科学的成色和项目的势头。他还写进备忘录里说，实验室安全九成是心理问题，一成是标识牌。

"恐惧是一种习惯，"那个星期四他对她说，"人们把东西弄炸，是因为他们本来就等着它炸。"

"人不把东西弄炸，"内尔说，"是东西把人弄炸，而且通常是在凌晨四点。"

他说，相对论是所有现代物理学赖以成立的前提。内尔念过三本书，记得两本，她说相对论也是物理学家吵输的时候最爱引用的一句话。他听了很兴奋，还把它记了下来，平心而论，这在二十九岁的人身上算是难得。他拒绝与房产处合作，理由是房产处提不出任何有价值的意见；而且他想当然——他对万事都是这个假设——凡是没发生在他自己身上的事，就根本没发生过。他弄不明白，一个在罐子里养虫子的女人凭什么对他的仪器有发言权。他身上有着那种从未在公开场合错过一次的人的劲头，而他亲手起了一个傻名字的那件发明，唯一的作用就是把实验台一分为二。总而言之，一个年轻人要被冤枉，该有的条件他全有了。

内尔管理煤渣室，就像别人管理一个教区：靠认识里头的每一个活物。

有一只老鼠，叫布拉姆，住在柜子后面；根据前六次事故的记录，它自己带了一只探测器：每次爆炸前大约四十分钟离开房间，一小时后回来。社会学系曾经想把这个事实写成论文发表，题目叫《啮齿动物对工业事故的预感》。还有一只蜘蛛，住在排风柜的挡板滑轨里，它的网是这间屋子里最老的固定装置；每逢要紧的早晨，它的习惯就是把网收成一根丝，然后坠下去不见了。

还有那些虫子。

十九年来，内尔在窗台上一只浅浅的搪瓷盆里养着一种虫子，来自院子尽头那条小溪。二〇〇七年她分离出了一个克隆系。她从一个标本出发，养了四百代后代。从最严格的意义上说，她是一个没人想要的动物的一个基因、一条染色体上全世界最权威的专家。她用燕麦和苹果喂它们，它们以一种她私下里叫做异乎寻常的热情不停地繁殖。它们的组织能够再生——这是生物学的一个小花招，她始终觉得奇怪。有一年夏天，一种寄生虫把整个种群拖垮了，她就一个一个地在显微镜下把它们数回来，也正是从那次她明白了：耐心不过是用在活物身上的算术。那只罐子的生态是这栋楼里唯一一次都没出过岔子的系统，她常说。

肯布尔交给她的东西，写在纸上是侮辱；落到实处，却是三个星期她本来求不到的查阅权，而她一分钟都没浪费。

她从自己的日志开始：一本从事故甲记到现在的黑皮横格本，每一次爆炸的每一条数据都按发生的顺序写在里面，因为写下来的东西是没人能用密码删掉的。而学院的维修数据库，巧得很，有七年的保存期限，也就是说六次事故里有四次是被自动化抹掉的，不是出于恶意，可这反而是丢掉它更糟的一种：因为没人是存心要这么干的。她六年来每月都给房产处写书面反馈，房产处把每一页都归档了。于是她一头扎进纸张还能活下来的地方：房产处的档案室、锅炉房的日志，还有屋顶上那间属于天文学会的屋子——他们的望远镜正对着煤渣室上方，会员们在十一年的观测记录里记下了六次无法解释的震动，而每一次，他们都把它归咎于"视宁度不好"。

她把一切收进一个文件夹：机房的记录曲线、电力日志、十一个冬天的室外温度读数，还有一捆楼上的投诉。她做了分析。那分析理性到了枯燥的地步。她画了图。这算不上什么高明的数学，就是小孩子也会做的算术，而统计数字说的只有一件事。每一次爆炸都发生在凌晨四点十二分，前后不到一分钟的误差，而且都在室外温度计低于四度的时候。每一次爆炸之前，记录仪上都会有一次几伏的电压跌落，小得根本跳不掉闸，又规律得绝不可能是天气。谁也没想过去看一眼时间，而时间恰恰是六次事故唯一吻合的那个维度。

她的假说跟化学毫无关系；这事儿根本没有任何化学上的原因。

她在日志里写了一行：这里的实验室不会自己爆炸。这里的实验室是被炸的。 下面她把这套机理的轮廓列成四样东西：热空气、一根生锈的杆、一扇卡住的挡板、一个火花。在这页中间某处，她写了一句话，很久没给任何人看：六份报告里，被归咎的都是操作者；而操作者是这里唯一一样从来不会炸的东西。

要到下面去看一眼，她得动用一个大人情。

地下二层的进入权掌握在仓库管理员弗娜·阿丹太太手里。她想当然地认为——这一点她没错——内尔不该下去；又想当然地认为——这一点她错了——这是个拒绝的理由。内尔从事故戊那次起就欠弗娜一个人情，这回把它兑现了；弗娜等了十一年才等到有人来问，于是掏出一把巴掌大的钥匙。房产处的木匠米克·塔洛跟着来，带了一根撬棍、一只手电和一把斧头——那把斧头是他一九九四年从一个玻璃柜子里取出来的，之后再也没能放回去。罗伊·霍伊特是从上个世纪起就给这栋楼的锅炉做保养的技工，他来，是因为米克答应他有热闹看。

下去之前，内尔先上了一趟楼。

科学史家哈尔瓦德·斯内尔教授把这个地方的历史收在一间只有柜子那么大的屋子里；十年来第一次有人来问他问题，他高兴坏了。有，他说：凯尔的笔记本还在，十一卷，在保险柜里。有：那套仪器是一九〇八年从汉堡用轮船运来的，由六个人和一匹马抬上山，整套操作的配方就草草写在一张账单背面。还有，斯内尔说，而他讲这句话时脸上有点泛红：有一份电报。一九〇八年三月。归档在"锅炉房"名下，原因现在谁也说不清：东竖井在蒸汽疏水阀拆除之前不得封堵 凯尔 完。它从来没有被译进目录，因为目录是做目录的人编的，而没人会告诉他们电报的事。

他们是星期二下去的，穿着靴子。

凯尔楼的电梯只到地下室，而且自一九九八年起就是靠一段铁丝和一个祈祷拼在一起的，所以他们走了楼梯。地下二层是一盆两厘米深的黑水，冷得隔着橡胶都扎人。米克手电的光柱里：旧煤滑槽；一台拆了一半的涡轮机；四十米包着保温层的管子，里面结着一层白色的钙质硬壳；一个衣柜大小的热水罐；一只冷凝水罐，还是温的。而在东竖井的井口上，横着一块复合板，湿透了，每一条边都烂掉了，用六颗钉子和一小段铁丝固定着——一九七四年有人把它当作墙签字验收了。

它后面那口竖井是一根砖砌的管子，直径八十厘米，沿一条轴线向上十一米，尽头就在煤渣室排风柜的背面，那里有一扇窗框和它的连杆，像喉咙一样坐在气流里。再往里是一片旧竖井组成的网络，大部分砌死了，有一个没有；内尔觉得，整个这套东西有一个固有的缺陷，四个字就能说清：有人赶时间。

墙是热的。暖意顺着竖井以一道缓慢的辐射柱往上走，砖墙后面某处，现代锅炉轰响了一声，又安静下来。齐肩高的墙上，挂在一只有裂缝的铜壳里的，是那种会保留最高读数的老式仪表：一支最高温度计，一九〇八年装上的，它的液柱冻在了六十一度。一九六一年有人拿一块化石当门挡，之后就一直搁在那儿。旁边的窗台上，在一只四十瓦的灯泡下面，立着一辆黄铜做的玩具火车头，是看门人的儿子从煤滑槽掉下去的，再也没取上来；罗伊·霍伊特把它捡起来，翻过来看看，然后放进了口袋，像是从九岁起就想要过这么一件。同一个窗台上有一只铅盒，里面是这栋楼里唯一的放射性标本，从一九五二年就在那儿，七十年里从没伤过任何人。

"嗯，"过了一会儿米克说，"下面挺热的。"

"是热，"内尔说，"二十六年来，它一天热两次；而它每一次在不该热的时候热起来，楼上就有人丢掉工作。"

内尔把一支探头夹在管子上，测了，算了，然后把手平放在砖上站了很久。接着她在日志里写下来，用的是她专门留给事实的工整字迹。四点十二分，自控箱为夜间程序打开旋转阀。气流冲上东竖井，因为西竖井在一九七四年砌得规规矩矩，东竖井却是用一块板和一句谎话封上的。热空气渗进排风柜的背板，让柜内的空气每秒获得大约两米的推力。那根连杆自一九七四年起就腐蚀着，浸透了硫磺和旧的镍粉，会卡住九十秒。挡板没有制动装置，靠自身重量落下。气流反向，而那只柜子本来每小时换二十次气，这下干脆不换了。氢气和氧气以它们最喜欢的比例相遇。窗框电机里的那个电气继电器，把一颗没人让它扔的电子，扔给了一个没人让它遇上的分子。 她翻过一页。这里的每一样都是固定装置。没有一样是科学家。

那个程序错误，等她找到的时候，只有四个字符宽。

一九九八年，有人把设定值以04:12敲进了控制箱，而那个字段要的是二十四小时制；那个循环是个大方的东西，于是把它读了两次：一次当成凌晨四点，一次当成下午四点。内尔花了六天把这两个时刻联系到一起，又花了大半个第七天接受这个联系是真的——因为这件事所牵涉的范围，比她的任务书大，也比她的胆子大，而她的胆子本来就这么点。她写道，下一次爆炸几乎可以肯定会在十九号十六点十二分到来，因为派克把机械臂、投影仪和那几个有钱人约在了那个时候。这栋楼二十六年来一直试图在四点十二分爆炸，一天两次；而楼上的房间只在有人忘了关气的时候，才客气地配合一下。

然后，在一个标着地下室，杂项，请勿销毁的文件夹里，她找到了那件让她坐下来的东西。

四页，打字机打的，日期是一九九八年：《论建筑设备对地下实验室燃烧的影响》，作者A·肯布尔，研究员。它讲的，实质上就是她刚算出来的那一套，而且是用数据讲的。它是理性的。它是系统的。它是出色的。在最后一页的下端，用内尔在十一年议程上见惯了的一种笔迹，有人写道：太抽象。不算学术。改投工程类。 那年夏天，肯布尔的奖学金没有续。他转去做了行政，然后花了二十六年，变成了那个说"问题出在人身上"的人。

内尔对着它坐了很久，就像她对着一罐虫子坐很久那样。后来，主任办公室派来一个送信的，试探性地敲了敲门，递来一张条子，问她有没有进展；她回了一个字：没有。

前一天晚上，内尔坐在大门对面那家咖啡馆里，面前是一杯茶和一盘灰扑扑的东西；朱妮看凯尔楼的窗户看了十一年，第六次的模样她闭着眼都认得，她问明天是不是就是那一天。内尔说是。朱妮问会不会有人受伤。内尔说不会；然后，因为这件事她想了六年，她又说：那间屋子里从来没人受过伤。这是唯一没人相信的一件事。

演示定在十九号下午四点，观众是出资人，还有一台摄像机。派克选四点，是因为四点拍出来好看。他还书面要求，向出资人介绍这间屋子时，要把它说成"新一代技术"。内尔认为热空气那套技术比化学本身还古老，就把这句划掉，改写成"凯尔的实验，再做一次"。学院有一套申请单独使用他人装置的手续，足有四页；内尔绕开了它——她在星期五四点半派克累了的时候开口问了他。他不肯在时间安排上配合，也不肯在排风柜上配合，到头来内尔两个都不再问他了。她只是低声地、以书面形式要了一样东西：十九号早上单独和那台装置待一个小时。派克答应了，是一时冲动；因为对一个男人来说，被求一件顺手的人情再便宜不过。

她用那一个小时做了四件事。

她把气瓶换成氮气，把比例核对了两遍。她把一袋面粉放在柜子里的搁板上，气流会找到它的地方——因为世界上每一粒面粉都在等这样一个下午。她在整个装置外面支起了一个透明塑料布的帐篷。她告诉派克那是挡风用的。派克很高兴，对着摄像机把它形容为"洁净室美学"。最后，她把窗框原样留着：生锈、干涩，闲闲地停在错误的位置上；她把好袖子卷起来，双手微微发抖，因为她四十一岁了，这辈子还从来没有故意破过一次规矩。

然后她在那个黑本子里写了一行字，上楼，泡了茶。

四点整，出资人坐了下来。派克容光焕发，先介绍了凯尔一九〇八年那项工作的前提，又请大家观赏机械臂的表演。四点十二分，分秒不差，正如日志所说：柜子后面的墙吐出一长柱热空气，竖井里的温度计爬过六十度，挡板落下，压力表上的指针跳了一下，面粉在塑料布里炸开，发出一声刺激、吓人、却完全无害的巨响，像一件非常昂贵的派对礼炮。它白茫茫地鼓了起来。没有人受伤。派克的头发白了一个星期；而那些本来是为一台激光器而来的出资人，事后在雨里站了二十分钟，互相描述自己刚才看到了什么。其中两个要求退钱，一个相当大声地要求派克出来。第四位是个老太太，从一九七四年起每年给学院捐钱，这辈子从没进过实验室；她在外面的湿台阶上坐下来，笑得不得不扶住栏杆，然后问他们能不能六点再来一次，为她丈夫。

录像六点就上了网，七点时半个网络空间都看过了。有那么一个下午，煤渣室不是掉出了雷达，而是正处在雷达的最中心；学院的电话响了三天。

肯布尔四点二十才到，刚看完牙，半边脸还麻着。

内尔没有嚷。她把东西一件件摆在实验台上，就像摆一排虫子罐那样：那只裂了壳的老仪表；那条在十六点十二分有日常电压跌落的曲线；一九〇八年的那份电报；凯尔的笔记本，翻到三月；她自己的黑本子，翻到关于竖井的那一行；最后，是一九九八年的那四页。

肯布尔把自己的报告读了两遍。然后他说了他唯一能说的一句话，而半边嘴不听使唤："我当时二十八岁。"

"二十六年，"内尔说，"一天两次。这栋楼从我没出生起就一直在说这件事。"

"你想要什么？"

内尔想过的。"东竖井砌死。控制箱换掉，在这间屋子安装任何其他东西之前。一个新的过滤器，一个新的吊车，还有给窗框加个止动装置。"她停了一下。"另外六封信，写给被归咎的六个人，一人一封。你来写。以学院的名义寄。"

"六封信，"肯布尔说。

"六个人，"内尔说，"一件器具。"她拍了拍水壶——那是这间屋子里唯一的电器，也是里头唯一被好好上过油的东西。

他写了。写了一个星期，而且据他自己说，喝掉了大半瓶什么好喝的东西；每一封里他都引用了一九九八年的那份报告，写到第六封时，他把她关于竖井的那句话抄了进去——这是内尔没料到的，也是她不会忘记的。房产处派了一个女人负责协调回信；六个人里有四个回了信，四个里有两个亲自来萨克穆尔看了那口竖井。回信的四个人里，一个当了老师，一个在店里做工，一个开了六年货车，压根不想谈萨克穆尔。第四个是事故甲那次的女人，当年二十六岁，在走廊里哭了一个小时；她回了一页纸，说她从来没弄明白自己身上发生了什么，却为此相信了十一年那是自己的错。东竖井在十一月被砌死了，干活的是个专砌烟囱的承包商；他看见那辆玩具火车头，问能不能拿走，罗伊·霍伊特说不行，那个承包商没料到会被一个技工拒绝，只好说这也公平。参数是房产处的一位工程师改正的，他把说明书读了两遍，九分钟就找到了那个错误，他还嫌这算慢的。派克在一个星期六自己给挡板上润滑油，拿着一把黄油枪，袖口卷了起来；他和内尔合作写了一篇论文——《论建筑设备对地下实验室燃烧的影响，附六起事故的回顾性分析》——发表在一本萨克穆尔没人订阅的期刊上，而在摘要里，署名排在第一位的是"技术员内·卡罗"。

那份从一九九八年起一直闲置的奖学金续上了，肯布尔把它给了她。

她拒绝了，这件事让他乐了一年；她转而要的是保留弗娜·阿丹的职位、一台像样的升降机，和一把自己的钥匙。三样她都拿到了。她没法拒绝、也没有拒绝的，是布兰韦尔·凯尔的笔记本——学院把它给了她，条件是她要继续往下写；而她至今仍把它放在那些罐子上面的搁板上。

蜘蛛回来了，不到一个星期就在新的滑轨里重新结了网。布拉姆退到实验台下面的柜子里，从此再没预言过什么。它们一如既往地进食、再生，对它们住的那间屋子的故事完全无所谓，也对"曾经有人有过错"这个说法完全无所谓。派克那台机器也被改名成了布拉姆，把所有人都搞糊涂了；而派克——他来萨克穆尔本是为了重现一个实验——留下来把它做对了，这又花了他一年，最终让他成了一个科学家。

现在煤渣室的墙上有一张卡片，镶在框里；内尔在上面写下了她从事故甲起就想写的那句话。那张卡片是从装面粉的袋子上剪下来的一块，她觉得很好笑；对面人行道上咖啡馆的女招待朱妮说，这是十一条街上十一年里有人做过的最好的一件事。朱妮为第七次爆炸开了好几年的盘口，一个下午就输了；她欠内尔十一英镑，用咖啡还了，内尔觉得这再公道不过。

卡片上写着：

这间实验室里从来没有一样东西想爆炸。它只是暖，而且只是四点十二分。

chapters.title: 爷爷的最后一局棋
chapters.content:
"His," he said. "I have owed him fifty-two years. A debt like that earns two moves before an answer." The board was still on the table when I came down. The black knight was gone, and Grandpa had set a hazelnut in the empty square. He moved it for me. One square. Another. "Whose move is it?"

"Name him."

The hospital had given him a deadline two days before. Twelve weeks, the doctor said. Sixteen if a man stays moderate, and nobody guarantees a day beyond that. He closed one eye and looked at the board. Brown. Polished by thumbs. Hardly bigger than a button, and it was not a coin with an emperor on it that he had never spent. "Anselm Rooke."

"Twelve," I said. "That is nothing."

"For a man with fifty-two years to wait," he said, "it is almost a long time." He put his coat on.

The nurse had taped a calorie chart to the fridge; over it he had taped a card of his own. MIND YOUR OWN BUSINESS. "What will you do with them?" I said.

On the step outside he turned. "Then I had better find him. A debt should not be left rude." "Finish a game," he said. "And finish it in front of them, so that they see the man and not the picture."

"You have not said his name in fifty-two years."

"Then say it." "Anselm Rooke." "I have said it," he said. "Every night for nineteen months, in a camp, to a wall."

The comrade was Anselm Rooke. The fire was in a bakery in the port of Vardene, where a grey fleet lay offshore all that winter. Every November the town hung his image on a nylon banner in the central square, three metres wide: BELLMERE REMEMBERS, and under it the sentence the town settled fifty years ago and never thought to check, WHO CARRIED HIS COMRADE FROM THE FIRE.

It ran: Private Tobias Kerr, nineteen, half the size of his gun, went back into the flames and carried his friend out on his back. The poet of Bellmere made a poem of it every year, glorious and thoroughly ridiculous. My son could say the last line of it at six.

"They put me in a comedy," he said. "And the part they gave me is the comic one." It was not true. I only knew that he could not stand the attention, hated being called a hero, and wore the name of the town's leading citizen like a wet coat. It provoked him, and it took very little provocation.

Mrs Pellow kept two lambs behind the house and breeds sheep for wool. She bosses the whole lane about and had called one of them Tobias. Grandpa pretended to resent it and adored it. He lived four doors from the pond, at the fringe of Bellmere, with a rosemary bush by the door and a fridge that hummed loud enough to hear from the road.

In the front room stood a glass cabinet: the badge, a bible that did not belong to him, and Nell's pearl, which came off her dress on their wedding day and had lived in a matchbox ever since.

"A jewel in a bank is only an excuse to be rude to the dead," he said. Nell's death was eleven years ago, and after that he kept her cup and the habit of filling it.

One week each spring I conduct an audit of the Remembrance charity, the money that pays for the military band and the tea.

Four years running I had calculated the same fundamental error in the same column and reported it to the four women who were the nucleus of the committee. "It is not difficult," I said. "The figures do not add up."

They were enthusiastic, generous with the butter, liberal with the honey, and quite unable to correct anything.

Prudence was not their method. It was my grandfather's, and it had won him fifty-two years of being decorated for something he never did, besides championing three lost causes and losing all.

I am a diligent woman. That is my occupation, and possibly my personality. Three days a week I work for the county records office, and my hours are flexible, which is the principal reason I could drive to Marlfield on a Thursday.

Anselm Rooke's workshop stood in a yard behind a baker's shop, and smelled of oak shavings and glue, a blend I go back to on purpose since. Not a major matter, but mine: Marlfield was ninety minutes away, downtown, by the main road and the castle ruin on the peak.

An oar leaned in the corner. He rowed on Sundays, because there is no peace in a church and a great deal of it on water. Guitars hung from hooks like sleeping bats. He had made forty-one and guaranteed every one for life, because he had spent thirty years on marine engines first and could hear a piston before he saw it.

Ninety and tall, and merry in public: his disposition had the patience of a long, careful life, and I understood that late.

"He has had fifty-two years to lose an argument," I said. "He would like to lose it properly. He is dying." Anselm went very still. "Your grandfather has had fifty-two years to write a letter," Anselm said, before he had even looked at me.

Apparently I had been doing it the whole time. He put down the wood he was shaping and made tea in a pot that had been black for forty years, pouring it to the brim. "Sit down," he said. "And do not imitate your grandfather's face. It does not suit you."

I persisted, which I had not done since I was fifteen and a rebel of a modest kind. My rebellion was a bad haircut and an instrument I could not play. After that there were four more afternoons, and the story came out of him in pieces, the way a bad tooth comes out: slowly, with almost no pain, and then all at once.

The winter campaign became a long, muted misery of distant cannon, shouted commands, and boys asleep in their coats. To combat the chill they wore everything they owned, which is why every photograph of that winter looks like a photograph of furniture. The winter of the invasion was the worst in forty years. The allied army pushed inland from the port and stopped, as armies do, in the mud.

Anselm and Tobias were detached with nine others to hold a cellar under a bakery. Their officer was a nineteen-year-old lieutenant with a pistol he did not know how to load. He went up the street at four and did not come back.

By the third day the battery in the radio was dead, the water was gone, and the alarm had stopped meaning anything. "Nothing left," Tobias said, "but wait." "There is the game," said Anselm. "So we play." They waited for the assault, while the battle went back and forth over their heads like weather. "There is nothing left to do," Tobias said, "but wait."

They had a pocket set of metal, the cheap kind that magnetises, and it was missing the black knight. "We are a knight short," said Anselm.

Both kept that rule, with the dignity of men who have nothing left to be faithful to except a game. A pool of light from one candle sat between them on the board, and outside the horizon flared and went opaque with smoke. "Use this," said Tobias, and put a hazelnut on the board. "A nut cannot be eaten. A knight cannot be eaten. Call it a knight."

Anselm was rash, aggressive, reckless, and brave in the careless way of the young. He attacked, confident they would be relieved before the week was out, and he said so with the confidence of a boy of nineteen, and at nineteen that is what courage consists of. Tobias was prudent. He played as he did everything, nine moves ahead, controlling the centre with the patience of a long wait.

The first game went to Anselm in thirty-one moves, the only defeat my grandfather ever admitted. He could not fight it and could not let it rest. He demanded a rematch on the spot. The core of it: my grandfather was never brave. He was careful, the town called his carefulness courage, nobody blamed him, and he let them.

What happened, in the force of it and the burst of flame that came down the stair: Tobias was ejected into the street by the blast itself, thrown clear, with nothing worse than fright and a burn on his right hand. They were eleven moves into it when the bomb hit. That is where Bellmere's story begins, and where the true one breaks away from it.

The town read that scar for fifty-two years as proof that he had gone in. Anselm was buried under the counter with both legs broken. Tobias, nineteen and conscious, was on his feet and ran, because his gut told him with the horror of it that nothing in that cellar was alive. He ran, and he swallowed it whole, and it stayed down for fifty-two years.

She got him to the allied line, where he was captured by people who were capturing everything that week. He was carried out by Marfa Sandow, the baker's wife, sixty-one, weighing less than a load of wood. She dragged him through the cellar hatch on a table-top, in the open, under missile fire, while the flames consumed her own house.

Nineteen months in the north, with nothing to eat and nothing to do but imagine the board.

When he came home in the spring, the town had already decorated my grandfather.

I ascertained the rest in the capital, where the regimental headquarters files are kept, in a small room with a window like a lens. The file contained four documents and one obscure sheet of carbon paper nobody had looked at in fifty years. The desk lady gave me a chair and a pen: "Sign for every box, dear. Every one."

Under the heading CIRCUMSTANCES it said: Pte. A. Rooke removed from a wrecked building by a civilian female, name unknown, at grave personal risk. Pte. T. Kerr detached; whereabouts at the time of the explosion unconfirmed. The first was a preliminary report, drafted three days after the attack by a clerk who had not been there.

The third was a form in Anselm's own hand, filled in the day he was released. The second, typed four days later, corresponded in general shape and was entirely different in essence: by his comrade, Pte. T. Kerr, who returned through hostile fire and bore him to safety.

Underneath lay Marfa Sandow's statement, in a feminine hand and ink of another colour, and no one in fifty-two years had encountered it beside the first sheet. It took me an hour to detect what that meant. In the box marked marital status he wrote no. In the box marked mother's maiden name, which nobody had asked him for, he wrote Kerr, my grandmother's maiden name, on his own paper.

The men in the capital had wanted a hero. The public had wanted a story. A civilian woman of sixty-one had been edited out of both, and the temptation to let it stand was real; I felt it too. I am not a curious woman by trade but a methodical one; I inferred a decision taken by a man with a rank and his own timetable.

It was October, and he sat by the window where the glass had gone opaque with steam from the pot of onions I had fried in butter. A man with twelve weeks wants onions at four in the afternoon. The point, said out loud, was that he had let a woman be edited out. He was a man of integrity, and that is why one lie had eaten him.

He punched the air and cheered, because he had asked the week before whether Grandpa was nuclear now, on account of the radiation, and Grandpa had said yes.

Six in March, he was. The kettle on the stove went on whistling, and I opened the window. The smoke alarm went off as it always did. "That is the bacon," he said. "I know. Leave it and open a window." Ivo was on the floor with a toy monkey and a polar bear.

Grandpa had not melted for a soul in twenty years. He melted for a six-year-old and gave him the burnt crust off his own plate.

"Marfa Sandow," I said. He closed his eyes. The scar on his right hand was white and looked elastic, and he caressed it with his thumb the way other men touch a coin.

"You never went back." He opened his eyes. "No."

"Then you ran," I said. He waited. "I ran."

"Why did you let them?" He was quiet a long time. A frog started up behind the house, and somewhere in the town a band was practising the wrong pace for a march.

"Because I was nineteen and frightened," he said. "When I got back to the line there was a colonel with a medal in his hand and a gap where a story should be, and I lacked the courage to fill it with the truth."

"The devil of it is that it was easy. It was the easier thing, and it was easy every day after that, and easier every year. That is my conquest, and that is the whole of it."

"You could have told them." "I could have. And Nell would have suffered, the town would have had nothing to commemorate, and Mrs Sandow was dead by then and could not be insulted by it."

"I told myself that a lie nobody chooses to check is a comfort to everybody," he said. "I told myself that for fifty-two years." He had a host of reasons and not one excuse.

"Lest you think I am asking for pity, I am not," he said. "I am asking you to fetch him. I want to lose the second game in front of the whole town. It is a modest amendment, and I want it more than I have wanted anything since I asked your grandmother to marry me."

He had been writing a letter and had drafted it eleven times, and on the table beside his chair lay the eleven drafts under an elastic band. "There is no honor left in the medal," he said. "There is a little in the table."

On top of them lay the thing he had kept all that time: Anselm's bible, small and black and holy to a Catholic woman, who had pressed a card into it and sent her boy to a war with it in his breast pocket.

So I fetched him. I encountered Anselm Rooke in his yard with a case under his arm, and he got into my car without a word. Grandpa had never opened it. "A guilty man does not read," he said. "He cherishes. Those are different trades, and mine is the humble one."

"It took me a great deal to get into that car, and I have overcome my share of the road," he said. "If you would not ask me to talk about it, I would be obliged." On the way he told me he had sung in the opera chorus at Saltmarch for twenty-two years as a bass, and that the norm in his family was to say nothing about anything.

He greeted my grandfather in the hall with a nod, a handshake and one line: "You took your time." He was discreet about exactly one thing. He never asked about Nell. Not once in all those years, and I have thought about that ever since. In that generation loyalty was a religion with no services.

They played at the oak table in the front room with the door open, so the town could stand in the yard, because the bulletin had gone round the parish and half of Bellmere was overflowing the path while the rest listened on the radio in the shop. "Traffic," said Grandpa.

Each afternoon Ivo bounces on the step; he hops, and hops, on one leg. Mrs Pellow brought the lambs to the fence as if they had asked, and the militant wing of the parade committee arrived and was persuaded, with difficulty, to leave it outside.

Anselm looked at it a long moment and laughed. Grandpa frowned at him. Grandpa set the board out himself. The metal men were rubbed to a dull shine, and in the place of the black knight, after fifty-two years, still the hazelnut, brown and polished by thumbs, hardly bigger than a button.

They played. It was slow and complex, and I understood a third of it. Anselm came out from the first move in the aggressive, reckless way he had at nineteen, while my grandfather gave ground, took it back, and controlled the middle with the patience it takes to work a board since 1969. "It is a knight," said Anselm. "It is a nut," said my grandfather. "It is a knight."

The two sounds met over the fence in a way that should have been ridiculous and was not, and Bellmere's poet stood at the fringe of the crowd with a poem in his pocket he had been writing all week and did not read out.

Outside, a naval band struck up in the square; the navy had sent thirty men and a conductor who had never conducted anything smaller than a cathedral, and somebody put pop music on a radio in the shop.

"Play it," I said. "Not yet," he said. "Play it, Tobias." Two hours in, my grandfather had the better position. Three hours in he had the power to win it, and I could see that he knew it. His hand went to the knight and caressed it, and came away.

"I am not going to finish this," said my grandfather, "until you have heard me. I did not go back into that cellar. I ran into the street and I did not look behind me."

"Marfa Sandow carried you out on a table-top and nobody in this town has ever said her name. I have worn your medal for fifty-two years and let them enlarge my image three metres wide and commemorate a lie with a band."

He was breathless and overcome by coughing. When he could speak again: "I do not want your forgiveness. I want it acknowledged. Those are different things, and I have had fifty-two years to choose between them."

The lane outside had no traffic on it by then, only the wind. The room went quiet. Somebody's radio made a small sound. Out in the square the cannon on the green stood in the cold doing nothing at all, the one Grandpa had told Ivo was a dragon asleep, and which Ivo had believed in for three full years.

Anselm leaned back in his chair. He was ninety years old, and he said, "I know."

"You know?" "I saw you," he said. "I was on my back under the counter. The roof was coming down, and there was a hole in the wall where a window had been, and I saw you in the street, and I saw which way you went."

He picked up the knight and turned it over. "I have known since 1969."

"Then why did you never say?" "Because you came back," he said. "You did not come back to the cellar. You came back to the table."

"You carried letters for a postman's wage for forty years," I said, "and you were not lazy, not greedy, not rash with anybody's money or anybody's heart. You sat with Nell while she was dying. You greeted that boy at the door every day of his life, and it took you nine seconds to give in."

He put the piece down on its square. "A man can be frightened for four minutes and steady for fifty-two years, and the reflection in the window is the same man both times. That is not comfort; it is the truth, and it does not make a glorious story, but it is considerably more useful."

Then he did the thing I will remember. He stood up, came round the table, took the medal off my grandfather's breast and pinned it to his own coat.

"There," he said. "Now it belongs to the man who was carried, which is honest, and I am giving it to your granddaughter, who will file it where files go, with a note saying who earned it."

"Who earned it?" He looked at me over his glasses, the look of somebody who has mastered one hard thing and will not be asked for another.

So I filed it; I am a diligent woman, and the accounts were due anyway. It went into the county archive in the capital with a note in my hand and a copy on carbon paper, because the essential thing was never the badge itself but the sentence under it. "Marfa Sandow," he said. "Sixty-one years old. She put me on a table-top and she pulled."

The corresponding entry runs to three lines: Private Anselm Rooke was carried out of a bakery in the port of Vardene by Mrs Marfa Sandow, who received nothing; Tobias Kerr ran; and the record was wrong for fifty-two years lest the town hear a harsh thing about a man it liked. I had been naive about that man for thirty-one years, and his correction did me no harm.

A gentleman from the dairy, who had fought in another war, rose to say the town had no issue with the truth and merely preferred its own version, and was ruled out of order. The committee debated it six weeks. The militant wing wanted to keep the old banner; the moderates wanted a stone for Mrs Sandow by the pond; the nucleus wanted both, and got both, as always.

It was read out, it went in the bulletin, and the poppies were not sold. Somebody proposed selling poppies in the square. "That is not remembrance," Grandpa wrote on a card from his chair. "That is capitalism."

They shook hands. Anselm picked up the book, his own and unread and handy as a stone for fifty-two years, put it in his pocket, and took it out again at the table. My grandfather finished the game; he did not win and he did not lose. Anselm said that was like him: a draw, at his own pace, on the movement he had been calculating since nineteen.

"Ah," said Anselm. "She was faithful to you," said Grandpa. "She kept faith with the truth," said Anselm, "which is the same virtue and a harder one." There he found what my grandfather had never found: a card from his mother, and a photograph of a girl with a pearl at her throat.

There is no moral in any of it and no glory.

We buried him next to Nell, in the fresh cold, with the band playing the march at the right speed for once, and Ivo cheered. Grandpa died in the first frost, on the ninth of November, eleven days less than Dr Vell had allowed him, before the ground could freeze, and he bore it with the dignity of one who had set his own deadline.

The banner went up and came down. The frog came back in April. Mrs Pellow breeds her sheep, the fence still leans, and the bush by the door has grown over the hook where Grandpa hung his coat. I consoled myself with work. In the spring I finished the audit: the money was short by four hundred pounds, and the four women covered it, as they always do.

In the cabinet now there is nothing official: a chess set with a knight missing, a nut, her bead in a matchbox, and a note my grandfather wrote that morning. Anselm sent Ivo a guitar, small, of the same wood, with a promise it would last his life, and one scratch on the back where he said a fox got into the workshop one night and burst a string.

I have read it a hundred times and will read it a hundred more. It is four lines long, it contains no excuse and no desire for forgiveness, and it says: I did not go back. But I came back to the table, and I sat down, and I finished what I had begun, and that is the whole of the courage I had.

When Ivo asks me what his great-grandfather was, I do not say hero any more. I say: he was one who came back, and sat down.
chapters.translation:
"他的。"他说，"我欠了他五十二年。这样的债，得先走两步才轮到回答。"我下楼时棋盘还摆在桌上。黑马不见了，爷爷在那空格里放了一颗榛子。他走给我看。一格。

再一格。"

该谁走了？""说出他的名字。"两天前医院给他下了一个期限。医生说，十二周。一个人若能保持节制，能撑到十六周，再往后谁也保证不了一天。他闭上左眼，看那张棋盘。棕色的。被拇指磨得发亮。几乎不比一颗纽扣大，也不是一枚印着皇帝头像、他从来没花出去过的硬币。"安塞尔姆·鲁克。"

"十二，"我说，"那算不了什么。"

"可对一个要等上五十二年的人来说，"他说，"那几乎算长了。"他穿上外套。

护士在冰箱上贴了一张卡路里表；那上面，他又贴了一张自己的卡片，写着：少管闲事。"你打算怎么处置它们？"我说。

他走到门外台阶上，转过身来。"那我最好把他找着。欠着债就这么了了，太不体面了。""把一盘棋下完，"他说，"当着他们的面下完，让他们看见的是这个人，不是那张画像。"

"这五十二年里，你一次也没叫过他的名字。"

"那你就说。""安塞尔姆·鲁克。""我说过，"他说，"有十九个月，每晚，在一个营房里，对着一堵墙。"

那个战友就是安塞尔姆·鲁克。火是在瓦尔登港的一家面包房里着的，那年冬天，一支灰色的舰队整冬都停在近海，什么忙也没帮上。每年十一月，全镇把他的画像挂上中央广场的尼龙横幅，三米宽，上面只有一行字：贝尔米尔不会忘记；横幅底下，是五十年前全镇定下、却从没想过要核对的一句话：谁把他战友从火里背了出来。

字是这样写的：二等兵托拜厄斯·克尔，十九岁，个头还没有他的枪高，转身冲进火里，把他的朋友背了出来。贝尔米尔的诗人每年都要把它写成一首诗，辉煌，又十足可笑。我儿子六岁就能把最后一句倒背如流。

"他们把我塞进了一出喜剧，"他说，"分给我的还是最滑稽的那个角色。"这话不假。我只知道他受不了那份关注，恨别人叫他英雄，把"全镇头面人物"这个名号穿在身上，像穿一件湿外套。这惹恼了他，而惹恼他实在用不着什么由头。

佩洛太太在后屋养着两只羊羔，还养羊取毛。她把整条巷子指挥得团团转，还给其中一只起名叫托拜厄斯。爷爷装出一副不高兴的样子，其实偷偷喜欢得要命。他住在离池塘四户人家的地方，就在贝尔米尔的最边上，屋门口一丛迷迭香，冰箱嗡嗡响，响到路上都听得见。

前屋立着一个玻璃柜：那枚勋章、一本不属于他的圣经，还有内尔的那颗珍珠——结婚那天从她裙子上掉下来的那颗，从那以后一直住在一个火柴盒里。

"把一颗珠宝塞进银行，不过是给对死人失礼找个借口，"他说。内尔是十一年前走的，那以后他留下了她的杯子，也留下了把它斟满的习惯。

每年春天有一周，我要为"纪念"慈善基金做一次审计——就是那笔付给军乐队和茶水的钱。

连着四年，我在同一栏里算出同一个根本性错误，报给那四个女人——她们是委员会的核心。"这不难，"我说，"数目对不上。"

她们热情，舍得放黄油，蜂蜜给得大方，却怎么也改不掉任何一件事情。

谨慎不是她们的办法。谨慎是我爷爷的办法；这办法让他拿了五十二年的勋章，所表彰的事他一件也没做过，此外他还拥护过三桩注定失败的事业，三桩全输了。

我是个勤快的女人。这是我的职业，大概也是我的性格。我每周有三天在县档案室上班，时间灵活——这是那个星期四我能一路开到马尔菲尔德的主要原因。

安塞尔姆·鲁克的作坊在一家面包店后面的院子里，闻起来是橡木刨花和胶水的气味，那股混在一起的味道，后来我还特意回去闻过。不算什么大事，不过是我自个儿的事：马尔菲尔德在市中心那一带，车程一个半小时，走主路，经过山顶那处城堡废墟。

墙角斜靠着一支桨。他星期天去划船，因为教堂里没有平静，而水上有的是。吉他挂在钩子上，像一排睡着的蝙蝠。他做过四十一把，每一把都保用终身；他敢这么保证，是因为在那之前的三十年里他一直修船用发动机，凭声音就能听出一个活塞好不好。

九十岁了，个子还高，在人前总是快快活活：他的性情里有一种漫长而小心的耐心，这一点我懂得太晚了。

"他有五十二年的时间可以输掉一场争论，"我说，"他想输得体面。他快死了。"安塞尔姆一下子定住了。"你爷爷有五十二年的时间可以写一封信，"安塞尔姆说，这话他说出口时还没抬眼看我。

原来我整个下午干的都是这件事。他放下手里正在削的那块木头，用一把黑了四十年的壶泡了茶，斟到壶口。"坐下，"他说，"别学你爷爷那张脸。那张脸不适合你。"

我还是坚持了下来；十五岁以后我再没这么坚持过，那时我算是个温和的小叛逆者——我的反叛是一个难看的发型和一件我不会弹的乐器。那之后还有四个下午，故事一点一点从他身上掉出来，像拔一颗坏牙：慢慢地，几乎不疼，然后一下子全出来了。

那场冬季战役变成了一场漫长而闷声的苦难：远处的炮声，喊出来的命令，穿着外套睡着的少年。为了抵住寒气，他们把身上所有的东西都穿在身上，这就是为什么那个冬天的每一张照片看上去都像家具的照片。入侵的那个冬天是四十年里最糟的一个。盟军从港口往内陆推进，然后像所有军队那样，停在泥里。

安塞尔姆和托拜厄斯连同另外九个人被派去守一家面包房下面的地窖。他们的长官是个十九岁的中尉，带着一把他自己都不会装弹的手枪，四点钟上了街，没有再回来。

到第三天，无线电里的电池死了，水也喝光了，警报早就不代表任何意义。"什么都没剩下，"托拜厄斯说，"只剩等。""可还有一盘棋，"安塞尔姆说，"那就下。"他们等着进攻，头顶上的战斗像天气一样来来回回。"没有别的事可做，"托拜厄斯说，"只剩等。"

他们有一副金属袖珍棋，是那种带磁性的便宜货，缺一个黑马。"我们少一个马，"安塞尔姆说。

这条规矩两个人都守着，守得极有尊严，像两个除了这盘棋再没什么可忠诚的人。一支蜡烛的光池落在他们之间的棋盘上，外面地平线闪着火光，又被烟熏得不透明。"用这个，"托拜厄斯说，把一颗榛子放到棋盘上，"坚果不能被吃。马也不能被吃。就叫它马。"

安塞尔姆莽撞、好斗、不计后果，勇敢得带着年轻人那种漫不经心。他进攻，坚信这一周过完之前他们会换防，说这话时带着一个十九岁男孩的自信，而在十九岁，勇气就是这么回事。托拜厄斯谨慎。他下棋跟做任何事一样：往前算九步，用一个长久等待的人的耐心控制住中路。

第一盘，安塞尔姆三十一步取胜——这是爷爷唯一承认过的败绩。他没法反抗，也没法就这么算了，当场要求再下一盘。事情的核儿就在这里：我爷爷从来就不勇敢。他只是小心；全镇把他的小心叫作勇敢，谁也没因此责怪他，他也就由着他们。

当时发生的事是这样的：在爆炸的力道和顺着楼梯扑下来的那阵火舌里，托拜厄斯被气浪本身抛到了街上，摔在空地上，除了惊吓和右手上一处烧伤，什么也没落下。炸弹落下来的时候，他们下到了第十一步。贝尔米尔的故事就是从这里开始的，真实的那一个也是从这里分岔出去的。

那道疤，全镇五十二年来一直把它当成他冲进去过的证据。安塞尔姆被埋在柜台底下，两条腿都断了。托拜厄斯，十九岁，还清醒，站在了地上，然后跑了——他的直觉带着当时的恐惧清清楚楚地告诉他：那个地窖里已经没有活着的东西。他跑了，把这件事整个吞了下去，它在他肚子里待了五十二年。

她把他送到了盟军的防线，在那里，他被那群那阵子什么都俘获的人俘获了。把他背出来的是玛尔法·桑多，面包房的老板娘，六十一岁，体重比一担柴火还轻。她把他放在一张桌面板上，从地窖的盖板口拖出去，就明晃晃在露天里，在炮火底下，而火焰正吞掉她自己的房子。

在北方十九个月，没东西吃，除了想象那副棋盘，无事可做。

春天他回到家的时候，全镇已经把勋章给了爷爷。

其余的部分我是在首都查明的，团部的档案就在那里，在一间小屋子里，有一扇窗，小得像一枚镜片。那份卷宗里有四份文件，还有一张五十年没人看过的不起眼的复写纸。柜台后的女士给我搬了把椅子，递了支笔："每个打开的盒子都签字，亲爱的。每一个。"

在"事发经过"这个标题底下写着：二等兵安·鲁克被一名平民女性从一座塌了的房子里移出，姓名不详，其本人冒极大风险；二等兵托·克尔被派出；爆炸时其所在位置未确认。第一份是初步报告，由一位当时并不在场的人在袭击三天后起草。

第三份是安塞尔姆亲手填的表格，填在他获释的那天。第二份是四天后打出来的，大体形状跟前一份对得上，实质却完全不同：……由他的战友二等兵托·克尔冒着敌方炮火返回，将其背至安全地带。

在这几份下面躺着玛尔法·桑多的证词，女性的笔迹，另一种颜色的墨水；五十二年来，没有人把它和第一张纸放在一起看过。我花了一个小时才弄明白那意味着什么。在"婚姻状况"一格里他填了"无"。在"母亲婚前姓氏"那一格——根本没人要他填这一格——他填了"克尔"：我祖母的婚前姓氏，写在他自己的纸上。

首都的人想要一个英雄，公众想要一个故事，而一个六十一岁的平民女人被从这两样里一并删掉了；让档案就这么摆着的诱惑，是真实的，我也尝过那个滋味。论职业我不是一个追根问底的人，我是一个按部就班的人；我从文件排列的顺序里推断出了一个决定：那是一个既有军衔、又有自己时间表的人做的。

那是十月。他坐在窗边，窗玻璃被一锅洋葱的蒸汽熏得不透明——那锅洋葱是我用黄油煎的。一个只剩十二周的人，会在下午四点想吃洋葱。说出口的要点是这个：他让一个女人被删掉了。他是个正直的人；正因为正直，一个谎言才能把他吃空。

他朝空中挥了一拳，欢呼起来；前一个星期他问过爷爷，因为做了放疗，现在是不是也算"核"的了，爷爷说是。

到三月，真的只剩六个星期了。炉上的水壶开始吹哨，我把窗打开。烟雾警报器照例响了。"那是培根，"他说，"我知道。别管它，开扇窗就是了。"伊沃坐在地板上，身边是玩具猴子和一只北极熊。

二十年来爷爷没有为谁软过心；他为一个六岁的孩子软了，还把自己盘子里那块烤焦的脆皮给了他。

"玛尔法·桑多，"我说。他闭上眼。他右手上的疤又白又像有弹性，他用拇指抚过它，像别人摸一枚硬币那样。

"你从来没有回去过。"他睁开眼。"没有。"

"那你跑了，"我说。他没吭声。"我跑了。"

"那你为什么由着他们？"他安静了很久。屋后池塘里的青蛙叫了起来，镇上某个地方，一支乐队正用错误的节奏练着进行曲。

"因为我十九岁，我害怕，"他说，"等我回到防线上，有位上校手里拿着一枚勋章，还有一个本该有故事的空缺，而我缺少用真相把它填满的勇气。"

"最要命的是，那太容易了。它是更容易的那一条，之后的每一天都容易，每一年更容易。这就是我的战功，也就是全部了。""你本来可以告诉他们。"

"我本来可以。可内尔会跟着受苦，镇上就没有东西可以纪念了；再说桑多太太那时已经死了，也受不到这份侮辱。"

"我告诉自己，一个谁也不去核实的谎，对大家都是一种安慰，"他说，"这话我对自己说了五十二年。"他有一大堆理由，没有一个借口。

"免得你以为我在求你可怜——我不是，"他说，"我是求你去把他接来。我要当着全镇人的面输掉第二盘。这是个很小的补救，而我想要它，胜过自从向你祖母求婚以来想要过的任何东西。"

他一直在写一封信，写了十一遍；他椅子边的桌上摊着那十一张草稿，用一根橡皮筋扎着。"那枚勋章里已经没有荣誉了，"他说，"这桌子上还有一点。"

最上面压着的就是他一直留着的那件东西：安塞尔姆的圣经，小小的，黑色，对一个信天主教的女人来说是神圣的，她把一张圣卡夹在里面，让她的孩子带着它上了战场，揣在胸口的口袋里。

于是我去把他接来了。我在院子里遇见安塞尔姆·鲁克，他胳膊底下夹着一只琴盒，一句话没说就上了我的车。那本圣经爷爷一次也没有打开过。"有罪的人是不读的，"他说，"他只是珍藏。

那是两种不同的行当，而我干的是低贱的那一门。""我能坐进那辆车，费了好大劲；这辈子的路我也算闯过一段了，"他说，"你要是别再逼我谈这件事，我就感激不尽了。"路上他告诉我，他在索尔特马奇的歌剧合唱团唱了二十二年男低音；他家的规矩是，任何事都一个字不说。

他在门厅里跟爷爷打了个照面：点一下头，握一次手，就一句。"你可真够慢的。"只有一件事他拿捏得极有分寸：他从不打听过内尔。那么多年，一次也没有；从那以后我一直想着这件事。在他们那一代，忠诚是一种没有礼拜的宗教。

他们就着前屋那张橡木桌下棋，门开着，好让全镇的人站在院子里看——公告已经传遍了教区，半个贝尔米尔把小路挤得水泄不通，另外一半在铺子里听收音机转播。"堵车，"爷爷说。

每天下午伊沃在台阶上蹦；他单脚跳，跳个不停。佩洛太太把两只羊羔牵到栅栏边，好像是它们自己要求的；游行委员会那帮激进派也来了，好说歹说才被劝着把那东西留在门外。

安塞尔姆盯着它看了好一会儿，笑了。爷爷朝他皱起眉头。棋盘是爷爷自己摆的：金属的棋子被摩挲成暗淡的光；黑马那个位置，五十二年之后，仍然还是那颗榛子——棕色的，被拇指磨得发亮，几乎不比一颗纽扣大。

他们下起来。棋下得又慢又复杂，我看懂了三分之一。安塞尔姆从第一步就进攻，使的是十九岁那年那股好斗、不计后果的劲头；爷爷让出地盘又夺回来，用一种从一九六九年起就跟这副棋盘打交道的人才有的耐心控制着中路。"它是马，"安塞尔姆说。"

它是坚果，"我爷爷说。"它是马。"这两种声音在栅栏上方撞到一起，本该荒唐，却没有；贝尔米尔的诗人站在人群最边上，口袋里有一首诗，他写了一整个星期，最后没有念出来。

外面，广场上起了一支海军乐队；海军派了三十个人，还有一位指挥，这位指挥这辈子没有指挥过比大教堂更小的场子；铺子里有人把收音机开成了流行音乐。

"放吧，"我说。"还不到时候，"他说。"放吧，托拜厄斯。"下了两个小时，爷爷的局面更好；三个小时，他已经有赢棋的力量了，我看得出他自己也知道。他的手伸向那颗"马"，摸了一下，又收了回来。"我不会把棋下完，"爷爷说，"除非你把我的话听完。

我没有回到那个地窖里。我跑到了街上，我没有回头。""是玛尔法·桑多用一张桌面板把你抬出来的，而这个镇上从来没有一个人叫过她的名字。

我戴着你的勋章戴了五十二年，还由着他们把我的画像放大成三米宽，用一支乐队去纪念一个谎言。"他喘不上气，咳嗽压了上来。

等他又能说话的时候："我不要你的原谅。我要这件事被承认。这是两回事，而我有五十二年的时间在这两者之间做选择。"

那时候巷子里已经没有车了，只有风。屋子里静下来。不知谁的收音机发出一声轻响。广场那边，草坪上的那门大炮在寒气里站着，什么也没干——就是爷爷告诉伊沃的那条睡着的龙，伊沃整整信了三年。

安塞尔姆往椅背上靠回去。他九十岁了，他说："我知道。"

"你知道？""我看见你了，"他说，"我仰面躺在柜台底下，屋顶正在往下塌，墙上有个洞，那里本来是一扇窗；我看见你在街上，我看见你往哪边跑了。"

他捡起那颗"马"，翻过来。"我从一九六九年就知道了。"

"那你为什么从来不说？""因为你回来了，"他说，"你回来的不是那个地窖。你回来的是这张桌子。"

"你拿了四十年的邮差工钱去送信，"我说，"你不懒，不贪，对谁的钱、谁的心都不鲁莽。内尔临走的时候你守着她。那孩子一辈子每一天进门你都迎他，而你只花了九秒钟就肯让步。"

他把那颗棋子放回它的格子里。"一个人可以害怕四分钟，也可以稳当五十二年，窗玻璃里的倒影前后都是同一个人。那不是安慰，那是真相；它编不出一个辉煌的故事，可它有用得多。"

然后他做了那件我会记一辈子的事。他站起来，绕过桌子，把勋章从爷爷胸前摘下来，别到了自己的外套上。

"好了，"他说，"现在它归那个被背出来的人——这才诚实；我再把它交给你孙女，她会把它存进档案该去的地方，附一张条子，写明它该归谁。"

"该归谁？"他从眼镜上方看我，那眼神属于一个已经精通一件难事、再也不打算被要求精通第二件的人。

于是我把它归档了；我是个勤快的女人，账目反正也到期了。它进了首都的县档案馆，附着我亲手写的条子，还有一张复写纸的副本，因为要紧的从来不是那枚勋章本身，而是它底下那句话。"玛尔法·桑多，"他说，"六十一岁。她把我放上一张桌面板，然后她拖。"

相应的条目一共三行：二等兵安塞尔姆·鲁克是由玛尔法·桑多太太从瓦尔登港的一家面包房里背出来的，她什么也没有得到；托拜厄斯·克尔跑了；还有——档案错了五十二年，为的是免得全镇不得不听一句关于一个他们喜欢的人的难听话。关于那个人，我天真了三十一年，被他纠正，对我并没什么坏处。

一位奶品店的绅士，打的是另一场战争，他站起来说，全镇对真相并没有意见，只是更喜欢自己那一版，随即被裁定为发言违规。委员会为此争了六个星期。激进派要留下那条旧横幅，温和派要在池塘边给桑多太太立一块石头，核心那几个人两样都要——从来如此，两样也都得到了。

那句话被当众念了出来，登进了公告，虞美人花没有卖成。有人提议在广场上卖虞美人花。"那不是纪念，"爷爷坐在椅子上，写在一张卡片上，"那是资本主义。"

他们握了手。安塞尔姆拿起那本书——他自己的，五十二年来没读，顺手得像块石头——放进口袋，到了桌边又掏了出来。我爷爷把那盘棋下完了；他没赢，也没输。安塞尔姆说，这就是他的风格：一盘和棋，按他自己的节奏，走他从十九岁起就在算的那一路变化。"啊，"安塞尔姆说。"

她对你很忠诚，"爷爷说。"她守的是真相，"安塞尔姆说，"这是同一种品德，只是更难。"就在那本圣经里，他找到了我爷爷一辈子也没找到的东西：他母亲留下的一张卡片，还有一张姑娘的照片，她的脖子上有一颗珍珠。

这一切里没有寓意，也没有荣耀。

我们把他埋在内尔旁边，在新的寒气里，乐队难得地把进行曲奏对了节奏，伊沃欢呼起来。爷爷死在初霜里，十一月九日，比维尔医生给他的日子少了十一天，地面还没来得及上冻。他承受这一切的样子，属于一个自己给自己定下期限的人。

横幅挂上去，又取下来。青蛙在四月回来了。佩洛太太还养她的羊，栅栏依旧歪着，门口那丛迷迭香已经长过了爷爷挂外套的那个钩子。我用干活来安慰自己。春天我把审计做完了：钱短了四百镑，四个女人把它补上了——向来如此。

如今那个柜子里一件正式的东西也没有了：一副缺了马的棋，一颗坚果，她那颗珠子装在火柴盒里，还有一张爷爷那天早上写的条子。安塞尔姆给伊沃寄来一把吉他，小小的，用同一种木头做的，附了一句保用终身的话；背面有一道划痕，他说那是有一天夜里狐狸钻进了作坊，崩断了一根弦。

我读过一百遍，还会再读一百遍。它只有四行，里面没有辩解，也没有求原谅的意思，它是这样写的：我没有回去。可我回到了这张桌子前，我坐了下来，我把开了头的事做完——这就是我全部的勇气。

伊沃问我曾祖父是什么人的时候，我再也不说英雄了。我说：他是一个回来了、并且坐下的人。
