chapters.title: 天台上的守夜人
chapters.content:
"Gatehouse, keep your eyes on the east wall."

"Why would I keep my eyes on the east wall?"

"Because a man is on it."

A silence came back with the rain filling it, and in that silence a whole shift passed. Marit Sohl had the night at Fenwick Wireless Works, nine years of it, and she had stopped expecting the works to explain itself. "Describe him," she said. "He is over the wall. He is at the pipe."

"What time is it?"

"Two."

"It is two in the morning, and you are counting pipes. Then come down and count him for me."

He had walked eleven years of it. Ovid Thorne was the sole employee of a works shut since 1994, because the insurance company did not believe in alarms. His card, printed in the gatehouse, said walk the yard once, the roof twice; he had walked the yard, and now he stood in the hut door with the town under, watching an east wall for a drunk.

"I can see him. He has sat down. He has lain down."

"Is he dead?"

"No. There is the dirt on his collar. He is only asleep."

"Then leave him. The police can have him at daybreak."

"The police cost money. So do you." She signed off and left the channel empty. He waited, laughed, went back inside and shut the door against the weather. Below, the drunk turned over and went on sleeping. The hut was a pine box the size of a capsule, wedged against the chimney above the old assembly shop.

Inside it was cosy in a way no other place in Ostwick was: a copper kettle, a rose in a cracked pot on the ledge, a wax candle, an analogue radio built in this shop in 1971, and a telescope on a tripod he had made out of the leg of a drill press.

On the door was a brass tag stamped 1994. He had been told repeatedly to take the telescope home and had repeatedly forgotten. The hut kept no lock, because nothing in Ostwick had needed one since the year the lead came off the north wall, and the only thing anybody had ever stolen from the works was that lead, who sold it for very little and spent it quickly.

"A star twinkles. A satellite does not. That is the whole of my method, and it took me eleven years to trust it."

On the third of October in 2015 he was sweeping the desolate area of sky between the chimney and the east ridge, peppered with stars he knew by heart, when a point of light came out of Cygnus and sailed across three fingers of dark in four minutes, steady as a bus.

He logged it the next night and the night after. By the end of those fourteen days he had a consistent arc, a constant period of ninety-six minutes, and a line in the margin of his notebook, in green ink: not a star, not a planet, not weather.

Ovid called it Object 41, because it was the forty-first thing in the sky he could not explain. Thirty-seven of the others had turned out to be balloons. One was a crow. One, memorably, was the red lamp on the mast of a pirate station out on the salt marsh.

Every page of those books carried a diagram at the top, a numerical table beneath, the time logged in universal time to the second, and in the margin the latitude and longitude of the works and the phase of the moon.

He corrected for lunar distance and for the influence of the moon on the brightness, and for the water that condensed on the lens in wet weather; he did not correct for the two mercury lamps in the yard, because he had paid to have them suspended from a wire and pushed to the far wall. One lamp, he liked to say, can pollute forty miles of sky.

Ostwick had been industrialized by the railway and undone by a chip. The works had assembled transistor radios, quartz oscillators and kit sets, and had produced a product for every room in the house; in its most productive year it made six thousand mechanical timers a week for a rival firm in Saltmarsh.

Production ended in the autumn of 1994, on a Friday, at four in the afternoon, when the tram on Fenwick Road stopped carrying four hundred people to that gate twice a day, and the founder, who had prospered enormously and read almost nothing, built the men a gymnasium and a gatehouse shaped like a small temple, and, inside it, a bronze sculpture of a sailor with a telescope under one arm.

Above the door, cut into the stone, was the slogan: FENWICK, WE REACH FURTHER. Ovid had been recruited as an apprentice fitter in 1989, at eighteen, five years before the end; his training was in fitting bearings, none of it astronomy, and silicon finished the works while redundancy finished the town.

A decade later Ostwick had been starving for work so long that nobody remembered it was hungry, and the town reaped nothing at all from the century it had built. "He was a fitter too," Ovid said into the radio. "My father. He joined the little astronomy club the works fostered for its apprentices in 1961, and the club gave him a telescope." "Is that how you came by it?"

"In a tea crate, in 2003. With a note from my sister. Come down off that roof, darling. It is not a career."

Marit clicked her tongue and asked whether his sister worried about him. He said she did, and that his mother, who had died young, used to say he was too imaginative for his own good. "She was probably right," Marit said, and Ovid told her he had found one thing in the sky, and that it was all he had ever wanted.

For about a week in the spring of 2016 Ovid allowed himself to hope that Object 41 was alien. He had read enough to know better and enough to enjoy it. In the end it turned out to be aluminum sheared in a shop two hundred yards away, which he decided was better.

Every two weeks since 2015 he had written to the university. Two hundred and eighty-seven letters, each concise, each with a table enclosed, each submitted by post, because he did not trust the machine in the library, and in the last of them he distilled eleven years onto a single page.

The replies came on a printed circular card with a gracious slogan at the foot, thanking him for his initiative, his interest and his rigour, which was the word that stung, because rigour was exactly what he had and exactly what they assumed he did not.

After two hundred the card stopped being polite and started being indifferent. Nothing discouraged him, which alarmed his sister; what hurt, to his dismay, was not the refusal but the interest they pretended to take. He did not despair. There was never time, because two weeks are only fourteen days, and he continued to write. "Two hundred and eighty-eight?" Marit asked. "Every one of them myself," Ovid said.

"Then somebody is reading them after all."

Letter two hundred and eighty-eight took a quiet courage, the sort nobody awards. Then, in March, the works was purchased by a company whose prospectus was folded around a poster: a soaring glass tower on the water, a rainbow drawn over the marsh, and the words A NEW QUARTER FOR A NEW CENTURY.

The young woman who came to tell him carried a briefcase and an assurance that nothing would happen quickly. She stood in the yard with it against her chest and said the hut must come down, that the roof was undergoing its last survey, that the gatehouse would be kept as a facility for the flats, and that his redundancy, delayed by an administrative disorder, would be processed in May.

"Salary runs to the end of June," she said. "Any questions?"

"Can the yard lamps stay where they are?" She wrote it down, was conscientious and did not once laugh, and Ovid, who had expected worse, admired her for it. He looked at the hoarding on the far wall with disgust, then went back to the sky, which had never once disappointed him on purpose. To lose the hut now would be disastrous.

What saved the gatehouse in the end was a petition: the Ostwick Industrial Heritage Society gathered four thousand names to preserve the little temple with the bronze sailor in it, and the council, after consideration and after an audio recording of its own meeting found its way to the pirate station on the marsh, agreed to suspend demolition for six months.

The settlement was signed in April. Everyone called it a desirable outcome, and Ovid disliked the phrase so much that he wrote it in his book and drew nothing beside it. He wrote: they are keeping the box and knocking down the thing that made it.

A reporter arrived on a Tuesday. Jo Pike was twenty-six and sent for a soft piece about the last watchman. Ovid shaved, which he did perhaps six times a year, and put on the silver tie his sister had given him and he hated.

He sniffed the air before she arrived and told her rain was coming, which she wrote down as local colour and which was, as it happened, wrong. She climbed the eighty-eight steps in shoes that were not for stairs, coughed at the thick petroleum smell of the tar, and peeped through the eyepiece. "What are you looking for?" "Lights that will not do what they are told." "Like what?"

"Like a light that refuses to twinkle to schedule. You would call it patience."

She wrote those down. He could see her already deciding the shape of the paragraph, and he tried to convey the one thing that mattered to him, and failed at it: that a man can be right for eleven years and still be a joke. She murmured something kind and wrote it better. "It is not blackmail," Ovid said, "to tell a newspaper what a university already knows."

Jo laughed. He had meant it as a joke, and it came out as an argument, which is what happens to men who talk to the sky. He did not relish being laughed at, and did not mind it either; he shared his tables with her freely, because data shut in a drawer is data that has decided to die.

The piece ran on page three with a shot of him against the chimney, squinting, holding the telescope as if it were a gun. He had been taught to shoot in the two years he spent at a depot outside Cray, and he had shot badly, and the photograph made him look as if he had it in mind.

Its heading was The Nightwatch Upstairs, and it referred to him twice as the last man in Ostwick with both a job and a telescope; the town thought it charming. Two hundred and eighty-seven letters had brought cards, and one paragraph in a local paper brought a telephone call on Thursday morning.

The caller was not a prominent professor. She was thirty-one, named Lena Vos, and she worked on orbital debris; on the telephone she said she had read the piece and looked up the patch of sky he described, and that she would like to see the books.

"Do you have a digital copy?"

"No." "That is indeed the correct answer," she said, and from that moment he liked her. She arrived with a laptop and a specification sheet she would not explain yet. She sat on the camp bed with the notebooks on her knees and read them under a scrutiny Ovid had not known since 1989, when a foreman half deaf from the drill shop had inspected his first thread.

She readily admitted that she had expected hobbyist nonsense, and did not suppress her surprise when she found none. Every entry was consistent with the one before it, the clock errors were logged, and the number did not move.

On page nine of book forty-one was a drawing of two paths that intersected, and beside it the point at which he had said they would cross. She photographed the pages, drove back to her department, and ran his numbers through a programme that simulated the paths of dead things. "Mr Thorne. Are you sitting down?" "I am always sitting down."

"Object forty-one is Vesper-2." He held the telephone and said nothing, because a telegram in the gatehouse that he had never read was about to be read.

Vesper-2 had gone up in 1980, on the second attempt of the national programme, from a range in the south that belonged to nobody Ovid knew. It was a spacecraft the size of a suitcase, carrying a transistor beacon, solar cells and one experiment, and for forty-one days it communicated with a relay station on Beacon Hill.

Then the beacon failed, the programme ended in 1982, and Vesper-2 was written off; the directory of tracked objects listed it as lost since 1998, in an orbit nobody had updated, at a height nobody had checked in thirty years.

It crossed the equator fifteen times a day. No astronaut had ever gone near it. No spaceship had ever come to fetch it. And Ovid Thorne, from a roof in a town that had stopped making things, had been watching it come down.

"Gravity is winning," Lena said. "The drag is real. Your ninety-six minutes is ninety-one now, and the rise in the decay rate fits re-entry inside a fortnight. If it comes over us it comes directly out of the west."

"Where does it land?" "The odds are on water. Everything is always on water. But the odds are not certainty and the risk is not nothing, and a thing that has been up forty-five years is made of older metal than anyone has simulated for a long time. I have to submit this. If nobody does, that is a disaster."

It was then, with the peaceful hum of the yard in his ear, that Ovid saw the prospect clearly for the first time. Forty-six years after his father had helped build it, Vesper-2 was coming home to Ostwick, and nobody in Ostwick was frightened yet.

He wrote the next morning and requested one thing: access to the works archive, which sat in the basement in a tin chest and had been in disorder since 1994. They gave him a key, and he went down on a daytime morning with the sunshine coming through the rotten floorboards above him and a rat watching him from a pipe.

There were ledgers, a staff list for 1979 with his father's name in it, a crate of contemporary cuttings, and one typed sheet for something called a Passive Reflector Panel. The specification ran three pages of intricate illustration and mechanical detail, its applicable factor being weight, always weight. PANEL TO BE SHEARED FROM 2 MM ALUMINUM. NO POWER SUPPLY REQUIRED. SURFACE TO BE FINISHED TO MIRROR GRADE.

At the foot, in the neat script Ovid had known all his life, in blue ink: for the watchers. Any fool can emit a signal. Only a mirror needs somebody looking. Folded inside the sheet was a telegram, dated the fourteenth of March 1979. PANEL ACCEPTED. CONGRATULATIONS SHOP FOUR. THORNE.

Vesper-2 had transmitted nothing since its forty-first day. It had no battery left, no beacon that worked, no solar cell worth the name. What it had was a flat mirror of sheet metal, cut by his father's hands, turning over and over at the end of its orbit through forty-six years of heat and cold.

Every ninety-one minutes, for four minutes at a time, it caught the sun and reflected it; the flash signified nothing at all except that somebody was looking. Ovid sat on the basement steps and reeled, not from grief but from the delight of it, a delight so profound that he put his head down between his knees. He had spent eleven years believing he had found something.

He had been found by something instead. That was the improvement, and there was no improvement in him that mattered. "It will not communicate any more. It is a mirror. It has been a mirror since 1979. Beware the sunset hour. That is when it will flash." She checked. It was, indeed, the hour he had said, and what followed was eleven days of the loudest quiet Ostwick had known since 1994.

The news was announced carefully, in language designed not to scare anybody, and the national papers announced it in language designed to; a man from a London paper called Ovid a rooftop amateur, and then, when the numbers held, called him the amateur who had been right.

In the old gymnasium the council held a public meeting. Four hundred people sat on the floor, and a man in the row behind Ovid asked whether the town would be emptied.

A prominent astronomer on a screen explained that it would not, that the chance of landfall over the marsh was one in nine, and that a spacecraft the size of a suitcase, made in 1979 of metal, copper and gold, with plated contacts, would mostly burn. "Mostly," said the man behind Ovid.

"Mostly," said the astronomer, who was conscientious and would not lie. The deaf old foreman came, and Ovid's sister came, and the young woman from the yard came and said nothing at all; a poster went up at the bus shelter: COME TO THE ROOF. Kestrel Quay had purchased a roof and inherited a spectacle.

It refused to open it, and then, after a second paper with nine thousand names on it, opened it gracious, with an assurance about insurance that Ovid did not read. He did not sleep. Each evening he sniffed the wind and peeped at the sky from the hut door, and wrote in his newest notebook the sentence he had avoided since March: I would like it to fall here.

He knew it was selfish, and he knew the desirable outcome was the sea. He wrote it anyway, because a man who has been refused indifferently for eleven years is allowed one desperate prayer, and watching had always been a kind of prayer in his family. The prevailing view in Ostwick was that the whole thing was either a disaster or a party.

"Anything on the east yet?"

"Nothing yet," came Marit's voice. "Hold on."

On the ninth evening a black bird landed on the chimney and did not move for an hour. On the tenth the weather broke and the rain came, and the thick cloud did not dissipate until dawn. On the eleventh Lena telephoned her last answer: nine hours, plus or minus two, and a track that intersected the salt marsh three miles away. Three miles, as the bird flies.

They came up the eighty-eight steps from six o'clock: the sister, the foreman, the young woman from the yard, Lena with her laptop, a photographer, four hundred people on the roof and two thousand along the quay.

Someone brought a sticky tin of biscuits. Someone poured tea from a tin urn and spilled most of it, and the mercury lamps stayed on because Ovid had asked, so the pollution nobody had wanted turned out to be the only reason anyone could see the person next to them.

The gatehouse below was lit for the first time since 1994, and looked, from where Ovid stood, like a small and foolish church; at the opposite end of the roof the children from Fenwick Road school were counting down loudly and getting it wrong.

A woman near the top of the steps was crying. When somebody asked her why, she said she did not know, and the people close enough to hear decided that this was the most honest thing anyone in Ostwick had said all week. "Lena, is that it?"

For forty minutes there was no sign of anything at all. Then it came in from the west at twenty-two minutes past nine. It did not shatter. It came down like a slow coin, whirling and spinning, trailing a rainbow of burning oxide, silicon and forty-six-year-old paint, and the spectacle eclipsed every firework Ostwick had ever paid for.

It did not twinkle either. By then it was not a thing in the sky but a streak, then a trail, then a curl of smoke that dissipated in the wind off the water, while two thousand people made a noise like a tide receding. "Well," said his sister in the dim light.

"That was pretty." The roof laughed, and something in Ovid's old self woke up and sat down again. It was a sight, and he watched it until sunrise, because he always did, and the dark retreated over a town that had not moved. It seemed appropriate that a town could not choose between a disaster and a party.

At seven the next morning a boatman from the quay telephoned the gatehouse to say that something had come down in the reed beds. "Flat?" Ovid said. "Flat and bright?"

"It is flat," she said. "One side black, one side still silver. It is lying in the reeds, ribs and all." Ovid took the marsh road, which bends east at the old pump house, with a deer watching him from the far ridge; he found it where the boatman had said, half sunk in mud and rock, small enough to hold in two hands.

The plate was warm. One edge had curled in the fire of coming home. He picked it up and cut his thumb on it, and the young woman from the yard, who had followed because everybody had, produced a bandage from her bag without a word. On the back, under a film of grey oxide, the words were still legible: FENWICK, WE REACH FURTHER.

And below them, in a hand Ovid would have known in the dark, scratched deep into the metal, four words his father had not been able to resist: FOR THE WATCHERS. A. THORNE. Nothing else survived. The rest of Vesper-2 came down as dust, and the dust settled on Ostwick for a week, a questionable sort of congratulation for a town told for thirty years it made nothing worth keeping.

A man asked whether he was disappointed that there was nothing to open. Ovid said he had never wanted a pod. He had wanted the mirror, and a mirror is the only thing you can send up that requires somebody to be awake.

The department reformed the way it answered public letters. Lena put his name on a paper as second author, and the settlement with Kestrel Quay was renegotiated: the gatehouse kept its sculpture, the works hall became a museum, and the hut was preserved on the roof exactly as it stood, wedged against the chimney, with the rose in the cracked pot under a glass case that fogged every August.

Inside, the museum's first exhibit is the panel; its second is book forty-one; its third, in a jar of yellow spirit on a shelf by the door, is a grass snake caught on the marsh in 1962 and kept there by a founder who liked reptiles, the only reptile in Ostwick and the only thing in the building that had never once been asked a question it could answer.

In the summer the place fills with schoolchildren, who are told to look into the mirror and say what they see, and who always, without being told twice, say the same thing: themselves.

The statue in the square has a plaque, and the plaque says the works manufactured radios, timers and one mirror, and that the mirror came back; the tram still runs down Fenwick Road, the rats still have the yard, the petroleum smell in the tar still rises out of the roof on hot afternoons, the pipes still knock, and the roots of the buddleia still work into the east wall.

Ovid Thorne, fifty-five now, who has not shaved since March, still climbs the eighty-eight steps at dusk with a book under his arm. He is not looking for anything now; he has acquainted himself with the sky the way other men acquaint themselves with a street, by going up and down it until the universe stops being alien and becomes a place he knows.

He has discerned, in eleven years, that a cosmic piece of bad luck is mostly a local one with better weather, that numbers which mislead are misleading only until somebody kind looks at them twice, and that a negative answer is not the same as a complicated truth.

Ovid attributes his own error, honestly, to wanting the thing to be wonderful; the one ingredient his books had lacked was somebody else's attention, and it took a paragraph in a newspaper to supply it.

What he cannot undo is this: for eleven years he believed he was watching a thing in the sky. He was being watched back, by a flat, sheared, stubborn mirror that had been up there since 1980, waiting, with the patience of a thing that does not care, for one man on one roof to be awake at the right hour.

You do not conquer the sky by going up into it. You conquer it by staying awake underneath.

Somebody has to be looking when it comes home.
chapters.translation:
"门房，盯着东墙。"

"我凭什么盯着东墙？"

"因为墙上有个人。"

沉默倒回来，里头灌满雨声。就这一小会儿，一整个夜班都过去了。玛里特·索尔上的是芬威克无线电厂的夜班，上了九年，早就不指望这座厂能跟自己讲明白道理。"描述一下他，"她说，"他翻过墙了，他蹲在管子那儿。"

"几点了？"

"两点。"

"两点，你还数管子。那你下来，给我数他。"

十一年都是这么走出来的。奥维德·索恩是芬威克无线电厂唯一的雇员，那厂子从1994年就关了门，因为保险公司不信警报器。门房里印着一张卡片，写着院子走一趟、天台走两趟。院子他是走完的；如今他站在小屋门口，城在他脚下，雨落在他背上，盯着东墙等一个醉汉。

"我看得见他。他坐下了。他又躺下了。"

"人死了吗？"

"没有。他领子上还有泥。他只是睡着了。"

"那就别管他。天亮的时候警察来收人。"

"警察要花钱的。你也一样。"她掐了通话，频道空掉。他等了一会儿，笑了，转身回屋，关门挡风。楼下那醉汉翻个身，接着睡。小屋是个松木盒子，只有太空舱那么大，楔在老装配车间上方的烟囱旁边。

屋里这么舒服，奥斯威克别处没有一处是这样：一只铜壶，窗台裂缝花盆里的一株玫瑰，一小截蜡烛，一台1971年在这厂里装的模拟收音机，还有一架望远镜，架在三脚架上——那三脚架是他拿一台钻床的床腿自己做的。

门上钉着一块黄铜牌，打着1994的字样。人家一遍遍叫他把望远镜搬回家，他一遍遍忘。小屋没加锁，因为从北墙的铅皮被人揭走那年以后，奥斯威克就没什么是需要上锁的；而这厂里唯一被人偷走的东西，就是那点铅皮，是个镇上人人识得的人偷的，卖了个便宜价，花得也快。

"星星会眨眼。卫星不会。我的全套办法就是这个，信它我花了十一年。"

2015年10月3日，他正在烟囱和东边屋脊之间那片荒凉的天区里扫，满眼都是他背熟的星；一点光从天鹅座里挪出来，四分钟横过三指宽的黑，稳得像一辆公共汽车。

第二天夜里他记了它，第三夜又记。到第十四天上，他有了条前后一致的弧、一个恒定不变的九十六分钟，还有本子页边上一行绿墨水字：不是恒星，不是行星，不是天气。

奥维德管它叫41号目标，因为这是他在天上弄不明白的第四十一样。剩下的三十七样最后是气球。一样是乌鸦。其中一样，说来难忘，是盐沼上那家电台桅杆顶端的红灯。

那些本子每页上方都有一张示意图，下面一张数字表，时间按世界时记到秒，页边写着工厂的纬度和经度，还有月相。

他修正月球距离带来的偏差，修正月亮对亮度的影响，也修正雨天凝在镜片上的水气；唯独不修正院子里那两盏水银灯，因为他自己掏钱请人把它们从电线上摘下来、挪到远处的墙上。一盏灯嘛，他爱这么说，就能污染四十英里的天。

奥斯威克是被铁路送进工业化的，又被一枚芯片打回原形。这家厂装配过晶体管收音机、石英振荡器和成套散件，也给每个房间都造过一件东西；出活最多的那一年，一周给索尔特马什的一家对手做六千只机械定时器。

生产在1994年秋天停了，停在一个星期五下午四点。芬威克路上的电车不再一天两趟把四百人送到那个大门口。那创始人发了大财，书却几乎不读，给工人们盖了座体育馆，又盖了一座神庙模样的门房，四根粗柱子，里面立着一尊青铜雕塑：一个水手，腋下夹着望远镜。

门楣上石头刻的标语是：芬威克，我们走得更远。奥维德是1989年招进来的装配学徒，那年十八岁，离关门还有五年。他学的是装轴承，天文一点没学。硅片毁了厂，裁员毁了城。

十年过去，奥斯威克饿工作饿得太久，久到没人记得自己还饿着；而这座城从自己建起来的那个世纪里，一样也没收割到。"他也是个装配工，"奥维德对着无线电说，"我爸。1961年他参加过厂里给学徒办的那个小天文俱乐部，俱乐部给了他一架望远镜。""那你这架是怎么到手的？"

"装在茶叶箱里，2003年。里头有一张我妹妹写的条子：从那个天台上下来吧，亲爱的。那不是一份事业。"

玛里特咂了下嘴，问他妹妹是不是为他操心。他说她操心；他妈死得早，生前总说他太爱想事，没个好。"八成她说得对，"玛里特说。奥维德告诉她，他在天上找见了一样东西，这就是他想要的全部。

2016年春天有那么一个星期，奥维德放任自己去盼41号目标是外星的东西。书他读得够多，知道不该这么盼；也读得够多，知道这么盼很来劲。到头来发现它是铝，是从两百码外一个车间里剪下来的一块板——他想，这样更好。

从2015年起，他每两周给大学写一次信。两百八十七封，封封简短，封封夹一张表，封封走邮局寄，因为他信不过图书馆里那台机器；最后一封里，他把十一年蒸馏成了一页纸。

回信是一张印好的圆形通告卡，底下印着句客气的口号，谢他的主动、他的兴趣，还有他的严谨。"严谨"这个词扎人，因为严谨恰恰是他有的，也恰恰是他们以为他没有的。

两百封之后，那张卡不再客气，开始冷淡。没什么能让他泄气，这把他妹妹吓着了；真正伤人的、也让他沮丧的是，不是那句拒绝，而是他们装出来的那点兴趣。他也不绝望——哪有时间绝望，两周也就十四天——他接着写。"二百八十八封？"玛里特问。"每一封都是我自己去的，"奥维德说。

"那总归有人在读。"

第二百八十八封信花的是一种不声不响的勇气，那种谁也不会发奖的勇气。三月里，厂子被买了。买主是一家公司，它的招股书里夹着一张海报：水边一座高耸的玻璃塔，沼泽上头画着一道彩虹，还有一行字——新世纪的新街区。

来通知他的那个年轻女人拎着一只公文包，还带着一句保证：什么都不会很快发生。她站在院子里，把包抱在胸前，说小屋得拆，天台正在做最后一次测量，门房会留下来当公寓的配套，而他的裁员——被一处行政上的紊乱拖着——五月里办。

"薪水发到六月底，"她说，"有问题吗？"

"院子里的灯能不能留在原处？"她记下来。她认真得要命，一次也没笑；奥维德本来预备听更糟的，因此倒有点服她。他望着远处墙上的广告牌，心里一阵厌恶，然后又回头去看天——天从来没存心让他失望过。如今要没了小屋，那可是一场灾难。

最后救下门房的是一份请愿书：奥斯威克工业遗产协会收了四千个签名，要保住那座供着青铜水手的小神庙。市政委员会斟酌了一通，又在自己那次会议的录音传到沼泽上那家电台之后，答应暂停拆除六个月。

和解协议四月签的。人人都说这是个好结果。奥维德讨厌这个词，讨厌到把它写进本子里，旁边什么也没画。他写的是：他们要留着盒子，却去敲掉造出这个盒子的那个东西。

记者是星期二到的。乔·派克二十六岁，报社派她来写一篇关于最后一位守夜人的软稿。奥维德刮了胡子——一年大概刮六回——又系上妹妹送他的那条银领带，他嫌它。

她到之前他嗅了嗅空气，跟她说要下雨，她把这当成地方风情记下来；而这句，凑巧，是错的。她穿着一双不是爬楼梯的鞋爬完八十八级台阶，被柏油地里那股浓重的石油味呛得咳嗽，凑到目镜上瞥了一眼。"你到底在看什么？""看那些不听话的光。""比如？"

"比如一盏不肯按时眨眼的灯。你会管它叫耐心。"

这些她都记了下来。他看得出来，她已经在想这段该怎么写。他想把要紧的那件事说出来，说了个白搭：一个人可以对上十一年，到头还是个笑话。她小声说了句体贴的话，写得比他说得好。"告诉报社一件大学早就知道的事，"奥维德说，"这不叫敲诈。"

乔笑了。他本来是想说个笑话，结果说成了一句顶撞——跟天说话的人都会这样。被笑他并不享受，可也不介意；他痛痛快快把自己的表都给了她，因为锁在抽屉里的表，是已经打定主意去死的表。

稿子登在第三版，配一张他靠着烟囱眯着眼的照片，手里端着望远镜，像端着一把枪。年轻时他在克雷城外一座仓库待过两年，那两年里学过打枪，也打得很糟；这张照片让他看着像是心里正惦记着这事。

标题是《天台上的守夜人》，文中两回把他称作奥斯威克最后一个既有工作又有望远镜的人。全城觉得这挺可爱。两百八十七封信换来的是通告卡；本地报纸上的一段话，换来了星期四早晨的一个电话。

打电话来的不是什么大教授。她三十一岁，叫莉娜·沃斯，搞轨道残片的。她在电话里说，那篇稿子她读了，他说的那片天她查了，她想看看那些本子。她问有没有电子版。

"有数字版吗？"

"没有。""那确实是正确答案，"她说，就从那一刻起他喜欢她了。她拎着一台笔记本电脑来，还有一张规格单，暂时不肯解释。她坐在行军床上，把本子搁在膝盖上，用一种奥维德自1989年就没领教过的目光把它们翻过去——那一年，一位在钻床车间里被震得半聋的工头检查了他的第一道螺纹。

她坦白说，本来以为会看到一堆爱好者的胡说八道；真没看到的时候，她也没装作不惊喜。每条记录都跟前一条对得上，钟的误差都记着，那个数字一动不动。

第四十一本第九页上画着两条相交的线，旁边标着他说过它们相交的那个点。她把内页拍下来，开车回了自己的系，把他的数字丢进一套模拟死亡物体轨迹的程序里跑。"索恩先生。您坐着吗？""我一直坐着。"

"41号目标是维斯珀二号。"他握着电话没说话，因为门房里那封他从来没拆过的电报，马上就要被拆开了。

维斯珀二号是1980年升空的，国家计划的第二次尝试，发射场在南边一处奥维德谁也不认得的地方。它是一只手提箱大小的航天器，带着一台晶体管信标、几片太阳能电池和一个实验项目；四十一天里，它一直跟信标山上的中继站通信。

后来信标坏了，计划1982年终了，维斯珀二号被当成死物一笔勾销。天体编目里，它从1998年起就挂在失踪上，轨道没人更新过，高度三十年没人查过。

它一天十五次穿过赤道。从来没有宇航员靠近过它。从来没有飞船来接它。而奥维德·索恩，在一座停止造东西的城市的一处天台上，一直在看着它掉下来。

"引力占了上风，"莉娜说，"阻力是真的。您那九十六分钟现在是九十一。衰减在加快，两周之内就会再入。要是冲我们头上过，它会直接从西边来。"

"它落在哪儿？""概率在水上。什么事不在水上。可概率不是定数，风险也不是零；一个在上面挂了四十五年的东西，用的金属比任何人很久以来模拟过的都更老。这份东西我得报上去。没人报，那就是场灾难。"

就在那一刻，耳边是院子里平和的嗡嗡声，奥维德头一回把前景看得分明：父亲帮忙造好它四十六年之后，维斯珀二号要回奥斯威克了，而奥斯威克还没有一个人害怕。

第二天上午他写信，只求一件事：让他进厂里的档案室。那批东西躺在地下室的铁皮箱里，从1994年起就一直乱着。他们给了他一把钥匙。他挑了个白天上午下去，头顶是烂地板缝里漏下来的阳光，一只老鼠蹲在管子上看他。

有账本，有一份1979年的职工名录，上面有他父亲的名字，一箱当年的剪报，还有一张打字的单子，写的是一种叫"被动反射板"的东西。规格单三页，画着细密的插图和机械细节，适用的要素始终是重量，永远是重量。反射板应由2毫米铝板剪切而成。无需供电。表面须加工至镜面级。

页脚，用奥维德一辈子都认得的那种工整笔迹，蓝墨水写着：致守望的人。傻瓜都发得出信号。只有镜子，必须得有人在看着。单子里折着一封电报，日子是1979年3月14日。反射板验收合格。祝贺四号车间。索恩。

维斯珀二号从它的第四十一天起就再没发过任何东西。电池没了，信标不亮了，没有哪块电池还配叫太阳能电池。它有的是一面平的镜子，是他父亲的手剪出来的，在四十六年的冷热里，在自己的轨道尽头翻过来又翻过去。

每九十一分钟，有那么四分钟，它接住太阳，再把它反射出去；那一闪什么也不表示，只表示有人在看着。奥维德坐在地下室的台阶上，一阵发飘——不是难过，是高兴，高兴得他低下头，把脸埋进两膝中间。十一年里他一直以为自己找到了什么。

结果是他被什么东西找到了。这就是那点长进，而在他身上，再没有别的长进要紧。"它不会再发信号了。它是一面镜子。从1979年起它就是一面镜子。当心日落那一阵——那阵子它会闪。"她核了一下。的确就是他说的那个钟点；接下来的十一天，是奥斯威克自1994年以来最响的安静。

消息是小心地放出去的，用一套专门设计来不吓着人的说法；全国性的报纸也放了出去，用的是专门设计来吓人的说法。一家伦敦报纸的记者管奥维德叫天台上的票友，后来数字站住了，又改口叫他那个说对的票友。

老体育馆里，市政委员会开了一场公众会。四百人坐在地板上。奥维德背后一排有个男人问，全城是不是要被清空。

屏幕上一位有名的天文学家解释说不会，说落到沼泽上的机会是九分之一，还说一只手提箱那么大的航天器，1979年做的，由金属、铜和镀金的触点构成，大部分会烧掉。"大部分，"奥维德后面那个男人说。

"大部分，"那位天文学家说。他很认真，不肯撒谎。半聋的老工头来了。奥维德的妹妹来了。院子里那个年轻女人也来了，一句话没说。公交候车亭贴出一张海报：上天台来。红隼码头买走了一座天台，也接手了一场好戏；它先不肯开，后来——在又一份压着九千个签名的请愿之后——很客气地开了，还附一份关于保险的保证，奥维德没看。

他不睡。每天傍晚他嗅一嗅风，从小屋门口偷看一眼天，在最新那本本子上写下那句从三月起他就一直躲着的句子：我希望它落在这儿。

他知道这太自私，他也知道最理想的结局是落进海里。他还是写了，因为一个被冷冰冰地退了十一年的人，是允许许一个不要命的愿的；而在他家里，看天向来就是一种祷告。奥斯威克普遍的看法是：整件事不是灾难就是一场聚会。

"东边有情况了吗？"

"还没有，"是玛里特的声音，"等着。"

第九天傍晚，一只黑鸟落在烟囱上，一个小时没动。第十天天气翻了，雨下来，厚云直到天亮才散。第十一天莉娜打来最后一个答复：九小时，正负两小时，轨迹跟三英里外的盐沼相交——三英里，直线距离。

六点起，人们往上爬那八十八级台阶：妹妹、老工头、院子里那个年轻女人、抱着笔记本电脑的莉娜、一个摄影师，天台上四百号人，码头沿岸两千人。

有人提来一罐黏手的饼干。有人从锡壶里倒茶，洒了大半。水银灯因为奥维德的要求亮着；于是谁也不想要的那点污染，反倒成了唯一能让人看清旁边站着谁的理由。

底下的门房亮了灯，是1994年以来的头一回；从奥维德站的地方看，像一座又小又蠢的教堂。天台另一头，芬威克路小学的孩子们在大声倒数，而且数错了。

一个站在台阶顶附近的女人在哭。有人问她为什么，她说她不知道；离得够近、听得见的人认定，这是整个星期奥斯威克有人说过的最老实的一句话。"莉娜，是那个吗？"

整整四十分钟，一点迹象也没有。九点二十分，它从西边来了。它没碎。它落得像一枚慢慢下沉的硬币，打着旋儿、转着圈，拖着一道由燃烧的氧化物、硅和四十六年前的油漆组成的彩虹。那场面把奥斯威克花钱放过的所有烟花都压了下去。

它也不眨眼了。到那时候它已经不是天上的一样东西，而是一道划痕，接着是条尾巴，接着一缕卷着的烟，在从水面上吹来的风里散掉；两千个人发出的声音，像退潮。"喏，"他妹妹在昏暗里说，

"还挺好看。"整个天台笑了起来，奥维德身上那个旧的自己醒过来，又坐了回去。那是个好场面，他一直看到日出，因为他向来如此；天黑在黎明时退开，退过一座一动没动的城。一座城分不清这是灾难还是聚会，在他看来正合适。

第二天早上七点，码头上一个船夫打电话到门房，说有东西掉进芦苇丛里了。"平的？"奥维德说，"又平又亮？"

"是平的，"她说，"一面黑，另一面还是银的。它躺在芦苇底下，跟泥一样平躺着。"奥维德上了沼泽边的路——那条路在老泵房那儿向东拐——鹿在远处的山脊上看着他。他在船夫说的那个地方找到了它，一半陷在泥和石头里，小得两只手就能捧住。

它是温的。有一边在回家的那把火里卷了起来。他把它捡起来，大拇指划了一道口子；院子里那个年轻女人——人人跟着，她也跟着——二话不说从包里抽出一条绷带。背面隔着一层灰白的锈，字还认得出：芬威克，我们走得更远。

在它底下，是一只奥维德在黑地里也认得出来的手，深深划进金属里的四个字，是他父亲没能忍住不写的：致守望的人。索恩。别的什么都没剩下。维斯珀二号剩下的部分化成了灰，灰在奥斯威克落了一个星期——对一个三十年来一直被人说造不出什么值钱东西的城来说，这是一种挺可疑的祝贺。

有人问他，什么也没剩下可以打开，是不是失望。奥维德说他从来没想要一个返回舱。他要的是那面镜子；镜子是唯一你送上去、却要有人醒着才管用的东西。

那个系改了答复普通人来信的办法。莉娜把他的名字署在论文的第二作者。和红隼码头的和解重新谈过：门房留下了它的雕塑，厂里的礼堂改成了博物馆，小屋原样留在天台上，还是楔在烟囱边，那株玫瑰连着那只裂缝花盆罩在一只玻璃罩里，每年八月都要起雾。

展馆里第一件展品是那块板，第二件是第四十一本本子。第三件在门边架子上一瓶黄颜色的酒精里，是1962年在沼泽上捉到的一条草蛇，由一位喜欢爬行动物的创始人泡在那儿——奥斯威克唯一的爬行动物，也是这栋楼里唯一从来没被问过一个它答得上来问题的东西。

夏天这地方挤满小学生，他们被叫着往镜子里看，说出看见了什么；而他们总是——不用说第二遍——说同一个：他们自己。

广场上那座雕像配了一块铭牌，铭牌上写着：这家厂造过收音机、定时器和一面镜子，而那面镜子回来了。有轨电车还在芬威克路上跑，老鼠还占着院子，柏油里那股石油味在热天下午还从天台上冒出来，管子还在响，醉鱼草的根还一个劲往东墙里钻。

奥维德·索恩，五十五了，从三月起没刮过胡子，黄昏时分还夹着一本本子爬那八十八级台阶。他现在不找什么了。他把天熟了起来，像别的男人熟一条街那样，上上下下走得够多，直到宇宙不再陌生，变成一个他认得的地方。

十一年里他弄明白了一件事：一场宇宙级的倒霉事，多半只是一场天气好些的本地倒霉事；会骗人的数字，只有在某个心软的人多看它两眼之前才算骗人；一个"不行"并不等于一个复杂的真相。

他把自己的错，老老实实归到太想让那东西了不起上；他那几本本子缺的那一味配料，是别人的在意，而补上它的，是报纸上的一整段。

他抹不掉的是这个：十一年里他以为自己在看天上的一样东西。其实是天上的一样东西在看他——一面平的、剪出来的、犟得很的镜子，从1980年起就在那儿，以一件无所谓的东西的耐心，等某个人在某座天台上，在对的时辰醒着。

你不是靠爬上天去征服天空的。你是靠待在下面醒着征服它的。

总得有人看着，它才回得了家。

chapters.title: 婚礼司仪手册
chapters.content:
"The pig is out."

"Two minutes," Ottie said. "Two minutes, Hugo." She walked to the cake table. The doll sat in twelve inches of Polish folk costume, a face painted with the fearful calm of a saint, and a folded edge showed at her seam. Ottie knelt and pushed a finger inside. It went in like paper.

The reporter was Marek, the groom's cousin, nineteen, breeding stock for the county show. "Nobody's crying," he said, pleased. "He is only frightened of the band."

"Write that down," said a bridesmaid, "and I will write it across your forehead." Ottie left them at it and went to find the bride. Blythe Kowalczyk stood by the door with a piece of bread in her hand. "You look like a woman waiting for a verdict," Ottie said. "I am a woman waiting for a verdict."

"Then sit. You are blocking the light." Blythe sat. Her grandmother came in then, and the barn lost its temperature. Ottie Sprague had written her first rule at twenty-four, on the back of a receipt, on the worst morning of her life. It was three words: the MC is never the story.

Since then she had compiled thirty-nine more, one for every disaster a barn, a church or a hired bus had produced, and the book had made her the foremost wedding MC in Thistledown, a town of nine thousand people who married four times on an average June weekend.

Her fame was small and entirely local: a badge on a cord, a card in the barber's window, four hundred and eleven weddings behind her. Thirty-eight of them, by her own count, ended in divorce. She had never written that number down.

She had accustomed herself to other people's bad days: warm fabric, plastic chairs that carried the dirt of whoever sat in them last, a portable speaker with a fault in the left channel, an aisle measured in fear. She associated June with smoke. What she dreaded, the way a housewife dreads a dead oven on the morning of a festival, was a wedding she could not fix.

They had spent forty years pretending the other did not exist, which was less a quarrel than an ideology. Ottie had known it since the introduction. Conventional wisdom said it began with a load of chairs. Conventional wisdom is only what a town agrees to stop asking about. Between them lay an outrage nobody in Thistledown could date.

Zofia Kowalczyk was eighty-four, Polish, and furious about the marriage. She called the Roys feudal and ignorant, and once, in the parish hall, she found a word that made the flower girl giggle for a week. She had raised Blythe after the girl's mother departed for a city nine hours away, with the intense, unsentimental passion of her trade and a low opinion of mercy.

Babcia to the mailman, to the owner of the hardware store, and to half the community. Ottie had escorted a hundred grandmothers to a hundred seats, and she esteemed this one while thinking her impossible. You could not humiliate her; in 1949 she had decided she was the elder thing in any room she entered. "You are the fourth grandmother I have escorted today," Ottie said. "Sit."

"I will sit when my daughter's daughter is married." Babcia removed one glove finger at a time. "You have a book. I have counted its rules."

"Thirty-nine." "Thirty-nine." Babcia gazed at her over the gloves with the keen interest of a philosopher testing a student. "You need forty." "It is not in the book."

"Rule Forty," Babcia said in English, with the customary calm of a grandmother who has waited all week to be difficult. "Then the book is not finished." Babcia sailed toward the cloakroom; the barn cooled by two degrees. Ottie stood in a barn that smelled of dust and smoke and felt the small cold episode of being corrected in her own trade.

It went everywhere in Babcia's hands. On the cake table at every family banquet it sat as a memorial to a wedding nobody in Thistledown had attended. "Ethnic," said the band's pianist, as if it were a diagnosis.

Ottie had seen it displayed at two christenings and one funeral, and at a summer party a cousin of the groom had tried to disguise it as a centrepiece and been glared at until he put it back.

The rehearsal, such as it was, degenerated in nine minutes. Ansel's mother wanted the aisle walked backwards. Blythe's mother wanted it walked twice. "Twice and we finish at midnight," Ottie said. "It is not about the aisle," said the Roys' side. "It is about who goes first."

"It is always about who goes first." Ottie wrote that one down. Ottie wrote nothing else and erased nothing. She found Blythe in the bathroom, which is where brides go. "My grandmother quoted your book at me last night," Blythe said. "Rule Forty. She has read it twice."

"She knows it because she wrote it." "You are very calm." "I am not calm. I am numb. Is that the same?"

"It is preferable to shouting and inferior to sleep." Blythe laughed, and then said the thing Ottie should have written down. "My grandmother knows Rule Forty. She put it in the doll in 1979 and waited forty-five years for somebody to knock it off a table." Ottie filed that, and went for a jog in the rain because she had left her coat at the hall.

She was not lonely; she told herself so with pessimistic cheer. She was busy, and hopeful for about eleven minutes every Thursday in a warm shop that smelled of bread and bacon. She ate a pie off the step at two in the morning. Vern had baked it at six.

The only identity she had ever trusted was the one pinned to her chest. By Tuesday the seating plan was done, and it was, in her own mental arithmetic, a neat compromise. The two families sat in their respective half-circles, facing each other across a buffer of out-of-towners, three male relatives and one tired usher whose only job was to avoid eye contact.

Rule Twelve held: never assume the gender of the person standing up. It was the only rule she had ever had to defend. She cut the order of service to seven minutes, then climbed a ladder into the hayloft to check the flower rigging. A loose iron ring stuck out of the wall. She wrote in the margin: rig left. defect.

Order was her obsession, so she folded the flaw into the machinery. Rule Twenty-Two said: fold the disaster in and it becomes a detail. Every Thursday she went to Tallow's, and Vern Tallow baked bread on Mill Street and had done for twenty-two years, and he had a philosophy he had explained to her eleven times: flour forgives everything.

"Flour forgives everything," he said for the twelfth time. "Everything forgives bread, bad blood and a bad marriage," Ottie said. "That is not in the book."

"No. Neither is everything." He was fifty, gentle, shaped like a barbecue grill, and he had stood at three hundred of her four hundred and eleven weddings, always in the same place: three rows from the back, on the aisle, in a casual jacket that had once been a good jacket. He caught the ring when it dropped and handed it back without a word.

Six years earlier he had slid a saucer across the counter with a note folded underneath it. Ottie had read the note and not answered it, and in six years he had never once irritated her about it. He had encouraged her to take the job, which was either faith or mad, and she had not decided which.

The venue was Harrow, and that was the first thing that ought to have struck her as mysterious. Harrow belonged to Bramwell Quist, seventy-one, who had spent two years quietly buying the infrastructure of every wedding in the county: the place, the hotel on Mill Street, the cellar beneath the old bank, and his proudest acquisition, a prosperous catering firm that fed four towns at once.

He ran it all from a board of ten people, one regulation about parking and one about alcohol before the toast. His plan was revolutionary and, to Ottie, only a lofty way of saying one invoice: consolidate, elevate the place into a destination institution, and put a single house MC inside it.

Three candidates remained. Ottie was one. The second was a casual woman from the county who charged by the hour. The third was Mr. Selkirk, who came from the city in June with an overcoat, a tan and a doctorate in ceremonial leadership from a college Ottie could not find on any map.

His credentials and his affiliation with Halcyon Events, an affluent firm with eleven affiliates, filled two folders. He called weddings domestic transitions and had once MC'd one aboard an airline at thirty thousand feet. "Where," he asked, "is the emotional structure?"

"Stacked in the hall," said Ottie. "Bread is the emotional structure." His ego was the largest object in the room, and she found it as fascinating as a snake on a path. Nothing excited him except the sound of his own script. What disturbed her was his bias. It was not apparent to him either.

He gave her the test on a Tuesday in the yard, where a coil of black cable lay in the mud and the likelihood of rain was high. "One wedding. The Kowalczyk girl. Work from the book, your book, and we will contact you inside a week."

"From whose book?"

"Yours." He said it like a threat. He offered it as a favor. It was not a favor. Ottie thanked him with courtesy, went home to her apartment and opened the familiar red binder. The competitive part of her wanted to win. The rest of her wanted the whole situation finished.

The farms surrounding Harrow held nothing but dull wind, and she would rather have been anywhere else. That was the week of the anonymous order. Forty copies of the book. Cash. No name. Shipped to Harrow, care of Quist.

She watched them travel into dwellings all over the county, into a bowl at a barbecue where somebody used one to prop a table leg, into the glove box of a driver who quoted Rule Nineteen, her favorite, to his lawyer. She never identified the buyer. The identification, when it came, arrived wrapped in cloth and seemingly asleep.

Friday, and the oven died with a bang Ottie heard from the yard. Vern's two colleagues stood over a hundred and twenty biscuits that would never rise, and the oven was likely to blame.

At ten the pit ignited, too close to a stack of crates, and filled the barn with fume so thick the band's triangle player huddled by the door and announced he could not see his instrument. All hell broke loose, tastefully, the way it does in a trade built on politeness.

Ottie accelerated. She connected the portable speaker to a cable running down to the storeroom, put the camera crew outside in the light, and told the beverage driver to use the north gate. Then she sent Marek down for ice, a boy with the enthusiasm of a puppy and the attention span of a mosquito. The ice run became an expedition.

Twenty minutes later she found him asleep on the sack. Ten minutes after that the gift box was gone. It was not a burglar. It was Hugo. Hugo was a pig of considerable importance to the Roys, a show animal with a ribbon, his photograph pinned in the freight office. Ansel's elder brother had brought him because a pig at a wedding seemed patriotic.

He escaped in the smoke, frightened the flower girl into a squeal Ottie would hear for years, trotted through the arch with a spare pair of the groom's pants in his mouth, and knocked the cake table as if it belonged to an enemy. And the doll fell.

She fell in slow motion, off the table onto the boards, and her red skirt split at the seam. Ottie was on her knees before she had decided to be. Inside the skirt, pressed four times into a square, was a pamphlet: cream, brittle, printed in 1978, and untouched by forty-eight years of a family's hatred.

On the cover, in faded green ink, a wreath that evoked a hundred other Thistledown weddings, and two names. The marriage of Zofia Kowalczyk and Bramwell Quist. Harrow. Fourteenth of June, 1978. By any honest estimate, holding what she was holding was impossible.

Four pages: a selection of readings, a note about the pit, one whole animal by courtesy of the groom's family, and a seating plan in the same hand that had drawn a thousand others. The name corresponded exactly. Quist had completed the acquisition of Harrow that spring, in a burst of optimism nobody in the county understood.

On the back, in her own language, and beneath it in English in a smaller and older hand: Rule Forty: the MC is never the story, except once, when the story is yours. Ottie sat on a floor full of smoke with a pig watching her.

She understood, in the way you know the shape of a thing before you can say it, that Blythe had not chosen Harrow for the light or the price. She had chosen it for Quist.

That one building was the only place in the county where Zofia Kowalczyk could not step without walking into 1978, and Blythe had arranged a wedding neither family could refuse. The wedding was real. The coalition of two households was real. Both were quietly and quite deliberately a pretext.

Weddings involve at least one disaster sooner or later. This one involved two old lovers and a clock. She found Blythe in the bathroom. "Your grandmother's wedding was booked here in 1978." Blythe looked at the page. Ottie could not read one emotion on her face. There was a feeling in the barn and it was not joy.

"I found it when I was nine," she said. "I was supposed to be dusting. I pulled the skirt off and there it was. I put it back. Nineteen times."

"You booked this place." "I booked this place." Her mood fluctuated between defiance and terror so fast that Ottie, who had seen every mood a bride can have, felt something very like envy.

"Ansel knows. Ansel helped. We did not know how else to get them into one room. They have not spoken since before I was born, neither will say why, and one of them is eighty-four." She paused.

"Ottie, please. I read your book. I read Rule One. I thought: the one person in this town who never gets into anybody's story is the only person who could get into theirs." It was mad, what the girl asked, and it was the bravest thing Ottie had heard in sixteen years.

"If I do this I lose the job, the fee, the contact, possibly the community." "I know."

"It is the first time in sixteen years I break my own first rule, in front of four hundred people, three of whom want my job and one of whom is a visitor from the city." Blythe said, "Please." Ottie said, "Go and get married. I will handle the rest."

The ceremony was, by every external measure, a wonderful one. The flowers held. The camera worked. The midges arrived at dusk and were forgiven. The county philharmonic, three men and a triangle, played a popular song from 1962, and then, at Blythe's request, something patriotic and unidentifiable, during which Babcia stood and nobody sat.

Ansel made his vows in his new grandmother's language, badly, and Blythe's kin applauded him for it. It was the first time in forty years a Kowalczyk had cheered a Roy, and the applause carried a kinship nobody in the room could account for.

Marek, awake at last and grateful to be, carried the ring on a cushion. The cake, destroyed by a pig, was replaced by a hundred and twenty biscuits and one enormous tart, baked at six that morning by a man from Tallow's, and he said nothing about it. Ottie preferred the tart, though nobody would have known it from her face. Ottie looked at him and thought: I am a coward with a badge.

Then the microphone malfunctioned. It did so at the worst possible moment: the slot for the father-of-the-bride toast, a moment with no father in it and, after a consecutive run of small disasters, no toast either. Blythe's uncle had gone out eleven minutes earlier and not returned. The speaker before him had muttered four phrases about engines and sat down.

Four hundred people looked at Ottie with the expectation of guests promised a feast and given dry cake. The hunger of them. A heat that oppressed the room like a held breath. Smoke overtaking everything. No toast at all. The timetable had held her hostage for sixteen years, and she had thanked it for the habit.

Rule Thirty-Nine said: shorten the silence. Rule One said: the MC is never the story. She took the microphone, found it dead, and raised her voice instead, the extreme remedy, the one the book kept for last, which she had never needed in four hundred and eleven weddings. "Ladies and gentlemen," Ottie said. "For goodness' sake, I am going to break a rule."

The silence was instantaneous. Even the pig listened. "Twenty-two years ago I stood at the front of a church in a dress my mother selected, waiting for somebody who did not come, and the only thing that saved me was four hundred people too polite to say anything."

"I wrote Rule One of a little book that morning. The MC is never the story. It has kept me safe. It has also kept me useless, and I have sold it to this town for four dollars a copy ever since."

"Somebody bought forty copies anonymously this week and had them delivered here. I have spent seven days working out who." She held the page up like an exhibit. "I know now. It was hidden in that skirt."

She read the order of service, the note about the meat and the two lines on the back. Then, because Rule Forty, which she had not written, told her to, she handed the microphone to an eighty-four-year-old woman in one glove and a black coat who had not spoken to Quist since 1978.

Babcia did not hesitate. She walked to the middle of the floor and took the microphone in both hands as if it were a weapon she had been trained on. "I came at eleven." The room went so quiet the rafters creaked.

"I came at eleven because the invitation said eleven. I sat in the cart until the sun moved across the yard. Then I went home, and I did not write, and for forty years I told this town that Bramwell Quist left me standing in his own building. That was not true. He was not there. I was early." She paused, and the pause was horrible and elegant at once.

"The ceremony was at two. I have known that since 1979. My English was bad. I read eleven where it said two. I was too proud to check, and by the time I understood I had built a coalition against him, a business against him, a life against him, and it was satisfying, and there was no way back into it."

She looked at Quist, who had gone very still beside the beverage table. "So. Here is the goodby I never said. It took forty years. I am sorry for the length of it." Quist put down his drink. "Zofia."

"Bram." "I kept the receipt," he said. "One whole animal, from your father's farm. It is down in the cellar."

"Of course it is," said Babcia. The banquet, four hundred guests, three candidates and a man from the city with a tan, stood and applauded for four minutes and eleven seconds, which Marek timed. Ottie entered it in the book later as Rule Forty-One: when the room stands up, let it stand.

What followed took eleven days and rearranged the county. The two families became an alliance in fact: bread and haulage, incorporated in September. Babcia and Quist were photographed by the camera crew, who were paid to shoot a wedding, sitting on the bench in the yard, eating bread and not speaking.

Babcia forgave nobody in words. The following Sunday she began to save him a seat, to indulge him in the argument about which loaf was superior, and to correspond with him by memo, which was how they had conducted their courtship in 1977. Guests at the next wedding mingled with guests from the last.

Selkirk left on the Monday, with his overcoat, his papers and his one credential that mattered. "Very moving," he said softly. "Of course, you have rather compromised your neutrality."

"Yes," said Ottie. "I hope so." He gave her a look that could murder. She had expected it, and she was astonished to find it pathetic. On the Wednesday Quist offered her the house job in front of the board: a contract, a salary, a membership in the new company, and a clause requiring her to adopt his regulations whole.

Ottie read it twice, in front of her prospective employers, who had expected her to cry. Then she did the thing she had learned from two lines written in 1978, which was to negotiate. She asked for Harrow on the first Saturday of every month. She asked for a seat at that table and the right to simplify anything she was handed.

And she asked, because she had once stood at the front of a room and waited, for a clause saying that no MC would ever be required to speak at a wedding she did not believe in. Quist asked why. "Because of Rule Forty."

Quist had paid for a whole animal in 1978 and kept the receipt in a cellar for forty-eight years. "Seems reasonable," he said. He signed. Somebody popped a cork. Hugo, by then a hero, ran once more through the arch, and four hundred people cheered him.

Vern found her afterwards by the bin, sweeping crumbs with the dignity of a woman performing housework in a cathedral. "You broke the rule." "I broke the rule." "Extra," he said. "Twenty-two years, one runaway and a dead kitchen."

"Twenty-two years, one pig, one dead kitchen, one burglar who was not a burglar, and an eighty-four-year-old woman with a pamphlet inside a doll." She looked at him. "You were three rows from the back the whole time."

"I am always three rows from the back."

Ottie looked at the bin and laughed. "That is the joke, is it not. Sixteen years and I never once looked behind me." "I know," she said gently. Vern nodded, as at a diagnosis, and did a thing he had not done in six years: he took a saucer from his pocket, folded a note and set it on the bin between them.

It said what it had said six years before, because a decent man does not edit a good sentence. You keep everyone else's story. When do you keep your own? Ottie read it, and the numbness that had held her since Thursday dissolved. "Thursday," she said. "Yours. I will bring the pie."

She kept the mystery unsolved for exactly as long as it took to walk back in, where Babcia held court with the patience of a monument. "You bought them."

"I bought forty. One for every year. I have read your little book for twelve months. It is helpful." She looked at Ottie with the cold, unsentimental eye of a woman appraising a loaf. "Thirty-nine rules. You need forty."

"Did you know it was in there?"

"Of course I knew it was in there. I put it there in 1979, and I waited forty-five years for somebody to knock that thing off a table." She waved away Ottie's gratitude like smoke. "It is not kindness. I am a selfish old woman and I wanted my forty years back."

Ottie decided then that she was the best philosopher of the seating chart in eleven counties, and she told her so. Babcia said, "Sit down. There is cake."

The fortieth rule went into the second edition that winter, on the last page, under two lines of Babcia's own tongue that Ottie could not read and had copied carefully from the back of that cream page. Babcia translated it for her three times, differently every time, and the last and shortest version was this:

Two people who love each other are allowed to be the story. Once. Thus the rest of it can be anybody's. Ottie still works the room, though she has slowed down. She charges more now and sells the book for six dollars, which Babcia called a scandal.

On the first Saturday of every month she opens Harrow to whoever wants it, and since that June she has MC'd sixty-one weddings and one renewal of vows, at which the pig was a guest of honour and the gift was a barbecue receipt in a frame.

She keeps, on the page after Rule Forty, a blank line, because she has learned from a boy who slept on a sack of ice and from a burglar that turned out to be an animal, that the last rule of any wedding is the one you have not written yet, and that it is always, in the end, about letting go.

Her memory for names is still the best in the county, which is the only qualification that has ever mattered, and the badge on the cord still says MC, though she has learned to read it differently: mostly coward, occasionally brave.

Rule Forty: the MC is never the story, except once, when the story is yours.

“猪跑了。”

“两分钟。”奥蒂说，“两分钟，雨果。”她走到蛋糕桌前。那个玩偶穿一身十二英寸高的波兰民族服饰，脸上一副圣徒才有的、令人敬畏的平静，裙摆的接缝处露出一道折边。奥蒂跪下去，把一根手指伸了进去。像纸一样，一下就进去了。

报信的是马雷克，新郎的表弟，十九岁，替县里的赛展养牲口。“没人哭。”他得意地说，“它只是怕乐队。”

“你记下来。”一个伴娘说，“我就把它写在你脑门上。”奥蒂不再理他们，转去找新娘。布莱思·科瓦尔奇克站在门口，手里捏着一块面包。“你看着像个在等判决的女人。”奥蒂说。“我就是一个在等判决的女人。”

“那就坐吧。你挡着光了。”布莱思坐下。她外婆紧接着进来了，谷仓里的温度当场降下去。奥蒂·斯普拉格二十四岁那年写下她的第一条守则，写在一张收据的背面，写在她一生中最糟的那个早晨。就三个词：司仪从不成为故事。

从那以后她又整理了三十九条，谷仓、教堂或者租来的大巴车造出来的每一种灾难都配一条；也正因为这本书，她成了蓟镇首屈一指的婚礼司仪。蓟镇住着九千人，一个平常的六月周末要办四场婚礼。

她的名声不大，而且完全是地方性的：一枚别在挂绳上的胸牌，一张插在理发店玻璃窗里的卡片，身后是四百一十一场婚礼。按她自己数，其中三十八场最后离了婚。这个数字她从来没写下来过。

她早就习惯了别人糟糕的日子：暖烘烘的衣料，沾着上一个坐过的人留下的泥土的塑料椅，左声道有毛病的手提音箱，用恐惧来丈量的过道。六月在她心里就等于烟味。她怕的是——像一个家庭主妇在节日早晨怕一只坏掉的烤箱那样——一场她修不好的婚礼。

两家人花了四十年假装对方不存在；这与其说是争吵，不如说是一种意识形态。奥蒂从他们被介绍认识那天起就知道这事。常识说，这一切始于一车椅子。所谓常识，不过是一个镇子全体同意不再追问的东西。两家之间横着一场愤慨，蓟镇没一个人能说出它始于哪一年。

佐菲娅·科瓦尔奇克八十四岁，波兰人，对这门婚事怒不可遏。她骂罗伊家封建、无知；有一次在教区礼堂里，她翻出一个词，让撒花的小姑娘咯咯笑了一整个星期。布莱思的母亲去了九小时车程外的城市，是她把孩子带大的，靠的是她这门活儿里那种强烈、不动感情的劲头，以及对仁慈的低估。

邮差管她叫巴布夏，五金店老板也这么叫，半个社区都这么叫。奥蒂护送过一百位祖母坐上一百张椅子；她敬重这一位，同时觉得她不可理喻。你羞辱不了这种人。一九四九年她就想明白了：凡是她走进的屋子，她就是最年长的那个。“你今天已经是第四个我送座的祖母了。”奥蒂说，“坐吧。”

“我女儿的女儿结婚那天我就坐。”巴布夏一只一只地脱下手套，“你有本书。我把里头的守则都数过了。”

“三十九条。”“三十九条。”巴布夏从手套上方凝视着她，像一个哲学家在考学生那样带着锐利的兴趣，“你需要四十。”“书里没有。”

“第四十条。”巴布夏用英语说，带着一位等了一整周、专挑麻烦的老太太那种惯常的平静。“那这本书就没写完。”巴布夏朝衣帽间扬长而去，谷仓当场凉了两度。奥蒂站在一间满是尘土和烟味的谷仓里，尝到了在自己这行里被人纠正的小小插曲。

它到哪儿都跟在巴布夏手里。每一次家族宴席，它就端端正正坐在蛋糕桌上，像一座纪念碑，纪念一场蓟镇没一个人出席过的婚礼。“民族风。”乐队的钢琴师说，那口气像在下诊断。

奥蒂见过它被摆出来，两次洗礼、一场葬礼上都有；有一年夏天聚会，新郎的一个表弟想把它伪装成餐桌中央的摆饰，被人瞪到只好又放了回去。

彩排——如果那也算彩排的话——九分钟就崩了。安塞尔的妈妈要过道倒着走。布莱思的妈妈要过道走两遍。“走两遍我们就干到半夜。”奥蒂说。“这不关过道的事。”罗伊家那边说，“这关谁先走的事。”

“永远是关谁先走的事。”奥蒂把这句记了下来。她别的什么也没记，也什么都没擦掉。她找到布莱思——新娘都往洗手间去。“我祖母昨天晚上拿你的书去引我。”布莱思说，“第四十条。她读过两遍。”

“她知道，因为她自己写的。”“你很平静。”“我不平静。我麻了。这是一回事吗？”

“这比大吼大叫可取，比睡一觉差。”布莱思笑了，接着说出一件奥蒂本该记下来却没记的事。“我祖母知道第四十条。她一九七九年把它塞进那个玩偶里，等了四十五年，等有人把那东西从桌上撞下来。”奥蒂把这话收好，然后冒雨去跑了一圈，因为她把外套落在大厅里了。

她不孤单；她用一种悲观的轻快这样告诉自己。她很忙；她每个星期四会在一家闻着面包和培根香味的暖店铺里，有大约十一分钟是抱有希望的。凌晨两点，她就着台阶吃了一块派。弗恩六点烤的。

她唯一信得过的身份，是别在胸口那一枚。到星期二，座位表定稿了，按她自己的心算，是一份干净妥帖的折中。两家人各占一个半圆，隔着一圈外乡人互相对望：三个男亲戚，还有一位累坏了的引座员，后者的唯一工作就是避免跟人眼睛对眼睛。

第十二条是这么写的：永远别假定站起来那个人的性别。这是她唯一一条不得不辩护的守则。她把仪式流程砍到七分钟，又爬梯子上了草料棚，检查花饰的吊挂。墙上有只松动的铁环。她在页边写下：左侧索具。缺陷。

秩序是她的执念，于是她把这个瑕疵折进安排里。第二十二条说：把灾难折进去，它就成了个细节。每个星期四她都去塔洛家；弗恩·塔洛在磨坊街烤面包，烤了二十二年，他有一套哲理，讲过十一遍：面粉宽恕一切。

“面粉宽恕一切。”这是第十二遍了。“一切都可宽恕：面包、烂掉的交情、一段该散的婚姻。”奥蒂说。“书里没写这条。”

“没写。‘一切’这个词也没写。”他五十岁，脾气温和，身材像只烧烤架；她那四百一十一场婚礼，他站过三百场，永远站在同一个位置：倒数第三排，靠过道，穿一件随便的外套，那外套从前是件好外套。戒指掉地上的时候，是他捡起来，一言不发地递回去。

六年前，是他把一只茶碟推过柜台，碟子底下压着一张折好的字条。奥蒂读了，没回答；六年里他一次都没为这事烦过她。是他劝她接下这份活，这要么是信，要么是疯，她一直没分清楚是哪一种。

场地是哈罗，这是第一件本该让她觉得蹊跷的事。哈罗归布拉姆韦尔·奎斯特所有，七十一岁，两年里不声不响买下了本县每一场婚礼的底座：地方本身，磨坊街上的旅馆，老银行底下的酒窖，还有他最得意的一笔收购——一家同时供四个镇子吃饭的兴旺餐饮公司。

他靠一个十人的董事会管着这一切，一条关于停车的规矩，一条关于祝酒前不准喝酒的规矩。他的计划很革命性；在奥蒂听来，那只是“一个人，一张发票”的堂皇说法：整合，把这儿升成一座目的地级的机构，里面只放一个驻场司仪。

候选人还剩三个，奥蒂是其中一个。第二个是本县一个按小时收费的散漫女人。第三个是塞尔扣克先生，他从城里来，六月里穿着大衣、晒着一身古铜色，还带着一张奥蒂在任何地图上都找不到的学院颁发的“仪式领导力”博士学位。

他的资历，还有他和哈尔西恩会展——城里一家有十一家分部的阔气公司——的从属关系，装满了两个文件夹。他把婚礼叫做“家庭过渡”，在三万英尺高空的客机上主持过一场。“情绪结构在哪儿？”他问。

“堆在大厅里。”奥蒂说，“面包就是情绪结构。”他的自我是这间屋子里最大的东西；她觉得它像小路上的一条蛇，挺迷人。除了他自己那套台词的声音，没有什么能叫他兴奋。让她别扭的是他的偏见——而连他自己都看不出来。

星期二他在院子里给她出了道题，一卷黑电缆躺在泥地上，下雨的可能性很高。“一场婚礼。科瓦尔奇克家的姑娘。照书办——你的书——一周之内我们联系你。”

“照谁的书？”

“你的。”他说这话像在放狠话。他说是人情，可这不是人情。奥蒂客客气气地道谢，回了家进了公寓，摊开那本熟悉的红皮活页夹。她身上好胜的那部分想赢。其余那部分只想让这一摊赶紧了结。

哈罗四周的农场除了无聊的风什么也没有，她宁可待在别的地方。那就是那笔匿名订单的那个星期。四十本书。现金。不留名。寄到哈罗，由奎斯特转交。

她看着它们流进全县各处的住家，流进一场烧烤上垫桌腿的碗，流进一个司机的手套箱里——那位司机向律师引用了第十九条，那正是她最喜欢的一条。她始终没查出买主是谁。而那个答案终于来的时候，是裹在一块布里送来的，看上去像是睡着了。

星期五，烤箱砰的一声坏了，奥蒂在院子里就听见了。弗恩的两个同事守着一百二十块永远发不起来的饼干，罪魁祸首很可能是那台烤箱。

十点，烟火坑着了，离一堆板条箱太近，浓烟灌满谷仓，浓到乐队里那位三角铁手蹲在门边，宣布他看不见自己的乐器。整个场面失控了，可失控得很体面，就像一门建立在礼貌上的行当里必然发生的那样。

奥蒂提速。她把便携音箱接上通往储藏室的电缆，把摄像组挪到外面的光里，让送饮料的司机从北门走。然后她派马雷克下去取冰——那男孩有小狗一样的热情，也有蚊子一样的注意力时长。这一趟取冰变成了远征。

二十分钟后她发现他睡在冰袋上。再过十分钟，礼品盒不见了。不是贼。是雨果。雨果对罗伊家是头相当重要的猪，得过绶带的展示用牲畜，照片钉在货运办公室里。安塞尔的哥哥把它带来，因为婚礼上有头猪是爱国的。

它在烟里跑出来，把撒花的小姑娘吓出一声奥蒂很多年后还会听见的尖叫；它小跑着穿过拱门，嘴里叼着新郎一条备用长裤；它撞蛋糕桌，撞得像那是敌人的东西。接着，玩偶掉了下来。

它像这类东西一贯的那样，以慢动作掉了下来，从桌子上摔到地板，红裙子在接缝处裂开。奥蒂还没决定要不要跪下，人已经跪在地上。裙子里面，折成四折压成一个方块的东西，是一份小册子：米黄色，脆硬，一九七八年印的，四十八年的一家人仇恨没碰过它。

封面上，用褪了色的绿墨水，画着一个花环，那种花环会唤起一百场别的蓟镇婚礼；还有两个名字：佐菲娅·科瓦尔奇克与布拉姆韦尔·奎斯特的婚礼。哈罗。一九七八年六月十四日。按任何诚实的估计，她手里正拿着的东西都是不可能的。

四页纸：一组选读经文，一条关于烟火坑的说明——一整头牲口，由新郎家好意提供——还有一份座位表，出自那只画过上千份座位表的手。名字完全对得上。奎斯特那年春天完成了对哈罗的收购，凭的是一股全县都没弄懂的乐观。

背面，用她自己的语言写着，下面又用英语写了一遍，字更小，笔更老：第四十条：司仪从不成为故事，除非有一次，当故事是你自己的。奥蒂坐在满地浓烟里，一头猪看着她。

她明白了，就在那种你还说不出一件事的形状、却已经知道它是什么的时刻：布莱思挑哈罗，不是为了光，也不是为了价。她挑的是奎斯特。

全县只有这一座房子，是佐菲娅·科瓦尔奇克跨进门就必然踏进一九七八年的地方；布莱思安排了一场两家都拒绝不了的婚礼。这场婚礼是真的。两家人的联盟是真的。而这两样，安安静静地，又明目张胆地，都是借口。

婚礼迟早至少卷进一场灾难。这一场卷进了两个老恋人和一只钟。她在洗手间找到了布莱思。“你祖母的婚礼，一九七八年就订在这儿。”布莱思看着那一页。奥蒂在她脸上看不出一丝情绪。谷仓里有一种说不清的感觉，那不是高兴。

“我九岁那年找到它的。”她说，“那会儿本该在掸灰。我把裙子一掀，它就在那儿。我又放了回去。十九次。”

“这地方是你订的。”“这地方是我订的。”她的情绪在顶撞和惊恐之间乱晃，快得让奥蒂——她见过新娘能有的每一种情绪——竟生出几分嫉妒。

“安塞尔知道，安塞尔帮了忙。我们不知道还有别的什么法子把他们弄进一个屋子。他们在我出生之前就再没说过话，谁也不肯说为什么，其中一个已经八十四岁了。”她停了停。

“奥蒂，求你。我读过你的书。我读过第一条。我当时想：这个镇上唯一从不钻进别人故事的人，是唯一钻得进他们故事的人。”这姑娘要的事很疯，而这是奥蒂十六年来听过的最勇敢的话。

“我要是做，就丢掉这份活、这笔钱、这条关系，很可能还有整个社区。”“我知道。”

“我要是做，这就是十六年来我头一回在四百个人面前破我自己的第一条规矩，那四百人里有三个想要我的工作，还有一个是从城里来的客人。”布莱思说：“求你了。”奥蒂说：“去结婚吧。剩下的我来收拾。”

单看外围，这场典礼好极了。花撑住了。摄影机在转。蠓虫在黄昏时来了，然后被原谅了。本县爱乐团——三个人加一副三角铁——先奏了一首一九六二年的流行曲，又应布莱思的请求奏了一首爱国的、谁也认不出来的曲子；吹到一半，巴布夏站了起来，没有一个人坐下。

安塞尔用他新祖母的语言念誓词，念得很糟，布莱思的亲戚们却为此给他鼓掌。这是四十年来头一回有科瓦尔奇克家的人为罗伊家的人叫好，那阵掌声里有一种谁也解释不清的亲近。

马雷克终于醒了，还庆幸自己醒了，用一只软垫托着戒指。被猪毁掉的蛋糕，换成了一百二十块饼干和一只巨大的果挞，是那天清早六点由塔洛家的人烤出来的，他一个字也没提。奥蒂更中意那只挞，尽管谁也看不出来。奥蒂看着他，心想：我是一个戴着胸牌的懦夫。

接着麦克风出故障了。坏在最糟的那一刻：本来排给新娘父亲祝酒的那一档——一个根本没有父亲的时刻，而且在一连串小灾难之后，连祝酒也没了。布莱思的舅舅十一分钟前出去了，没回来。他前头那个发言的人含含糊糊说了四句关于发动机的话就坐下了。

四百个人看着奥蒂，那眼神是被许诺了一场大餐、端到手里的却是干蛋糕的人的眼神。他们的饥饿。一股像屏住的呼吸一样压着这屋子的热气。烟味盖住了一切。一点祝酒都没有。那张时间表拿她当人质当了十六年，而她一直谢它成了习惯。

第三十九条说：缩短沉默。第一条说：司仪从不成为故事。她拿起麦克风，发现它是死的，于是改用嗓子——极端的补救，那本书留到最后才用的那一招，四百一十一场婚礼里她一次也没用过。“女士们，先生们，”奥蒂说，“看在老天的分上，我要破一条规矩了。”

沉默是瞬间的。连那头猪都在听。“二十二年前，我穿着我母亲挑的裙子，站在一座教堂的前排，等一个没有来的人；唯一救了我的，是四百个太有礼貌、什么也没说的人。”

“那天早上我写了一本小书的第一条。司仪从不成为故事。它保过我的命，也让我没了用；从那以后，我一直拿四美元一本的价格把它卖给这个镇子。”

“这星期有人匿名买了四十本，让人送到这儿。我花了七天想知道是谁。”她把那一页举起来，像举起一件证物。“现在我知道了。它就藏在那条裙子里。”

她读了仪式流程、那条关于肉的说明，还有背面那两行字。然后——因为那条她压根没写过的第四十条叫她这么做——她把麦克风递给一位八十四岁的老太太：一只手套，一件黑外套，从一九七八年起就没跟奎斯特说过话。

巴布夏没有犹豫。她走到场地中央，两只手捧起麦克风，像捧一件她受过训练要用的武器。“我是十一点来的。”屋里静得连椽子都在响。

“我是十一点来的，因为请柬上写的就是十一点。我在马车里坐到太阳挪过院子。然后我回了家，我没有写信，四十年来我告诉这个镇子，说布拉姆韦尔·奎斯特让我站在他自己的屋子里空等。那不是真的。他不在。是我来早了。”她停了一下，那个停顿既吓人又好看。

“典礼是两点。我从一九七九年起就知道。我英语不好。两点我看成十一点。我太骄傲，不肯去核对；等我弄明白，我已经搭起了一个针对他的联盟、一份针对他的生意、一种针对他的生活，而那很痛快，也再也回不去了。”

她看着奎斯特，他在饮料桌旁一动不动。“那么。这就是我从来没说出口的再见。它用了四十年。它的长度，我抱歉。”奎斯特放下杯子。“佐菲娅。”

“布拉姆。”“那张收据我留着。”他说，“一整头牲口，你父亲农场的。就在下面的酒窖里。”

“那当然了。”巴布夏说。这场宴席——四百位客人、三位候选人、一个晒着一身古铜色的城里人——全体起立，鼓掌四分十一秒，时间是马雷克掐的。奥蒂后来把它写进书里，成了第四十一条：全场站起来的时候，就让它站着。

接下来的十一天改动了整个县。两家人实实在在地成了同盟：面包和运输，九月注册成了一家。巴布夏和奎斯特被摄像组拍了——他们是拿钱来拍婚礼的——坐在院子里的长凳上，吃着面包，谁也不说话。

巴布夏没有用一句话宽恕谁。紧接着那个星期天，她开始给他留一个位子，由着他争论哪条面包更好，还用便签和他通信——一九七七年他们谈恋爱时就是这么来的。下一场婚礼的客人和上一场婚礼的客人混到了一起。

塞尔扣克星期一走了，带着他的大衣、他的文件，他那唯一管用的一张证书。“非常动人。”他轻声说，“当然，你已经相当损害了你的中立性。”

“是。”奥蒂说，“我正是这么希望的。”他给了她一个能杀人的眼神。她早料到了，而她诧异地发现那眼神有多可怜。星期三，奎斯特当着董事会把驻场的位置许给她：一份合同、一份薪水、新公司的会员身份，还有一条要求她全盘照搬他那些规章的条款。

奥蒂当着未来的雇主把合同读了两遍——他们本来以为她会哭。然后她做了一件她从一九七八年那两行字里学到的事：谈判。她要求每月第一个星期六归她用哈罗。她要求在那张桌子上有个位子，还有权把塞到她手里的东西简化一通。

她还要求——因为她曾经站在一间屋子的前排等过——加一条：任何司仪都不必在自己不信的婚礼上开口。奎斯特问为什么。“因为第四十条。”

奎斯特一九七八年为一整头牲口付过钱，把那张收据在地窖里存了四十八年。“听着合理。”他说。他签了字。有人砰地拔了木塞。雨果——这时候它已经是英雄了——又跑过一次拱门，四百个人为它欢呼。

事后弗恩在垃圾桶边找到她，她正在扫地上的碎屑，那架势像一个在大教堂里做家务的人。“你破规矩了。”“我破规矩了。”“还多一样，”他说，“二十二年，一个逃跑的，一间死掉的厨房。”

“二十二年，一头猪，一间死掉的厨房，一个不是贼的贼，还有一个把小册子塞在玩偶里的八十四岁老太太。”她看着他。“你全程都站在倒数第三排。”

“我永远在倒数第三排。”

奥蒂看着垃圾桶笑了。“这才是笑话，不是吗。十六年，我一次也没回过头。”“我知道，”她轻声说。弗恩像听诊断一样点了点头，接着做了一件他六年没做过的事：从口袋里掏出一只茶碟，折好一张字条，放在两人中间的垃圾桶上。

字条上写的和六年前一模一样，因为一个正派人不会去改一句好句子。你替所有人保管他们的故事。你什么时候保管你自己的？奥蒂读了它，那股从星期四起一直攥着她的麻木松开了。“星期四，”她说，“在你那儿。我带派来。”

她把这个谜留到刚好走回大厅那么久——屋子里巴布夏正以一座纪念碑的耐心端坐着等人来朝贺。“是您买的。”

“我买了四十本。一年一本。你那本小书我读了十二个月。它有用。”她用那种打量一条面包的、冷面无情的眼神看着奥蒂。“三十九条守则。你需要四十条。”

“您知道它在里面吗？”

“我当然知道它在里面。我一九七九年放进去的，我等了四十五年，等有人把那东西从桌上撞下来。”她把奥蒂的感激像烟一样挥开。“这不是好心。我是个自私的老太婆，我想把我那四十年要回来。”

奥蒂当下断定，她是十一个县里研究座位表最厉害的哲学家，并且把这话说了。巴布夏说：“坐下。有蛋糕。”

第四十条那年冬天进了第二版，印在最后一页，压在两行巴布夏自己语言下面——那两行奥蒂一个字也不认得，是从那张米黄色纸的背面一个字一个字描下来的。巴布夏给她翻译了三遍，一遍一个样，最后最短的那一版是这样的：

两个相爱的人是允许成为故事的。一次。于是剩下的部分，就可以属于任何人。奥蒂还在主持场面，只是慢了下来。她现在收得更多，书卖六美元一本，巴布夏管这叫丑闻。

每月第一个星期六，她对任何想用哈罗的人开放；自那个六月以来，她主持了六十一场婚礼和一次誓言重续，那一次那头猪是贵客，礼物是一张装在相框里的烧烤收据。

她在第四十条后面那一页留了一行空白，因为她从一个睡在冰袋上的男孩、从一个其实是头牲畜的贼身上学到：任何一场婚礼的最后一条守则，都是你还没写下的那一条；而它到最后，永远是关于放手的。

她记名字的本事仍是全县第一，这是唯一真正管用的本事；挂绳上那枚胸牌还是写着司仪，只是她已经学会了换个读法：多半是懦夫，偶尔是勇敢。

第四十条：司仪从不成为故事，除非有一次，当故事是你自己的。
