chapters.title: 替身演员第 42 次落地
chapters.content:
"Forty-one," Wick Dougherty said to the van window. "Forty-one, and still standing." Fisk turned a page of his log. "Forty-two," the rigger said. "By forty-two you write the last line yourself, or nobody does." He kept the count in a notebook the size of a cup. Forty-one lines in twenty-six years. Date. Height. Surface. What broke. 14 August. Forty-one feet. Gravel, dry. Left wrist. 2 November. Sixty feet. Canvas. Nothing.

19 March. Eighty-eight feet. Water. Three ribs and one tooth. Half of the forty-second was already down on the last page: 7 October. Eighty-one feet. Airbag. Six feet off the line. The rest he would write himself, or Dr. Prue, or nobody.

The origin of the count was a rigger named Fairweather, long dead. A body only gets so many falls, and nobody knows how many. Count them yourself, and stop before the count stops you.

"Forty-two sounded right at twenty-six," Wick said. "It rhymes with nothing, and it fits." He was forty-nine, this was the last week of his engagement, and the number had come up on him like a bill coming due.

The brickworks at Slag Hollow stood forty miles out of Vance at the end of a road built for carts. Four chimney stacks, and only one sound. A furnace shed with no roof, and no flame burning in it since Kennedy was alive.

"In the wet months the whole place drains into a ditch," Fisk said, "and a plague of midges comes off it of an evening." Frequent rain had turned the yard to a bog that smelled of rust. The wall of Number Four was homogeneous brick from boot to crown, eighty-one feet of it, no ledge and no mercy. As a location it was a magnificent ruin.

Old Pike kept the gate, and had been illiterate for seventy years, which is why the weight notice bolted to Number Four had always been, to him, a decoration. "The Marshal goes to work at four," Pike said. "On principle." The Marshal was a cock, and in the considered opinion of the unit manager a pest and a menace.

Social intercourse between the unit and Slag Hollow consisted of eggs, one disturbance call about the noise, and a goat.

The picture was The Brimstone Line, a joint venture between Kestrel Pictures and a German outfit nobody could name. "It's a kidnap," Rex Marchand said. "A train, an heiress, a ransom in a duffel bag, and eighty minutes of men falling off things." He played the hero.

Rex was fifty-four, vain as a diamond, and as for his own body, a thorough coward. He had a classic leading man's arrangement with the truth, which was to tell it nothing, and he disdained the men who did his falling. With one exception, which was his tongue.

Out of twenty-six years of interviews he had created a legend in which he did them all himself, and he had said it in so many columns that the fact had hardened into something nobody checked. He was famous across the globe, and the picture was sold for a global release on the strength of it.

I do my own stunts. "Then why does the sentence get shorter every year?" Hallie asked. Rex did not hear her. Rex's trailer was humid enough to grow mushrooms. He sat in it with a hot cloth on his neck, a flask of liquor under his pillow, and a spine he called too painful for a four-foot step-off onto a gym mat.

"Do you know what my spine is worth?" he said into the mirror. "Four feet."

Dr. Ines Prue, the production physician, looked at the spine and went back to her crossword. She was a patient woman with the patience of somebody who had stitched fishermen, and she carried a pharmacy. Prue gave Wick two pills for the pain in his knee. "You sound like a bag of bricks with a cough," she said, listening to the intermittent cough he had carried since August.

"Forty-one falls and you still cough," Prue said. "The ditch will finish you."

"If you land in that ditch, you will be in my care until spring, with pneumonia," she said. "The stuff in it is not water. It is a compound of rust, dead midges and one poison I do not care to name."

Hallie Sorn came up from the city on the Thursday. She was a correspondent for The Frame, a trade paper with a small format and a long memory, and she had come to interview Rex about his trade. "It's a craft," Rex told her, with the greeting of a man who has already decided on the quotation. "It's a craft, it's a gamble, and it's a feat."

She wrote it down like a copybook and wrote the same wall five times over before she understood it.

"And who is the man who goes over the edge?" Hallie asked. A runner with a clipboard looked at his boots.

Wick stood behind the monitor with a coffee and watched them both in the picture and neither in the photograph, which is why he had read enough of these pieces to generalize. The journalist asked about fear. The star answered. The man who went over was never in the shot.

The climax of The Brimstone Line was the Number Four drop, and it was the only reason the picture had come to Slag Hollow at all.

"Eighty-one feet off the crown, down the north face, onto a bag," the second unit manager said. "Get it in the can by half past ten." The bag was a prototype, cube-shaped, which is why the crew called it the Cube. "Merit is that it folds compact," Fisk said. "Drawback is page nine of the manual."

The drawback, printed in the smallest type Wick had ever seen, was that the bag had never been tested above sixty feet, and eighty-one necessitated a second bag underneath, which was with the second unit and could not be spared.

"Then I will build you a model," the art department said, and built one of the stack four feet high in a corner of the shed. Wick fell off the model eleven times in rehearsal.

On Wednesday the safety committee arrived: Yolanda Betts from the studio, a delegate from the completion insurer, and a local fireman named Tuck with a hose and an expression of neutral boredom. Betts was formidable, with the contempt of a woman who has read every rule twice. "Seven o'clock, compulsory briefing," she said into her mobile. "Gloves on, compliance sheet signed. I insist, and I will not say it twice."

She ran the briefing at seven each morning, handed out a compliance sheet nobody read, and insisted that every man comply with a rule about gloves. "And you," Betts said to Wick, "will not be exempt because you have fallen forty-one times."

"Has that ever been a reason before?" "It is now."

She opposed the drop in writing, in triplicate. Barrow discarded the triplicate in the bin by the catering truck, where Wick found it and read it, because reading things in bins had been, for twenty-six years, his most useful habit. The impetus for all of it had been a death on a picture in Antwerp, and a clash with the studio's insurer about who would pay.

"The prototype holds no certificate for that height," the sheet said. "The discrepancy between the tested height and the drop is twenty-one feet. That is not a discrepancy. That is a wall."

Barrow was notorious in three countries for finishing pictures, which he did by the drastic method of removing from them whatever cost money. He called this efficiency, and he liked to innovate, which in his mouth meant a saving that was his and a risk that was somebody else's.

"Money is no object," Barrow said at half past seven, with an envelope in his hand and a genuine smile that reached exactly as far as his teeth. "I want the drop at ten. The light is due at half past, the appraisal is Monday, and if the drop is not in the can, a couple of us will be looking for employment."

He held it up. "That is a bonus. There is also a replacement in the second van." He kept talking about the weather while he said it, the way a man talks to distract a horse. Wick did not open the envelope. Shouting at a producer is like shouting at weather: a futile trade, and the futility of it is the only part you can count on.

"Is Deke in the second van?" Wick asked. "He is," Toby said. "Warming up."

The replacement was a boy named Deke Sollis, twenty-two, with a neck like a pillar and the obedient face of a man who will fall where he is told. He excels at going down and has not yet learned to arrive. "Mr. Barrow says if you are not up there by ten, Deke is," Toby said.

Toby Vane was Wick's nephew, a runner, and the only reason Wick took the job. He was nineteen, obedient to a fault, and juggled three things badly. "Bring coffee at seven," Wick said. Toby had enlightened him about the outbreak that had taken out half the second unit from the catering truck, not wanting to intrude on a silence he did not understand.

It frustrated him to be told the time. He had entered the trade at nineteen himself, carrying cable for a man named Sollis, Deke's father, a job the business found common and Wick found difficult. He had hunted for work all that winter, and he had never envisaged ending it in a van at Slag Hollow being told when to go up a wall.

He dozed for twenty minutes in the makeup chair, the only diversion on offer, and then walked out to look at the rig.

The yard at ten to nine was a circus with the tent left off. The Cube lay flat beside the loading dock, pink, with a white X painted at its centre, being filled by a compressor of heroic horsepower from a bottle of gas the size of a man.

"That cable runs through a puddle," Sonia the electrician said to Barrow. "It is dangerous." "Facilitate the shot." Barrow despatched a runner to Vance for an adapter, the runner was slow, and Sonia made one. Above them Number Four went up into a gradual grey light that diffused through the dust, and she held a fuse in one hand and thought better of it.

A crowd of extras, grips and office people had gathered at the fence in the way they do when a human body is about to be involved, and Pike's cock walked along the top of the fence, ignoring everybody. The catering truck was a magnet for anyone with a spare hour.

Wick inspected the bag himself, because he had learned to inspect things himself. He kneeled beside it, ran a hand along the seam, then along the four tie-downs, then over the valve, which was compatible with the compressor only by an adapter Sonia had made from a fragment of pipe and a great deal of tape.

"Valve's homemade," Wick said. "It holds," Sonia said. "For now."

The material smelled of a factory in a country he could not name. He read the indication on the gauge, the level of the fill, and the minimum distance the manual gave between the bag and any hard edge.

"Six feet from the water," Wick said to Fisk. "Six and a half," Fisk said.

The rigger had installed the rope on the stack at six, inserted the anchor bolts with a wrench and a great deal of opinion, and fixed a lever at the crown so the camera could see the moment of release. "Centred and tensioned," he said, and commended the bag to Wick as though it were a horse.

Wick started up at twenty past nine, gripped the first rung of the iron ladder on the north face, and climbed. For thirty feet the friction of iron on his palm and brick on his boots was the whole of his attention. "How long can you hold a knot?" Fisk called up. "Long enough."

He groped along the wall for the latent crack the survey had mentioned, found a chip out of the brickwork the size of a fist, and went on. At fifty the wind found him and hurled dust in his face. He grabbed the rung and waited, because fighting the wind on a ladder is arguing with the ground, and you lose.

At sixty-five the ladder ended and the rope began. He groped for the first knot, inserted a boot, and went up the last sixteen feet hand over hand, his left leg complaining in the plain manner of a leg that had complained since 1998. The rope constrained him there, and the constraint was a comfort, because the function of a rope on a wall is to hold a man there.

The crown was level, three feet across, hot even at that hour. He did not look at Slag Hollow, but down the drop line, at the Cube, pink, the white X on it, and the marker flag the camera crew had planted where the rehearsal had put the bag.

"Marker's off the X," Wick said into his chest radio. "Six feet toward the water."

The marker and the X were not in the same place. Six feet. A mere six feet, and at eighty-one feet of fall it was the distinction between a feat and a fatal collision with the lip of that water.

Wick tried to divine it. Either the ground crew had moved the bag for the convenience of a shot that wanted water in frame, or they had moved it and had not re-tensioned the tie-downs afterward, so anything landing off-centre would slide. On the way down both meant the same thing.

He hesitated for two heartbeats, which annoyed him. He had not hesitated at a height since he was thirty. Then he did the arithmetic Fairweather had taught him: the bag's current position, the excess air it would discharge on the near side, the minimum he would have to divert. Six feet of drift, bought with a twist of the hip, the old trick off a water tower in Fresno.

A gamble of the ordinary kind, and crucial for one reason. It was the only way down that did not involve explaining himself to a boy named Deke.

He focused on the white X, extended an arm, found the lever, and put his fist on the radio at his chest. "Bag is six feet off the line," he said. "Repeat. Six feet off the line."

Static, the continual static of a cheap radio, and under it the continuous hum of the generator.

"Stand by, Wick," Betts's voice, tight. "We are burning daylight," Barrow's voice, warm. "The light goes at half past. Execute the drop."

"It sits where the camera wants it," Barrow went on, in the even tone of somebody assuring a child. "Six feet. You can handle six feet."

Wick looked at the marker and at the X. He thought of the bonus in the van, the holder of the completion bond, and the inertia of a picture that had already spent its money.

He understood, with the calm of a man reading a sentence he has read before, that the bag was not going to be moved. He was compelled to put his body where the camera wanted it, as he had been compelled for twenty-six years, and the compulsion felt nothing like courage. It felt like being told the time. He kicked off.

The first twelve feet were the worst, as they always are: the immediate drop, the motion of a body that has not yet agreed to what is happening to it, the flash of pure objection behind the eyes. Then he folded into the drop position, arms in, chin down, and the curve of the fall took him.

At forty feet the wind came round the stack and tried to hurl him back into the brick. He diverted with a shoulder and drifted left, paying for it. At sixty he focused on the white X again, which was not where it should have been, and he turned hard: hip, shoulders, the whole of his left side, six feet of travel bought out of eighty-one feet of air.

The impact came up through his boots. The bag discharged with a liquid hiss, four vents expelling the excess air in a second and a half, and he went down through the material and hit the ground underneath it hard enough to see white. The collision with the earth was not loud. It was dull and final, and brick chips came down after him like a small private weather.

He gasped and could not stop. There was pain, the ribs, a bright new line of it down his left side that had not been there at breakfast, and he moaned and did not move while the pink walls of the bag rose on four sides. That is not an airbag. That is a pillow with a hole in it.

Then the noise arrived. Somebody clapped once, uncertainly, and then the whole crowd did, and the clap ran for six seconds before it became embarrassing and stopped. Prue was over him in eleven seconds with her tackle box, explored his side with two fingers, told him not to move, told him the left side was painful but not paralyzed, and gave him a pill and water.

"Will there be another take?" somebody interrupted, and Wick, lying in the dirt, found it funny in a way he could not explain. The extras pressed in and were pushed back, a mob of them. He turned his head. Six feet away, at the corner nearest the water, one of the four tie-downs lay loose in the dirt, and the rope had not torn.

"Who moved the bag?" Wick asked. "Ask the man who signed the log," Fisk said.

It had been cut, a neat cut, clean through, the work of a blade and not of a collision, and the knot above it was Fisk's, tied in the way he had tied everything for twenty years. He signed the rig log at half past nine, the last entry in it, and illustrated the release for the committee by dropping a brick off the shed roof.

"Who cut it?" Wick said. "The rope," Fisk said. "Not a fall."

Wick extended an arm, grabbed the cut end, and extracted from the dirt a fragment of the same rope and a chip of brick, and put both in his pocket, because anyone who has fallen forty-two times knows that the truth of a thing is usually small enough to put in a pocket.

"That is the climax in the can," Barrow said, coming through them with a folder. "Insurance will carry it. We will take care of you, Wick. A hospital bill would exhaust the contingency, and we do not intend to incur one." Insurance will carry it. The appraisal was Monday. The water had been in frame.

Wick asked for his notebook and his nephew, and Toby came running with both, and with the photographs on his mobile, because Toby had photographed everything since the day he arrived, which everyone had called a nuisance and Wick now called evidence.

The photographs were stamped. At 9:31 the bag was centred on the white mark. At 9:52 two men had moved it six feet toward the water, because the camera wanted water in the shot, and nobody had re-tensioned anything afterward.

Fisk's rig log said bag final, tie-downs tensioned. True at half past nine, false at ten, and in the format the insurer required, a forged application for a payout. The deceit was small and had deceived nobody for longer than an afternoon, which was exactly as long as it needed to.

Wick had not intended to go to the press. What changed his intention was Barrow saying, in the yard, that the drop would be edited into the trailer as a genuine feat by Rex Marchand, and that no one could expose it, because the only man who had been up on the crown was going to be paid to keep quiet.

Barrow exerted no pressure at all. He said it in the plain mode of a man stating the weather, and Wick understood then that the motive had never been the shot. The motive was the claim.

The second thing he found in his own notebook, and it took him until the evening, in the lavatory of the shed, the only room on the lot where a man could sit with a book and not be interrupted. He had taken the liberty of carrying both notebooks in.

Line nineteen: 23 May. Sixty-six feet. Airbag, secondhand. And at the foot of it, in his own hand, twenty years old and quite forgotten: bag off line six ft, tie-down cut, Barrow. He had written it down once and had not thought about it in twenty years, because a faller cannot think about the ones that nearly worked. He had never disclosed it, never escalated it, and nobody had ever asked.

There had always been an exception in the way the business treats its own accidents, and for Wick Dougherty it had been that he was too tired to make trouble. "Disclose all of it?" Hallie said that night, in the lavatory, which gave her story its ending and gave the magazine its column. "Every word," Wick said. "And four words in the margin, if you can read them."

The Frame ran it under the headline The Man Who Falls, with an excerpt from Fisk's log beside an excerpt from Toby's photographs, and with a real photograph, taken by Sorn's own man from the fence at nine forty, of the crown of Number Four, on which, at the moment of release, was the face of Wick Dougherty.

It was, the editor said, the shortest line in the business: the distinction between a man who does his own stunts and a man who says he does. What had intrigued Hallie afterwards, she said, was not the rope. It was the four words in the margin of a notebook kept for twenty-six years.

The completion insurer refused the claim. Barrow was held liable for a sum he described, in a statement his own people would not print, as drastic, and to the end he maintained that he had not known about the rope.

Kestrel dropped the picture and revived it, and edited the drop into a shot of the stack on a table, which the critics hated and the schoolchildren of Slag Hollow thought magnificent. Fisk forged nothing himself but signed a log he had not re-read, and lost his employment and his employer in one week. He took to loading containers on a dock in Vance, the same labor with less illusion.

Rex, at the wrap party, said I do my own stunts once more, out of habit, and the room went mute. The guild never nominated him again, which is how the picture business damns a man.

He donated a bench to the town on the understanding that his name would not go on it, and the town put his name on anyway, in paint, the ordinary revenge of ordinary people, which suited Wick very well. Nothing was allowed to interfere with that bench, and nothing did.

The drop was never repeated. Deke Sollis went home at twenty-two with his neck intact, and Wick liberated himself from the trade on the number he had chosen at twenty-six, the only number in this story that anybody chose for himself. He did not so much escape the business as walk off the end of it.

At Slag Hollow he organized a small school: a yard, a furnace shed with a new roof, forty feet of rope an old mate donated, a plaster cast of Wick's left wrist by the door as a teaching aid, and a rule that no student is exempt from the ladder. Kestrel endowed it with a modest annual sum and asked that the studio's name not appear on the wall.

Pike still keeps the gate and is still illiterate. The Marshal still goes to work at four. The bog still drains and still breeds midges, and there is a flag on top of Number Four that the students put up each term and take down each term, because the wind takes it.

Every native of Vance knows the story, most of them tell it wrong, and a couple have made a contribution to the school fund on the strength of it.

"Why forty-two, Mr. Dougherty?" a boy asked on the first morning. "Because I picked it," Wick said. "Pick yours and keep it." "What if the bag is wrong?" a boy asked. "Then you count it," Wick said.

Wick teaches the arithmetic: the inspection before the climb, the knot before you trust the wall, the minimum before you take the step. The ground does not care how brave you are. The ground only cares where somebody put the bag.

There are forty-two lines in the notebook. The forty-second is finished now, in his own hand: 7 October. Eighty-one feet. Airbag, off line, cut. Six feet, bought in the air. Nothing broken that will not mend. Under it, added years later in the same even hand:

Forty-two, and not one more. A tumbler can be pushed off a chimney a hundred times; the one he walks away from is the one he chose.

"四十一次，"维克·多尔蒂对着面包车的玻璃说，"四十一次，还站着。"菲斯克翻了一页索具日志。"四十二，"那个索具师说，"到四十二你自己写最后一行，或者谁来写都不算。"他把这笔账记在一个杯子大的本子里。二十六年，四十一行。日期。高度。落点。摔坏了什么。8月14日。四十一英尺。砾石，干的。左手腕。 11月2日。

六十英尺。帆布。没坏。3月19日。八十八英尺。水。三根肋骨，一颗牙。 第四十二行他已经在最后一页写下了一半：10月7日。八十一英尺。气垫。偏离落线六英尺。

剩下那半句他自己写，或者普鲁医生写，或者谁也不写。这个计数的源头是一个叫费尔韦瑟的索具师，早死了。

一个人一辈子只能摔那么多次，谁也不知道是多少次。所以你自己数着，要在数到头之前停下来。"二十六岁时觉得四十二顺耳，"维克说，"押不上什么韵，可它合用。"

他四十九岁，这是他这份合约的最后一周，这个数字像一张到期的账单一样找上门来了。斯拉格霍洛的砖厂在万斯城外四十英里，一条为马车修的路的尽头。

四座烟囱，只有一座还结实。一间没有屋顶的窑棚，自肯尼迪还活着的时候起，里面就没再燃过火。"雨季里整个厂区的水都排进一条沟，"菲斯克说，"天一黑，成群的小咬子就从沟里冒出来。"频繁的雨水把院子泡成一片发臭的泥沼。四号窑的墙从上到下是一色的砖，八十一英尺高，没有一道棱坎，也不讲一点情面。

作为外景地，这是一片壮观的废墟。老派克看大门，已经当了七十年的文盲，所以钉在四号窑上的那块承重告示牌，在他眼里一直只是块装饰。"'元帅'四点上工，"派克说，"凭原则。"那是一只公鸡，在剧组制片主任看来，是个讨厌鬼，是个祸害。

剧组和斯拉格霍洛之间的往来只有三样：鸡蛋、村里为噪声打来的一次投诉电话，还有一只山羊。

那部片子叫《硫磺线》，是凯斯特雷尔影业和一家谁也叫不出名字的德国公司的合拍片。"是桩绑架，"雷克斯·马尚说，"一列火车，一个女继承人，一只帆布包里的赎金，还有八十分钟男人往下掉的戏。"

他演男主角。雷克斯五十四岁，虚荣得像颗钻石，而在自己身体这件事上，是个彻头彻尾的懦夫。他和真相之间有一套经典的男主角式安排，那就是什么都不告诉它，而且他瞧不起替他挨摔的那些人。

只有一个例外，那就是他的舌头。二十六年的采访里，他编造出一个传奇，在这个传奇里每一次都是他自己摔的；他说这话上过太多报纸的版面，以致于这个事实硬成了没人再去核实的东西。他名满全球，这部片子就靠这个卖出了全球发行权。

我自己的特技我自己来。 "那为什么这句话一年比一年短？"哈莉·索恩问。雷克斯没听见。雷克斯的房车潮湿得能长出蘑菇。他坐在里面，脖子上捂着一块热毛巾，枕头底下塞着一瓶烈酒，还有一根据他形容疼得连四英尺高的垫子都跳不下去的脊椎。

"你知道我这根脊椎值多少？"他对着镜子说，"四英尺。"

剧组的执业医生英尼斯·普鲁看了看那根脊椎，看了看维克，回去做她的填字游戏。她是个有耐心的女人，有着曾经给渔民缝过针的那种耐心，随身带着一个小药箱。她给了维克两片治膝盖痛的药。"你咳起来像一袋砖头，"她说，一边听他从上八月起就断断续续咳个不停。

"摔了四十一次还咳，"普鲁说，"那条沟能要你的命。"

"要是你落进那条沟，就得在我手上躺到开春，还得落个肺炎，"她说，"里面那东西不是水。是铁锈、死蚊蚋和一种我不愿意说名字的毒药调出来的东西。"

哈莉·索恩周四从城里上来。她是《取景框》的记者，一份开本很小、记性很长的行业小报，她来是想采访雷克斯聊聊他的活儿。"这是门手艺，"雷克斯告诉她，那神态像一个已经想好了自己要被引用哪一句的人，"这是门手艺，是场赌博，是项绝技。"

她像抄本一样记下来，同一面墙抄了五遍，这才明白自己抄的是什么。

"那真正翻过那道边的人是谁？"哈莉问。一个抱着夹纸板的跑腿的盯着自己的鞋看。

维克端着咖啡站在监视器后面，看着他们两个都在画面里、都不在照片里，所以这类稿子他读得够多了，足以放心地概括一番。记者问害不害怕，明星答了话，而真正翻过去的那个人从来不在镜头里。

《硫磺线》的高潮是四号窑那一场坠落，这也是全片跑到斯拉格霍洛来的唯一理由。

"从窑顶往下八十一英尺，顺北面，落在垫子上，"二组制片说，"十点半以前给我进罐头。"那只垫子是个原型，立方体形状，所以剧组都管它叫"方块"。"好处是收起来紧凑，"菲斯克说，"坏处你看说明书第九页。"

这个坏处印着维克见过的最小的字号：这只垫子从没在六十英尺以上测过。而八十一英尺本来需要在下面再加一只垫子，第二只在二组手里，抽不出来。

"那我给你做个模型，"美术组说，就在棚子角落里堆了个四英尺高的窑模型。排练时维克从那模型上摔下来十一次。

周三，安全委员会到了：制片厂来的约兰达·贝茨、完工保险方派来的一名代表，还有一名叫塔克的当地消防员，拎着水龙带，脸上是一副中立的无聊。贝茨不好对付，带着一个把每条规章都读过两遍的女人的那种轻蔑。"七点，强制开会，"她对着手机说，"手套戴上，合规单签了字。这是硬性要求，我不打算说第二遍。"

她每天早上七点开这个会，发一张没人看的合规单，坚持要求场上每个人都要遵守一条关于手套的规定。"还有你，"贝茨对维克说，"摔过四十一次，也不是你可以免了的理由。"

"这种理由以前有过吗？""现在有了。"

她反对这场坠落，书面反对，一式三份。巴罗把三份纸扔进了餐车旁边的垃圾桶，维克从里面捡出来读了——二十六年来，翻垃圾桶一直是他这行最有用的习惯。这一切的起因是安特卫普一部片子上死过人，还有制片厂跟自己的保险公司为谁付钱起的冲突。

"这只原型没有那个高度的认证，"那张纸说，"测过的高度和要摔的高度差了二十一英尺。那不是什么差异。那是一堵墙。"

巴罗在三个国家以"把片子拍完"出名，他的办法是把片子里一切花钱的东西拿掉，他管这叫效率。他喜欢搞点新名堂，而在他嘴里，新名堂意味着省钱的是他，担风险的是别人。

"钱不是问题，"巴罗七点半说着，手里捏着个信封，脸上挂着一丝只到牙齿那么远的真诚的笑，"我要十点摔。光线点半就得走，保险公司的估价在周一，这场坠落要是进不了罐头，我们中间就得有两三个人另找工作。"

他把信封举起来。"这是奖金。第二辆面包车里还坐着一个替补。"他说这话时一直在聊天气，就像一个人为了分散马的注意力而聊天。维克没有打开那个信封。冲制片人吼就像冲天气吼：白费力气，而唯一靠得住的就是这份白费力气本身。

"迪克是不是在第二辆面包车里？"维克问。"

在，"托比说，"正热身呢。"那个替补是个叫迪克·索利斯的男孩，二十二岁，脖子像根柱子，长着一张让摔就摔的顺从的脸。他擅长往下掉，还没学会怎么落地。"巴罗先生说，十点您还没上去，就上迪克，"托比说。

托比·韦恩是维克的侄子，剧组里的跑腿，也是维克接下这活的唯一理由。他十九岁，顺从得过分，能同时应付三件事，件件都应付得糟糕。"七点把咖啡送来，"维克说。托比已经跟他讲过餐车那场闹腾放倒了二组一半的人，讲完又咽回去了，不想贸然闯进一种他并不明白的沉默。

被人告诉他时间让他恼火。他十九岁入行，给人扛电缆，主顾叫索利斯，正是迪克的父亲——这活儿在这行里觉得平常，维克觉得难办；那年冬天他一直找活干；而他从来没设想过自己的收场，是在斯拉格霍洛的一辆面包车里，被人告知什么时候该上墙。

他在化妆椅上打了二十分钟盹，这是唯一可得的消遣，然后走出去看索具。

差十分九点，院子里像个没搭帐篷的马戏团。方块平躺在装卸台旁边，粉红色，正中刷着一个白十字，正被一台马力大得离谱的空压机从一瓶一人来高的气体里充气。

"那根电缆从水坑里过，"电工索尼娅对巴罗说，"危险。""想办法让这场拍成，"巴罗说。他派了个跑腿的去万斯城买转接头，跑腿的太慢，索尼娅就自己做了一个。他们头顶上，四号窑升进一片渐渐亮起来的灰光里，光线透过尘土散开；她一手捏着保险丝，想了想还是收了手。

一群临时演员、场务和办公室的人聚在栅栏边，那种聚法是每当有一具人的身体快要卷进去的时候人群都会有的聚法；派克的那只公鸡沿着栅栏顶踱步，谁都不理。餐车对任何一个有一小时空闲的人来说都是块磁铁。

维克自己检查那只垫子，因为他早就学会了自己检查东西。他跪在旁边，一只手顺着接缝摸过去，再摸过四根系绳，最后摸过气阀——那气阀只有靠索尼娅用一截管子和大量胶带做出来的转接头才跟空压机接得上。

"这阀门是现做的，"维克说。"撑得住，"索尼娅说，"暂时。"

那材料闻起来像某个他说不出名字的国家的工厂。他看了看表盘上的读数、充气的水位，还有说明书上规定的垫子与任何硬边之间的最小距离。

"离水六英尺，"维克对菲斯克说。"六英尺半，"菲斯克说。

那索具师早上六点在窑上装好了绳子，用一把扳手和大量的个人见解把地脚螺栓插进去，还在窑顶装了一根拉杆，好让摄影机看得见脱扣的那一刻。"居中，拉紧了，"他说，然后像夸一匹马那样把垫子夸给维克听。

维克九点二十出发，抓住北面铁梯的第一级往上爬。头三十英尺，他全部的注意力都在铁与掌心的摩擦、砖与靴底的摩擦上。"一个结你能撑多久？"菲斯克在上面喊。"够用。"

他沿着墙面摸索测量报告里提到的那道潜伏的裂缝，找到一块拳头大小的砖茬，然后继续。到五十英尺，风找到了他，把尘土摔到他脸上；他抓住横档等着，因为一个在梯子上跟风较劲的人，早就输掉了和地面的那场争论。到六十五英尺，梯子到头，绳子开始。

他摸到第一个结，塞进一只靴子，倒着手爬完最后十六英尺，左腿用一条从一九九八年起就在抱怨的腿的那种直白方式抱怨着。绳子在那里约束着他，而这种约束是一种安慰，因为绳子在这面墙上的用处就是拴住一个人：它意味着风没法把他从墙上掀下去。

窑顶是平的，三尺见方，就连那个钟点也是热的。他没有看斯拉格霍洛，只顺着坠落线往下看：那只方块、粉红色、上面的白十字，还有摄影组插在排练时垫子位置上的那面标记旗。

"标旗偏了，"维克对着胸口的对讲机说，"朝水那边六英尺。"

标记旗和十字不在同一个地方。六英尺。仅仅六英尺，而在八十一英尺的坠落里，这就是绝技和撞上那片水沿来个致命冲突之间的距离。

维克拉了拉对他的解释。要么是地面组为了让摄影机取景里有水，把垫子挪了；要么是挪了以后没把系绳重新拉紧，于是任何落在偏心的东西都会滑下去。往下掉的时候，这两种可能一个样。

他犹豫了两下心跳，这让他恼火。三十岁以后他在高处再没犹豫过。然后他算了费尔韦瑟教他的那笔账：垫子现在的位置，近侧那面会排掉多少多余的空气，冲击的角度，最少要偏多少。六英尺的偏移，用腰一扭换来的，老把戏，早年在弗雷斯诺从一座水塔上抖落过，当时跟前一个人也没有。

一场再平常不过的赌博，要紧只因为一个理由：这是唯一一条不用跟一个叫迪克的小伙子解释的下来方式。

他盯着那个白十字，伸出手臂，摸到拉杆，拳头顶在胸口的对讲机上。"垫子偏离落线六英尺，"他说，"重复。偏离落线六英尺。"

沙沙声，一台破收音机那种没完没了的沙沙，底下是发电机不停的嗡嗡。

"待命，维克，"贝茨的声音，绷着，"光在烧钱，"巴罗的声音，温吞，"点半光线就没了。执行，跳。"

"它落在摄影机想要的地方，"巴罗接着说，用的是哄孩子那种不疾不徐的口气，"六英尺。六英尺你应付得了。"

维克看着标旗和十字。他想到面包车里的奖金、周一那笔估价、完工保单的持有人，还有一部已经把钱花光的片子的那种惯性。

他明白了，像一个重读早读懂过的一句话的人那样平静：那只垫子不会挪了。他被逼着把身体摆到摄影机要的地方，二十六年来一直被这么逼着，而这种逼法一点都不像勇气。它像被人告知时间。接着他就踢开了。

头十二英尺最难过，一向如此：那一瞬间的失重，一个身体还没同意正在发生在它身上的事时的那种动，眼睛后面纯粹的反抗一闪。然后他缩进坠落姿势，手臂收住，下巴压低，坠落的弧线把他带走了。

四十英尺处，风绕着烟囱兜回来，想把他又摔进砖墙里。他用肩膀一转，往左飘，为此付了代价。六十英尺，那个白十字又在他眼里浮上来，而它根本不该在那个位置；他硬生生扭过去：胯、肩、整个左侧——用八十一英尺里的六英尺空气换来六英尺的位移。

冲击从靴底顶上来。垫子"滋"地排掉一口气，四个排气口一秒半里把多余的空气全吐出去，他穿过那层材料砸在下面的地面上，砸到眼前发白。跟地面那一下不响，闷得吓人，而且到头了。碎砖末跟着他落下来，像一场小小的、私人的天气。

他喘不上气，停不下来。疼，肋骨，左边一道亮亮的新印子，早饭时还没有；他哼了一声，一动不动，而那四面粉红的垫壁一堵堵立起来。那不是气垫。那是个漏了洞的枕头。然后声音来了。

有人先拍了一下手，没把握地；接着整群人都拍，掌声跑了六秒才变得难堪，停了。十一秒，普鲁就带着她的工具箱扑到他边上，两根手指探了探他的身子，让他别动，说左边疼但没瘫，又给了他一片药和水。"还要再拍一条吗？"

有人插嘴问，而维克躺在泥里，觉得这好笑，可又说不出为什么。临时演员们往前挤，又被推开，一群乌合之众；就在刚才，那儿还排着队。他转过头。六英尺外，靠水最近的那个角上，四根系绳里有一根松松地摊在泥里，绳子没断。

"谁把垫子挪了？"维克问。"去问签名签日志的那位，"菲斯克说。

那是被剪断的，剪得干净利落，一刀过，是刀刃的活儿不是撞出来的，上面那个结是菲斯克的结，二十年来他打的结都是这个打法。他九点半签了索具日志，那是里面最后一条记录，还为了给委员会演示脱扣，从棚子顶上扔过一块砖下来。

"谁剪的？"维克说。"绳子，"菲斯克说，"不是摔。"

维克伸出一只手，攥住那截断口，从泥里抠出一小段同样的绳头、一块砖茬，两个都塞进兜里，因为摔过四十二次的人都知道，一件事的真相往往小得能塞进口袋。

"这就是成片里的高潮了，"巴罗穿过人群走过来，手里拎着个文件夹，"保险会扛的。我们会照顾你，维克。一张住院账单会把备用金掏空，我们可不想惹上。"保险会扛的。估价是周一。水，已经在画面里了。

维克要了他的本子和他的侄子，托比抱着两样跑来，还抱着手机里那批照片——托比从进门那天起什么都要拍，大家都说这是讨人嫌，维克现在叫它证据。那些照片都盖了章。

九点三十一分，那只垫子正压在白标上。九点五十二分，两个人把垫子往水那边挪了六英尺，因为摄影机想要画面里有水，而事后谁也没把绳子重新拉紧。

菲斯克的索具日志上写着垫子就位，系绳拉紧。九点半真，十点假，而在保险公司要的那个格式里，这是一份伪造的理赔申请。这点欺骗很小，一下午都没骗过谁，而它也只需要骗一下午。

维克本来没打算找媒体。让他改主意的是巴罗在院子里说的话：这场坠落会剪进预告片，做成雷克斯·马尚亲自完成的绝技；谁也揭不穿，因为唯一上过窑顶的那个人，会拿钱换个闭嘴。

巴罗一点压力都没施。他只是用一个人报天气那种平平的口气说出来，维克这才明白，动机从来不是这场镜头。动机是那笔索赔。

第二样东西是他自己本子里翻出来的，翻到天黑才找到，在棚子里的厕所，是整片场地唯一一个能坐着看书、没人来打断的屋子。他自作主张把两个本子都带进去了。第十九行。

5月23日。六十六英尺。气垫，二手的。 而在这行下面，他自己二十年前的手迹，早就忘干净了：垫子偏离落线六英尺，系绳被剪，巴罗。这件事他写过一次，二十年没再想过，因为靠摔活的人不该去想那些差一点就成了的。他从没抖出来过，从没往上报过，也没人问过。

这行里对待自家事故，总留着一个例外，而对维克·多尔蒂来说，那个例外就是：他太累了，没力气惹事。"全抖出来？"哈莉那天夜里在厕所里问——这一问给了她故事一个结尾，也给了那本杂志一整版。"一个字不剩，"维克说，"还有页边四个字，你要是在这个尺寸上还认得出。"

《取景框》把它登在头条下面，标题是《掉下去的那个人》，一边配菲斯克日志的摘录，一边配托比照片的摘录，还有一张真照片——索恩自己的人在九点四十从栅栏后面拍的，拍的是四号窑的顶，而在脱扣那一瞬，顶上是维克·多尔蒂的脸。

用编辑的话说，这是这行里最短的一句话：一个说自己的特技自己上的人，和一个说自己是自己上特技的人，之间的区别。哈莉后来说，最勾她好奇的不是那根绳子。是一本记了二十六年的本子，页边上的四个字。

完工保险公司拒赔。巴罗被判赔一笔数目——他自己人都不肯印出来的声明里，他管这数目叫狠；到最后一刻他还是坚持说他根本不知道那根绳子的事。

凯斯特雷尔先砍了这部片，又捡回来，把高潮剪成桌上摆着一个模型的镜头，评论家恨死了，斯拉格霍洛的小学生却觉得壮观。菲斯克自己什么都没伪造，只是签了一份他没重看的日志，一周之内丢了工作和老板，跑去万斯码头上集装箱——一样的活儿，少一点幻觉。

雷克斯在杀青宴上又说了一遍我自己的特技我自己来，纯属习惯，全场鸦雀无声。行会再没提名过他，这就是这行搞臭一个人的办法。

他给镇上捐了一条长凳，条件是别把他的名字刻上去；镇上还是把名字漆了上去，用油漆，普通人最普通的报复，维克觉得挺解气。什么都不许打扰那条长凳，什么也没打扰。这场坠落再也没有重拍。

迪克·索利斯二十二岁就回了家，脖子好好地架着；维克用二十六岁自己挑的那个数字从这行里脱了身，这是这个故事里唯一一个由自己挑出来的数字。他不是逃出这行，他是走出了这行的尽头。

他在斯拉格霍洛办了一所小小的学校：一块院子，一间补了新屋顶的窑棚，四十英尺绳子（一个老伙计捐的），门边一尊维克左手腕的石膏模型当教具，还有一条规矩——谁也不许免了爬梯子。凯斯特雷尔在和解款里给了它一笔不多的年度资助，并要求片厂的名字别出现在墙上。

派克还看着大门，还当着文盲。"元帅"还四点上工。那片泥沼还排着水，还养着小咬子，四号窑顶上还飘着一面旗，学生每学期挂上去，每学期再收下来，因为风总要把它带走。

万斯本地人谁都知道这个故事，大多数讲错了，还有几个人听了感动，给学校的基金捐了点钱。

"为什么四十二，多尔蒂先生？"头一天早上一个孩子问。"因为是我挑的，"维克说，"你也挑一个，记着它。""垫子要是不对呢？"一个孩子问。"那就数着它，"维克说。

维克教的正是这笔账：爬之前先看，上结之前先摸拉杆，迈步之前先看最小值。地面不在乎你有多勇敢。地面只在乎有人把垫子摆在哪儿。本子里有四十二行。

第四十二行现在写完了，是他自己的笔迹：10月7日。八十一英尺。气垫，偏线，剪断。六英尺，在半空里买回来。没有摔坏的东西是养不好的。 底下是很多年以后，用同样的手迹添上的：

四十二，一个不多。一个人可以被从烟囱上推下去一百次；他走下来的那一次，是他自己挑的那一次。

chapters.title: 末班高铁
chapters.content:
Carriage four held forty seats and six passengers, and a diverse six they were: a boy with a cartoon on a tablet, a handsome guy in a good coat with his paper folded to the sport, and the bride three rows ahead in a white gown that had waited forty years in a wardrobe for a wedding that would not happen. Forty seats, and she had counted them twice, because counting makes the mind go slow.

"This is the wrong train," she said. "Then sit where I can see you. I would like a witness to my departure." "I know why," said Nell. "That is why I boarded it."

She sat three rows behind with a canvas bag on one shoulder and a bundle of documents under her arm. Her accommodation for the night was an inn two streets from the harbor, and the fare had been granted her by the firm, which would grudge her even that. She had been at the office since seven in the morning.

The board had shown one hole at twenty to twelve, and the line was due to terminate at midnight. A counter with its shutter down, a clock whose hand went clockwise, and a stern young guard with a beard who kept his eyes on the barrier.

On the wall a faded poster showed an aeroplane above a beach, and somebody had drawn horns on it in biro. The train lay along the platform like a liner in a dry dock. "Carriage four," said the guard. "The barrier is up. Ninety seconds. Run, miss." "Where are you going?" said the man opposite. "Southvale," said Nell, "and a hearing at ten. I carry the file that will settle it."

"I teach geology," said Mr. Kovac. "I am going toward the coast, but the coast can wait. What brought you aboard this one?" "An excursion to the reservoir. The bus left without me."

It was meant to have been an outing for the whole class, and now he sat in his own coat with his own helmet, explaining it to anybody who looked. "It was never my fault," said Kovac. "It was the bus." He had a helmet on his knee, a canoe paddle leaning sideways against his leg, and the mild air of a man who has explained the same thing four hundred times and will do it again if he is asked.

"Geology. Geometry," said Nell. "And grammar, when they let me." His name was Mr. Kovac, and for the rest of the night the old captain behind them called him Kovac, and Kovac answered to it.

Behind him an old man in a cap bellowed for the hostess like a ship in a storm. "Ahoy! Tea!" "The buffet is shut," she called down the corridor, "the tea is hot, and it is free because the till is shut."

"Free," roared the old man. "I have sailed forty years, and never once have I been hailed by a woman with a trolley." The hostess came on with her trolley and poured a gallon of it, announcing in the gay voice the company paid her for that there was nothing else on board.

The old man folded his cap face up on the table as though it were a cat. A retired sea captain, by the cap and by the fond way he wore it. "My hearing went at sea," he said. "I can hear a bell down the line and not one word you say." "Forty years of watches," said Nell. "You call that a fair trade?"

"It is, and I would do it again," said the captain, folding his hands. "And again, and again. A man gets used to having nothing."

The train crawled out under the overpass, past the junction where the southwest branch deviated toward the coast, then upward along the northern edge of the city. The arches went over them one after another like a row of shut eyelids.

Then the city vanished. There was only the track, the dark and the humidity, and nobody on board could have said what lay beyond the far window. Beyond it there was nothing to see and nothing to want.

"Twenty-four centigrade," said the little display over the door. The glamor of night travel lasted eleven minutes; the glamour evaporated around the third suburb and never came back.

A train is a finite box: forty seats, one night, six people thrown together by nothing at all. The intriguing thing about it was also the terrible one, and from the outset this night had already decided to be odd.

Nell's first impression had been that the bride was asleep. Her second, reached on the subway, stationary in a tunnel under the eastern half of the city, was that she had been crying, because the veil was dry at the top and wet at the bottom.

Mr. Pell hauled her into his office at half past six and, at his customary length, formulated the one guideline he had never diluted in thirty years: a clerk who carries papers carries the firm. "Four minutes, Farrow," he said. "Four." Furthermore, he had furnished her with a handful of copies, a ticket the firm would grudge her, no fancy hotel on the firm, and four minutes in which to fetch her coat.

She had heard that same sentence from him on eleven previous Mondays. The Trench file had been her whole life for six weeks, and she had taken the train four times a week to Southvale without once looking out of the window.

Old Elias Trench died in March and left a narrow house on Marl Lane, a garage holding a bicycle, two canoes and a can of gasoline. By a will signed in 2019 it all went to Winnie, the heir under it, who kept a retail stall in the market and could not have paid the firm's fee in cash if she had sold it twice over.

Three days before he died a second will arrived by fax, and it said: to my wife Cassia. Winnie called it fraud, Pell called it fraud, and Nell called it louder than either, and spent six weeks building the case that would establish it at a hearing at ten.

If she reached Southvale with the papers she kept the house; if she did not, Winnie would forfeit the lot to a woman nobody at the firm had ever met.

The heart of the case lay in a finding about handwriting. A man in Southvale who charged by the millimeter had compared a fax of the disputed signature with Mr. Trench's hand on the former will, and reported that the weight of the line was too even to be written at all. "Trace it," Nell had written on her own wall. "Trace it."

"Traced is not written," she said now. "I have read that sentence six hundred times." She looked grave, which was a strange look on a wedding dress.

At Wray Junction the doors opened at twenty to midnight: a jolt, a shout, the emergency brake, and the train halted in the middle of a ploughed field. Duff set it forth later with the weary skill of a man who does it four times a week.

"Doors open. Nine minutes. Otherwise we lose our slot and crawl in at dawn." "A pickup collided with the barrier at the intersection by the bridge. The barrier is down across the line, and the driver had a shipment of auto parts in the back and one goat loose in the cab. He let the goat out rather than wait."

"The creature is on the platform now, eating a grocer's crate of carrots and grapes. A procession of porters and one small dog have gone to catch it. Its front wheel is disabled, so it can only hop."

Nell got out into air that smelled foul with ozone and wet rubber, and watched the animal gallop backward along the platform with a mouthful of greens, the shopkeeper tramping behind with a sack of flour. "There it goes," said the driver, thumping the side of his truck. The ground was cold under her shoes.

"A helicopter went over farther south," said the captain, who had seen worse weather. "And a jet above it. And a tanker running along the road with fuel for somewhere else."

There, in the cold light of that platform, she saw the handsome man lean down and say something into the veiled woman's ear. The woman bowed her head and did not answer. His hand stayed on her arm a beat too long.

"What did he say?" asked Nell. "Nothing," said the bride, and did not look up.

"Who is he?" said Nell. "Nobody." "Then you are not a bride. I was at nine. Now I am nobody's."

They embarked again at one minute to midnight. The nine minutes lost would offset the ten she had gained by running, and the equation interested nobody. She opened the file on her knee and read one page.

Then the woman screamed.

"My jewelry. It is gone." Hallow was on his feet, bellowing for the police, and the man in the good coat rose slowly, like a man who had been waiting for something.

"He was here. The foreigner was here the whole time," he said in a fierce, reasonable voice. Mr. Kovac opened his eyes and said nothing, which everybody took, as people do, for guilt.

Nor did he say anything again, because silence is its own confession, and silence says guilty. Six passengers, six ways of not speaking. Nell closed the file. She had not meant to get up; she meant to sit still, deliver the papers in the morning and keep her job.

Her handicap in life, as Mr. Pell had pointed out on four separate occasions, was that she tended to care about the wrong end of a case.

The woman was dizzy with fright, and the coach had turned, in the way of coaches, into a court with no judge in it. A court needs a judge, and a judge needs a name, which was why Nell knew one thing highly well. She knew how to take a statement, and by now something in her had come to the fore.

"Everybody sit down. Please." What followed was a procedure, and the frank truth was that procedure was the only thing she had ever been good at. She had taken two thousand statements in six years and never read one of them twice.

They believed her, which fascinated her afterward, because the total authority she had exerted in her life until that moment was zero. "A clerk," said the boy. "A clerk with a pad." In her canvas bag there was a toothbrush, a sandwich of doubtful nutrition and, because it was her quirk and people deride a clerk for it until the night they need one, a pad of forms.

"Write what you saw," she said. "Not what you think. Voluntary, and you may stop whenever you like."

The captain wrote two pages about the animal, and the boy glanced up from his cartoon, drew a picture of the goat and signed it.

Mr. Kovac wrote four lines: he had boarded at Northgate, he had not left his seat, his baggage had been on the rack the whole time, and he would abide by whatever Duff decided. Nell gauged him while he wrote and decided, on no evidence at all, that he was telling the truth.

Then she asked the woman, and the woman lifted the veil. Nell found herself looking at somebody else entirely: a thin face, bare of paint, bewildered, frightened, about thirty-two. "My name is Mrs. Bly. I left the feast at nine and slipped out by the kitchen door." She said it in the roundabout way of a woman who has rehearsed a lie, and the gown was gorgeous and forty years out of fashion. It had come from a garment bag hanging on the rack, and moreover it was unlike anything that had been in that coach since 1998.

"Your mother wore it in 1979. She did. It waited forty years in a wardrobe for a wedding that went wrong." "May I look at your bag?"

It smelled of face powder and old glue. The whole bag had been shut for a week. There was a purse, a handkerchief monogrammed C and T, and, at the bottom under the sash, a small parcel wrapped in brown paper and sealed. Nell turned it over twice.

"The glue. It has not set." "I don't follow." "You sealed this during the journey. Within the hour. Nobody cut it open, because nobody had to."

An awkward pause followed, and the woman's mouth opened and shut.

"There was no theft," said Nell, in the flat tone she used for reading documents aloud. "Would you like to give me an explanation?"

What came next came in a whisper, in haste, with her hands working the handkerchief into a knot.

The man in the good coat was not her brother, though he had said he was. He had invited himself onto this journey and held a reservation at a motel east of the city. She was to be taken there and kept until the case was over. Before that there had been a cycle of letters, then a raid on her flat: drawers turned out, nothing taken, which is the part that stays with you. She had not gone to the police of her own accord, though she had thought about it for weeks. "He found me at the door," she said. "He found me and I let him in."

He had flattered her for a month and harassed her for three weeks, and the relation between the two was that neither had ever once been about her. "So I wanted them aboard," she said. "That is the whole of it. I am a fool."

Nell opened the file, and there was a fax in it she had read a hundred times: the copy of a marriage register showing the entry of Elias Trench, widower, and Cassia Bly, spinster, with two signatures and two witnesses and a date in December.

Her Christian name was there in black and white, and so was the small, tight, oddly even hand that had just written four lines on a form in a coach running through the dark.

It was Cassia Trench: the woman Nell had hunted for six weeks and called a fraud in writing, in three separate documents, with her own name at the bottom of each. Six weeks of it, and not one hour spent guessing what she looked like. The dilemma arrived like weather.

She could sit there and say nothing, deliver the papers in the morning, win the case and put this woman in the street. Or she could read the copy again, the radical thing, the thing no clerk ever does, with no guide but the page and the opportunity at last to be wrong in public.

Nell read it. The train ran southeast, the generator under the floor hummed, and nothing fogs a mind like six weeks of certainty.

The copy was printed on thermal paper, curling at the edges, and it was made of dots: a mixture of gray dots, coarse as sand. Held up to the light, every stroke carried the same weight, because a copy carries no weight at all. "It is dots," she said. "It is nothing but dots."

A fax dilutes a signature to a shape. It throws away the pressure, the speed, the hand itself and keeps the outline, and the outline of a genuine signature and the outline of a traced one are identical, because that is what a trace is.

Worse, on the fax of the register Cassia's genuine handwriting showed the same even weight the expert had called too even. His own test would condemn a signature that was not in doubt at all. "The test is broken," said Nell.

Hence the finding was worth nothing, and not entirely the expert's fault. The file embodied six weeks of certainty, and certainty is the heaviest thing a clerk can carry.

Her exterior was calm, and her inward state was fluid, hot and close to tears. "Sit still, Nell Farrow," she told herself. "Sit still." Outside the window a signal went past, red then green.

"A fax of a signature is a photograph of a voice," said Kovac. "It keeps the shape and throws away the weight." "A photograph of a rock will tell you its shape," he said. "It will not tell you how heavy it is."

Then she found the note. It had slipped down beside the purse, folded once, in a hand she did not know: a large, forward-leaning hand, the hand of a man who writes seldom and hard.

Say you never saw him sign it. Say you were not in the house that day. Say nothing else to anyone. The motel is booked. I will be waiting at the terminal with the van.

She folded it into the papers and went further down the corridor, through the gap between the coaches where the wind came up cold, to where the man in the good coat sat with his paper folded to the sport, and nothing outward about him at all.

"Mr. Tolly," she said. "Bram Tolly."

He looked up slowly, and the easy superiority on his face was the first thing about the night that made her angry rather than frightened. It was the look of a man who has never once been told no.

"You are a clerk," he said. "A girl with a pad. Open your mouth in court and you will see the street before the week is out. She signed nothing. She saw nothing. Whatever she has told you in this coach is the talk of a woman who has had a nightmare and wakened up believing it."

"A note," said Nell, "is a document." "I don't follow." "No," said Nell. "You wouldn't."

Tolly rose, and Duff was there with his radio, wearing an expression like a closed door. "Mr. Tolly. Sit down. The police will meet the train at Southvale. I have asked them to, and they have kindly agreed."

"The young lady asked me half an hour ago," said Duff, "in the compartment adjoining the luggage van, which the company equips with the only radio on this train that works."

Tolly sat down and did not speak again. The rest of the journey passed downward through the southern cutting, past the old gaol at Sedge and a yard of scrap, with a lorry standing on sideways at the gate, in a silence so complete that even the captain asked twice, in the direction of the ceiling, whether anybody had heard a bell.

Arrival at Southvale: twenty-five past one, four minutes late, which Duff called a miracle and the display called on time. It was warm and nearly bare, its international board showing one aircraft for six in the morning, its floor freshly paved, its buffet downstairs shut and dark. A dog barked once behind the fence and stopped.

Two officers met them at the gate, and the truck behind them carried a cargo of scrap. "This one?" asked the younger officer, holding up the parcel. Nobody at Pell and Quist had ever wanted her to be interesting, and Nell handed over the note, the statements and the parcel, giving her own statement last, written against a wall in the harsh light, and it ran to nine pages.

The inn could not accommodate her at that hour. The night porter said the book was full of people whose trains had also stopped for a goat. The hall had one armchair and a smell. "Full," he said. "Full of goats."

So she sat in the hall with a lamp on and worked until dawn, and the hall smelled of floor polish and old tea, and both finally made her dizzy. At ten the hearing opened in a small room with a dirty window.

Mr. Pell was there in his gown. Winnie was there with her handbag on her knee. Cassia was there in her mother's white dress with the veil lifted. Nell was there with nine pages of her own, and none of them were in order. "Nine pages," said Pell. "I have not read a single one."

Her opponent at the bar was a young woman from a progressive firm who had taken the case for nothing, and she kept looking at Nell as if Nell were either brave or mad.

"The original will has never been produced," she said. "It has been in Mrs. Tolly's sideboard since March."

Now the registrar looked at Winnie. Winnie looked at her handbag. Nell watched six weeks of work evaporate in the time it takes a woman to open a bag.

They brought the original up from the house at noon by cab. Elias Trench's hand on it was shaky, uneven, heavy at the end of every word: the hand of a dying man who held a pen with difficulty and signed anyway. It matched the copy in every respect that a copy can show and differed from it in the one respect a copy cannot.

Every hand is unique, the expert had written, and he had been right about that and wrong about everything else. It was the only sentence in his report worth keeping. Nell had been right about the shape and wrong about the weight, and she said so aloud, in a voice that shook exactly once.

The firm's payment never came. Winnie had paid in cash, week by week, and there was no more, so on the Monday Mr. Pell dismissed her with a letter of two lines. Cassia kept the house on Marl Lane, the bicycle with the bent pedal, the two canoes and a can of gasoline.

She wrote to say that the animal, bought from the grocer at Wray Junction out of sheer sentiment, had eaten most of the barley in the field behind the house. She wrote one further line: You could have carried the papers and said nothing. I would not have blamed you.

Nell went to work for the progressive little firm in the city, and learned there what Mr. Pell had never nurtured in her and what she had to harness for herself: that a file is a story somebody wrote down first, and the clerk who carries it is obliged to read it.

And she learned the reciprocal of that, which is harder. A story somebody wrote down first is a story somebody can get wrong, and the resultant wrongness travels faster than any train, for a train can only transport paper, and paper carries anything you give it.

By midnight the line had closed on the night she rode it, and there was an editorial in the local paper about the last train, written by a man who had not been aboard it, calling the whole business a pity and a sign of the times. The captain read it aloud in the buffet at Wray, deaf as a post and his opinions intact. The last coach was swept at six and again at eight, and empty both times.

"They took the rail because the rail was ours," he said. "That is the whole of it." He was something of a Marxist after a second cup, and he would come down by the coast road again in a friend's auto whenever they let him.

Anyway, getting a seat on that train had been a lottery, and Nell won it, and the prize was a nightmare with a good end and a hole in her life where six weeks of certainty had been. The seat numbers had run in decimal order down the coach, she had been in four and seventeen, and she remembers the number for no reason at all.

On the wall above her desk she keeps a plain brown frame with a piece of thermal paper in it, on which a dead man's signature has gone the color of weak tea. The frame cost eleven pounds and she has never been sorry about that. Under it, in her own hand, is the sentence she owes to a geology teacher with a canoe paddle and a helmet: the sentence that cost her one job and bought her another.

A fax of a signature is a photograph of a voice: it keeps the shape, and throws away the weight.
chapters.translation:
四号车厢有四十个座位和六名乘客，六个人各色各样：一个男孩，平板上放着动画片；一个穿好外套的英俊小伙子，报纸折在体育版；还有新娘，坐在前三排，一身白礼服，在衣柜里等了四十年，等一场不会发生的婚礼。四十个座位，她数了两遍，因为数数能让脑子慢下来。

"这趟车不对，"她说，"那你坐到我前面来。我想要个目击者，看我上车。""我知道为什么，"内尔说，"所以我才上车。"

她坐在后面三排，一只肩挎着帆布包，一只胳膊底下夹着一捆文件。这一夜的住处，是港口边两条街外的一家小旅馆；车票那点车费是事务所给她批的，事务所连这点儿也会跟她算。她从早上七点就坐在办公室里。

十一点四十，牌子上十二点那一格是个空档；这条线要在午夜终止。一只柜台卷帘门拉着，一只钟指针顺时针走着，还有一个年轻列车员，留着胡子，板着脸，眼睛一直盯着栅栏。

墙上一张褪色的旧海报，画着一架飞机飞在海滨上空，有人用圆珠笔给它添了两只角。列车横在站台上，像干船坞里的一艘远洋班轮。"四号车厢，"列车员说，"栅栏起来了，九十秒。跑，小姐。""你上哪儿去？"对面那位问。"索斯韦尔，"内尔说，"十点一场听证会。我带着那份能一锤定音的卷宗。"

"我教地质学，"科瓦奇先生说，"我要去海边，可海边可以等等。你上这趟车干什么？""一次郊游，去水库。大巴没等我开走了。"

本来是全班都该去的一次远足，可他现在穿着自己的外套、戴着自己的头盔，逢人便解释。"这不能怪我，"科瓦奇说，"怪那趟巴士。"他膝上放着一只头盔，一支独木舟桨斜靠在腿边，还有那种温和的神情——把同一件事讲过四百遍、你再问他还肯再讲一遍的人才有的神情。

"地质学。几何学，"内尔说，"还有语法，只要他们肯让我教。"他姓科瓦奇，这一夜剩下的时间里，后面那位老船长都叫他科瓦奇，科瓦奇也应。

他后头，一位戴帽子的老头像船在风暴里那样冲女乘务员大喊。"喂——！茶！""餐车关了，"她顺着过道喊，"茶还热，而且收银机关着，茶不要钱。"

"不要钱，"老头吼道，"我跑了四十年船，从来没人推着小车喊我一声、夸我一声。"女乘务员推着小车过来，倒了一大壶茶，用公司花钱雇来的那种欢快的嗓子宣布，车上别的什么也没有了。

老头把帽子正面朝上折好放在桌上，像那是一只猫。看他的帽子和他戴帽子的那份深情，他是个退休的船船长。"我的耳朵是在海上丢的，"他说，"我能听见铁轨尽头有铃声，你说一个字我听不见。""四十年表，"内尔说，"你管这叫公平买卖？"

"公平，而且我还愿意再来一次，"船长把手拢在桌上，"再来，还再来。人总会习惯了两手空空。"

列车从立交桥底下爬出去，经过西南支线朝海边拐出去的那个岔口，再沿城市北缘往上开。桥拱一道接一道从头顶过去，像一排闭上的眼皮。

然后城市消失了。只剩下轨道、黑暗和湿气，车上谁也说不出远边窗外是什么。那边什么也没有，没什么可看，也没什么想要。

"二十四摄氏度，"门上方的小屏说。夜行的那点光鲜只撑了十一分钟；那点诱惑在第三个郊区就蒸发了，再没回来。

列车是个有限的盒子：四十个座位，一晚上，六个人被什么都不是的东西塞进了同一个盒子。它最耐人寻味的地方，也正是它最可怕的地方。这个夜晚从一开始，就已经决定要不平常。

内尔对新娘的第一个印象是：她睡着了。第二个印象是她在哭——这第二个印象是在地铁里得到的，人待在城市东半区底下的隧道里一动不动，因为面纱上端是干的，下端是湿的。

六点半，佩尔先生把她拖进办公室，照他一贯的冗长，把三十年来从不肯稀释的那一条准则重新讲了一遍：一个拿着文件的书记员，就是拿着整个事务所。"四分钟，法罗，"他说，"四分钟。"此外，他塞给她一沓复印件、一张车票——事务所连这张票都会记恨她——还有一间不花事务所钱的小旅馆，他说可不是什么高级酒店，再批给她四分钟，让她去取外套。

前许多个周一，她听他说过同一句话。特伦奇那份卷宗是她六周来的全部生活；她一周搭四趟车去索斯韦尔，一次也没往窗外看过。

老伊莱亚斯·特伦奇三月死了，留下马尔巷一栋窄房子、一间车库，车库里有一辆自行车、两条独木舟和一罐汽油。按二〇一九年签下的遗嘱，这些全归温妮，那份遗嘱之下的继承人；温妮在市场里摆了个零售摊，就算把摊子卖上两回，也掏不出事务所要的现金律师费。

他死前三天，第二份遗嘱用传真送了过来，上面写着：给我的妻子卡西娅。温妮说这是欺诈，佩尔说这是欺诈，内尔喊得比谁都响，并且花六周把案子打造成能在次日上午十点的听证会上把这桩欺诈钉死的东西。

只要她带着文件赶到索斯韦尔，房子就保住；赶不到，温妮就得把这一切全赔给一个事务所里谁也没见过的女人。

案子的核心是一份关于笔迹的鉴定结论。索斯韦尔有个按毫米收费的人，把那份有争议的签名的传真件和前一份遗嘱上特伦奇的笔迹比了比，然后报告说：笔画的力度太匀了，根本不像是写出来的。"描的，"内尔在自家墙上写过这两个字，"描的。"

"描的不算写，"她这会儿说，"这句话我念过六百遍。"她脸上神色凝重，这在这条婚纱上显得很怪。

雷伊岔口，午夜前二十分钟门开了：一晃，一声喊，紧急制动，列车停在一片刚犁过的田里。后来达夫把经过讲了一遍，带着一个一星期要讲四遍的人的那种疲惫的熟练。

"开门。九分钟。不然就赶不上点，只能一路爬到天亮。""一辆皮卡撞上了桥边十字路口的栏杆。栏杆倒下来横在铁轨上。司机后头装着一批汽车零件，驾驶室里还关着一只山羊，他宁可把羊放出来，也不肯等警察。"

"那畜生现在在站台上，吃着杂货店板条箱里的胡萝卜和葡萄。一队搬运工和一只小狗已经出去抓它了。它的前轮报废了，只能蹦。"

内尔下车，钻进那股臭氧加湿橡胶的臭味里，看着那东西倒着沿站台飞奔，嘴里叼着满口青菜，杂货店老板扛着一袋面粉在后面跋涉。"瞧它跑的，"司机拍着卡车帮说。地很凉，硌着她的鞋底。

"一架直升机在更南边过去，"船长见过更糟的天气，"顶上还有一架喷气机。路边一辆油罐车，燃料是运给别处去的。"

就在那儿，在站台清冷的光里，她看见那个英俊的男人俯下身，对着蒙着面纱的女人耳朵说了句什么。女人低下了头，没有答话。他的手在她胳膊上，多停了一拍。

"他说什么了？"内尔问。"什么也没说，"新娘说，头也没抬。

"他是谁？"内尔问。"没人。""那你不是新娘。九点我还不是。现在我是谁的也不是了。"

他们在一分钟前重新上车。损失的九分钟，会抵掉她跑出来的那十分钟；这个算式很简单，这个钟点谁也不感兴趣。她打开膝上的卷宗，看了一页。

然后那女人尖叫起来。

"我的首饰。没了。"哈洛一跃而起，扯着嗓子喊警察；那个穿好外套的男人慢慢站起来，像一个一直在等什么的人。

"他在这儿。外国人一直在。"他用又凶又讲道理的嗓门说。科瓦奇先生睁了下眼，什么也没说，大家都当他是心虚——人向来就是这么想的。

他还是一句话没说，因为沉默本身就是招供，沉默就是在说有罪。六名乘客，六种不说话的方式。内尔合上卷宗。她本来没打算起来；她本来打算坐定不动，明早把文件送到，保住这份差事。

她这辈子的短处，佩尔先生点过四回：她总爱把力气使在案子的另一端。

那女人吓得发晕；车厢变了，像车厢总变的那样，变成了一间没有法官的法庭。法庭需要法官，法官需要一个名字——内尔由此深知一件事。她知道怎么录口供；这时候，有什么东西浮了上来。

"大家都坐下。请。"接下来是一套程序，而一句实话是：程序是她这辈子唯一拿手的东西。六年里她录过两千份笔录，一份也没重读过。

他们信了她，后来她想这事还觉得着迷——因为在此之前，她这一生活使出来的全部权威，等于零。"一个书记员，"男孩说，"一个拿本子的书记员。"她的帆布包里有一支牙刷、一个营养也好不到哪儿去的三明治，还有——这是她的怪癖，人家要笑话一个书记员，笑到哪天夜里需要她了，就笑不成了——一本空白的笔录本。

"写你看见的，"她说，"别写你想的。自愿写，什么时候不想写就停。"

船长写了两页，写的都是那头牲口。男孩从画片上抬起眼，画了张羊，签上名。

科瓦奇写了四行：他在诺斯盖特上的车，没离开过座位，行李一直在行李架上，一样没动；达夫说了算，他照办。内尔一边看一边掂量他，一点证据也没有，就断定他在说真话。

然后她问那个女人。她掀开了面纱。内尔看见的是另一个人：一张瘦脸，脸上没化妆品，迷茫，害怕，三十二岁上下。"我叫布莱夫人，"她说，"九点我从宴席上溜出来，从厨房门走的。"她说得转弯抹角，像个把谎话排练过的人；那件礼服华丽得很，过时了四十年。它是从行李架上挂着的一只衣服袋里取出来的；再说，它也不像这节车厢自一九九八年以来出现过的任何东西。

"那是你妈妈一九七九年穿的。她穿过。它在衣柜里等了四十年，等一场没能办成的婚事。""我可以看看你的包吗？"

那包里有一股香粉和陈胶的味道。整个包封了一个星期。里面有只钱包、一条绣着姓名缩写的手帕，还有——在腰带的底下——一个用牛皮纸包着、封了口的小纸包。内尔翻了两遍。

"这胶，"她说，"还没干。""我不懂。""你是在这趟路上封上的。顶多一个小时。没人切开过，因为没必要。"

接着是一阵尴尬的沉默，女人的嘴张开又合上。

"没有什么盗窃，"内尔用她念文件时那种平板的调子说，"你要不要给我一个解释？"

接下来是压着嗓子的耳语，急匆匆的，她的手把那块手帕绞成了一个结。

那个穿好外套的男人不是她哥哥，虽然他一直说是。他是自己缠上这段路的；他在城东一家汽车旅馆订了房，要等案子了结，就把她带走关着。在那之前，先是来而复去的一堆信，再来是一通通电话，再后来是抄她家：抽屉全拉出来，什么也没拿走——可这一样最忘不掉。她没自己去找警察，虽然想了整整几个星期。"他在门口找到我的，"她说，"他找到我，我把门开了。"

他奉承了她一个月，骚扰了她三个星期；这两者之间的关系是：从来就没人真的在乎过她。"所以我想让他们在车上，"她说，"就这些了。我是个傻子。"

内尔打开卷宗，里面有一份她读过一百遍的传真件：一份结婚登记簿的抄件，登记着鳏夫伊莱亚斯·特伦奇和未婚女子卡西娅·布莱成婚，两个签名，两个证人，日子在十二月。

她的名字清清楚楚印在上面；还有那只手——小小的、紧绷的、出奇均匀的手——刚刚在飞驰的车厢里的一张纸上写下四行字。

她是卡西娅·特伦奇。六周来内尔到处找的就是这个人，白纸黑字三份文件指着她喊欺诈，每份底下都签着内尔自己的名字。六周，没花一个小时猜过她长什么样。进退两难的处境像天气一样来了。

她可以坐在那儿什么都不说，明早把文件送到，赢了案子，把这女人赶到街上去；或者，她可以把那份抄件再读一遍——那才是根本的一步，是从没有书记员肯做的事——没有旁人指路，只有一页纸，还有最后一次当众犯错的机会。

内尔读了。车往东南开，地板底下的发电机嗡嗡响；六周的确信能把人的脑子糊住。

那抄件印在热敏纸上，边缘卷着，是一堆小点组成的：灰点掺在一起，粗得像沙。她把纸举到光下，每一笔的力度都一样，因为一份抄件本身没有力度。"都是点，"她说，"全是点。"

传真件把签名稀释成了一个轮廓。它把压力、速度、那双手全扔了，只留下边线；而一份真签名的边线和一份描出来的签名的边线，一模一样，因为所谓描，就是照着一个轮廓描。

更糟的是：结婚登记簿的那份传真上，卡西娅本人的真笔迹，正是那位专家说过的"太匀"。他那一套检验，能把一个根本没人怀疑的签名也判死。"这套检验坏了，"内尔说。

所以那份鉴定一钱不值，而且也不全怪那位专家。那卷宗装的是六周的确定，而确定是书记员能背的最重的东西。

她的外表很平静，内里的那一摊却晃荡着、滚烫的、快要哭出来。"坐住，内尔·法罗，"她对自己说，"坐住。"窗外一道信号闪过去，先红后绿。

"传真是签名的照片，是声音的照片，"科瓦奇说，"它留下轮廓，把力气扔了。""一张石头的照片只会告诉你它什么形状，"他说，"不会告诉你它有多重。"

后来她找到了那张纸条。它从钱包旁边滑下去，折了一道，是她不认识的一只手写的：笔画大而前倾，一个很少写字、又写得很用力的男人的手。

你没看见他签。别说你那天在屋里。别的什么都别说。汽车旅馆订好了。我会开着面包车在车站等。

她把纸条折进文件里，往过道更深处走，穿过两节车厢之间的缝口，那儿风一上来就是凉的；走到那个穿好外套的男人跟前，他的报纸折在体育版，身上一点也看不出来。

"托利先生，"她说，"布拉姆·托利。"

他慢慢抬起头；他那副轻飘飘的优越，是这一夜里头一件让她生气而不是害怕的东西。那是一个从来没被人拒绝过的男人的眼神。

"你是个书记员，"他说，"一个拿本子的小丫头。你在庭上张一张嘴，不出一周你就得卷铺盖。她什么也没签，什么也没看见。她在这节车厢里跟你说的那些，全是一个做了噩梦、醒来当真的女人胡说八道。"

"一条纸条，"内尔说，"就是一份文件。""我不懂。""不，"内尔说，"你不懂。"

托利站了起来，达夫就站在那儿，手里端着对讲机，脸上一副关门的样子。"托利先生，坐下。火车会在索斯韦尔停，警察接车。我开口请了，他们痛快地答应了。"

"那位小姐半小时前跟我说的，"达夫说，"就在连着行李车厢的那个隔断间，全车只有那间屋的对讲机是好的。"

托利坐下，再没开口。剩下的路程从南边那段路堑往下走，路过塞奇那座老监狱，还有一片废铁堆，大门口歪着一辆侧过来的卡车；安静到了这个份上，连船长都朝天花板问了两遍，有没有人听见铃声。

抵达索斯韦尔：一点二十五分，晚四分钟。达夫说这是奇迹，显示屏说正点。这里暖和，也几乎空着，国际航班牌上写着清早六点有一架飞机；地面新铺过，餐车在楼下关着，黑着。 栅栏后头一条狗叫了一声，不叫了。

两个警察在门口等他们，他们身后那辆卡车上装着一车废铁。"这个？"年轻的那个举起纸包问。佩尔与奎斯特从来没人盼她出风头；内尔把纸条、笔录和纸包交了上去，自己的那份笔录压在最后，靠着墙写的，光很晃眼，写了九页。

那家小旅馆这会儿容不下她。夜班门房说登记簿满了，全是不些火车也让一只山羊拦下来的客人。大厅里只有一张扶手椅，还有一股味儿。"满了，"他说，"满了一院子羊。"

于是她点着一盏灯坐在大厅里，干活干到天亮；大厅里是地板蜡和陈茶的味道，这两样最后都把她熏晕了。十点，听证会在一间小屋里开。

佩尔先生穿着长袍在。温妮膝上放着手提包在。卡西娅穿着母亲那身白衣裳、面纱掀起，在。内尔在，手里九页纸，一页也没按顺序排。"九页，"佩尔说，"我一页也没看。"

她的对方律师是新派事务所一个年轻女律师，这场官司她一文钱不收就接了；她不住地看内尔，看得内尔要么很勇敢，要么很疯。

"最初那份遗嘱一直没拿出来，"她说，"三月起它就托利太太家的碗柜里放着。"

这会儿登记官看着温妮。温妮看着她的手提包。内尔看着六周的心血蒸发——只够一个女人打开提包的工夫。

中午他们用出租车把原件从房子里取了上来。伊莱亚斯·特伦奇在上面签的那只手抖得厉害，每一笔的收尾都重：一个快死的人握笔吃力，还是签了。它在每一个一份抄件能比出来的方面都对得上，只在那个抄件比不出来的方面不一样。

每一只手都是独一无二的，专家在报告里写过；这一点他是对的，别的地方他全错。这是他那份报告里唯一值得留的一句话。内尔对了轮廓，错了力气，她当着所有人的面说了出来，声音只抖过一下。

事务所的工钱始终没来。温妮一周一周地拿现金付，付到没有了；到了周一，佩尔先生用两行字的信把她辞退了。卡西娅保住了马尔巷那栋房子、踏板歪了的那辆自行车、两条独木舟和一罐汽油。

她写信说，那只牲口——她就凭一点心软，从雷伊岔口的杂货商手里买来的——把屋后地里的大麦吃了大半。她又多写了一行：你本来可以照常把文件送到，什么也不说。换了我也不会怪你。

内尔去城里那家新派的小事务所上班，在那儿学到了佩尔先生从来没在她身上培养过、而她必须自己驾驭的那样东西：一份卷宗，是有人先写下来的一个故事；背着卷宗的书记员，是有义务把它读一遍的。

她还学到了它的反面，那更难。有人先写下来的故事，就是有人能读错的故事；而因此而来的错，跑得比任何一列火车都快，因为火车只能运纸，纸却什么都装得下。

她搭这趟车那一夜，这条线到午夜就断了。本地报上有篇关于末班车的社评，写的人从没上过这趟车，把整件事说成一件可惜事、一个时代的记号。船长在雷伊的餐车里把它念出声来，耳背得像根柱子，意见却一整套。最后那节车厢六点扫一次、八点又扫一次，两次都是空的。

"他们要铁路，因为铁路是我们家的，"他说，"就这些。"喝了第二杯，他有点马克思主义了；只要人家肯，他会再从沿海那条路搭朋友的车来一趟。

反正，在这趟车上搞到一个座位是一场抽签，内尔中了签；中签的彩头是一晚噩梦，收场倒是好的，她心里被六周的确定挖出一个洞，那地方原来就空着。座号按十进位一路往下排，她坐的是四号十七座；她记着这个号，一点理由也没有。

她书桌上方墙上挂着一个素色的棕色相框，框里一张热敏纸，上面一个死人的签名已经褪成了淡茶的颜色。这相框花了十一英镑，她一点也不后悔。底下是她自己的笔迹，写着她欠一位地质老师的一句话——那位老师带着一支独木舟桨和一顶头盔：那句话让她丢了一份工作，又换来一份工作。

传真是签名的照片，是声音的照片：它留下轮廓，把力气扔了。
