chapters.title: 补课
chapters.content:
"I copied it off the board," Arthur Kew said. "Every word of it. I never read a line."

The board on the workshop door was painted in letters a hand wide: Nobody is an idiot at six o'clock. Under it, smaller, because the black paint had run: Bring a pencil. Leave your shame on the step. And smallest of all: No money. Ever.

"Pencil," she said. "You came without one."

He went down the step and came back with a stump of one. The shop by the cemetery had shut at five, so it was a penny from home, and she did not ask him about the penny.

The workshop stood behind her father's house at the bottom of Cutler's Row, where Terrence Vail had turned the clay of Calder's pit into chimney pots. The predominant smell was wet clay, the frames were quietly beginning to rot, and after he died he left the wheel, the stove, the photograph of the ox that turned the pugmill, and his ledger of clients.

"Is it free?" the boys asked in the first week. "It is free." "Then why does she do it?" "Ask her." He never told them; he had been a slave to the school semester for thirty-one years, sitting deep in the same comfortable rut with a zeal about the business that read badly on paper.

"Snob," Mr Wace said behind her back. "You teach the refuses and call it a vocation." "Not a cent," she told the coal man. "No tuition. Not a cent changes hands. Thirty-one years and never a cent earned." Every October to March she lit that stove and taught whoever came, and the quickest of them got chocolate on Friday for finishing a page.

"That was the whole of her method. It looked repressive in an inspector's notes. The six-o'-clocks were not clever children; they were the ones the place had dropped." "I can take an engine apart," said Denny Pratt. "Then read the instruction sheet," she said. "Nowhere will you find the engine." The Rudge boys were upright, slow, and kind to the dog.

And worst of all there was Arthur Kew, the worst reading score of his year, fourteen, naughty and inventive, sentimental about machinery. His belly growled in fourth period with a regular and humiliating rhythm. His mother Marla worked nights on overtime at the hospital laundry and slept with rolled socks in her ears; his father had gone west in a lorry and never come round the bend.

"Fourteen," she said. "What do you want to be?" "A pilot." "Then you will have to learn your numbers." "I can read numbers. It is the letters I cannot do." He said it flatly, without a scrap of shame, and that was how she knew how much shame was waiting for him.

Sixteen years earlier she was nineteen and a sophomore at the university reading English, when something came loose in her head. She had been copying a passage in a seminar at the back of the room when the letters went slippery and slid down the page like wet type.

It lasted eleven minutes and cost her the rest of her education. She called it weather; it recurred every dark season and spared no faculty but the one she needed most. "I can hear him cheat," she would say, and it was true: she could hear a boy read aloud and tell you where he had cheated.

What she lost was the page. Print turned to bramble and would not hold its depth, and it always strengthened towards evening. She could recall a face years afterwards and never the sum it had failed to do; what she could recollect perfectly was the first rule.

So every morning she copied one dull line and dated it, and knew before she faced a class whether she could read. Five shoeboxes of them lived under her bed. "What is in the shoeboxes?" Marla Kew asked once, on a night when the laundry ran late. "Nothing," she said. "Old paper."

The pills had become a preoccupation. The only remedy was a powder, and Dr Halloran, a practitioner of the old school on Grange Street, prescribed two packets a week. Twice the dose would have been poisonous; it relieved the ache only if taken before the warning, but the price ate most of what was left once the insurance and the coal man were served, so she took half.

Money went elsewhere: eighty paperbacks, Artie helping her unload the crates, and the school clothing store, for half the six-o'-clocks were clothed by nobody. Her mouth went dry as cloth; she lost the whole of her saliva by noon and her stomach revolted at anything she put in it to quench the taste. "I am merely economical," she told Mrs Dill. "That is all there is to it."

The trouble came on a Tuesday of the third week of the autumn semester, comprehension week at Wrayford Secondary. Miss Vail walked between the desks with a purple pen behind her ear, and Artie's paper said exactly what the girl's next to him said, including the spelling of barge, which the girl had got wrong.

He had copied, and by his own admission he had copied in a hurry, which she held the graver fault. "A copied answer," she said, laying both papers down, "is louder than a wrong one. A wrong one is a fact. This is an opinion about my eyesight."

His face went the colour of wet brick, the most troublesome boy in the second year, and he did not look at her while she said it, and most liars look straight at you.

"Cheating is discipline," said Mr Bodkin, the headmaster. "It requires a document, and the parents, in accordance with county rules." His deputy, Mr Wace, said it more cheerfully, having a tuition club at eleven shillings a head, though there was a flaw in his arithmetic and to some degree he knew it.

"Send him to me," said Bodkin. "Every evening until Christmas." "Your workshop?" "To my workshop." "The insurance cannot be made to stretch to it in ninety-four days." "I am not asking the insurance to stretch. I am asking for the boy."

Bodkin, who loved conformity the way other men loved gardens, gave way in the wrong direction, and realised it even as he agreed in a low voice. It was settled badly, on the understanding that nobody wrote anything down, and she left wishing she could get anywhere near him. He went home and sat an hour with a response he never sent.

He came at two minutes to six in a coarse wool jersey two sizes too small, hands up the sleeves, with a shiver he would not admit to. From the step the whole panorama of the town went down to the reservoir.

She put the kettle on to boil; inside there was a circle of lamplight, five chairs, and cocoa that did not begin to quench him. "Read it," she said, and handed him a page. He read it beautifully, round and even, the commas honoured, the way a reader reads a timetable he loves.

"What did it say?" "Nothing." "It is not nothing. It is a content. Say it back." The boy could not. Not the gist, not one domain of it; another page, another refusal. There was an encyclopedia he knew by heart and could not summarise; his ignorance was nine feet of unfocused air. His toe worked at a crack in the floor, and there was a silence before he spoke.

"I cannot see the board. I can hear all right."

"How far can you see?" "Four feet. No further." "And the chart last year?" "I passed it. I read it backwards." "Why?" "My father said spectacles were for soft lads." "And you believed him for five years." It was elementary, and she had missed it for two terms.

She took off her own reading glasses and pushed them across the table. The strength was wrong, so he had to take a posture with his head back and squint; the print came slowly up out of the dark, and she repressed a smile, and he said a word seldom heard in that room.

"Oh."

He was hotly ashamed afterwards and resented her the whole walk home. Nobody wants to be handed spectacles by someone who might have noticed sooner, and he hated being dependent on anybody's charity.

The glasses came out of the school welfare fund, in accordance with the policy, and Bodkin saw to it quietly, saying only that he had a responsibility, that he was responsible, and that he would not discuss it. He also had an obligation to say something, and delayed it over a chat about the boiler.

"In ninety-four days the county comes," he said. "Your name is third on the list." She poured tea and reminded herself, mid-pour, that he had come to warn her rather than catch her.

Three weeks later it happened in front of the boy. They were working through a textbook borrowed before dawn and due back before eight, and he pushed his page over, expecting to be told he was wrong, only to find her holding the paper too far away.

There had been no warning: she had written her morning line and dated it and read it back, all in order. She could see shapes. She could not read one word of his answer. "Tell me what you have written." "I copied it off the board." "Tell me anyway."

So he told her, and she understood it, and showed him where he had gone wrong. By Wednesday she knew she could not teach the next module without learning it first. At quarter to twelve each night, stove banked and curtain drawn, she taught herself one chapter, so as to be one chapter ahead of Arthur Kew on Thursday. Nothing sharpened her limits like a page of algebra.

She had no knowledge of numbers beyond marking them and no expertise whatsoever. Fractions lay outside the realm of anything she had ever been educated in, and she went after them in pursuit of a boy's life.

Long division became integral to a fourteen-year-old's chances, a small nightly revolution in one damp room, and she practised it like a girl with a forbidden piano, learning on Tuesday what she must impart on Thursday.

Everything depended on nobody asking one question, and the boy asked none. He worked it out, of course. He began arriving at ten to six, reading the day's work aloud first, before the dictation, never asking why. "No soft pencils," he said. "I have a preference." She had no preference to offer him and let him keep his hard ones.

"You can read me," she told him once, and despised the sentiment of it at once. "You can read me," he said back, and read. He received it with a nod, as a man receives a tool. It was a solitary arrangement, and they were both solitary in it. Nothing romantic; a stove and two people being careful.

The ninety-four days were spent by Bodkin in a state the staffroom called beneath its breath the Siege. The county was coming: curriculum, basic standards, equipment, whether the third-years could find their own region on a map, whether the junior intake was counted within the fortnight. A mission statement drafted by the deputy and distributed in triplicate contained the word productivity four times and the word child once.

Pook was a politician of the kind Wrayford breeds in damp weather, short and ripe and redolent of committee rooms, whose politics came down to being present at whatever may later be called a triumph. He was responsible for several good things, including the lights at the Grange Street crossing, but his political instincts were sharp about any room he had not licensed.

At an evening meeting Pook presided to explain that a survey is no judgement upon anybody's profession. "Nobody pays her," he said. "Nobody counts her. Then nobody can defend her." Pook went home and wrote a letter, because a woman nobody pays for is easy prey for anyone aiming to promote himself by being seen to protect children.

The county man came on the second Tuesday of November in a grey car. That morning she knew; she always knew. No saliva at all, the ceiling jogging faintly, fingers not to be trusted twice, so she fastened every button slowly and walked up Cutler's Row in her wool coat, and stood before the second year at nine exactly.

She could not read. Not the register, not the board, not the opening line of the passage she had chosen, chosen because she knew it by heart and could therefore be trusted with it. Mr Pike sat at the back with a clipboard; on her desk lay the textbook open at page forty-one, a sham of a prop.

"Books shut. This is dictation. Pens when I start, down when I stop, no catching up, no looking over. This is not a test of memory. It is a test of listening, which is half of comprehension and none of the examination."

"Shut your eyes," she said. "Say what it was about." "The canals," someone said. "And the barges," someone else said. Then she put a single word on the board in her own hand: because. Twenty-five minutes she spent asking everything that one word can be made to do, and forbidding writing about transcendental sunsets.

Twenty-eight pupils responded as one animal. It was the best hour anybody in that room ever had in a classroom, and it was done entirely in the dark. "Worth a satisfactory, then?" "Satisfactory," he wrote, twice, and wrote that the session showed careful preparation, an adequate vocabulary, the department helpful, the librarian candid to indiscretion.

On the last page, small: The teacher did not look at a single printed word in fifty-five minutes. I have seen this twice in thirty-one years and never once been wrong about what it meant. Nobody trouble her. — G. Pike.

"A reprieve," said Bodkin, not rejoicing, having learned that she could smell comfort at forty paces.

Pike stayed behind when the others had dispersed, shut the geography room door, and asked his sly question without softening it: unable to read the textbook, or unwilling? "Unable. On Tuesdays." He did not react. He nodded.

"Do you want me to write it down? There is a promising young man in the county office emerging into an opening for exactly this kind of finding, and he would enjoy it." "Not yet." "Why not?" "Because there is one boy a chapter behind me, and I intend to be a chapter ahead of him until March."

"Then write nothing," she said. He looked at her a long while, tucked his clipboard under his arm, and wrote nothing for ten weeks. The historical record suggests a professional man who had once been unable to do something himself; he knew the breadth of what can be lost in eleven working minutes.

It was the powder that finished it. She had left the tin in her desk drawer on the Friday, and by eight the signs were on her. Dry mouth. Sliding words. Pressure behind the eyes. By twenty past eight Arthur Kew had decided, with the ruthless logic of fourteen, to go and get it. The window had been jammed open since September by Denny Pratt.

He was coming back along the corridor with the tin in his pocket when Mr Knapp, the caretaker, returned for his teeth and put a torch in his face. The police were extremely nice; there is a kind of policeman who grasps at once that this is not his evening, and Wrayford had two.

They stood in the Kews' kitchen holding their caps while Marla came off nights and heard what her son had done and why. "You idiot," she said to him, then to Miss Vail in the doorway, then, wildly, to the police.

He felt himself a traitor to the one teacher who had assumed he could learn. "You never told your mother," she said. "She would have killed me." Marla Kew knew nothing of the inside of a teacher's head, and he swears that was how it was meant to be.

By Tuesday Pook had rallied a committee and delivered a discourse on standards using the word minors eleven times. It became a scandal in the way small things do when a politician needs a staircase. Rage came afterwards, at himself, at being called a thief, and worst of all at being caught doing something nearly kind.

His reign as chairman lasted nine years and produced one idea: a teacher who cannot be counted cannot be defended. He gave his temper full rein.

The Board met on Thursday. "I will stop the evenings," she said. "Then the minutes will say so," said the clerk, "and the minutes will be read." They could not accept, since to accept would admit there had been something to stop.

So she resigned, though the Echo's word was sacked. A younger teacher waited to displace her by Easter, and she wanted no revenge, did not expect Pook to repent, and would not obey a rule she judged stupid. Six weeks on she was the recipient of a county letter requiring two textbooks back, a wall map and one tin mug.

She walked to the pub and sat under the sign of The Royal Ox until Bodkin came in with two half-bitters, and the whole business had begun to shrink to a paragraph by then. The six-o'-clocks stopped coming at six, and came at midnight instead, over the wall, each contributing a penny a week toward the coal, never asked.

What finished her was not the resignation. It was that the work was what held her up, and nobody was left to notice the difference. She fell on the sixteenth of December, walking home past the cemetery on the slippery path above the rails, twenty minutes after dark.

There was a prick at the back of the skull, then a widening circle of nothing, then gravel. Marla Kew, coming off nights, sat her up in the road and gave her the whole of her mind about a town that lets a woman teach for thirty-one years and then lets her fall over in the dark.

They admitted her that night to the department serving the whole region: a long ward with a radio that played a symphony at ten and nothing at eleven. Someone took her pulse every four hours, someone came for blood, and a senior doctor examined the back of her eyes and said hmm in the voice of a man pricing a secondhand bicycle.

"Nothing malignant," he said. "And talking?" she asked. "Beneficial, they tell me." He said functional, and nervous, and at your time of life, which she took with the gratitude of a person who had not known she was afraid.

Thirty-one years of keeping it to herself, he explained, was a form of repression he had read about in a periodical and half understood; patients often did well with psychiatry. "And how many of those winters was it?" he asked. She said nothing. He wrote the number down himself.

It was Halloran who dealt with him. She arrived next morning carrying five shoeboxes and set them on the bed. "Here. Read." Thirty-one years of weather, one line a day, dated. Whatever else illness is, it leaves a record: the hand steady while the sense goes out of it, then the letters crowding, then the slant, then nothing until March.

The young man read eleven of them, went quietly pink, and said recurrence twice. He wrote out a prescription and a regime of powders at a strength she had never been able to afford, a dark room, and one instruction she has kept ever since: tell one person immediately, every time. He offered reassurance and went away.

Recovery was not quick; she was slow to recover, and was rebuilt by a woman with five shoeboxes and a grudge. Fear occupied the room where language had been, and there was no quiet anywhere in that ward, and less in her head.

On the twenty-third, at six in the evening, with the symphony on and the man opposite asleep, Arthur Kew came in with a paperback. "Same arrangement?" "Same as ever."

So it ran backwards: he read aloud about engines and weather while she instructed him, fifty minutes at a stretch, to a ward with nothing else to do. The nurses drifted over; the man opposite asked for the second volume. Nobody could digest a chapter until they had heard it twice.

"Eleven pounds," Artie said, looking at the gate. "Where from?" "Savings," she said. Eleven pounds she did not have, most of it the coach, and she did not tell him that part. They came for the orientation talk in a hall the size of a chapel, where a learned man told three hundred parents how their children would be taught to think.

Afterwards they strolled the campus: a fountain full of somebody's detergent standing two feet proud of the ground, dorm windows drying socks in every one. "Did you finish it?" "No. Eleven minutes in, I stood up and walked out." Noticeboards advertised documentary films, a symposium on water, a theological society, a society arguing for a republic, and nine ways to take credit for a module.

The great hall was where the chancellor presides each June over the handing out of diplomas; they never went near it. She had walked out eleven minutes into a final examination in her last semester and never returned for the paperwork, which is what happens to the frightened and the proud. Her undergraduate thesis, comprehensive and trivial, about canals, with a bibliography of four pages, sat unfinished under her bed.

They had come for a lecture: Professor Emeritus Ludo Crayle, who had flown mail planes over water for eleven years, was to speak in the aeronautics department on what really kills engines. In the third row, in his new spectacles, Artie did not stir for fifty minutes.

Afterwards he walked to the front, the only walk he ever called difficult, and asked the question he had saved. "Could I do it if I am no good at the numbers?" "No." "I thought not." "You could do it if you learn the numbers, and there are not many."

"Aviation is elementary arithmetic with a disaster attached to it, which is why anybody bothers to learn it. Come on Thursday." He went on Thursdays for two years, then applied. The reference came from a one-eyed lunatic in aeronautics who wrote that Kew had the hands for it and the temperament for it and no fear of being corrected, the rarest trait in thirty years of applicants.

He was admitted in the autumn, having scraped through the medical with eleven seconds of eyesight to spare, and money toward the tuition. He wrote and told her. "Well," she said aloud in the empty workshop. "That's that." It was not that.

When he came to say goodbye she gave him her father's fountain pen, black, its nib renewed every year since 1974, which he had expected her to keep and she had expected to keep, and neither said a word about it. He went down Cutler's Row with his kit on his shoulder, turned at the rail at the top, lifted one hand, and she lifted hers.

Two things remain. The first happened ten years afterwards, in the great hall in June, before the chancellor, thirty-one years late. She had finished the thing in the shoebox, an Elementary Account of the Water-Roads of the North, which the examiners called authentic and nobody has read except an examiner, a professor, and Arthur Kew, who read it to her aloud over eleven weeks while she checked it by ear.

When her name was called, fifty-one people stood up, eighteen of them strangers to Miss Vail. They were six-o'-clocks grown to full height, in suits and uniforms and one fish-van: a vicar, a woman pilot, Denny Pratt with his own diploma in a tube, Maisie Toll with handwriting still resembling a plan of the cemetery.

"Are you here?" someone asked at the back. Arthur Kew, unable to sit down, said nothing. Eighteen in all: somebody had counted. Five hundred more, with ninety qualifications between them, could not be there. The Echo ran it under the word HEROINE, which repelled her so violently that she regretted reading it; she insisted the word be used of the aircraft, which had in truth been somebody's friend.

Second is the board on the door. Still black, still her hand, reading now, the last line added the year she came home, because paint runs: Nobody is an idiot at six o'clock. Bring a pencil. Leave your shame on the step. No money. Ever. My eyes are tired, bring yours.

"Licensed?" asked whoever came next. "Licensed," she said. The workshop is a registered evening recreation class now, with a license framed by the door, in accordance with everything that ever frightened Arnold Pook. There is a stove, and not a cent has ever changed hands in it. Every teacher there knows the first rule, the second and the third.

There is a fourth, never written down, which the room runs on anyway: if somebody else's eyes are tired, you read.

We were not making anything up, Hesper Vail wrote in the flyleaf of her own weather book, on the last day she could see the page perfectly. We were simply the only two who knew which of us was being taught.
chapters.translation:
「我照着黑板抄的，」阿蒂·邱说，「一个字不落。一个词我都没读进去过。」

门上那块黑板，字有一个巴掌那么宽：六点钟这儿没有白痴。 底下小一号，因为黑漆流了下来：带支铅笔。把羞耻留在台阶上。 最小的一行是：不收钱。永远不收。

「铅笔，」她说，「你没带。」

他走下台阶，转回来时手里捏着一截铅笔头。墓地旁那间铺子五点就关门了，所以这一趟是从家里花了一便士；那一便士的事她没问。

作坊就在她父亲房子的后头，卡特勒巷最底下那一段。特伦斯·维尔从前拿卡尔德那个泥坑里的黏土，做成一摞摞烟囱管。最冲的味道是湿泥，窗框在悄悄发朽。他死后留下的是一台转盘、一台炉子、一张拉碾的公牛照片，还有一本记着老主顾的账本。

「免费吗？」头一个星期，那几个男孩就问。「免费。」「那她图什么？」「问她去。」他一句也没跟他们讲。三十一年，他给一学期的课当牛马，坐在同一个舒服的坑里，那股对教书的热情印到纸上，难看得很。

「势利眼，」韦斯先生在她背后说，「你教的是让人扔掉的一群，还管这叫事业。」「一文钱都不收，」她对送煤的说，「不收学费。一文钱都不经手。三十一年，从来没挣过一文钱。」每年十月到次年三月，她把那炉子点着，谁来教谁。谁最快读完一页，星期五就多发一块巧克力。

「这就是她全部的法子。督学的本子上记着，看着挺吓人。六点班的不是聪明孩子；他们是那地方扔掉的那些。」「我能把一台发动机拆开，」丹尼·普拉特说，「那就把说明书念一遍，」她说，「你去哪儿也找不到发动机这种东西。」拉奇家的几个男孩站得笔直，慢，对那条狗很和气。

最糟的还有阿蒂·邱，全年级阅读分最低的那个，十四岁，皮，点子多，对机器全是感情。第四节课上他的肚子按时按点地咕噜，节奏规整得叫人丢脸。他妈玛拉在医院的洗衣房上夜班加班，睡觉拿卷起来的袜子塞住耳朵；他爸坐着货车往西去了，再没绕过那个弯。

「十四分，」她说，「你想当什么？」「飞行员。」「那你就得把数字学明白。」「数字我认得。是字母我不认得。」他说得平平淡淡，一点羞耻都没有。她就是凭这个看出来，他身上攒了多少等着来的难堪。

十六年前，她十九岁，大学二年级，读英语，脑子里有东西忽然松了。她本来在教室后排的讨论课上抄一段课文，忽然那些字母发滑，像浸了水的铅字，顺着纸面往下淌。

那阵子长了十一天，把她往后剩下的书全赔进去了。她管这叫天气；每到暗下来的季节它就回来，除了她最要用的那一点功能，别的全放过。「我能听出他在作弊，」她常说。这话是真的：一个男孩念书，她听得出来他哪儿抄的。

她丢掉的是纸。印的字变成黑刺莓，撑不住那个深度，而且一到傍晚就加重。过了好些年她能想起一张脸，偏偏想不起那道没算对的算术；她记得最清楚的，是第一条规定。

于是她每天早上抄一行枯燥的话，写上日期，再去面对学生之前就知道自己今天能不能读。五只鞋盒就这么搁在床底下。「鞋盒里是什么？」有一夜洗衣房干到很晚，玛拉·邱问。「没什么，」她说，「旧纸。」

药片成了她放不下的一件事。唯一的方子是那种粉剂，格兰奇街上老派头的霍洛兰医生给她开的是一周两包。两倍的剂量会要命；可必须在发出警告之前吃下去才管用，而买了保险、付了送煤的钱之后，价钱就吃掉剩下的一多半，所以她只吃一半。

钱还流到别处去：八十本平装书，阿蒂帮她卸箱子，还有学校的旧衣铺——六点班有一半是谁也没给做衣服的。她的嘴干得像块布；到了中午口水一点不剩，往里头塞什么压嘴，胃就反什么。「我只是会过日子，」她告诉迪尔太太，「就这么回事。」

出事是秋天第三个星期的某个星期二，雷德福中学的理解力那一周。维尔小姐夹着一支紫钢笔在桌子中间走。阿蒂卷子上写的，跟他旁边那女孩一字不差，连「驳船」的拼写都跟着她错。

他抄的，自己认了，而且抄得很急。这一点她判成更重的那条罪。「抄来的答案，」她说，把两张卷子并排放下，「比答错的还响。答错是个事实。这是对我眼睛的意见。」

他的脸僵成湿砖那个颜色——二年级最讨人嫌的那个男孩。她说话的时候他一直不看她，可大多数撒谎的人是直勾勾盯着你的。

「作弊也是一种纪律，」校长博德金先生说，「那就得有文书，还得有家长签字，按郡里的规矩来。」他的副手韦斯先生说得更轻松些，因为他开了个补习班，一人十一先令——他算术里有个漏洞，而且多少知道有这个漏洞。

「交给我，」博德金说，「每天放学，到圣诞节。」「你的作坊？」「我的作坊。」「九十四天，保险挪不出这么大一块。」「我没让保险挪。我要的是那个男孩。」

博德金爱规矩，别的男人爱花园就是这么爱。他让了步，让错了方向，同意的时候压着嗓子，心里其实明白。这事就定得很难看，条件是谁都不许写下来；她走的时候恨不得离他近一点。他回家坐了一个钟头，写了一封从没寄出去的回信。

他差两分钟到六点来的，穿一件小了两号的粗毛线衫，两只手缩在袖子里，还有一身他不肯承认的哆嗦。从台阶上望出去，整个镇子的全景一直落到蓄水池。

她坐上去烧水壶；屋里一圈灯光，五把椅子，一杯可可，一点也压不下他身上的干。「念念，」她说，递过去一页。他念得漂亮，圆，稳，逗号都照规矩停，像一个人念自己喜欢的时刻表。

「说的什么？」「没什么。」「不是没什么。这是个要点。你复述一遍。」那男孩做不到。要旨一点没有，一个领域都没有；换一页，再一次拒绝。有一本百科全书他能背下来，可一句也概括不出；他的无知是九英尺没有焦距的空气。他的脚趾在地板缝上碾来碾去，开口之前先静了一阵。

「我看不见黑板。耳朵好使。」

「你能看多远？」「四英尺。再远就没有。」「去年的图表呢？」「我过了。我是倒着念的。」「为什么？」「我爸说戴眼镜是软蛋人才干的事。」「那你信了他五年。」这再简单不过，可她白瞎了两个学期。

她摘下自己的老花镜，推过桌子。度数不对，他得把头往后仰、眯起眼才看得清；字从黑里一点点慢慢浮上来，她把笑憋了回去——然后他说了一个那个屋子里极少听见的字。

「哦。」

散了以后他臊得厉害，走一路都在生她的气。没人愿意让一个早该看出来的人递给你一副眼镜；他讨厌靠别人的施舍过活。

这副眼镜走的是学校助学金，按规矩办的。博德金悄悄一手张罗，只说自己有责任，自己负这个责，别的不再谈。他其实也有一个非说不可的义务，于是拿锅炉的事搭了个话茬，把这事一直拖下去。

「九十四天以后，郡里的来人，」他说，「名单上你排第三。」她倒茶，倒到一半提醒自己：他是来给个信的，不是来抓人的。

三个星期以后，当着那男孩的面，事情发生了。他们正啃一本天不亮借来、八点前要还的课本。他把卷子推过来，等她说一句不对；结果发现她把纸拿得太远了。

一点预兆都没有。她早上那一行照旧写了、署了日期、又念了一遍，样样在序。她看得见形状。他写的那些字她一个也读不出。「写的什么，说给我听。」「我照黑板抄的。」「照样说一遍。」

于是他说了。她听懂了，指出他错在哪儿。到了星期三她明白，不先学会，下一单元她就教不了。每天十一点四十五，炉子压好火，帘子拉上，她自己啃一章，好让星期四那天比阿蒂·邱多懂一章。

没有什么比一页代数更能逼出人的极限。她除了打分对数字一无所知，也完全谈不上有学问。

分数除法落在她所受过的全部教育之外；她去追它，是为了一个男孩的前程。竖式除法从此成了这个十四岁孩子全部的指望，是这间潮湿屋子里每晚一场小小的革命。她练它，像姑娘偷练一架不许碰的钢琴——星期二学的，星期四就要讲出去。

全靠没有人问那一个问题；那男孩一个字也没问。他当然心里有数。他开始六点差十分就到，先大声把当天的功课读一遍，再开始听写，从来不问为什么。「别用软芯铅笔，」他说，「我有我自己的偏好。」她拿不出什么偏好给他，随他留着那几支硬芯的。

「你念给我听，」有一次她跟他说，说完立刻嫌这句话太肉麻。「你念给我听，」他回了一句，然后就读。他点头接过去，像一个男人接过一件工具。这桩往来是孤的，他们两个在里面都是孤的。没什么情爱；一个炉子，两个人互相小心着。

那九十四天，博德金过得像受围。办公室的人管这阵子压低嗓子叫「围城」。郡里要来了：课程、基本标准、设备、三年级的能不能在自己国家的地图上找出本地区、新招的初中生这半个月里有没有点清。副手起草、一式三份发的那份使命书，「效率」一词出现了四次，「孩子」一次。

普克是雷德福那种阴雨天养出来的政客，矮，熟，一身的会议室气味；他的政治全在于：什么事情以后能叫「政绩」，他就要在场。他也办过几件好事，包括格兰奇街口那几盏灯；可凡是他没发过许可证的屋子，他的政治直觉就锋利得吓人。

一个晚上开会，普克主持，讲一份调查不算是对谁职业的判断。「没人给她开钱，」他说，「没人数她。那也就没人护着她。」普克回家写了一封信。因为一个没人付钱的女人在别人看来是块好咬的肉——那人只想靠「保护孩子」把自己抬上去。

郡里那位是十一月第二个星期二来的，坐一辆灰车。那天早上她就知道；她每次都知道。嘴里一点口水都没有，天花板轻轻晃，手指头使第二回就不作数。于是她一个扣子一个扣子慢慢扣好，穿毛大衣沿卡特勒巷走上去，九点整，站在二年级教室里。

她读不了。点名册读不了，黑板读不了，连她自己挑的那段开头一句也读不了——挑它是因为她背得熟，这样才敢用在课上。派克先生坐后排，抱着一块写字板。她桌上摊着课本，翻到四十一页，是个假得不能再假的道具。

「书合上。今天听写。我开始你们下笔，我停你们收笔，不许回头补，不许翻看。这不是考记性。这是考听话——听话是理解的一半，考试里一点不含。」

「眼睛闭上，」她说，「说一说刚才讲的是什么。」「运河，」有人说。「还有驳船，」另一个人说。然后她用自己手写的字在黑板上落下一个词：因为。二十五个分钟，她就围着这一个词问它能干的所有的活，还禁止他们写落日那种超脱的东西。

二十八个学生像一只畜生那样一起应声。那是屋里所有人上过得最好的一节课，而且全程在黑里做的。「给个「合格」，行不行？」「合格，」他写了两遍，还写上：本堂课准备认真，词汇量够用，本组配合，图书管理员坦白得有点没分寸。

最后一页上，字很小：这位老师在五十五分钟里没有看一眼任何印出来的字。三十一年我见过这样的事两次，从来没判错过。别去难为她。——吉·派克。

「算宽赦了，」博德金说。他并不高兴，因为他早就知道，隔着四十步她就能闻出安慰是什么味儿。

别人散了以后派克留下来，关上地理教室的门，把那个滑头的问题原样问出来：是读不了那本课本，还是不肯读？「读不了。星期二读不了。」他没反应。

他点了点头。「要我写下来吗？郡办公室里有个挺有出息的小伙子，正等着这类发现腾出位置，他会乐坏的。」「还不到时候。」「为什么不到时候？」「因为有个男孩比我落后一章。到三月为止，我都要比他快一章。」

「那就什么都别写，」她说。他看了她很久，把写字板夹在胳膊底下，十周一个字没写。后来留下的材料说，这是个正经职业人，自己曾经有一件事干不成；他知道十一个小时上班时间里能丢掉的东西有多大一片。

把事情彻底推过去的是那罐粉剂。星期五她把铁罐落在抽屉里。到了八点，症状全挂在她身上了。口干。字发飘。眼睛后面有压。八点二十，阿蒂·邱拿十四岁孩子那股不讲情面的理路，打定主意去把那东西拿来。那扇窗打九月起就让丹尼·普拉特顶着开着。

他揣着铁罐顺着走廊往回走，管理员纳普先生回来取假牙，正好一道手电照在他脸上。警察非常好。有一种警察一眼就明白今晚不是他的班；雷德福有两个。

他们站在邱家厨房里，手里捏着帽子和玛拉一起等她下夜班回来，听她儿子干了什么、为什么干。「你个傻瓜，」她先冲儿子说，冲门口的维尔小姐说，最后发疯一样冲警察说。

他觉得自己对不起全年级唯一一个相信他能学的人。「你从没跟你妈说，」她说，「她非掐死我不可。」玛拉·邱不懂一个当老师的脑子里装着什么；他赌咒，事情本来就该是这个样子。

到了星期二，普克已经拉起一个委员会，做了一场关于标准的长篇讲演，「未成年人」这个词用了十一遍。这事闹成风波，是靠一件小事在有政客要台阶下时那种长法。火气是后到的——对自己发的，对被人叫小偷发的，最难堪的是被人撞见一件几乎还算好事的事。

他当主席坐了九年，只弄出一个想法：一个不算数的老师，就没人护得住。他的脾气被放开了全套。

校务会星期四开。「我要把晚上的课停了，」她说。「那会议记录上就这么写，」书记说，「而且会议记录是要念出来的。」他们不能接受。接受了就等于承认本来有东西该停。

于是她辞职了——虽然《回声报》用的字是「被开除」。有个更年轻的老师等着复活节把她顶掉。她不报复，也不指望普克悔过；一条她判断为蠢的规矩，她不肯听。六个星期以后，她收到郡里一封信，要她还两本课本、一张挂墙地图、一个白铁缸子。

她一路走到皇家公牛酒吧，坐在招牌底下，等博德金端着两杯半品脱的苦啤进来。到那时候，整件事已经开始缩成报上一段了。六点班那几个人不再六点来了。他们改在半夜翻墙过来，每周出一个便士凑煤钱，谁也没问过他们。

真正把她撂倒的不是辞职。是那点活儿撑着她，如今没人剩下的工夫去看有什么不一样了。十二月十六日，天黑二十分钟以后，她抄近路从墓地旁边回家，走在铁轨上方那条滑的路上，摔了。

后脑勺先是一下刺，接着一圈空白慢慢散开，然后是碎石。玛拉·邱刚下夜班，把她扶坐在路当中，把一整座城的怨气都倒给她：一个女人教了三十一年书，然后由着她在黑地里摔倒。

那天夜里她被送进管整个片区的那家医院：一间长长的病房，十点放交响乐，十一点就什么也不放。每四小时有人来摸一次脉，有人来抽血。一位老医生翻看她眼睛的内侧，嗯了一声，那声音像在给一辆旧自行车估价。「没有坏东西，」他说。「那说话呢？」她问。

「说有好处，」人家这么跟她说。他说的是功能性的，神经的，还有到你这个岁数——这几句她接过来，接得真心存的，就像一个人到这会儿才发现自己原来一直怕着。

他解释说，三十一年一个人闷着不说，是一种压抑；她在某本期刊上读到过，只明白了一半；精神科对这类病人常常管用。「那些冬天，到底有几个？」他问。她不说话。他自己把那个数写上去了。

是霍洛兰去对付他的。第二天一早她抱了五只鞋盒来，往床上一放。「给。念。」三十一年的天气，一天一行，都署了日期。病不管别的，总留一份记录：手还是稳的，意思先走了；然后字挤成一堆，再然后歪斜，再到三月之前什么都没有。

那年轻人念了十一本，脸悄悄红起来，「复发」说了两遍。他开了一张处方，还有一套吃粉剂的规矩——浓度是她从来负担得起的那种；一间暗屋子；还有一条她从此一直守着的话：每次都要立刻告诉一个人。他给了她几句宽慰，就走了。

好得并不快。她恢复得慢；把她重新搭起来的，是个带着五只鞋盒和一股怨气的女人。恐惧住进了语言腾出来的那间屋子。那间病房里哪儿都不安静，她脑子里更吵。

二十三日晚上六点，交响乐放着，对面床上那人睡熟了，阿蒂·邱拿着一本平装书进来。「还是老样子？」「老样子。」

于是事情倒着走：他念发动机的书、念天气预报，她在一边给他讲，一口气五十分钟，讲给一间无话可做的病房听。护士们飘过来；对面那人要第二卷。一本书得听过两遍，才有人消化得下去。

「十一镑，」阿蒂盯着大门说，「哪来的？」「攒的，」她说。十一镑她根本没有，大头是助学金；那一截她没跟他说。他们来听入学介绍，在一间和礼拜堂一样大的厅里。一位有学问的人对三百个家长讲，他们的孩子以后是怎么被教着去思考的。

之后他们在校园里慢慢地走：一个喷水池里满是别人家的洗衣粉，整座池子高出地面两英尺；宿舍的窗户，每一扇都在晾袜子。「听完了吗？」「没。听了十一分钟，我站起来走了。」

布告栏上贴着纪录片、一场关于水的研讨、一个神学社、一个争共和的社团，还有九种为一门课的学分争功的办法。大礼堂是每年六月校长发文凭的地方；他们一次也没靠近过。她最后一个学期曾在一场期末考里走到第十一分钟站起来走了，从此再没回去办手续——胆小又要脸的人就是这么收场的。她的本科论文又全又碎，写的是运河，参考文献四页，还摊在床底下没写完。

他们其实是来听讲座的：荣休教授卢多·克赖尔，飞了十一年海上邮机，要在航空系讲什么才能真正弄死一台发动机。第三排，戴着新眼镜的阿蒂，五十分钟一动没动。

讲完他走到最前面——这是他唯一一次说「走这段路真难」——把攒了很久的那个问题问出来。「我要是数字不行，还能干这个吗？」「不能。」「我就知道。」「你要学了数字就能干，而数字也没多少。」

「飞行其实就是一道会出事的算术题，正因为这样才值得学。星期四来吧。」他连着去了两年星期四，然后报了名。推荐信来自航空系一个独眼的疯子；信上说邱这只手生得合用，性子也合用，还不怕被纠正——三十年的申请者里，这一条最稀罕。

秋天他收到了录取，体检是压着线过的，剩十一秒的视力余量，还有一笔抵学费的钱。他写信告诉了她。「嗯，」她在那间空作坊里大声说，「就这么着了。」并不是就这么着了。

他来告别那天，她把父亲的那支黑钢笔给了他，笔尖从七十四年起年年换。他原以为她会留下，她原以为自己会留下；两个人都一个字没提。他背着行囊沿卡特勒巷往下走，到顶上那道栏杆拐过身，举起一只手；她也举起了自己的那只。还剩两件事。

第一件在十年以后，六月，大礼堂，校长面前，晚了三十一年。鞋盒里那本书她写完了，叫《北方水路初级志》。考官说它是真的；除了一个考官、一位教授和阿蒂·邱，没人读过它——他在十一个礼拜里念给她听，她用耳朵一句句校。点到她名字的时候，五十一个人站了起来，其中十八个跟维尔小姐并不相熟。

那是长个子后的六点班：穿西装、穿制服，还有一个人开一辆卖鱼的货车。一个牧师，一个女飞行员，丹尼·普拉特（自己的文凭卷在筒里），梅茜·托尔（字还像那片墓园的一张平面图）。「你在吗？」后排有人问。

阿蒂·邱坐不住，一句没说。一共十八个，有人数过。另外五百个，合起来有九十张文凭，来不了。《回声报》把这条新闻压在「女英雄」这个标题底下；那词让她反胃到后悔自己看了。她坚持这个词该用在飞机上——那架飞机真正当过某个人的朋友。

第二件是门上那块黑板。还是黑的，还是她的手写的，如今读得通了。最后那一行是她回来那年添的，因为漆会流：六点钟这儿没有白痴。带支铅笔。把羞耻留在台阶上。不收钱。永远不收。我的眼睛累了，把你的带来。

「有执照吗？」下一个人进门就问。「有，」她说。如今那作坊是一堂正式备案的夜校文娱班，门上架着框好的执照，样样都合阿尔诺·普克当年吓破胆的那套规矩。有一台炉子。从来没过一文钱在里头经手。每个在这儿教书的人都懂第一条、第二条、第三条。

还有第四条，从没写下来，可这间屋子照样靠它活着：要是别人的眼睛累了，你就念。

我们什么都没编，赫丝珀·维尔在自己那本天气笔记的扉页上写道，那是她最后一天把纸看得很清楚的日子。我们俩只是仅有的两个，知道到底是谁在被人教。

chapters.title: 钟表匠之死
chapters.content:
He died among his own gears. Forty-one clocks stood round him on their shelves, and not one of them was running. I turned a wheel over with two fingers. It rolled off the bench and stopped against my shoe. "You haven't touched anything," Sergeant Halloway said. "Not yet. I touched it coming in. Nine feet from counter to wall. It is a narrow room."

She let that go. I appraise the goods of dead men for Mordaunt and Leaf, auctioneers of Hollowmere, an inland town set in a saucer of drained swamp, in a locality where no floor has ever been horizontal. This urban little valley bred watchmakers the way other places bred bakers. The damp gets into the joints of a house and the joints of a man.

"How long has he been down there?" "Since overnight. Nobody heard him." "No one hears him," I said. "That is the trouble with clocks. The tower rang him at eleven. Eleven of what?" "Of everything else. That is the one thing the Board will not write down."

The tower stands on St Aldous, a cathedral in name and a shell in fact. A bomb destroyed its roof on a Tuesday in 1941, and the destruction took eight minutes and sixty years to mend badly. The remains went to the Hollowmere Preservation Foundation, founded the year the pits closed: a secular trust, four paid staff, eleven volunteers, a quarterly forum, and a quarrel nobody has won.

"Does the canon know the time?" "He knows whose. That is the whole town's trouble; there are two of them and the valley has never settled it."

The tower held a great clock of 1791: hands the length of a forearm, a pendulum rod sturdy as a fence post, a weight of some eighty thousand gramme that needed two men to heave. A full winding lasted eight days, poor endurance now and a boast in its own era.

An ancestor fitted a new escapement in 1889 and was never paid, owing to a churchwarden who died in debt, so the Quillets came back every generation to collect. Ambrose climbed to it every Thursday from fourteen, three thousand climbs in one careless lifetime. At fifty, in his prime, he could wind forty-one clocks in eleven minutes.

He had been married eleven years and widowed thirty-one, with no children, and the tower was wife to him in turn. He never surrendered its key, and no one ever got it. The Foundation voted for a modernization of the tower. The strategy was plain: a sponsor, a plaque, a tea-room with no purpose but tea, space for the occasional concert, and a small theater nobody would fill.

"A tea-room," Halloway said. "In a town that runs on water and a lean." They erected a scaffold in a fortnight, put up a temporary hut for the men who built it, and into the belfry went a biscuit tin: an electronic unit that listens to the national signal and corrects itself, a solenoid to strike, and a speaker playing a recording of the lost bell.

"So we don't get a bell any more. We get a memory of a bell." The papers said eleven thousand visitors would enrich the town, a figure no reliable person could trace to a source and never correct.

Nothing here forgave that speaker. It was the cheap counterpart of everything the modernization had done, and since it switched on, Hollowmere heard on the hour not a bell but a memory of one.

Ambrose was pensioned as Honorary Keeper, a rank with no authority, and given a carriage clock and a farewell card signed by eleven, two of whom could not spell his name. "Where is his card?" "On the shelf, above the nineteen." He kept it there.

His acceptance took four seconds and eleven months, and he told Mrs Tebbit he felt persecuted by people who did not know they were persecuting him. "Feels persecuted," she said. "Then let them persecute him somewhere else."

In his capacity as Keeper he had no duties, so he made one. On the Thursday after he retired he set every clock in his shop eleven minutes slow and held them there. No one permitted it and nobody prevented it, and his landlord Boggis found the row favorable to trade.

"What is that for?" "So the shop keeps Hollowmere time. When it is noon here it is eleven past in London. London can wait."

That was all he meant. But the card left the town with two honest times, so no one could say when anything happened without answering one question, namely whose clock. Everything I am telling you took place in the epoch that card opened, and the sometime keeper had eleven months to live.

The shop stood on Crowstep Lane, ground floor of a medieval wool store, a blackened beam overhead, a floor of blue tile hollow in patches. In 1840 a drainage board took the bends out of the river and six inches out of the parish, and thereafter every floor in the old quarter leaned toward the water.

In the whole period he owned it the place was never spacious. He owned forty-one clocks in a set order written in a cloth book he called the Order, and each had its line. The four slow ones lived upstairs.

When he wound the last he wrote one word: bed. The span of that round, nightly, was fifty-two years. His hands were deformed by fifty years at a bench, the little fingers hooked like question marks, and lately the stretch took twice as long, which he treated as nobody's business.

To watch him was to watch a ritual older than the wires in the wall. At nine by his clocks he took the winder, opened the regulator, wound, drew one breath, and moved along the shelf in a sequence invariable since 1971.

"He is punctual to the minute. You can set your watch by Quillet's shadow." A recurrent joke on Crowstep Lane, and he was impatient when his hands lagged.

What preceded the round never changed: post face down, a look at the sky, half a minute still. He invariably stopped at nineteen to put the kettle on, and invariably worked right to left. "Right to left, or you will have the devil's own mess."

He tolerated no help and believed in no genius, only patience, and his father's little hammer of forty gramme, with which he tapped a case shut when it was good and open when it was not.

One precaution he kept fifty years, the only effective one I know: nothing belonging to a customer was ever wound without a note. He never learned to roll a cigarette, so the shop smelled of tobacco and oil in that order.

Infinite patience. He could sit with a hairspring for a week, and his only pastime was argument, pursued at leisure, like someone with all the time in the world.

His apprentice could do the round in the dark. Tobias Cree is twenty-six and has wound that house since fifteen, and Ambrose noticed what that meant. "He is not clever with his hands," Tobias said once. "But he never leaves one out."

Ambrose enrolled exactly one apprentice in fifty-two years and never said a kind word. Tobias's initial job at fifteen, unable to spell more than his name, was sweeping.

In his first month he took apart a toy nobody had asked him to touch: a clockwork tiger of painted tin, kept in a glass case and refused to every dealer. It was the only object in the shop never priced.

Tobias dropped a wheel into the mud on his shoe, wept, and spent that winter learning what the inside of anything looks like. He persevered, and the perseverance was the only useful thing he brought.

When the tiger walked again, Ambrose watched it cross the counter. "That will do. Put it back." "Yes, sir." On the Thursday before he died he signed a will leaving everything to that boy, and told him nothing.

The row began on the eve of Easter, Maundy Thursday, when half the shops shut and the children came in from the outskirts. The Cask held a darts tournament no one has won twice.

"Half the shops shut and you could not buy a pie." "You never could on Maundy Thursday. That is what pies are for." The perpetual argument about the hour is the local staple. The council cleared a slum here years ago and moved everyone four miles off, to a place still called Newtown.

Cyrus Quillet, the nephew, sells second-hand tractors off the bypass and lives in a suburb called Bramble End. "Sixty thousand," he said. "Forthcoming." "Forthcoming in what?" "In a deal. You would not understand a deal."

He got nothing, a lecture on durable goods and undurable men, and left shortly before eleven, returning at a quarter to twelve to apologise. "You are sorry now," Mrs Tebbit said. "You were not here an hour ago."

Ned Pargeter, a plumber fitting a stopcock next door, heard through the wall a young voice asking and an old voice refusing, in the flat parallel rhythm of a quarrel they had had before. "I caught no words," Pargeter told Halloway. "Just a moan with an edge on it. I took the young voice for the lad's." "The lad was on a bus." "So they say."

Halloway saw Tobias at Cobb's Cross in the rain, hands in pockets. "Out at twenty past ten," she said. "Thirty-three minutes for the bus. His card tapped. Chips on his grandmother's sofa. A stadium poster over him. The rural bus was a destiny of its own that night."

"And his grandmother says he was home before the news. She would have scolded him for the bus." "She would. She has known him from birth." At eleven exactly, as the speaker played its small memory across the valley, Ambrose set down his winder, took the brass key, and went to the foot of the staircase.

The obstruction was his own. Three weeks earlier he had carried two boxes of stuff to the top room and set them on the turn. "My legs are feeble," he told Mrs Tebbit. "I will move them at the weekend." She never heard him say it again.

"That is your obstruction," Halloway said. "He never moved them. He put his foot on the third step, caught a box corner, stumbled, and went forward with both hands out." The damage to the man was done in the first second; the damage to the clock was nothing at all. He thrust out his arm. He fell. He broke his wrist against the wall.

He was eighty and thin as a winder. There was a momentary silence, then the house went on ticking. "Eleven minutes to eleven," I said. "And the house went on." "It does," she said.

He did not die then. He lay at the foot of his stairs four hours and twenty minutes, awake for most of it, listening to the house ticking and to the tower calling eleven, twelve, one, two. Four hours elapsed. Nothing exciting happened that night, nothing overnight, and no medicine could prolong what the floor had begun. That, in the end, is what happened to him.

Somewhere in that long duration he found something sharp and cut four marks into the paint of the skirting, each with a vigorous stroke, and a fifth begun and left to run sideways. "What do they denote?" "I don't know that. I only know he counted something."

He died near twenty past three. The police surgeon put it down to the head injury, worsened by exposure on a cold floor. "She put the time first. Ten to eleven. She is not foolish."

Then someone said murder. Easier to say than prove. Three facts were available to anyone who could read: Cyrus was sixty thousand short and had quarrelled with his uncle; the old man had signed a will to the apprentice and not to his own blood; and owing to one card the file held two times no one could tell apart. "Sixty thousand short," Halloway said. "A will. And two times."

"Twenty-nine minutes is plenty for a strong young lad to go back and forth, push an old man down his own stairs, and stand at a bus stop looking ordinary." "Against a boy with a will in his pocket, twenty-nine minutes is overwhelming. That is not a lapse in the file. That is a card in a window."

That morning the Foundation wrote, prompt as ever, to notify the executors that the premises must be inspected, and asked me to call at ten. Mr Mordaunt, my superior, whose eyebrow does his thinking, told me to be prompt, not to linger, and to act on behalf of the executors.

I had snatched a nap in my van, changed into clean jeans, and walked up with a tape, a camera, and written permission to look at anything. "Whose paper?" "Mine. It says anything. Irrespective of who objects."

Canon Preece brought his keys. He had been the last priest the town employed, and he kept the ruin, the storage room, three unidentified swords and two Home Guard spears. He says the socialism left this valley with the mines, and nothing replaced it but heritage, which pays worse and argues longer.

"I call the board a senate." "You call it a senate. I call it four men and a postbox." With him was Mrs Tebbit, who came twice a week to dust and called herself Ambrose's maid, though she was plainly independent and his match.

Cyrus arrived. "What do you think you are doing in my shop?" "I am making a list." "Whose list?" "Mine. With a pen that writes."

I got on with it. With the door shut the shop was a vacuum: nothing flowed, nothing glided across a dial, no footstep in a house whose clocks had stopped. Chalk marks were everywhere, a lump of plasticine where a print was lifted, the glitter of broken crystal in the boards. Some want their proof visual. I photograph everything first. Nothing in that room moved.

"Every clock in this room is eleven minutes slow." "He has told us that for eleven months," Mrs Tebbit said. "We only started listening in March." None had stopped together, but all forty-one agreed within twenty seconds, and the whole house lag eleven minutes behind my telephone. By dusk I had the shutters open and forty-one faces before me.

Owing to the swamp nothing here has been level, and a pendulum out of plumb lies. "Nothing here is level," I said. "He levelled them anyway." "With a spoon," she said. "And cold coffee." He synchronized forty-one machines in a house that tilts.

"A spoon for a ruler. Do you want that written down?" "Write it. That is the trade." He had made two honest times in one town. "Apprentice walks out at twenty past ten." "By the shop. Twenty past ten by the shop."

Quarrel heard at ten thirty-five, card tapped at seven to eleven, fall at eleven, nephew out at ten fifty-eight. Read the right column and Tobias is clean.

Correlate the ticket machine with the plumber's van and the signal and you reach the conclusion the police should have reached: the lad was miles away when his master fell. Read the left column, which every witness spoke from, and the alibi collapses. "And the left one?" "The one every witness spoke from. The one that kills."

Twenty-nine minutes. A temper. A hundred and eighty yards. A will. Read either column about the nephew and something else appears: on whichever clock you use, Cyrus left two minutes before the old man fell. "Arguing with a dead man's ledger is a poor tactic," Halloway said. "What would you write?" "Interesting."

I wrote that on the back of a bill and went upstairs. The boxes still sat on the turn of the staircase, two cases of catalogues and thin layers of brass, in their own track in the dust. Meanwhile the rain did what March does to a market town.

There had been no push. No one else was on those stairs. "Four feet wide," I said. "Nobody else was on it." Ambrose tripped over his own housekeeping: a minor tragedy nobody writes down, and the missing item on an inventory is always where the money went.

I knelt at the foot of the stairs and found what Halloway had missed: four marks, and a fifth running out. The Order lay open, and Thursday's page held forty-one ruled lines, a tick beside each.

"Who ticked them?" "One to thirty-three in soft graphite. And thirty-four to forty-one in blue ballpoint." "Pressed, slanting wrong, made by a man against his nature. Underneath, in pencil: done. bed." Someone had finished his round, and understood that forty-one ticks meant the old man was up and about past eleven, uncommonly organized for a corpse. I glimpsed the whole shape of it then.

What that someone did not know was line thirty-nine. Number thirty-nine is a small dial clock Ambrose had stripped to its frame on the preceding Monday, because the great wheel had worn oval. "And thirty-nine?" "A clock with no wheels. It could not have been wound."

Its movement stood in three pieces under a cloth, and there is no winding a clock with no wheels. Whoever ticked line thirty-nine had never touched it. "Then who ticked it?" "Someone with a biro, four hours, and a reason."

The watch explains why. It lay in a tray beside a magnetic dish of screws, intact but for its glass. A case of that age will withstand a fall; this one did, and the glass did not, cracked in one clean slit from the rim across the little window that tells the day.

The hands said ten to one and the window said THU 28. Those cannot both be true. A calendar is driven by the works, not the hands; the hands can lie, the little day wheel cannot. "You can corrupt a witness. Can you corrupt a calendar?" "No. And everyone who read it hitherto read the hands and stopped."

Four hours and twenty-eight minutes is what he gained. One death, and another death. The gap between them was ninety-six thousand pounds that year, because a transfer made to the nephew seven years earlier fell out of the tax man's account the instant the clock passed midnight.

Once the lawyers deducted their share there was still ninety thousand, and no decrease anyone in Bramble End could shoulder. He had demanded sixty thousand on Thursday and been refused.

By Friday he stood to keep ten times that, if only the hour would turn, and Ambrose's own body had done his arithmetic all night. He simply had not finished the sum before midnight. He had brought the old man six cups of tea and not one word of comfort.

I keep a picture I cannot rid myself of. A man comes back at a quarter to twelve to say sorry, and finds his uncle at the foot of the stairs. Alive. Cold. Whispering. He understands at once that the old man is finished and that at midnight the seven years run out. He kneels.

He is not a man to fling money away. He sits down beside it, and at that instant decides that thinking is not doing, the sort of thought that has spoiled more lives than speed has.

Then he stands and rings no one, and lets a cold floor finish the job, then walks the shop giving the house one more turn and finishes the round with a biro from his pocket.

"Everything he wanted was going to happen anyway. All he had to do was walk out." "He might have rung a doctor. What he did was nothing." Halloway came back, sat where I sat, read my column twice, and had to summarize it into four lines, a summary she did not enjoy giving, for a chief inspector on the telephone.

"Cree taps his card at seven minutes to eleven." "Yes." "And the old man falls at eleven." "At eleven. Simultaneous with nothing at all, five feet from his own stairs." It took forty minutes to be heard and three hours to free him, and in the meantime he had sat eleven hours in a cell.

He came out blinking into the wet evening, grey and hungry, unable to stop looking at his hands. "Are you okay?" He nodded without speaking. The first thing he asked about was not himself.

They detained his cousin on the Tuesday. The day wheel did most of it, and the fifth scratch helped. You cannot say he was cold and gone when I got back when four cuts say he was alive at two in the morning. The biro helped. It was a bank pen with the branch printed on the barrel, the sort of luck that favours the police.

The rest he confessed in four tedious hours on tape, in a low voice. He denied everything for an hour, which is characteristic; then he denied nothing, which is also characteristic. There was no murder charge, for there was a plain deficiency of proof, and I do not think anyone wanted one.

He faced the lesser business, tending to pervert the course of justice, and the harder thing that is no charge at all: he bent over his uncle, heard the breath, and sat down to think about money.

The judge did not punish him as hard as the street wanted. Eighteen months. There was adverse comment about the call no one made. He was fortunate in his solicitor and unfortunate in all else.

For a week the town ran a fever of opinion, and the sentence was reported in one local paper under a headline about a tragic end to a Hollowmere tradition, the ending no one in my trade believes.

The inventory took eleven days. My interim figure came to nine hundred thousand, inclusive of everything, a great deal of money for forty-one broken machines, a box of springs and a tin tiger, though the density of worth in that room was higher than its weight.

The Foundation bought the lot for an enormous sum from a grant nobody can explain, though its destination had been settled in pencil fifty years before. It opened as a museum, admission free. By every measure but his own it is a success, and nowadays it is the most visited small museum in the county. Tobias is the keeper now. Presently he lives above the shop.

On Thursdays he climbs to the tower with his own key, which the trust did not want to give and gave in the end, after a mobilized campaign by the Cask's darts team, much persuasion from Canon Preece, and one vigorous letter from Mrs Tebbit.

Monthly, on the first Thursday, he lets the two clocks alternate, the network for the hours and his own for the first, in memory of a thing his master never apologised for. He keeps the Order going, and the forty-one lines, taken in succession, are the only tradition handed him.

Regarding the two clocks he has made his choice and will not discuss it. At the foot of Thursday's page, under a blue tick he will never remove, you can still read what Ambrose wrote fifty years ago.

"done. bed." We buried him a year later, in Easter week, on the wrong day, which everyone noticed and no one minded, because Hollowmere has never been good with calendars. It rained, and Canon Preece said what needed saying in a voice much diminished by the years, then did the bravest thing: he stopped, looked at his notes, and told forty people the truth.

Mrs Tebbit, who had been his maid for twenty years, was the only one who did not stare at the floor. "Get it out," Tobias said. He took the clockwork tiger out, wound it until it grumbled, set it on the edge of the memorial table, and let it go.

It walked the entire length with its tail swinging, and fell off the end into an elderly hand, and forty people who came to be miserable laughed out loud in a medieval building in the rain.

A spontaneous, indecent noise in a place that has heard little of either. It was the best thing since the pits closed. Eleven minutes is nothing. It is also eternal, if you are the man under it.

Nobody murdered Ambrose Quillet. He was killed by eleven minutes. By two boxes he carried up himself. By a man willing to sit and let an hour pass. Of those three the third is by far the most deadly, because it was the only one anyone had a choice about.

He did not deserve it, which is a different thing from saying anyone owed him better. That hour, and the man who let it pass, will be forever the part of the story nobody can unsay.

Two clocks can both be right, and a man can still be dead between them. That is why I now set my watch by the thing I can least afford to be late for.
chapters.translation:
他死在自己满地的齿轮中间。四十一座钟立在架子上围着他，没有一座在走。我两根手指把一只大轮子翻过来。它从台子上滚下去，撞在我鞋边停住。“你还没碰任何东西，”哈洛韦警长说，“先别碰。”“我进门就碰了。柜台到墙九英尺。这屋子窄。”

她没再追究。我是替莫尔当特与利夫拍卖行清点并估价死人遗物的，那家行号在霍洛米尔，一座排干沼泽后陷成盆地的内陆小镇，这一带没有哪块地板曾经水平过。这座城似的谷地当初养钟表匠，就像别处养面包师。潮气钻进房子的关节，也钻进人的关节。

“他在下面躺了多久？”“从昨夜起。没人听见。”“没人听得见他，”我说，“钟的麻烦就在这儿。塔楼在十一点敲给他听。十一点，是哪套时？”“是别的钟。这是董事会死也不肯写进文件的那一条。”

塔楼立圣奥尔本斯，名义上是大教堂，实际上只是个空壳。一九四一年一个星期二，一颗炸弹炸掉了它的屋顶，那场破坏只用了八分钟，却花六十年才勉强修好。残骸后来归了霍洛米尔保护基金会，那是矿场关门那年成立的机构：一个世俗信托，四名带薪职员，十一名志愿者，一个它非要称作论坛的季度会议，还有一场谁也没赢过的争吵。

“那个牧师知道几点吗？”“他只知道按谁的钟。这正是全城的问题；城里有两套时，这个谷地至今没定下来。”

塔上挂着一座一七九一年的大钟：指针有人的前臂那么长，钟摆杆结实得像根栅栏柱，一个约八万克的重锤要两个男人才抬得动。上一次满弦能走八天，如今算不得耐力，在它自己的年代却称得上夸口。

一位祖先曾在一八八九年装过一个新擒纵机构，始终没拿到工钱，因为经手的那位教区委员欠着一屁股债死了，于是奎利特家每代人都得回来讨账。安布罗斯从十四岁起，每个星期四都爬上那座塔，一生漫不经心里爬了三千趟。五十岁正当壮年，他能在十一分钟里给四十一座钟上完发条。

他结过十一年婚，守了三十一年寡，没有孩子，那座塔先后做过他的伴侣。他从不交出钥匙，谁也没拿到过。基金会投票要给塔楼搞现代化。策略明摆着：拉个赞助、立块铭牌、开一间茶室，留出偶尔办场音乐会的空地，外加一座谁也不会坐满的小剧院。

“茶室，”哈洛韦说，“在这种只靠水和稀粥过日子的镇子上。”他们两星期就搭起脚手架，给干活的人搭了间临时棚屋，钟楼里塞进一只饼干罐似的东西：一台电子装置，收听国家标准信号自行校准；一个电磁铁敲钟；还有一只扬声器，里头录着那只丢了的钟。

“这样咱们就听不见钟了。听见的只是一段钟的记忆。”报纸说这一万人次的游客能让镇子发财，一个数谁也追不出来源、而且从来没算对过。

这儿没谁原谅那只扬声器。它是那次现代化干的一切的廉价复制品。从它一开机，霍洛米尔在每个整点听到的都不是钟，是钟的一段记忆。

安布罗斯被养起来当名誉看守——一个没有半点实权的头衔——另给了一只旅行钟和一张告别卡，卡上十一个签名，其中两个连他的名字都拼不对。“他的卡片在哪儿？”“在架子上，十九号上头。”他一直把它搁在那儿。

他“接受”这件事，四秒钟就完了，十一个月才做完。他跟特比特太太说，自己被一群根本不知道在迫害谁的人迫害着。“受迫害？”她说，“那就让他们到别处去迫害他。”以看守的身份他毫无职责，于是给自己派了一桩。

退休后第一个星期四，他把店里每座钟都拨慢十一点，从此一直拨着。没人允许，也没人拦，房东博吉斯反倒觉得这一场吵闹对买卖有利。

“这是干什么？”“让本店守霍洛米尔时间。这儿正午的时候，伦敦已经是十二点十一分。伦敦可以等。”

他就只想干这个。可那张卡给一座镇子安放了两种都诚实的时间，于是此后谁也别说清一件事发生在什么时候，除非先答一个问题，即：按谁的钟？我要讲给你听的这一切，都发生在那张卡开启的那个时代。那位曾经的看守，只剩下十一个月的活头。

铺子开在克劳斯泰普巷，是一家中世纪羊毛仓库的底层，头顶一根熏黑的梁，脚下是东一块西一块空洞的蓝瓷砖。一八四零年，一个排水委员会把河弯裁直，也从教区里挖走六英寸的地基；自那以后，老城区的每片地板都朝水那边微微倾斜。

他拥有这地方的整段年月里，这里从来不算宽敞。他拥有四十一座钟，次序固定，记在一本他称作“秩序簿”的布面册子里，每座钟占一行。慢的那四座住在楼上。

给最后一座上完弦，他写一个词：睡。那一圈活计的跨度，一夜一夜，是五十二年。他的双手被台子前五十年弄变了形，小指弯成问号；近来这一圈伸展要花过去两倍的时间，他把它当作与旁人无关的事。

看他干活，就像看一场比墙里电线还老的仪式。按他自己的钟九点，他取下上弦柄，打开调速器，上弦，吸一口气，然后沿着架子走过去，那次序从一九七一年起就没变过。

“他守时到分。你尽可以按奎利特的影子对表。”这是克劳斯泰普巷一个反复出现的老笑话；他两手一滞，就急得不行。

那一圈之前的事也从不变：信正面朝下压着，抬头看一眼天，静半分钟。他总在十九分那座停下烧水，也总是从右往左干。“从右往左，不然你手里就得乱成一锅粥。”

他不许任何人搭手，也不信什么天才，只信耐心，和他父亲那把四十克重的小锤子——钟壳够好就敲上，不够好就敲开。

他守了五十年的一条防备，也是我认得的最有效的一条：凡是属于顾客的东西，上弦前必在簿上记一笔。他始终没学会卷烟，所以铺子里按先后次序闻起来是烟草和油。

无限的耐心。他能对着一根游丝坐一星期；他唯一的消遣是争论，在闲暇里慢条斯理地争，像个怀里揣着全世界时间的人。

他的学徒能在黑地里走完那一圈。托拜厄斯·克里今年二十六，从十五岁起就给这屋子的钟上弦，安布罗斯看明白了这孩子意味着什么。“他手不算巧，”托拜厄斯有回说，“可他从不漏一样。”

五十二年里安布罗斯只招过一名学徒，一句好话也没说过。托拜厄斯十五岁头一份活是扫地，连比自己名字更长的字都拼不出。

到第一个月，他拆开一个没人让他碰的玩意儿：一只上了漆的锡皮发条老虎，一直摆在玻璃柜里，对每个上门的贩子都拒售。它是这屋里唯一从不标价的东西。

托拜厄斯把一个小齿轮掉进自己鞋边的泥里，哭了，整个冬天都在弄明白一样东西的内部长什么样。他撑下来了，那股撑劲儿是他带过来的唯一有用的东西。

老虎又能走动那天，安布罗斯看着它走过柜台。“行了。放回去。”“是，先生。”他死前那个星期四，立下遗嘱把一切留给那孩子，一个字也没提。

风波起在复活节前夕，也就是濯足节星期四，半个镇子的铺子关门，孩子从郊区跑进来。卡斯克酒馆摆了一场飞镖赛，没人连赢过两次。

“半个镇子都关了门，你还买不到一个派。”“濯足节你本来就买不着。派就是派这种日子的。”关于钟点的永久争执是这儿的日常主食。议会多年前清掉一片贫民窟，把所有人迁到四英里外，那个地方到今天还叫纽敦。

侄子赛勒斯·奎利特在环城路外倒卖二手拖拉机，住在郊区布拉姆布尔恩德。“六万英镑，”他说，“快了。”“快在哪儿？”“在一笔买卖上。一笔买卖你不懂。”

他什么也没得到，只挨了一通关于耐用货和不耐用男人的训斥，十一点前不久离开，十一点三刻又折回来道歉。“你现在是来道歉的，”特比特太太说，“一小时前你还不在。”

内德·帕吉特是个水管工，在隔壁装一个截水阀，隔着墙听见一个年轻声音在问、一个老声音在回绝，一遍一遍，是一场上一次的争吵那种平齐的节奏。“我一个字也没听清，”帕吉特告诉哈洛韦，“只听见一声带锋芒的呻吟。那年轻声儿我当成了那小子的。”“那小子在辆巴士上。”“话是这么说。”

哈洛韦在雨里看见托拜厄斯站在科布十字口，两手插兜。“十点二十分出来的，”她说，“等了三十三分钟的巴士。卡打过了。薯条是在廷德尔巷他祖母家的沙发上吃的。头顶一张体育场海报。那趟乡下的巴士，当夜自有一份命。”

“他祖母说他新闻传出来前他就到家了。她早该为这趟车骂他一顿的。”“她会骂。她从他出生就认识他。”十一点整，当扬声器把那段小小的十一点记忆送过整个谷地，安布罗斯放下上弦柄，拿起那把黄铜钥匙，走到楼梯脚下。

那障碍是他自己造的。三个星期前他把两箱杂物扛上顶层，搁在楼梯转角，本打算周末挪开。“我腿软了，”他跟特比特太太说，“周末我搬。”她没再听他说过这句。

“这就是你的障碍，”哈洛韦说，“他没搬过。他踩上第三级，撞着箱角，一趔趄，两手往前扑出去。”对人的伤在第一秒就造成了；对钟的伤一点也没有。他猛地伸出胳膊。他倒下。他手腕砸在墙上。

他八十岁了，瘦得像根上弦柄。有那么一瞬的静，然后这屋子接着嘀嗒。“差十一分十一点，”我说，“屋子照走。”“它一直走，”她说。

他那时并没死。他在楼梯脚下躺了四小时二十分钟，大半时间醒着，听屋子嘀嗒，也听那座塔一声一声喊着十一、十二、一、二。四个小时流逝了。那一夜没什么叫人兴奋的事，一夜之间也没发生什么；而到头来，发生在他身上的就是这个。

那段漫长的持续里，他在某处摸到一件尖东西，在踢脚线的漆面上刻了四道痕，每一道都下笔很重，还有第五道起了头就丢开，往旁边斜着跑了。 “这是什么记号？” “我说不上来。我只知道他在数东西。”

他死于三点二十分前后。警察的法医把死因归到头部伤，又加上在冷地板上长时间受冻——法医的说法其实意思是：他被人撂在那儿了。“她先把时间放第一位。差十分十一点。她不糊涂。”

于是有人说谋杀。说起来总比证明容易。有三条摆在那里、只要会读就看得见的理由：赛勒斯短了六万英镑，又跟叔叔吵过；老人把遗嘱立给学徒，不立给自己骨血；还有，因为一张卡片，卷宗里躺着两个谁也分不清的时间。

“少六万，”哈洛韦说，“一份遗嘱。还有两个时间。”“二十九分钟，足够一个壮实的小伙子来回一趟，把老人推下他自己的楼梯，再站在站台上装得跟平常一样。”“对一个口袋里揣着遗嘱的小子，二十九分钟是压倒性的。这不是卷宗里的疏忽。这是一扇铺面窗里的卡片。”

那天上午基金会照例及时地写信通知遗产执行人，说这处房产必须勘查，并请我十点到场。我的上司莫尔当特先生——一个用眉毛替他思考的人——说，要快，别磨蹭，记住我们是代表执行人来的。

我在车厢里抢了个小睡，换了条干净牛仔裤，带着卷尺、相机和一张书面许可上门，看什么都可以，不管谁反对。“那是谁的条子？”“我的。它什么都能批。谁反对都不管。”

普里斯牧师自带钥匙。他是镇子雇过的最后一个牧师，守着那片废墟、那间储藏室、三把来历不明的剑和两支本土防卫军的矛。他说社会主义随着矿场离开了这座谷地，替上来的什么都没有，只剩遗产——工钱更差，吵得更久。

“我把董事会叫作元老院。”“你管它叫元老院。我管它叫四个男人一个邮筒。”跟他同来的是特比特太太，一星期来两次掸灰，自称安布罗斯家的女仆，其实明摆着独立，也明摆是他的对手。

赛勒斯到了。“你以为你在我的铺子里干什么？”“我在列一张单子。”“谁的单子？”“我的。一支写得出的笔。”

我干起活来。门一关，这屋里就是个真空：没有东西流动，没有东西在表盘上滑过去，在一座钟都停了的屋子里也没有脚步声。白粉印子到处是，一块取指纹用的橡皮泥团，木板缝里闪着碎水晶的光。有人要的是看得见的证据。我什么都先拍一遍。那屋里没一样东西动过。

“这屋里每一座钟都慢十一点。”“这件事他讲了一整年，”特比特太太说，“我们是到三月才开始听的。”没有一座是同时停的，可四十一座在二十秒之内彼此一致，整座屋子比我的电话慢十一点。到黄昏，我已经把百叶窗全打开，四十张脸摆在我面前。

由于沼泽，这儿没有一样东西水平过；一个失了铅垂的钟摆就是个骗子。“这儿没有一样是平的，”我说，“他还是给校平了。”“拿一把勺子，”她说，“还有一杯凉透的咖啡。”他让四十一台机器在一栋歪着房子的屋里同步起来。

“拿勺子当尺。这你要写进报告？”“写。这就是我这行。”他在一座镇子里放进了两套都诚实的时间。“学徒十点二十分出门。”“按店里的钟。按店里的钟是十点二十分。”

争吵听见是在十点三十五，打卡是差七分十一点，跌倒在十一点，侄子十点五十八分离开。看右栏，托拜厄斯干净。

把车票机跟水管工那辆货车跟信号对起来，你就能得出警察本该得出的结论：他师傅倒下时，那小子在几英里外。看左栏——每一位证人都照它开口——不在场证明就塌了。

“那左栏呢？”“每位证人都照它开口的那栏。要命的那栏。”二十九分钟。一场脾气。一百八十码。一份遗嘱。不论看侄子的哪一栏，另一样东西会浮上来：你用哪套钟，赛勒斯都在老人跌倒前两分钟离开了。

“跟一具死人的账本抬杠是下策，”哈洛韦说，“你打算写什么？”“有趣。”我把那两个字写在一张账单背面，上了楼。箱子还搁在楼梯转角，两箱目录和薄薄几层黄铜，在灰里压出自己的辙印。这当口，雨照老规矩泼向一座集贸小镇。

没有人推他。那段楼梯上没别人。“四英尺宽，”我说，“别人上不去。”安布罗斯栽在自己收拾屋子时绊在自家锅碗上——一场没人记载的小悲剧；清单上少掉的那一项，永远就是钱不见了的那个地方。

我跪在楼梯脚下，找到了哈洛韦漏掉的东西：四道痕，还有一道跑偏的。秩序簿摊开着，星期四那页有四十一道竖线，每条旁边一个勾。

“谁勾的？”“一到三十三号是软铅笔。三十四到四十一号是蓝圆珠笔。”“压得重，斜得歪，出自一个跟自己本性拧着的人写的。底下是铅笔：完。睡。”有人替他把这一圈干完了。有人明白四十一个勾意味着老人过了十一点还起来活动过——一具尸体这么有条理，可真少见。我这时瞥见了整件事的形状。

那个人不知道的是第三十九行。三十九号是一座小表盘钟，安布罗斯在前一个星期一把它拆到只剩框架，因为大齿轮磨成了椭圆。“那三十九号？”“一台没有轮子的钟。它上不了弦。”

它的机芯摊成三块，盖着布；没有轮子的钟是上不了弦的。勾第三十九行的人从没碰过它。“那是谁勾的？”“一个拿着圆珠笔、有四个钟头、还有个理由的人。”

怀表解释了原因。它躺在一个螺丝盘旁的托盘里，除玻璃外都好。那个年头的壳能扛住一摔，这一只扛住了，玻璃没扛住，从边沿裂开一道干净的口子，横过那个报日期的小窗。

指针指着差十分一点，表窗写着周四·28。这两样不可能都对。日历是机芯推的，不是指针推的；指针会说谎，那个小日历轮不会。“你买得通一个证人。买得通一本日历吗？”“买不通。而且到今天为止，每个看过它的人都只读了指针就停下了。”

四小时二十八分，是他挣来的。一次死，又一次死。这中间的差价那年值九万六千英镑，因为七年前做给侄子的那份房产转让，会在钟声越过午夜的那一刻从税务员的账上掉出去。

律师们扣完他们的那份，还剩九万；布拉姆布尔恩德没人扛得动这个数。他星期四张嘴要六万，被拒了。到星期五，只要钟肯走一走，他就能留下十倍于此。

安布罗斯自己的身体替他算了整整一夜的账。他到底没在午夜前把这笔算完。他给老人端过六杯茶，一句宽心话也没说。

我脑子里有一幅甩不掉的画面。一个男人差一刻十二点回来道歉，看见叔叔躺在楼梯脚下。活的。冷的。在气若游丝地说话。他一下子就明白老人完了，也明白到了午夜七年就到期了。他跪下去。

他不是个把钱甩着扔的人。他坐到钱旁边，就在那一刻认定：想不等于做——正是这种念头，比速度害死的命还多。

然后他站起来，没给任何人打电话，让一块冷地板把活干完；之后绕着铺子再给这屋子上一回弦，从口袋里摸出圆珠笔，把这一圈收了尾。

“他想要的每一样，反正都会发生。他只需走开而已。”“他本可以打电话叫医生。他做的事是——什么都没做。”哈洛韦回来，坐在我的位置上，把我的表读了两遍，还得给电话那头的警督归纳成四行，一份她并不乐意指出的摘要。

“克里，在差七分十一点打了卡。” “对。” “老人十一点跌倒。” “十一点。跟什么都不在同一时刻，离他自己的楼梯五英尺。”要有人肯听，花了四十分钟；要放出人来，花了三小时。这中间他在号子里坐了十一个小时。

他眨着眼走进湿漉漉的傍晚，脸色灰白，饿得发慌，止不住地看自己的手。“你还好吧？”他点了点头，没说话。他头一个问起的不是他自己。

他们在星期二拘留了他的表兄。那个日历轮做了大半贡献，第五道刻痕也帮了忙——当踢脚板上的四道刻痕说他在凌晨两点还活着时，你很难再说“我回来时他已经冷了、没了”。圆珠笔也帮了忙；那是一支银行笔，笔杆上印着分行地址，是那种只照拂警察的好运。

剩下的是他在磁带前用低嗓子坦白的，四个冗长乏味的小时。他头一个小时否认一切，这很符合他的性子；然后他什么都不否了，这同样符合他的性子。

没有谋杀指控，因为证据存在明显的不足，而且我想没人真想要一个。他面对的是轻的那桩——妨害司法；还有更难的那桩，根本算不上指控：他弯下腰，听见叔叔还有气，然后坐下来盘算钱。

法官没有按街坊的意思重罚他。十八个月。关于那通没人打的电话，有难听的议论。他的律师让他侥幸，其余一切让他不幸。

整整一个星期，镇子陷入舆论的发热；那份判决登在某家本地报上，标题写的是霍洛米尔一门传统的悲惨收场，这个结局，我这一行里没人真信。

清点花了十一天。我交出去的初步数字是九十万，什么都算在里面——对四十一台破机器、一盒发条和一只锡皮老虎来说是大钱，可那屋里价值的密度比它的分量还重。

基金会用一笔谁也解释不清的拨款出了个吓人的数目把全部买下，尽管这一切的去向早在五十年前就用铅笔定死了。它开门成了博物馆，免费入场。拿除他本人以外的一切尺子量，它都是成功的；时下它是全郡人数最多的那家小馆子。托拜厄斯现在是看守了，眼下他住在铺子楼上。

每个星期四他带着自己的钥匙爬上塔楼——信托起初不肯给，后来还是给了，起因是卡斯克酒馆飞镖队发起的一场动员、普里斯牧师好一番说合，还有特比特太太一封很硬的信。

每月第一个星期四，他让那两座钟轮着走：整点用网络，头一个钟点用自己的，为的是记念他师傅从没道过歉的那一桩。秩序簿由他接着记下去；那四十一条线，一条接一条，是他接过来的唯一传统。

关于那两座钟他早就做了选择，不再谈。在星期四那页的页脚，在一个他永不抹掉的蓝勾底下，你至今还能读到安布罗斯五十年前写下的一句话：

完。睡。我们在一年后的复活节那一周埋了他，日子还选错了，人人都瞧出来，却没人在意，因为霍洛米尔向来不擅长对付日历。下雨了。普里斯牧师用被岁月掏得大不如前的嗓子说了该说的话，然后做了那天最勇敢的一件事：他停住，低头看看笔记，对四十个人讲出了实话。

特比特太太做了他二十年女仆，是四十个人里唯一没盯着地板看的。“拿出来，”托拜厄斯说。他把那只发条老虎取出来，上到它咕噜作响，摆在纪念桌的边沿，撒手。

它甩着尾巴走完全张桌子的长，从尽头掉进一只年迈的手里；四十个本来是来难过的人，在一栋中世纪的屋子里、雨中，放声大笑。一种自发的、不成体统的响动，在一个两种都不常听见的场合。这是矿场关门以来这边最好的一件事。

十一点钟算不得什么；如果你是躺在它底下那个人，它也是永恒的。

没人谋杀安布罗斯·奎利特。他是被十一点钟杀死的，被他自己扛上楼的两只箱子杀死的，也被一个肯坐着放过一小时的人杀死；这三样里，第三样远为致命，因为它是唯一一样需要有人主动选择的事。

他并不该落得如此——这和“有谁欠他更好的下场”是两回事。那个小时，以及放着它溜走的那个人，将永远是这个故事里谁也收不回去的一块。

两只钟可以都对，而一个人仍可能死在它们中间。所以我现在去对表的时候，挑的是我最耽搁不起的那一件事。
