chapters.title: 九十岁的马拉松
chapters.content:
"Ninety," said the postman, dropping a package on the rug. He had a van, a dog, and a jacket with a pen in the pocket. "They still hand out racing bibs to ninety, you know." Mabel Quill was ninety, and she had been sewing for this rural parish since the mill closed. She saw no reason to stop.

Inside was a biography of her late husband, published by the parish, and a note about the old Ridge Run. "Read it," the postman said at the door. "Half the parish has read it." Mabel scanned the first page, then the second, then the first again.

Under a tidy pile of textile scraps she found her husband's typewriter. A page sat on the roller, dry as a bone, and at the top one unfinished verse: Run the stride that outlives the body; all the rest is vanity.

She read the words twice, laid it by the fire, and looked at the cat. The roller still turned when she pushed it with one finger.

"A poem," she said. "And a curtain for a back." Outside, a sparrow took its morning bath in a puddle by the step. The cat watched from the stone windowsill while the kettle sang on the stove and the lane outside stayed asleep under a violet dawn.

Ned had been gone twelve years. The mill had closed, the school had shrunk, and most of her friends had retired to the coast to be near their children. The post came late in the winter now, and the bell at the parish church had a crack in it that sang flat.

His boots stayed by the door, not for his return but for the shape they gave the empty floor, and the usual quiet of the cottage held that shape like warm water in a cup.

"Still at the needle, then?" Mrs. Alder teased her at the gate every morning. "You'll have the whole parish in rags one day." "Only the ones who come back," said Mabel. "The rest I kept."

Her fingers knew the work better than her eyes did. A coat, a curtain, a seam let out twice, a button sewed back on where the dog had taken it, and the mending kept half the village warm for a crust and a cup of tea. She had raised two children here, buried a husband, and watched the trees at the garden's end go from sticks to shade.

In that winter she had walked ten miles a day to the river, pregnant, a tin of biscuits in her coat. She remembered her paternal grandfather, a versatile man who joined a bowling league and played volleyball with the boys, and the thief who took her purse on that very lane.

Poppy, her little princess in a paper crown, called the wicker chair by the fire her throne. Mabel guarded her privacy as the last thing the years had not removed. The women of Cedar Fell were gone, and it was a fine life, slow but steady, held by the ordinary quiet.

The biography was wrong about a dozen things, and the desk had forgiven none of them. What it did not lie about was the score: at three miles Ned had led the competition by a full mile, and then he had to withdraw to help a pedestrian who had suffered a fall by the fence.

Ned had been the fastest and the most notable runner Cedar Fell had ever had, until bad luck and not bad legs had stopped him. "He withdrew," she said aloud. "After leading by a mile. At his age. At his best age."

The record shed no light on the reason yet, and the page after it was blank. She sobbed into her sandwich, a small honest sob, and the kitchen filled with the smell of rain over the distant hills.

She phoned Dr. Iris Hale, the specialist and surgeon who had mended her knee, and the clinic screen showed an old scar from that surgery. Hale had opened half the village and argued with all of it.

"As a rule," said Hale, "I recommend rest. I will restrict you, and I will refuse." "Refuse?" said Mabel. "You haven't even watched me run." "I don't need to watch your knees," said Hale. "They are sore, your breath is scarce, and you are susceptible to a strain that tips into a second stroke."

"One mile," she said. "The Ridge is five." "One mile at ninety is a stroke waiting," said Hale. "Give me the tablet and the therapy," said Mabel. "And keep the watch, not the race."

Hale was smart enough to be kind. She gave her a tablet of vitamins and a specific therapy, and warned her that the symptoms of a syndrome she would not name would spiral without care. Mabel said nothing. She put Ned's watch in the safe and retorted that the ruler on the wall measured nothing of the heart. The clinic never rang back, and she never phoned again.

She would not qualify by the clinic's rules. She would qualify by will. No result from a machine would restrain her.

The next morning she went to the village hall to register for the Ridge. Nobody clapped, and nobody even looked up. There was a mat, a broken pen, a notice about the sweeping rota, and a list of names belonging to men who had never come back from the war. The clerk rejected the form twice on her behalf and said one thing only.

"It says ninety," the clerk said. "It says a fall." Then she handed Mabel a pencil and turned away.

The next morning Theo Vance came, a thin young man with a satchel and a calm way of speaking. "I came home to look after my grandmother," he said. "She fell ill from sitting still. I see too many people lost to a chair."

"I see one kept from it," said Mabel. "That's your job. Mine is the knees. Are you telling me no?"

They walked the garden while he watched how she moved, and he made notes in a small book. He had a sister in the city, no wife, no children, and a pair of old running shoes kept for the sake of them. He did not laugh at her plan. "What do you hope to prove?" he asked. "That I can finish," said Mabel.

"Then we start at dawn," he said. "Will you supervise it?" "Every morning."

His grandmother sat in the same chair at the same hour. The wireless clicked, and the old woman's hands went flat on her knee. It ran on without them. "She has not stood in a year," Theo told her. "Say something to Mabel." The old woman raised her eyes. "Run, then."

The plan was simple on paper and hard in the body. He timed her with a cheap watch and wrote the numbers down as if they were gold.

By the third week she could feel the difference in her knees. "You don't have to come out," she said on the mornings she did not want to leave the house.

"I'll stand at the gate," he said. "You'll come out. Or I won't come in." She opted to train, knowing the difference between a plan and a wish. She would prepare each dawn, optimize her optimum pace by a process she could control, and place herself under the intensive care Theo offered twice a week.

Her primary and practical plan was settled: pray before the mirror, utilize the garden rail, and dictate her own small laws. She had a resolution, and a quest she would not name to the women at the gate.

"Time is at a premium," she told him. "I knew poverty as a child. Do not let age overturn me. Do not let it overthrow me."

A calm permeated the cold field. When Theo asked about the grammar of effort, she laughed and told him the plural of stride is strides, and she meant to make many. The special quality of that dawn was a wind off the Pole that turned her ears red and made the work real. The grass was wet on both sides of the path, and the wet did her good.

The training was a string of strenuous mornings. She yawned, pulled the zip of her jacket up to her chin, and selected her shoes. He waited by the gate with a whistle. "Shoulders down," he said. Then she rotated her ankles, rubbed her knees with liniment oil, and paused to relax her tense shoulders.

"Rub them," he said. "Slowly. Press them into the bone." She did as she was told, and the liniment went in warm. Each morning the same small orders, and each morning a little further than the last. None of it asked for courage, only for the next dawn.

After that came the slow arithmetic of mornings. A few minutes here, a few yards there, a hill they would not skip, and she swayed her arms like a pendulum and pumped them on every step. "Forty," Theo counted. "Forty." He wrote it in the book with a pencil down to an inch.

The following morning she skipped once and scrambled up the stone bank, then tossed her head against the whip of the wind. A rabbit startled her and scattered the sand from her shoe. "Watch the nettles," said Theo.

A nettle sting made her quiver, and she sneezed in the cold air. Dogs barked across the field, and a kite stayed stuck in the elm. She shoved the rusty gate that hung on one loose screw, and the rust came off on her fingers.

Later she passed the shuttered shed where the slaughter had once been, and she puffed up the split in the road to tackle the hill her friends said to avoid. On the stool by the door she stitched a glove and felt a stitch of pain, a sudden stab, and then nothing.

She winked at her own wrinkled face in the kettle lid, and the wink came back at her. Before a run she ate peas from the garden and drank a pint of milk and a quart of water. The cat followed her to the gate and turned back at the step.

Her breath grew stable. Sudden cramps came and reversed, and she repeated the repetition until the motion took hold and the pace would stick. "Again," said Theo. "Again." In retrospect every small succeeding step had been a significant thing, and not an ounce of that week had been lost.

She was prone to doubt, reluctant to hide a grin, and vocal about the stupid fear that the warm bed would tempt her. The gate had a hinge that sang, and it sang on the mornings she almost turned back. "Let the town subsidize my entry," she said. "But the stakes are my own pride." "The sacrifice of comfort is no substance to me," she added. "I have seen worse."

A torrent of rain vibrated the pane. She trailed the quiet path at a pace her spirit could sustain. The road ran beside the field, and the field had never once let her down. "Oldest in the northern hemisphere," a passerby said, touching his cap. "Good luck to you." The news went round, and passersby began to salute her each morning. She nodded back. She nodded at everyone.

The women at the gate had long since given up guessing. She kept her own small map in her head, and outside it there was only the road and the weather.

She segregated the field in her mind by courage, not age, and chose a remote refuge of quiet when the uproar of doubt grew loud. She did not tell the parish about the verse. That one was hers alone. At the sermon that Sunday the vicar spoke of the long race, and Mabel toned her legs and ticked the days on a clear calendar within a radius of a mile.

"Ninety is not the point," he said from the pulpit. "Stopping is." She sang half a line of it and forgot the rest, which seemed fair.

The primitive pump in the yard still worked, if you had two hands and a shoulder. A rope marked the start of the field, where she would press her palms together and postpone the moment no longer. The cold would stimulate her lungs. She would rush nothing, and she would signal her own small wins with a nod.

Down at the lane the smell of bread mixed with the river and the cut grass. An old man with a dog nodded as she passed. "Going far today?" he asked. "To the hill," she said. "And then further."

She made a game of it. Each post was a small country, and by the time she reached the hill she had visited ten. The cold air rose off the water and caught her cheeks, and she learned to breathe through it low and slow.

Her shadow walked beside her on the grass, long in the early light, and she talked to it as if it were Ned. In June came a setback. Her knees were sore again, a trouble she could not name, and she sighed in sorrow in her chair by the fire.

Sweat stained her shirt. The garden gave her lettuce and a few torn leaves, and the lettuce kept her going. A vague memory of the threat of a stroke made her pause. The hill felt tough. She took the entry form out of the trash, looked at it, and gave it one rip into the trash again.

For a week she stepped back and let the garden be her refuge, until the removal of her fear came slowly by a subtle change in her gait. "A setback is a turn, not an end," Theo reassured her. "On the worst days we substitute a walk for a run." "Not despair," she said. "Just the next morning."

Her legs thrived again, slower, and she fixed the process until it held.

Poppy came after school with a drawing of a woman with very long legs and a medal around her neck. "This is you," said Poppy. "Winning." She kept the drawing rolled in her pocket next to a dead dandelion.

Mabel pinned it above the fire, where it joined the bills and the recipes, and she told the child about the winter she made a whole coat out of three old coats.

The week went by in the kitchen, sorting buttons and threads and watching the rain write its small script on the window. She had mended more seams than that in one winter, and still the parish had not gone cold.

That pain was not the sharp kind that warns. It was the dull kind that simply stayed, a visitor with no manners. But the visitor left when she began again, and she marked the day the fear lost its lease. That bed had other names, and one of them was Saturday.

Back in the yard the women of Cedar Fell had made her a light shirt with her name on the back and left her a tin of biscuits. The baker kept a loaf each morning. "For the old lady," the baker told the queue. "She's running the Ridge."

Even the councillor's office sent a letter, and it said only that the path would be swept. Mabel read it twice and laughed twice, because a sweep of a path is the smallest kindness and sometimes the largest.

What underlies her will, she saw, was not vanity but unity: a collective promise to the man in the verse. The book showed only half of it. Ned had not merely withdrawn; he had witnessed the child of that pedestrian saved, and had counted the sacrifice worth what it cost him.

She retrieved the watch from the safe and wound it, and its tick was a small signal that time could be held. It went on a cord now, and the ticking kept the house company after dark. She would run not to win but to finish what he had started, and there was a principle in it: a true will can propel a solid frame.

The secret he had carried was this, and the reveal made her sob again. Somebody had to finish the sentence, and nobody else had picked up the pen. She left an oral account of the day for the parish, and not an ounce of fear remained in her.

On the morning of the Ridge Run the atmosphere was splendid and the sky a crystal blue. "Balloons," said a girl. "And a band." Balloons rose over the green, and the contest drew a crowd whose uproar she could hear a street away. The race had prestige across the county. A man sold coffee from a folding table and called the cup a victory.

Councillor Bramwell, a local statesman, opened it and saluted the oldest runner with a small crystal trophy he did not yet know she would take. "Mabel Quill!" shouted the provocative reporter. "Why run at ninety?"

"Because ninety is where I stand," she retorted. "The noteworthy thing is that I refuse to quit." "Would you take a trophy?" he pressed. "Nothing that fits in a box," she said.

Cameras rolled. A video of her warm-up would spread worldwide, and a paper would publish and publicize the story by night. She was a striking sight before she moved at all, and the skill of her calm was its own superb answer. The photographer asked her to smile; she asked him to hold the gate.

The green filled with people in bright clothes, and two boys raced a pram up the bank and lost. She found Theo by the fence. He raised a hand. She raised hers. "Ninety," he said. "And here you are."

That morning the teacher brought her class down to the green and set them in a ragged line. "Numbers first!" she called. "Then noise!" The children shouted until the band stopped playing, and Mabel shouted with them, which made a passerby cheer.

She bathed her face in the cold river before the start, then found a vigor that felt vital. She stood vertical and sustained a rate her spirit could hold, breathing in rapid, scarce pulls of air. Two swallows argued over the awning of the school, and the sun was warm on her back. A classmate of Ned's, now ancient, waved from the fence.

"There he goes, the young lad," said the old woman, meaning Ned. "Still leads, doesn't he, your husband?" She leaned on the fence with both hands and laughed at nobody in particular. Theo predicted, correctly, that she would finish.

At the first mile a young woman in a red shirt fell into step beside her. "You'll finish," the young woman said, and then dropped back. She counted her breaths the way Theo had taught her, and the counting made the distance a thing she could eat one spoon at a time.

A child offered her a sweet and she took it, laughing. The crowd along the route grew thicker as the miles fell away, and people leaned from gates and stood on low walls.

Then a small girl in a red hat ran beside Mabel for a few steps, then fell back laughing, and the laughter followed her like a gift. Thin voices were lifted over the noise, and the sound of it caught in her throat.

At the water stop a boy pressed a cup into her hand without a word, and she drank. The cup was cold and the water was colder. The simple act, a cup, a hand, a nod, seemed to contain the whole of what the town had become to her.

She thought of Ned, somewhere ahead in the story she was finishing. There was no bell at that corner, no band, no banner, and she liked the plainness of it. The distance had never been the point. The point was the moving, the refusing to sit, one step after another.

The last mile had no gate and no wall and no shadow, only the road, the river, and the longest hill Cedar Fell had to offer.

That hill before the finish was the worst, everyone said so, a short steep wall that tested the slow. Mabel took it the way she had taken everything that spring: one stride, then the next, then the next.

The crowd rose as she climbed, a wave of sound that seemed to lift rather than push. The final hill reversed every expectation. She propelled herself upward, utilized the garden rail, and the crowd screamed her name.

She crossed the line to a victory no scoreboard could show. Behind her the church clock gave its half hour, and a man was still running with a paper cup on his head. A woman in a blue coat kept shouting her name in the wrong order. It was the supreme moment of a splendid day and a superb proof that the true race is the one against the chair.

A woman at the fence wiped her eyes and shook Mabel's hand, and two small boys pushed a plastic cup toward her as though it were a crown. "Are you the ninety one?" they asked. "I am," said Mabel.

The watch in her pocket was a symbol of the precious, valuable thing she had witnessed in herself. Theo retrieved her, safe and sane, and the solidarity of the town came like warmth.

She had succeeded where the clinic had predicted she would fail, and the result was a significant sum of small stubborn steps. She left an oral word for the archive: not an ounce of doubt, only a vivid memory of Ned.

They walked home at the soft end of the day, Theo carrying the trophy she had at last been given, and Mabel carrying nothing but her own tired, happy weight. The street was quiet, a few lights had come on behind curtains, and she stopped at the gate to look back the way they had come. The hill had gone quiet again, the way hills do at dusk.

Down the street the baker was still at his window. "Did you see it?" he called from behind the glass. "I heard it," said Mabel. "From the bakery, I heard the whole thing."

The next morning she did not go to the road. She sat by the window with her tea and watched the light come, and the trophy stood on the shelf, not because it mattered, but because it proved a thing can be both true and small. She put a new button on a man's coat and thought about the road. The morning was pale and the road was empty. The milk came late, and the milkman waved from the van.

Somewhere a page stayed blank, which was its own kind of finished. Ned's boots were where they had always been, behind the door. In the quiet after, Mabel sat on her throne by the fire, a violet in her lap, and looked at the virgin page of the typewriter she would never fill.

She was sane, tidy, and ready to begin again tomorrow. The words had been right: the rest is vanity, but the stride is real.

What she had optimized was nothing but her own refusal to stop, and on the verge of ninety-one she felt a unity of body and will that no clinic could measure.

She had seen, at last, what underlies a long life: not the record of miles, but the will to take one more. Nine months later the paper came again, and the words were still on the desk where she had left them. She had started a sentence about the cold, and about the girl at the fence.

The stride outlives the body. The rest is vanity. I finally understand the verse — and the only race a soul can lose is the one it will not begin.
chapters.translation:
"九十，"邮差说着，把包裹丢在地毯上。他有一辆小货车、一条狗，口袋里插着一支笔。"你还不知道吧，九十岁的人照样发赛号布。"梅布尔·奎尔九十岁，从磨坊关上门起，她就给这一带的村子缝补衣裳。她看不出有什么理由停。

包里是她亡夫的传记，由教区印了出来，还有一张关于老山脊跑的纸片。"读啊，"邮差在门口说，"半个村子都读过了。"梅布尔把第一页扫了一遍，又扫第二页，再回头扫第一页。

在一堆整整齐齐的碎布底下，她翻出了丈夫的打字机。滚筒上搁着一张纸，干得发脆，纸顶上有一行没写完的诗句：跑出那超越肉身的步幅；其余皆是虚空。

她把那些字读了两遍，把纸搁在炉边，抬头看猫。她用一根指头推了推滚筒，滚筒还会转。

"一首小诗，"她说，"给后脑勺当个帘子也行。"门外，一只麻雀在台阶边的水洼里洗了个晨澡。猫蹲在石窗台上望着她，炉上的水壶唱着，屋外的小巷还在紫罗兰色的晨光里睡着。

内德已经走了十二年。磨坊关了，学校缩了，她的老朋友大半退到海边去陪孩子。冬天的信来得晚，村口那口钟裂了道缝，敲出来是走调的。

他的靴子还留在门边，不是等他回来，而是为了那对空地板的形状，屋里的惯常安静像温水盛在杯里一样，托着这个形状。

"还捏着针呢？" 守着门口的阿尔德太太每天早上在门口打趣她。"有朝一日，你得把整个教区都缝成破布。" "只缝还回来的人，"梅布尔说，"剩下的我都留着。"

她的手指比眼睛更认得这活计。一件外套，一副窗帘，一道放开过两回的针脚，一枚被狗叼走又缝回去的扣子，缝补让半个村子暖着，代价是一块面包皮和一杯茶。她在这屋里养大两个孩子，埋了一个丈夫，看着园子尽头那些树从棍子长成荫凉。

那年冬天她怀着身孕，一天走十英里去河边，外套兜里揣着一罐饼干。她记得她祖父——一个多才多艺的男人，能进保龄球联赛，也能跟小子们打排球——也记得那个在这条巷子里偷走她钱袋的贼。

波比，她那个戴着纸王冠的小公主，把炉边那把柳条椅叫作她的宝座。梅布尔把隐私当成岁月唯一没能夺走的东西守着。雪松谷的女人们都散了，日子依旧是好日子，慢，也稳当，被惯常的安静托着。

传记里有十几处写错了，桌上那几个也没饶过任何一处。唯一没撒谎的是成绩单：三英里处内德曾领先整场一英里，然后他不得不退下来，去扶一个在栅栏边摔倒的路人。

内德是雪松谷跑得最快、也最出众的跑者，一直跑到霉运拦了他，不是腿脚不中用。"他退了，"她出声说，"领了一英里之后退的。他那个年纪。他最好的年纪。"

书里的记载还没说清缘由，它后面那页是空的。她对着三明治啜泣起来，一小声老实的啜泣，厨房里满是远处山丘送来的雨意。

她打电话给艾里斯·黑尔医生，那个给她缝过膝盖的专科医生兼外科医生；诊所的屏幕上，是那次手术留下的旧疤。黑尔给半个村子开过刀，还跟所有人吵过架。

"按规矩，"黑尔说，"我建议休息。我会限制你，而且我拒绝。" "拒绝？"梅布尔说，"你连我跑都没看过。" "我不用看你的腿，"黑尔说，"它们又酸又僵，你的气不够用，你容易染上一种劳损，能把你推成第二次中风。"

"一英里，"她说，"山脊跑是五英里。" "九十岁跑一英里，等于等一场中风，"黑尔说，"把药片和疗法给我，"梅布尔说，"还有，手表你留着，比赛别留。"

黑尔聪明，人也厚道。她给了她一片维生素和一种明确的疗法，警告她说，她不肯点名的那种综合征，症状若不加照料就会恶性螺旋。梅布尔没吭声。她把内德的手表塞进保险箱，回嘴说墙上的尺子量不出心的分毫。诊所再也没有回过电话，她也没再打过。

她不按诊所的规矩取得资格。她凭意志取得资格。机器出的任何结果都拦不住她。

第二天一早，她去村礼堂给山脊跑报名。没人鼓掌，连抬眼瞧一下的人都没有。地上一张垫子，一支秃了尖的笔，一张关于扫街轮值的通告，还有一长串名字——那些从战场上再也没回来的人的名字。办事员替她把表退了两次，只说了一句。

"上头写的是九十，"办事员说，"写的是摔一跤。"说完递给她一支铅笔，转过身去。

第二天清晨，西奥·万斯来了，瘦瘦的小伙子，背个书包，说话不慌不忙。"我回乡照顾我奶奶，"他说，"她坐太久，坐出病来了。我见太多人败给一把椅子。"

"我倒见过一个没败的，"梅布尔说，"那是你的活。我的活是腿。你这是不让我跑？"

她在园子里走，他看着她怎么动，小本子上记着。他有个姐姐在城里，没娶妻，没孩子，还有一双留着给人家看的旧跑鞋。他没笑她的打算。"你想证明什么？"他问，"我想能跑完，"梅布尔说。

"那我们从天亮开始，"他说，"你让我管着？" "天天管。"

他奶奶坐在同一个椅子上，同一个时辰。那台无线电厂咔地响了一声，老太太两只手平平地搭在膝上，机器自个儿响下去。"她一年没站起来了，"西奥对她说，"跟梅布尔说句话。"老太太抬起眼，"那你就跑。"

计划写在纸上简单，落在身上难。他用一只便宜的表给她计时，把数字记下来，像记金子。

到第三个礼拜，她能觉出腿上的不同了。那些她不想出门的早上，她说，"你不用出来。"

"我站在门口，"他说，"你得出来。不然我就不进屋。"她选择训练，心里分得清计划和心愿。她每个天亮预备，用自己能把控的步骤把最佳配速调到最好，把自己交给西奥一周两回的悉心看护。

她首要而务实的计划就这么定了：对着镜子祷告，用上园里的栏杆，口授几条自己定的小规矩。她有决心，也有一个不肯对门口那些女人说出口的追寻。

"时间是金贵的，"她跟他说，"我小时候知道什么叫穷。别让年纪把我掀翻，也别让年纪把我打倒。"

一片安静漫过冷田。西奥问起用力的文法，她笑了，跟他说起用力的文法：迈出去的那一脚，加上许多许多脚，就是一大串步幅，而她正要迈出许多。那个清晨特别的地方，是极地吹来的风把她耳朵冻红，把活计逼成真的。路两边草都是湿的，那点湿对她有好处。

训练是一连串费力的早晨。她打了个哈欠，把外套拉链拉到下巴，挑好鞋。他在门口等着，手里一只哨子。"肩膀放下来，"他说。然后她转转脚踝，用药油揉揉腿，停一停，放松紧绷的肩。

"揉，"他说，"慢点，按进骨头里。"她照办，药油热乎乎地渗下去。每天早上都是这几句小命令，每天早上都比前一天多走一点。这些都不需要勇气，只需要下一个天亮。

再往后，是每天早上慢腾腾的算术。这儿几分钟，那儿几十码，一道绕不过去的坡，她摆动手臂像钟摆一样，一步一摆。"四十，"西奥数着，"四十。"他用快没了的铅笔头记在本子上。

第二天早上她跳过一次，手脚并用爬上石岸，迎着风的抽甩甩了甩头。一只兔子惊着了她，把她鞋里的沙抖散。"当心荨麻，"西奥说。

荨麻的刺让她一哆嗦，她在冷空气里打了个喷嚏。狗隔着田地叫，一只风筝卡在榆树上不走。她推开那扇挂着一颗松螺丝的锈门，锈掉在她指头上。

后来她经过那间关了板的旧屠宰棚，顺着路上的岔口喘着上了坡，去攻朋友们让她躲开的那座山。门边的凳子上，她缝一只手套，感到一阵刺痛、一下猛地扎来，然后没了。

她冲着水壶盖里自己满是皱纹的脸眨眨眼，那眨眼又从盖子里眨回来。跑步前她吃园里的豌豆，喝一品脱奶和一夸脱水。猫跟着她到门口，在台阶上停住。

她的呼吸稳了下来。突然的抽筋来了又退，她把那动作反反复复，直到动作定住，配速也定住。"再来，"西奥说，"再来。"回头看，那一周每一小步的向前都算要紧的事，一点没丢。

她容易犯疑，不肯藏住笑，嘴上也爱讲那蠢念头——暖被窝会勾她。"让镇上替我把报名费出了吧，"她说，"可押的本钱是我自己的脸面。" "舍弃舒适对我没什么分量，"她又添一句，"我见过更糟的。"

一阵急雨震得窗格发颤。她沿着安静的小径，以心神撑得住的配速前移。路在田边跑，田从没丢下过她。"北半球最年长的，"一个路人说着，抬手扶了扶帽子，"祝你顺利。"消息传开了，过路人每天早上冲她敬礼。她也点头。她对谁都点头。

门口那些女人早就懒得猜了。她自己在心里留着一张小地图，地图外面只有路和天气。

她在心里按勇气而不是年岁把这一片分开，等怀疑的喧哗变响，就选一处远的安静躲着。她没跟教区提那首诗，那是她一个人的。那个礼拜天的布道里，牧师讲起漫长的赛跑，梅布尔把腿绷住，在清楚的日历上划日子，范围不出一英里半径。

"九十不是要紧的，"他在讲台上说，"停下才是。"她跟着唱了半句就忘了后头，也算公平。

院里那架老泵还管用，只要你有两只手一只肩膀。一根绳子标着地边的起点，她要在那儿把两只手合上，不再往后拖。冷气会激她的肺；她不抢什么，只用一点头给自己小小的赢利打信号。

巷子里飘着面包、河水和割草的气味。一个遛狗的老人朝她点头。"今天走得远？"他问。"到山坡，"她说，"再往后。"

她把它当成游戏。每过一根柱子就是一个小国，等她到坡顶，已经到过十个国家。冷气从水面上起来，扑上她的脸颊，她学着低低地、缓缓地透口气。

她的影子在草地上伴她走，清晨光里拉得老长，她对着它说话，像对着内德。六月来了一次挫折。她的腿又酸，一种说不上来的毛病，她在炉边的椅子上叹着气，满心哀伤。

汗洇湿了她的衬衫。园里给她几棵生菜和几片撕坏的叶子，生菜把她支住了。一段关于中风的模糊记忆让她停步。坡显得难。她把报名表从垃圾桶里捡出来，看看，又一把撕了扔回去。

有整整一周她从路上退回来，让园子收留自己；恐惧的消去来得很慢，靠步态里一处细微的改变。"挫折只是转弯，不是完，"西奥宽慰她，"最糟的日子，我们用走代替跑。" "不是绝望，"她说，"就是第二天早上。"

她的腿又缓过来了，慢一点，她把整套做法调稳，直到它立得住。

波比放学回来，画了一个腿很长、脖子上挂奖牌的女人。"这是你，"她说，"在赢。"画卷在口袋里，挨着一支蔫了的蒲公英。

梅布尔把它钉在炉上方，和账单、食谱挤在一起，还跟孩子讲起那年她用三件旧衣拼出一件整外套的事。

这一整周都在厨房里过，分拣扣子和线，看雨水在窗上写它小小的字。一个冬天她缝的针脚比这还多，村子照样没冷过。

那疼不是示警的锐痛，是赖着不走的钝痛，一个没规矩的访客。可她重新开步时访客就走了，她把那一天记成恐惧丢了租约的日子。那张床还有别的名字，其中一个叫星期六。

院子里，雪松谷的女人们给她做了一件背后绣名字的薄衫，还留了一罐饼干。面包师每天早上留一条面包。"给那位老太太，"面包师跟排队的人说，"她要跑山脊。"

连议员办公室也寄了封信，信上只说路会扫干净。梅布尔把信读了两遍，笑了两遍——扫一条路，是最小的善意，有时候也是最大的。

她渐渐看清，撑着她意志的，不是虚空，是团结：对诗中那个人一份共同的承诺。那本书只露了一半：内德不止退了下去，他看见那个路人的孩子得救，也把这份牺牲算成抵得过代价。

她从保险箱取出手表，上了发条；它的滴答是个小信号，说明时间能被握住。现在表挂在绳子上，夜里的滴答给屋子作伴。她跑，不为赢，只为完成他开个头的事；这里头有个道理：真正的意志能推动结实的身架。

他藏着的那个秘密就是这个，揭开它她又哭了一场。总得有人把这话说完，别人没拾起笔。她给教区留下这一天的口述记载，心里不剩一丝恐惧。

山脊跑那天，气氛好得不得了，天是水晶般的蓝。"气球，"一个女孩说，"还有乐队。"气球在草地上空升起，这一场把一群人引了来，那喧哗她隔着一条街都听得见。这赛跑在整个郡都有声望。有个人支一张折叠桌卖咖啡，把那杯叫"胜利"。

布拉姆韦尔议员是本地的政治家，他宣布开跑，向最年长的跑者敬了个礼，递上一座小水晶奖杯——他还不知道她会捧走。"梅布尔·奎尔！"一个爱挑事的记者喊道，"九十岁还跑什么？"

"因为我人就站在九十，"她回嘴，"值得注意的不是我，是我不肯放弃。" "奖杯你肯要吗？"他追问。"盒子里装不下的都不要，"她说。

摄像机转起来了。她热身的一段视频会传遍世界，天黑前一张报纸会把这故事登出来、宣传出去。她还没迈步就已经是惹眼的一景，而她那份从容的功力，本身就是顶好的回答。摄影师让她笑；她让他先扶着门。

草地上挤满了穿鲜亮衣裳的人，两个男孩推童车往坡上冲，输了。她在栅栏边找着西奥。他举起一只手，她也举起自己的。"九十，"他说，"人就在这儿了。"

那天早上老师把全班带到草地上，让他们排成一列歪歪扭扭的队伍。"先喊数！"她喊，"再吵！"孩子们一直喊到乐队停了，梅布尔也跟着喊，一个路人被喊得也喊起来。

开跑前她在冷河里洗了脸，随即找到一种觉着生机勃勃的劲儿。她笔直站着，以心神撑得住的配速往前，吸进短促而稀少的空气。两只燕子为学校门檐吵个不停，太阳暖暖地晒在她背上。内德一个如今也老了的同年，在栅栏边朝她挥手。

"瞧那儿，那个小后生，"老太太说，说的是内德，"还不是领着跑？你丈夫。"她两只手撑着栅栏，冲谁也没具体笑。西奥猜对了，她会跑完。

第一英里，一个穿红衫的年轻姑娘落到她身边并肩。"你会跑完的，"那姑娘说，随即退了下去。她按西奥教的数呼吸，数数把距离变成能一勺一勺吃下的东西。

一个孩子递给她一粒糖，她笑着接了。沿途人群随里程消逝愈发稠密，人们从门里探身，站上矮墙。

接着一个戴红帽的小女孩在梅布尔身边跑了十几步，大笑着退下，那笑声像礼物一样跟着她。盖过噪声的细嗓子抬起来，那声音卡在她喉头。

补水站，一个男孩一声不响把杯子按进她手里，她喝了。杯子是凉的，水更凉。就这么一只杯、一只手、一点头，似乎盛下了镇子对她而言的全部。

她想起内德，在正在收尾的故事里走在前头。那个路口没有钟，没有乐队，没有横幅，她喜欢这份素净。距离从来不是重点。重点是挪动，是拒绝坐下，是一步接一步。

最后一英里没有门，没有墙，也没有影子，只有路、河，和雪松谷给得起的最长那道坡。

终点前那道坡最糟，人人都这么说，一道又短又陡的墙，专破快的，试慢的。梅布尔像对付那年春天一切那样对付它：一个步幅，再来一个，再来一个。

她往上爬，人群的声浪涨起来，像托着她而不是推她。最后那道坡把一切指望都翻了个个儿。她往上撑着，用上园里的栏杆，人群尖叫着她的名字。

她冲过那条线，赢得一块计分板显示不出来的胜利。她身后教堂的钟敲了半点，还有个男人顶着纸杯继续跑。一个穿蓝大衣的女人不停喊她名字，一次都没喊对。这一天里最要紧的一刻，是这极佳的一天里至高的时刻，证明一件极好的事：真正的那场比赛，是对着椅子那一场。

栅栏边一个女人擦了眼睛，握了握梅布尔的手；两个小男孩把一只塑料杯朝她推过来，像推一顶王冠。"您就是那位九十的？"他们问，"我是，"梅布尔说。

口袋里的表，是她在自己身上看见的那件珍贵、贵重的东西的一个象征。西奥把她接过去，人是清醒的、好好的，全城的团结像暖意一样漫过来。

在诊所断言她会失败的地方，她成功了；结果是许多小倔强步子的一个要紧总和。她给档案室留下一句口述：不剩一丝怀疑，只有关于内德的一帧生动记忆。

他们在天将尽时软软地往家走，西奥扛着终于颁给她的奖杯，梅布尔什么也没扛，只扛着自己疲倦而欢喜的份量。街上很静，几扇窗帘后亮起了灯，她在门口站住，回望来路。那道坡又安静了，坡在黄昏时就这般安静。

街那头面包师还趴在窗上。"看见了吗？"他隔着玻璃喊。"听见了，"梅布尔说，"在面包房里，我听见了整场。"

第二天清晨她没去路上。她坐在窗边喝茶，看光进来，奖杯立在架子上，不是因为它要紧，而是因为它证明一件事可以既真又小。她给一个男人的外套钉上一枚新扣子，想着那条路。天色是淡的，路上一个人也没有。牛奶送晚了一回，送奶的人隔着货车挥了挥手。

有一页始终空着，那本身就是一种完结。内德的靴子还在老地方，门后头。事后安静里，梅布尔坐在炉边的宝座上，膝头一朵紫罗兰，望着那台她永远不会填满的打字机上崭新的一页。

她是清醒的，收拾得利利索索，准备好明天重头再来。那些话说得对：其余皆是虚空，唯独步幅是真实的。

她除了自己的不肯停步，什么也没优化；在九十一岁的门槛上，她感到一种肉体与意志的团结，是任何诊所都量不出的。

她终于看见，什么撑着漫长的一生：不是里程的纪录，而是再迈一步的意志。九个月后报纸又来了，桌上那些字还在她搁下的地方。她起头写了一句话，写的是冷，还有栅栏边那个姑娘。

步幅超越肉身。其余皆是虚空。我终于读懂了那首诗——而灵魂唯一会输的赛跑，是那场它不愿开始的。

chapters.title: 镇长是一份兼职
chapters.content:
"Eleven pounds," said Old Skell. "In March. In coin." Birdie did not lift her eyes from the collar she was folding. "And the jug." As a mayor she ought to have been articulate, and at the typewriter she was extraordinary.

Two thousand four hundred and eleven people inhabited Thrumm, and she knew what roughly nineteen hundred of them wore next to their skin. That is a position no framework has ever found a label for. The mayor's pension was a jug of cider at Christmas, and the town paid her eleven pounds a year in coin and disregarded inflation.

A chain of office had no jewel on it, only a washer off the mangle, which the town thought proper and Marle thought a myth. Marle was their neighbor and, in a way, their oldest relative.

The mayor's office was a folding table beside the second dryer, the hall and the archive in one. On it sat a biscuit tin, a comb lost in 1997, and a stamp nobody could find. At six that Tuesday an envelope came in with a window cut in it. "For the mayor," said Old Skell. He put it down without meeting her eye.

She slit it with a fingernail. The county had launched an overhaul of municipal administration across the district, in the tone of a man mentioning a leak, and an immense sheet of questions came with it, and a form so intrusive that Old Skell asked aloud why Marle wanted to know his sex.

Every parish beneath a threshold of two thousand five hundred constituents must show twelve lawful meetings in the previous year: advertised in advance, minuted, signed, filed inside seven days. What the circular did not indicate was why. Miss that and the town folds into Marle, and the notice board on Barrow Street, the only medium they trust, would go with them.

"Twelve," said Old Skell. "We did eleven." "We did twelve," said Birdie. "One of them was standing in water." "Where?" The rear room of the shop. Concrete floor, a metre of wet wool on the rack, somebody's stocking still on the iron. Old Skell counted on his fingers and stopped at eleven. "The twelfth was the parking. Three meters on Barrow Street, and the middle one froze in January."

A jolly salesman from the city with an imitation leather case had kicked it, and eleven pounds forty had been released into the gutter, where the offspring of the school scrambled for it in the rain with the joy of people who find money in the street.

"That was our finest hour," said Birdie. "The only innovation Thrumm has had this century." "Would you believe it," said Old Skell, "we took eleven pounds in one kick and nobody has complained since." The jam lasted an hour, and it was the best thing to happen to Barrow Street.

The poll had been held in the shop too, in March, in the rain. The ballot box was a large jar with a slit cut in a card; the poll opened at seven and closed at half past, because Birdie had to start the machines.

She had been elected because the last mayor, who had wanted to flee to Marle, had finally gone, and somebody had to lead the citizens through a winter in which the welfare of three pensioners and one orphan hung on a form. Nine years she had devoted to that, and never called it a career, nor ever justified it. She had been a typist by trade since nineteen.

Eleven. On the Friday she took the tin down and counted the meetings she could prove. There had been twelve; she remembered the twelfth the way she remembered her mother's funeral: six in the morning, in the dark, the item being the parking.

On the lawn outside the hall, in the mist of the next morning, she counted again, Old Skell holding the tin and saying the numbers had not improved since 1971.

"We could hold it again," said Old Skell. "Nobody counts till March." "Nobody counts till the county sends somebody," said Birdie. "And then they count backwards."

The town met at six because Norris Haig worked nights and Old Skell would not be out late. Seven, a quorum: the pad had run out, so the signature sheet was a laundry docket with a duplicate carbon. There was no executive or clerk, only the stamp in a tin. The room was cold enough to harden a sponge and inhibit the nib, so all seven signed in pencil.

"What is the item?" asked Norris. "The item is the business," said Old Skell. "Then write something," said Birdie. "Seven lines. Then we open the shop." At half past seven Norris put the docket in his jacket and went to work, and the jacket went into the machine with eighty hotel sheets.

Birdie plunged a hand in, fished it out, peered. The docket came out at the bottom of the drum like the remnant of something drowned. Six pencil signatures had survived: the ink had gone, the pencil had stayed. "It came out reading clear," she told them. "If it had been ink it would have been soup."

The county sent an official. His name was Aldous Cade, a subordinate of a subordinate, with a clipboard, a tape measure and a lean grey jacket. "Hello," he said to the shop. "I am from the department. I am here about administration in parishes." "Then you are the one who counts the meetings?"

"I count what is on the sheet," said Cade, in the jargon of a man reading a shopping list. "I have been asked to impose a schedule. Monday for documents, Tuesday for the board, Wednesday for what the ministry calls engagement." "Engagement?" "To be seen," said Cade. "To be available. To interact."

He was not a bad man. He was a patient man with a rule, and he measured the hall door, found it inaccessible to a chair, found the roof leaked, and found the notice board obstructed the pavement by four inches, which had been true since 1908.

"Four inches in a town of two thousand four hundred and eleven people is a serious obstruction," he said. "It has to be dealt with. Who is responsible?" "The weather," said Old Skell. "Say that to Marle," said Birdie. He settled it all in a calm, linear hand, under a heading he called findings, with a restraint Birdie found worse than rudeness.

Then, on the Friday night, somebody hijacked the board. A poster appeared across it, printed on the school machine and pasted with flour, in letters eight inches high: THRUMM WELCOMES FENNIMORE. Underneath, in a smaller hand: and about time too.

"No form. No fee. No stamp," said Cade, standing in front of it with his mouth open. "This is illegal." "Illegal," said Old Skell. "A good word. Say it three more times and I will paint it under yours." Birdie said the orthodox way was a form and nine days, and the Thrumm way was Mrs. Kipp's flour. He called it indicative; she said it was quicker.

"Do they know we are here?" asked Old Skell. "They know," said Birdie. "That is why they send the scholarship." Fennimore was an isle beyond the frontier, in the province of Alterra, three hours from anywhere anybody had heard of, and a commonwealth for three hundred years until a prince's great-grandfather took the title and most of the fishing.

Nine islands belonged to a federation whose president was elected at a congress every four years and whose patron was the prince. The twinning had been revived in 1974 by a clerk who thought he was joining a chess league.

Every year the federation sent one Thrumm child a scholarship: prestigious, hotly contested, endowed by a native who had left the isle an orphan and come back with a fortune he could not explain. Every year Fennimore sent a diplomat to check that Thrumm still existed, and every year the diplomat ate too much and went home with a recipe.

This year Fennimore was sending an ambassador, which is like sending a celebrity. "The invitation is diplomatic," said Old Skell. "Too diplomatic. Read it again." Birdie read it three times before she understood that it was a complaint. Madame Orette Vane was due on the twentieth of December, two days after the hearing in Marle and nine days before the money was paid out.

The favourite was Tilda Rooke, fifteen, who had taught herself enough Latin to read the sign on the church and had stuck there. Her father had gone, and Mrs. Rooke, no scholar, had decided the child would reach Fennimore if the road had to be built by hand. "Who filled in the form?" asked Old Skell. "Mrs. Rooke did," said Birdie.

"Miss Thwaite," said Tilda. "I never applied." "You are eligible by age and by school record," said Birdie. "That is the only test. Then who filled in the form?" "My granny did," said Tilda. "She is very good at forms."

Birdie looked at the form, and the form looked back. It asked for sex, for age, for racial group, and for the position of every single citizen in the parish. "She has been filling in forms since 1974," said Birdie. "Good hands, bad hands, nobody knows which is which."

"Without a charter," Cade said slowly, "there is no town. Without a town there is no twinning. Without a twinning there is no visit, and without a visit there is no scholarship. Shall I write it down?" "Write it," said Old Skell. "Then read it back in a voice."

Thrumm had a reputation in the district for two things: minutes, and a peculiar idiom. The idiom was it'll wash, and it did not mean what it means. Birdie was no prophet, but she had reckoned in the first week of November that this would not wash. "It'll wash," said Cade, hopefully. "It'll wash," said Birdie. "Now open the window, because the hypocrisy of it is sticking in my throat."

Marle had cut its own staff since the recession; it could not reconcile its own accounts and it relied on Thrumm's three meters for a share of the parking revenue. Yet it now demanded twelve proper meetings from a town of two thousand four hundred and eleven people with one part-time employee.

The cost would leap from forty to four hundred and pinch two hundred and nine into nothing. The benefit of any of it would go to Marle, and Thrumm's most treasured possession after the mangle was its exclusive right to post on its own board, held since 1908.

That night Birdie did what she always did. She closed the shop, extinguished all but one lamp, sat on the stool and read something old under a light that illuminated the scene badly: the mangle, the rack, the odor of wet wool and synthetic detergent, and a book pushed under the short leg.

It was her grandmother's journal, hard-backed and ruled, with a postcard of Fennimore folded in as a marker. She had been town clerk before Birdie, and a justice of the peace, and the first woman in the county to stamp a notice upside down on purpose.

The entry was dated March 1948: Took the charter to the Institute. The Latin is plain when a scholar looks at it, and the dean affirmed it in writing on the twelfth. It says what I have always said it says. The town is not a building. A record is any mark a willing hand makes, and the mayor is whoever is willing, for as long as they are willing.

I showed it to them and they said it was superfluous, and that a charter in Latin is not legislation. "A charter is not legislation at all," I said. "It is a promise, and promises are older." Nobody laughed, which was worse.

Below, from 1953: They have asked me again. I have sent the letter to the department. The department has filed it. To file a thing is not to read it. Under that, the week she died: The law is not the point. The point is who is willing. Moral: never be ashamed of a pencil.

Birdie sat until the dryer stopped and the shop went quiet in the way only a laundry goes quiet, absolutely, like a church with the heating on. A colony of jackdaws invaded the lawn and were gone. She judged the whole thing as she judged a stain, by age and by fibre, and her judgement was that it would come out.

She telephoned the Institute and obtained the address of a retired dean in a neighborhood of Marle. She held the docket to the lamp. And she reserved the back room for the week of the hearing, because she trusted neither the roof nor Cade.

The town cleaned, the way towns do when they are afraid. Norris Haig, nineteen, technician at the hire shop and the most juvenile councillor in the county, repaired the aerial and upgraded the amplifier with a part off a bus. "Nobody is coming to my meeting," said Norris. "Are they?"

Mrs. Kipp, Thrumm's one immigrant, who had emigrated at nineteen, a baker who had come over on a scholarship in 1974, married a Thrumm man and never got back on the boat; she baked for three days and refused to be paid. Old Skell painted the notice board and painted the poster out, then painted the board back again badly, in the night.

Two highland farms sent wood for the hut on the plantation, which had stood doorless for forty years. The salesman came back with a case of new meters and a smile you could borrow money on.

"The meters will repay themselves in eighteen months, sir," he said. "The scheme is profitable, the profit is split three ways, and I refund the whole sum if it is not. And Marle is offering a grant to any town that can reckon its revenue to the penny."

"How many forms?" "Four." "Can four tell a parish from a shop?" "No." "Can they differentiate a parking meter from a bus stop?" "That," he said, "seems reasonable. Old Skell can distinguish a parish from a shop with his eyes shut. Can your forms?" "The transition will take six weeks," he said, and opened the door.

Birdie said the town had three meters, two hundred and nine in the bank, and one part-time employee. He evaded every question about the disposal of the old meters, and she said nothing, because a salesman's silence is a reply.

Sunday, and the budget meeting at the back of the shop. "Sell the plantation," said somebody. "The money upgrades the meters. The willow is dead anyway." "The willow was planted by men buried on the hill," said Old Skell. "It can wait."

"The hut can be let," said Cade, who had brought his chair without being asked. "It is a most convenient size." Tilda, who had no vote at all, then spoke: "Ask Fennimore to lend it the money."

"No," said Birdie. "A town that borrows from a friend has sold something it cannot buy back." "What have we left, then?" said Old Skell. "A pair of socks?" "A willow," said Birdie. "No left. A whole." The survival of Thrumm was not a matter of money but who turned up at six in the morning. She said that, and being embarrassed went to make tea.

Birdie said no vicious word about the branch office. What unified the town was not anger, only boredom with being explained to itself.

"Civilization sits in one room," said Birdie. "Hot water, soap, and someone willing to listen." "Explain it again," said Old Skell. "No," said Birdie. The shop was invaluable for that reason and lucky in a way no form could measure, the only place Thrumm interacted with itself without an agenda.

Cade had come to avert a merger and stayed to watch one. His cheeks were hollow and his manner acute, and by the second week he was tolerant of the steam and jealous of the noise. The cognitive load of a single form had nearly finished him. An ideal solution, Marle called it: expand the district, unify the records, and give Thrumm a branch office open on Thursdays.

The hearing was in the county hall, in a room off the lobby. Cade sat on one side of the long table with two colleagues; Birdie sat on the other with Old Skell, Norris, Tilda, and the docket in a plastic sleeve. "The smell is noticeable," said Cade, in the doorway. "That is laundry." "That is my town," said Birdie. "I keep it. I also wash it."

There was no jury and no judge, only a table, a tape machine, and a woman from Marle who asked them all to speak up. "There is no jury because there is no case," said Cade. "There is no case because there is no town," said Birdie.

Cade's manner was judicial, his case short and rigid. Eleven meetings on the record. The twelfth held on premises that were not municipal. The sheet was not a legal document. The writing in pencil. Nothing filed within seven days. He said legitimate twice, inevitable once, said he had no discretion, and said, with what he believed was civility, that he was sorry.

Old Skell was indignant, and his indignation filled the room like a boiler. "Say it in the kitchen, then," he said. "Say it where the tea is." Birdie's own sat further down, where she kept her pride. Tilda despised him in silence, with the flat stare of a fifteen-year-old watching an adult be stupid in public.

Cade drew the inference himself and stated it. The twelfth meeting had never happened. It was queer, he said, that a town could not produce one sheet of paper.

Birdie thought of the innumerable sheets that had gone through her machines in thirty-one years and said nothing. Then Birdie stood up and placed two things on the table.

The first was the docket. "Seven signatures," she said. "Six in pencil. One in what my granny called a frozen finger."

"It went through a machine at half past seven with eighty hotel sheets, immersed in hot water and synthetic detergent, and it came out reading clear. You will say pencil is not legal. I am telling you it is indispensable, because that morning it was the only thing in Thrumm that would write."

The second was the journal. She read the entry of 1948 aloud, and the one from 1953, and the last line, then stopped, because her vision had begun to blur as it did when she stayed up typing, and she would rather be blind than pitied in front of Cade.

"My grandmother took this there in 1948," she said. "A dean affirmed it. The department filed it. Nobody read it. She set it aside for thirty years, and never opened it either."

"I am not asking you to take my word for the Latin. I am asking you to read what a scholar wrote, in English, sixty-one years ago, and then to tell me in front of these four people that a town is a building."

A silence. The potted plant dropped a leaf. Cade's colleague wrote the word premises on his pad and crossed it out. Then the door opened, and Norris came in with a retired teacher: eighty-seven, deaf, arrived by bus, with his own copy.

His name was Brackett. He had taught at the Institute for forty years and had translated the charter twice for a journal nobody bought.

Norris needed the amplifier, which had been upgraded with a part off a bus, and it worked unfortunately extremely well. His confirmation went out into the entrance hall, down the stair, and, it was reported, into the washroom of the hall itself, where a woman ironing shirts heard the town is not a building and stopped ironing for a full minute.

He confirmed three clauses. That a meeting of Thrumm is wherever seven citizens stand and one writes it down. That a record is any mark made by a willing hand. And that the mayor is whoever is willing, for as long as they are willing, and not one minute longer.

The Latin was plain, and plainness was its whole virtue. "I am advanced in years," he added, unasked, "and advanced in nothing else. If Marle wishes to check my Latin, it should hurry." That raised the first laugh of the day and the first smile Cade had produced in three weeks.

Cade went pale in a way that was evident to everybody but himself. "May I have guidance?" The twenty minutes he was given became an hour, in which a lawyer was telephoned and a minister was woken.

When they came back the decision was short. "What is the decision?" asked Norris. The twelfth meeting stood. The docket was accepted as a record, and Thrumm kept its charter, its willow, its three parking meters and its notice board.

Cade stood in the lobby afterwards with sweat on his forehead and said, in the driest tone Birdie had heard from a loser, that he had been doing his job. "I know," said Birdie. "I implemented the rule as written. I know that too."

"The relationship between Marle and Thrumm has been damaged by the whole occurrence," he said. "It was damaged in 1908," said Birdie. "And nobody noticed till now."

"Eleven pounds a year," he said. "Is that right?" "Eleven pounds. The jug of cider is private."

"I would undertake it," said Cade, "for the cider."

Birdie looked at him a long moment. The offer was foolish and sincere, a combination she trusted in the shop and doubted elsewhere. Her one vice was overhearing, thirty-one years of it, and she had overheard enough of Cade to know he was lonely, jealous of Thrumm, and beginning, without meaning to, to enjoy himself.

"You would," said Birdie. "And you would do it badly, you would learn, and in nine years you would be saddled with it the way I am, and you would still be doing it wrong." She paused. "Come on Monday. Six in the morning. Bring a coat. And bring that form, and we shall fill it in properly, post it, and see."

The ambassador came ashore on the twentieth in the mist, with a small case and an accent that turned every sentence into a question and every question into a gift.

Her journey had taken two days and three boats. She had been a refugee of the flood of 1979, a scholar at twenty and a diplomat at thirty, and had served at an embassy in a federal capital where the paperwork was worse than Thrumm's and the coffee no better.

"Is this the town?" she asked. "This is the town," said Birdie.

"This is a photograph of the prince opening a fish stall," she said. "It is the premier duty of a prince in a commonwealth that has decided to stay a commonwealth in every respect but the name." She also brought a square of lace, made on Fennimore by a woman of ninety-one.

"The pope blessed our harbour in 1961," she said over lunch. "The pilgrim path to the old church is four hundred years old and still walked every spring."

"It is all true," said Mrs. Kipp. "It is all true," she said again, in a voice nobody in the room had heard before; then she cried, and then she gave the ambassador a hug that went on rather a long time.

"The scholarship is yours, Tilda Rooke," said Birdie. The excitement in the room was such that Old Skell kissed the ambassador and then apologised, a long formal apology delivered to the potted plant, which he took for the senior figure present.

There were subsequent consequences. Marle loosened the schedule for parishes under five hundred and called it a pilot, which let Marle claim the credit and Thrumm keep its own hours. The department wrote to the Institute to ask whether other charters might say the same thing, and the Institute replied that they probably did, and that it was impossible to say which.

The elite of Marle assumed the whole business was a fantasy, and wrote to the paper. They were answered, rather well, by Tilda. A republican club of Fennimore ran a piece in its journal calling Thrumm a noble example of civil disobedience, which amused Birdie, since the only thing she had ever disobeyed was a deadline.

Thrumm's unemployment, it should be said, was one man who refused to work indoors.

"Indoors ruins the hands," he said, and nobody argued.

There was an exchange of gifts, as there is every year, and an exchange of letters, which is rarer. Fennimore sent seed; Thrumm sent the speciality of the house, which was, unfortunately, a shirt, laundered and folded, with a note reading SHIRTS A SPECIALITY, because the town could think of nothing else and had refused, on a vote, to send a meter.

"And the docket went into a frame," said Birdie. "It hangs beside the notice board where the rain cannot reach it, and the town can point at it, as it points at the comb, when a stranger asks what this place is."

Under the glass, in Birdie's typing, are the seven signatures and one line she added that night: The meeting was proper. We were there. The pencil was willing. Birdie is still mayor, part-time, and still a laundry woman, the only job that ever paid her by the hour. She has slowed down and charges more.

On Monday mornings at six she unfolds the table beside the second dryer, sets out the tin marked RATES, and waits for whoever turns up: usually seven, occasionally eight, since Cade came in January and has not missed one.

"He still brings the form," said Old Skell. "And she still fills it in. Twelve years now, and he has not missed one."

Eleven pounds a year, she wrote in the ledger, and the town is not a building.

”十一英镑，“老斯凯尔说，”三月，还得是硬币。“伯迪眼皮都没抬，手里的衣领还在折。”还有那坛酒。“当镇长，她本该能说会道；可一坐到打字机前，她就是个厉害角色。

德拉姆镇住着两千四百一十一口人，其中近两千位穿什么贴身，她心里有数。这么个位置，哪套制度都懒得给它一个名分。镇长的养老金是圣诞节一坛苹果酒；镇上一年付她十一英镑硬币，对通货膨胀不闻不问，就跟它对别的事一样。

那条垂在脖子上的链子没镶一颗宝石，只挂了一枚从压面机上拆下来的垫圈。镇上觉得挺合适，马尔镇却说它是个神话——这话他们常当着人面讲。马尔是他们的邻居，说起来还是他们最老的那门亲戚。

镇长办公室是第二台烘干机旁边一张折叠桌，议事厅和档案室挤在一处。桌上摆着一饼干盒、一把九七年丢的梳子，还有一枚谁也找不到地址的印章。那个星期二，六点钟进来一个信封，剪了个窗口。”给镇长，“老斯凯尔说。他把信放下，没敢看她一眼。

她用指甲划开。县里在全区搞一轮市政整顿，口气像个男人提起屋顶漏水；随信附来一沓厚得吓人的问题，还有一张表格，无孔不入，连老斯凯尔都大声问出来：马尔凭什么要问他的性别。

低于两千五百选民的堂区，都得拿出过去一年里十二次合规会议：事先公告、做了记录、有人签字、七天之内归档。可这份通告压根没说是为什么。漏了这十二条，镇子就被并进邻居——对德拉姆来说就是马尔，而巴克街那块公布栏，镇上唯一信得过的媒介，也得一起并过去。

“十二条，”老斯凯尔说，“我们只开了11。”“我们有十二条，”伯迚说，“其中一次是站在水里开的。”“哪儿？”店里后屋。水泵地，架子上一米长的潿毛线，还有谁的裹子挂在熊斗上没掠。老斯凯尔掂着指头数，数到11停住了。“第十二次是停车。广克街1个呼商器，中间那个一月份冻住了。”

一个从城里来的推销员，乐呵呵的，拎着个仿皮箱子，一脚把它踢了出去；十一英镑四先令就这么滚进了水沟。镇上孩子们在雨里抢，抢得跟街上捡到钱的人一样高兴。

”那是我们最好的一小时，“伯迪说，”本世纪德拉姆唯一一次创新。“”你信不信，“老斯凯尔说，”一脚踢出来十一英镑，从那以后再没人抱怨过。“堵了整整一个钟头，是巴克街上有史以来最好的事。

投票也在店里，三月，下雨。票箱是一只大玻璃罐，卡片上割了道口子；投票七点开始，七点半就关——伯迪得开机器。

她能选上，是因为上一位镇长终于走了，那人从九八年起就想逃去马尔，总得有人带着这一镇人熬过这个冬天：三个领养老金的老头、一个孤儿，命都悬在一张表上。九年她就这么耗下去，从不说这是事业，也从不为它找理由。她从十九岁起就是个敲字员。

十一。到了周五她把饼干盒取下来，数自己能证明的会议，数完把盒子搁回原处。应该有十二次；第十二次她记得清清楚楚，就像记得她妈的葬礼：早上六点，天没亮，议题是停车。

第二天早上的雾里，她又在礼堂外的草地上数了一遍，老斯凯尔捧着盒子在旁边，说这数字从七一年起就没好过。

”咱们可以再开一次，“老斯凯尔说，”没人到三月才数。“”没人到县里派人来才数，“伯迪说，”到时候他们倒着数。“

镇上六点钟开会，因为诺里斯·黑格上夜班，老斯凯尔天黑以后不肯出门。七个人，够法定人数；记录本也用完了，于是签名页就是一张洗衣单，还打了份复写副张。没有行政班底，也没有办事员，只有饼干盒里那枚印章。屋里冷得能把海绵冻硬，笔尖也写不动，七个人只好都用铅笔签。

”议题是什么？“诺里斯问。”议题就是正事，“老斯凯尔说。”那就写点东西，“伯迪说，”七行。写完我们就开门营业。“七点半，诺里斯把那张单子塞进外衣口袋去上工；那件外衣跟着八十条宾馆床单进了滚筒。

伯迪把手伸进去，捞出来，凑近看了看。单子在滚筒底下出来，像从什么东西肚子里捞出来的残骸。六个铅笔签名活了下来：墨水没了，铅芯还在。”出来上头清清楚楚，“她告诉大家，”要是墨水写的，那就成了一锅汤。“

县里来了个官员。他叫奥尔杜斯·凯德，是部里的下属的下属，拿着写字板、软尺和一件瘦瘦的灰夹克。”你好，“他对着店里说，”我来自部里。我是来谈堂区行政的。“”那你就是数会议的那位？“

”我数纸上写了什么，“凯德说，口气像个念购物清单的人。”上面让我推行一套日程：周一办公文档，周二上公布栏，周三——部里管这叫'对接'。“”对接？“”就是让人看见，“凯德说，”让人找得着。让人搭得上话。“

他不是坏人。他是个守规矩的耐心人；他量礼堂的门，发现轮椅进不去；发现屋顶渗水；发现公布栏占掉了人行道四英寸——这事从一九〇八年起就一直如此。

”在两千四百一十一口人的镇上碍出四英寸，这是严重妨碍，“他说，”必须处理。谁负责？“”天气，“老斯凯尔说。”这话去跟马尔说，“伯迪说。他一笔一划把事情定了下来，标题写着'查证结果'，笔触冷静又直线条，那股克制劲儿在伯迪看来比无礼更叫人恼火。

接着到了周五晚上，有人把公布栏给劫了。一张海报糊在上面，学校那台机器印的，用面粉贴牢，八个英寸高的大字：德拉姆欢迎芬尼莫尔。底下更小的字一行：早该这样了。

”没有表格。没有手续费。没有印章，“凯德站在它面前，嘴张着。”这是非法的。“”非法，“老斯凯尔说，”好词儿。你再说三遍，我就把它刷在你那块牌子底下面。“伯迪说按规矩是填表加九天；德拉姆的规矩是基普太太的面粉。他管这叫”有指示意义的“，她说就是快。

”他们知道我们还在这儿吗？“老斯凯尔问。”知道，“伯迪说，”所以每年才给奖学金。“芬尼莫尔是边界外的一座岛，属阿尔特拉省，离任何有人听说过的地方三小时船程；三百年来它一直是个联邦，直到一位王子的曾祖父把头衔和大部分渔业都拿走了。

九座岛归一个联合体，主席每四年在代表大会上选出来，赞助人是那位王子。结为友好城市这事是一九七四年由一个办事员推动的，他以为自己是在加入一个棋类协会。

联合体每年给德拉姆一个孩子一份奖学金：名头响，抢破头；基金来自一个本地人——他小时候是岛上孤儿，后来带着一笔说不清的财富回来了。芬尼莫尔每年也派一位外交官来看看德拉姆还在不在；每年这位外交官都吃撑了，带一张食谱回家。

今年芬尼莫尔要派的是位大使，那相当于派个名人。”这份请柬太外交了，“老斯凯尔说，”太外交了。你再读一遍。“伯迪读了三遍才明白这是一封投诉。奥雷特·韦恩夫人定在十二月二十日到，比在马尔的开会晚两天，比发钱早九天。

热门人选是十五岁的蒂尔达·鲁克，她自学了够用的拉丁文，能读懂教堂门口那块牌子，然后就卡在那儿了。她爸不在了；鲁克太太不识字，却下了决心：就算要一锤一锤把路修出来，也得让这孩子到得了芬尼莫尔。”表是谁填的？“老斯凯尔问。”鲁克太太，“伯迪说。

”索斯韦特小姐，“蒂尔达说，”我从来没申请过。“”你够格——论年纪，论学籍，“伯迪说，”那是唯一的测试。那表到底谁填的？“”我外婆填的，“蒂尔达说，”她最擅长填表。“

伯迪看着那张表，表也看着她。它问性别、问年龄、问种族，还问堂区里每一个公民住在什么位置。”她从一九七四年就在填表了，“伯迪说，”手好的时候好，坏的时候坏，谁也说不清哪只手是她。“

”没有特许状，“凯德慢慢地说，像在对着墙讲，”就没有镇子。没有镇子就没有结为友好镇。没有友好镇就没有访问，没有访问就没有奖学金。要我记下来吗？“”记，“老斯凯尔说，”然后念出声来。“

德拉姆在全区有两样名声：会议记录，还有一句怪话。那句怪话就是”能洗掉“，可它并不等于它字面那个意思。伯迪不算先知，但十一月第一周她就算出来这事洗不掉。”能洗掉，“凯德满怀希望地说。”能洗掉，“伯迪说，”现在把窗打开，我这嗓子眼儿里卡的全是这号虚伪。“

马尔自经济衰退以来裁了自己的人；它连自己的账都理不清，还指着德拉姆那三个咪表分停车收入。可它现在要一个两千四百一十一口人、只有一个兼职雇员的镇，交出十二次像样的会议。

花销会从四十蹦到四百，把账上那两百零九压成一堆灰。好处一样都落不到德拉姆头上；除了压面机，镇上最金贵的家当就是独占那块公布栏的权利，从一九〇八年起就没变过。

那天晚上伯迪还是老样子。她关了店，只留一盏灯，坐到凳子上，就着那盏把场面照得挺糟的光看一本旧书：压面机、晾架、湿毛线和合成洗涤剂的味儿，还有一本被塞进短桌腿底下的书。

那是她外婆的日记，硬壳横线本，夹着一张芬尼莫尔明信片当书签。当镇长之前，外婆就是镇上的文书，还当过治安法官，是全县第一个故意把通知倒着盖印的女人。

第一条记在一九四八年三月：把特许状送到学院。拉丁文平铺直叙，学者一看就懂；院长在十二日书面确认，有两名见证人和一只猫。它说的正是我从来都说它说的。镇子不是一栋房子。记录就是肯动手的人留下的任何痕迹；镇长就是那个肯干的人，肯多久，就干多久。

我拿给他们看，他们说多余，说拉丁文特许状算不上立法。我跟他们说，特许状根本就不是立法。它是一种承诺，而承诺比法条更老。没人笑，这比笑更糟。

下面是一九五三条：他们又来问我要东西了。我把院长的信寄去了部里。部里归档了。归档一件东西不等于读过它。再往下，她临终那周：法的意思不是重点。重点是肯不肯干。箴言：别为铅笔害臊。

伯迪一直坐到烘干机停转，店里这才静下来——洗衣店的静是彻底的静，像开了暖气的教堂。一群寒鸦涌进草地，又呼啦一下走了。她像判断一块污渍那样判断这整件事，看年份，看料子；她的判断是：能洗掉。

她打电话到学院，问到了马尔某条街上一位退休院长的地址。她把那张单子凑到灯下。她又把后屋留给开会那周，因为她既不信任屋顶，也不信任凯德。

镇上开始大扫除，就像人一害怕就要打扫屋子那样。诺里斯·黑格，十九岁，租赁店的技师，也是全县最稚气的议员，修好了天线，还拿公共汽车上的一个零件把扩音器升了级。”不会有人来开我的会，“诺里斯说，”会不会有？“

基普太太是德拉姆唯一的移民，十九岁移民过来，是个面包师，一九七四年靠奖学金过来的，嫁了个德拉姆男人，就再没上过那条船；她连烤三天，死活不肯收钱。老斯凯尔把公布栏刷了一遍，也把那张海报盖掉，然后夜里又歪歪扭扭把牌子刷了回来。

两家高地农场送来木料，给种植园里那间小屋——它四十年没门，如今得装一扇。推销员又来了，提着一箱新咪表，脸上那笑容可以拿去借钱。

”咪表十八个月就回本，先生，“他说，”这买卖赚钱，利润三方分成，要不赚我全退。马尔还给任何能把自己的收入算到便士的镇子发补贴。“

”要几张表？“”四张。“”四张表能分出堂区和店铺吗？“”不能。“”那能分出停车咪表和公共汽车站吗？“”这个，“他说，”还算讲道理。老斯凯尔闭着眼睛都能分出堂区和店铺。你的表行吗？“”过渡期要六周，“他说着，拉门走了。

伯迪说，镇上三个咪表，银行里两百零九，一个雇员——就是她自己，还是兼职。他搪塞每一个关于旧咪表怎么处理的问题，她一声不吭，因为她早就懂得：推销员的沉默，就是回答。

到了周日，预算会议在店后头开。”把种植园卖了吧，“有人说，”钱用来升级咪表。那棵柳反正也死了。“”那柳树是埋在山上的人种下的，“老斯凯尔说，”它等得起。“

”小屋可以租出去，“凯德说，那把椅子没人叫他自己搬来的，”尺寸相当合适。“蒂尔达一点票也没有，这会儿开口了：”让芬尼莫尔借钱给它。“

”不行，“伯迪说，”向朋友借钱的镇子，等于卖掉了自己买不回来的东西。“”那我们还剩什么？“老斯凯尔问。”一双袜子？“”一棵柳树，“伯迪说，”那不叫剩下的，那叫一整个。“德拉姆能不能活下去，跟钱没关系，跟清早六点有没有人露面有关系。这话她说了，说完有点臊，起身去泡茶。

伯迪没对那个分处说过一句狠话。到头来让这个镇子拧成一股的，不是愤怒，是被自己人反复解释到自己听腻的厌烦。

”文明就坐在一间屋子里，“伯迪说，”热水、肥皂，还有一个肯听人说话的人。“”再讲一遍，“老斯凯尔说，”不，“伯迪说。就因为这，这家洗衣店才珍贵得没法估量；也因为这样才运气好——那是德拉姆唯一一个不带议程、自己跟自己打交道的地方。

凯德是来阻止合并的，最后留下来看合并怎么发生。他两颊凹陷，神情尖利；到第二周，他对蒸汽宽容了，却开始嫉妒这屋里的吵闹。一张表格带来的一点点脑力负担，几乎要了他的命。马尔管这叫理想方案：扩大辖区，统一档案，再给德拉姆开一个周四营业的分处。

听证在县礼堂，侧厅一间屋子里。凯德一边坐两个同事；伯迪另一边，身边是老斯凯尔、诺里斯、蒂尔达，还有套在塑料袋里的那张单子。”味道挺明显，“凯德站在门口说，”那是洗衣店。“”那是我镇子，“伯迪说，”我守着它，也洗它。“

没有陪审团，也没有法官，只有一张桌子、一台录音机，还有一位来自马尔、叫大家都大点声的女士。”没有陪审团，是因为没有案子，“凯德说。”没有案子，是因为没有镇子，“伯迪说。

凯德一副司法腔调，案子又短又硬。记录在案的十一次会议。第十二次开在原不属于市政的房子里。那张纸不是法律文件。写的是铅笔。七天之内什么都没归档。他”合法“说了两遍，”不可避免“一遍，说本人没有自由裁量权，还用好意的口气说了一句他以为算礼貌的”抱歉“。

老斯凯尔气得不行，那股气像锅炉一样撑满了屋子。”那你去厨房说，“他说，”去有茶的地方说。“伯迪自己的那口气压得更低，压在她放自尊的地方。蒂尔达闷声不响地鄙视他，用十五岁看大人当众犯傻那种平板的眼神。

凯德自己把结论推出来，又说了出来。第十二次会议从来没开过。他说这很”怪“，一个镇子连一张纸都拿不出来。

伯迪想起三十一年里从她机器里过掉的那些数不清的纸，什么也没说。然后她站起来，往桌上放了两样东西。

一样是那张单子。”七个签名，“她说，”六个铅笔。一个是我外婆叫'冻僵的手指'写上去的。“

”七点半，它跟着八十条宾馆床单进了一台机器，泡在热水和合成洗涤剂里，出来照样清清楚楚。你们会说铅笔不算合法。我告诉你们它不可或缺——那天早上，它是整个德拉姆唯一还能写字的玩意儿。“

另一样是那本日记。她把一九四八年的那一段念出来，把一九五三年的那段也念了，还有最后一行，然后停住——她的视线开始发模糊，跟她熬夜敲字时一个样；她宁可瞎，也不愿在凯德面前被人同情。

”我外婆一九四八年把这个送到那儿，“她说，”一位院长确认过。部里归档了。没人读过。她搁了三十年，自己也没翻开过。“

”我不是要你们信我的拉丁文。我是要你们去读一位学者六十一年前用英文写的东西，然后当着这四位，告诉我镇子是一栋房子。“

一片沉默。那盆植物掉了一片叶子。凯德的同事在本子上写下”处所“两个字，又划掉。接着门开了，诺里斯领着一位退休院长进来：八十七岁，耳背，坐公共汽车来的，自己带了一本书。

他叫布拉克特。他在学院教了四十年书，把那道特许状译过两遍，一九四八年一遍，一九八八年一遍，投给一本没人买的刊物。

诺里斯那台扩音器装了公共汽车上的零件，运气不好的是，它好使得吓人。他的确认声传到门厅，顺着楼梯下去，据说还进了礼堂自己的洗手间——有个在那儿熨衬衫的女人听见”镇子不是一栋房子“，足足一分钟没敢再熨。

他确认了三条。德拉姆的会议，就是七个公民站在一起、其中一人把它写下来的地方。记录就是肯动手的人留下的任何痕迹。德拉姆的镇长就是那个肯干的人，肯多久就干多久，一分钟不多。

拉丁文平实，平实就是它全部的好处。”我年岁已高，“他没等问就自报了一句，”别的方面也高。“”要是马尔要查我的拉丁文，它可得快点儿。“这一句换来了这天头一个笑声，也是凯德三周来脸上第一个笑。

凯德脸白了起来，这样子所有人都看得出来，只有他自己没发现。”能给我一点指引吗？“人家给他二十分钟，结果成了一个钟头；这钟头里，律师被电话叫醒过，文件被传真过来，部长也被吵醒了。

他们回来的时候，决定很短。”决定是什么？“诺里斯问。第十二次会议成立了。那张单子被认定为记录，德拉姆保住了特许状、柳树、三个停车咪表和那块公布栏。

散会后凯德站在门厅，脑门上冒汗，用伯迪听过的、从一个输家嘴里能听出的最干巴巴的口气说，他一直在照章办事。”我知道，“伯迪说，”我也照章办了。我都知道。“

”马尔和德拉姆的关系，被这一整桩事弄伤了，“他说。”一九〇八年就伤了，“伯迪说，”只是到这会儿才有人发现。“

”一年十一英镑，“他说，”对吗？“”十一英镑。那坛苹果酒是私事。“

”为了那坛酒，“凯德说，”我也肯干。“

伯迪看了他好一会儿。这个提议又蠢又真，是她在店里练出来的一套判断——店里信，别处不信。她唯一的毛病是爱偷听，三十一年偷下来的；她偷听过足够多的凯德，知道他孤单，嫉妒德拉姆，还正在无意间开始自得其乐。

”你会的，“伯迪说，”你会干得很糟，你会学，九年后你会像我一样被这差事套牢，而且到那时你还是做错。“她停了一下。”周一来。早上六点。带件外衣。把那张表带来，我们正经填一遍，寄出去，然后看看。“

大使在二十日那天雾里上了岸，提着一个小箱子，口音把每句话都变成问句，又把每个问句都变成一份礼物。

她路上花了两天、三只船。她是七九年水灾的难民，二十岁是学者，三十岁是外交官，还在一座联邦首府的使馆供过职——那里的公文比德拉姆还糟，咖啡并不比德拉姆好。

”这就是这个镇子吗？“她问。”这就是，“伯迪说。

”这是王子给鱼摊剪彩的照片，“她说，”在一个除了名字、处处都还把自己当联邦的联邦里，这是王子的头等大事。“她还带来一方蕾丝，是芬尼莫尔上年纪一位九十一岁的女人织的。

”六十一年，教皇祝福了我们的港口，“她吃午饭时说，”去老教堂那条朝圣小路有四百年历史，每年春天还有人走。“

”都是真的，“基普太太说。她又说了一遍”都是真的“，声音是这屋里谁都没听过的那种；接着她哭了，接着她给了大使一个拥抱，抱得有点太久。

”奖学金是你的了，蒂尔达·鲁克，“伯迪说。屋里的激动闹到这个份上，老斯凯尔去亲了大使，又立刻道歉——一长串正式的道歉，冲着那盆植物说的，他把它当成了在场最年长的人物。

后头的后果还在后头。马尔把两千五百人以下堂区的日程放松了，管它叫试点：好处让马尔捞了名声，德拉姆保住了自己的钟点。部里写信给学院，问别的特许状是不是也说得一样；学院回信说，大概一样，而且很遗憾，说不准是哪几份。

马尔的体面人原以为整件事是个笑话，于是给报社写了信。写信的人后来被蒂尔达回得相当漂亮。芬尼莫尔一个共和俱乐部在自家的刊物上发文，说德拉姆是不服从的崇高榜样，这可把伯迪逗坏了，因为她这辈子唯一一次不服从，是不服从一个期限。

得说一句，德拉姆的失业人口是一个不肯在室内干活的人。

”室内干活毁手，“他说，没人反驳。

每年都有互赠礼物，也都有通信，后者更少些。芬尼莫尔送来了种子；德拉姆回的是本店的招牌货——很遗憾，是一件衬衫，洗好叠齐，别着一张纸条：本店专做衬衫。镇上想不出别的东西，还投票决定不送咪表。

”那张单子后来装了框，“伯迪说，”挂在公布栏旁边，雨淋不着。有外人问这儿是个什么地方，镇上人就能指着它，就像指着那把梳子。“

玻璃板底下是伯迪打出来的字：七个签名，还有那天夜里她添的一句——会开得合规。人在场。铅笔是肯干的。伯迪还是镇长，兼职，还是个洗衣女；那是她唯一一份按钟点付钱的工作。她干慢了，也涨价了。

周一早上六点，她把第二台烘干机旁的那张桌子摊开，摆上写着”费率“的饼干盒，然后等不管谁来：通常七个，偶尔八个，因为凯德一月就进来了，一次没落过。

”他还带着那张表，“老斯凯尔说，”她也还填。如今十二年了，他一次没落过。“

十一英镑一年，她在流水账上这样写，镇子不是一栋房子。
