chapters.title: 赝品杰作
chapters.content:
"It's a fake." Cordelia Vane kept her voice flat. "Look at that sky. Four hundred years of sky, and it still smells new."

Senator Hale Renn stopped mid-sentence. The painting had arrived that morning in a crate padded with timber and tape, and the staff were already moving chairs around it. Nine people stood in the gallery and stared. "Nine educated people," she said. "Only one of them saw it first."

Cordelia Vane was the museum's chief conservator, an artist before she was a scientist. Her feel for texture and composition had made her the living authority on Cosimo Venn in three countries. She set the canvas under the lamp and located the first flaw in under a minute. The blue of that sky was a color no classical hand could ever have composed.

"Cosimo Venn's Concert in the Courtyard," the Senator said, "a Renaissance master, a gift from his mother's estate. The exhibition opens Thursday."

Madame Yvette Voss smiled, and her smile did not move. The artistic authority in this town, she had even designed the leaflet herself. "A marvelous return," she told the press, and the word spread through the nearby cafés like gossip. She managed every step of the project, and the same word went onto every leaflet printed and pinned to the booths in the courtyard.

The Halcyon Museum of Art stood on a plateau above the river Vellaine, brick and marble, a grand house with a dome that towered over the courtyard like a second moon. Its best feature, and its worst idea at once. In winter the river fog came up the hill and swallowed the attic windows.

No money had changed hands. The Senator had given the work as a gift; the mayor, an optimistic man with a love of ceremony, had promised to open the show himself. A subsidy from the culture ministry hung on the building owning a Venn, the building sat under a mortgage, and the mayor's outlook was sunny enough to tie the ribbon. One spectacular draw might yet lift it.

Up went a platform in the courtyard for the orchestra, and an acrobat was hired to balance on a rope above the dome. The mayor cut the ribbon in May and called that evening a triumph for art and for humanity. Nobody noticed that she had gone pale. The layout of the hall had been streamlined for crowds, and the crowds moved well, past the canvas, without stopping.

A famous actor and a rising actress accepted invitations. A musician friend promised a solo trumpet between the movements of a classical concert, and someone queued a rap track for the late crowd. The drum of the orchestra kept a tempo that lifted the whole square. Cordelia watched it all from the doorway with a headache she would not name.

Cordelia brought her niece to the rehearsal, a serious nine-year-old named Mara. She settled at a booth in the courtyard and drew a panda with a crayon, then taped it to the timber rail. The child's imagination had no prejudice in it yet. "A panda," Cordelia murmured. "The only honest critic in this building."

Under the lamp the old varnish told a story the certificate did not tell at all. The pigment in the sky was too pure for a work four hundred years old; real Venn blue carried grain, and dust, and four hundred winters. They had called it a masterpiece on the leaflet, and the label had been printed in the building's own press.

"Wrong texture," she said. "The grain runs the wrong way. It's painted, not weathered."

The canvas weave showed a modern press mark, and a pin of twentieth-century steel held the stretcher together. A nail with a factory head. A lid stamped by solvent, no older than the war. Small proof, and yet positive.

That flaw shouted. It did not ask. Cordelia refrained from speaking at once; attentive by habit, cautious by nature. The mystery deserved a method, not a panic. That evening, after closing, she wandered the gallery alone, the monotonous hum of the stereo in the guard's lounge following her like a melody she could not shake.

She compared the new painting with a genuine Venn drawing in the vault, a miniature study of a peasant drawing water at a well. One was four hundred years old, or so the story ran; the other had been finished in a week. The two were alike in manner, and that was the whole of the problem.

"They're alike in manner," she said. "Too alike. The forger copied the manner too well to be careless, and too well to be real."

Her reliance on instinct had limits, so she called Detective Hugo Barr. A plain man with a gift for silence and a nose for nonsense, he had solved the theft of a cathedral mosaic two years before. The crack in that case had been a hairline. This one she could amplify under a lens.

"The law obliges me to start with the obvious," he said. "Any fool would."

"Start there, then," she said. "Tell me about Tomas Quill."

The obvious suspect was the young apprentice painter who had cleaned the basement and carried the crate in. He had worked there since September, and he slept in a room above the stables. Barr had a note in the boy's own hand, found in the lab. There was no clue at first. Only a smell of turpentine and a list of names nobody printed.

"He left a note in his own hand," Barr said, "found in the lab. Me and him paint it, on account the money."

Clumsy English, and a boy's panic behind every word. Cordelia studied it the way she studied the varnish, until the shape of a lie showed through the shape of a confession. "Wrong pronoun," she said. "A literate clerk would write he and I."

"The preposition's wrong as well," she went on. "And the noun at the centre of it, money, is vague to the point of farce. A real forger names a method. A buyer. A date. This one names nothing and proves everything you want to believe, and that forged hand was instrumental in fooling a whole room of experts."

Barr raised an objection. "If the boy could write that, why pretend he cannot spell?"

The police proceeded anyway. The machinery of the law moved with a logic of its own, and Tomas was charged with forgery and fraud. He would plead not guilty, and his plea was a thin hope against an opinion that had already convicted him in the papers. Nobody in that room offered to ring his mother.

"He'll need a lawyer," Barr said, "and the front page is standing in for one. The offence carries years in prison, and the penalty includes a fine."

The prisoner's face looked back at them from the front page, and that face made the case simpler for everyone who liked simple things. Cordelia refused the simple version. She obsessed over the brushwork the way a mother obsesses over a child's fever. "The virtuosity is real," she said. "That forged hand fooled experts who trust surfaces."

Yet the highlights held a tell: a slight wobble, a tremor no steady hand would ever leave. She wanted to know whose hand had shaken, and why. A recording surfaced that week, a phone message left for the Senator's assistant, the voice masked but careless. "He pronounced Venn as if it rhymed with ten," she said. "No scholar speaks it so."

The true pronunciation ended on a soft consonant, almost on the n alone. Cordelia could say it correctly in her sleep. The word sat behind her teeth like a coin. The forger had learned his Venn from a book printed for tourists, not from a life spent at the canvas. "He worked inside this building," she said. "The means were right here."

Emerged the next day: the means. The fake had been painted in the museum's own basement, with a litre of synthetic medium, a kilo of pigment mixed to imitate the old, a drum of turpentine with its lid on a stool, and a pan of solvent under the bench. Someone had eaten there: a cup, a crust, a spoon left in the sink.

"He lodged a complaint against maintenance," Barr said, "to keep them away on the night he worked."

The mess in the lab was real. The alibi beside it was fiction. Cordelia assembled a cohesive theory and took it to Barr. "Then follow the coin," Barr said. "Follow it, and the trail ends in this building."

"Whoever painted this knows the rooms," she said. "The vault. The schedule of the guards who patrol the halls. He acquired the canvas through the project, then maneuvered the blame onto a boy who cannot defend himself. He walked these halls after hours and knew where the lamps went dark."

Barr nodded, slow. "You describe a person with a key and a grudge." "A key," she said, "and a reason. A money reason."

The reason was plain. The museum's income had fallen three years running, the mortgage payments loomed, and the subsidy would save the roof, but it required a proven Venn. Someone had decided that a fake work was cheaper than a closed one; the reward was continued work, and the risk was prison.

Cold calculus. The hand that made it was warm, and warm hands leave tells. She turned next to the certificate itself, the paper that praised the work as genuine; it called a figure in the chapel mosaic a negro servant, a word no sixteenth-century Italian document would use. "It calls a figure in the chapel mosaic a negro servant," she said. "No sixteenth-century Italian document uses that word."

"An English anachronism," she went on. "Lifted from a nineteenth-century catalogue that labelled the same figure with an offensive, out-of-date word. A real Venn paper would have named the man in Italian. In faking age the forger copied a later, prejudiced hand, and in doing so signed his own ignorance."

That ignorance pointed home, because only a handful of people had ever touched the old catalogue. Chief among them was Aldous Pryce, the museum's director, and not incidentally the author of the very book that had used the word. The property did not belong to the building at all; it belonged to whoever painted it last week.

A trained apprentice, the loyal successor to the Venn chair at the university, he had mentored Madame Voss, who was, the gossip whispered, his mistress. The two shared a pact: a secret and a debt. "A pact," she said. "A debt, and a long friendship between people with something to hide." He had taught for eleven years and had never once written a false date.

Cordelia wanted proof, not suspicion. She requested the security strip from the night the canvas arrived and sat down with Barr to watch it. A figure in a long coat appeared: tall, left-handed, limping on the right.

"That is Pryce," she said. "Ankle, two winters ago. The injury left a physiological tremor in his right hand."

The same tremor ran through the fake's highlights. The physical evidence and the physical tell agreed. "One hand," she said. "One shaking hand, and a very clever man." Still she did not confront him at once; she needed to understand Pryce before she accused him, so she spent a week reading everything he had written.

A novel about an apprentice's life, funded by a loan against his own house. A movie about Venn that he had consulted on. A literary friend who wrote poetry in praise of the master. The notion that a scholar could turn forger did not occur to most people, but it occurred to her the moment she saw the tremor.

The museum stood a short distance from the river dam, and beyond the dam rose a skyscraper of glass, the bank that held Pryce's debt. One afternoon she walked there with Barr and watched the water fall a hundred metres. The path between them was paved with broken plates. The noise of it filled her head and emptied it at the same time.

"A barren rock face," Barr said, "and a shabby little booth that sells coffee." A cat slept on the wall with its paw on a peel of old paint. Nearby a child peeled an orange and dropped the pit into a napkin. They learned that Pryce had patented a way of ageing varnish, a chemical trick of physics that made a fake look centuries old.

The patent was real. The honesty was not. He had pledged, under oath, to protect the collection, and that oath now read like a joke. He carried the pledge in a pocket notebook, still in his coat the night he painted the copy. The paper was genuine. The promise inside it was worth nothing.

Word spread at once. The discovery polarized the staff. Some supported Pryce, saying a fake work beat a closed building; others demanded his head. The town likewise split and the newspapers fed the fire, and Cordelia had assimilated too many lessons about pride to take sides. Her task was the truth, not the verdict. Within the hour someone had put a chair outside the director's office.

"A powerful man cornered is a dangerous man," Barr warned. "Pryce is influential, and he has friends in high places."

The risk of reprisal, of harassment, of a discrimination campaign against the witness who exposed him, was real enough to keep her awake at night. She described the forger to the board in plain terms: not a criminal by habit, but a man driven by fear and debt, capable of great craft and greater foolishness. From her perspective he was dangerous, and her perception had been right.

"Magic? No. It was betrayal, she told them. The magic of the fake is not its beauty, but a skill turned against the very tradition it pretends to serve."

The board listened in silence, then voted to suspend Pryce pending the proceeding. "And the boy?" the treasurer asked. "What becomes of him?"

Preparation never sleeps. She forced herself to ensure every fact was airtight, and she barely slept. The weeks went by in one continuous day. She choked on the dust of the lab and elbowed her way through crowds of reporters every morning.

An eccentric collector offered, as an option, to buy the fake for a limited sum. She declined. "Not at any price," she said. "God help this place if we sell our shame." The reproach in her voice was for herself as much as for him, though she did not say it aloud. The man left a card, a phone number, and no explanation of the suitcase.

Her resistance to fatigue was mostly stubbornness. She had limited faith in luck and limited patience for liars, and the examination of the canvas had been realistic in its demands: a steady eye, a clean lens, and a will to see what others refused to see. The work itself never once asked to be finished.

Besides the science there was simply attention, the same attention a mother gives a sleeping child. The shampoo-scented air of the lab reminded her of her first year, when she cleaned frames with a gentle shampoo and learned that paint yields its secrets only to the patient.

She had virtually memorized every Venn in existence. The dam, the skyscraper, the booth, the cat, the whole sterile list: all of it faded beside the one question that mattered, and she hardly had to say the words aloud. "It's a grid," she muttered. "There. Under everything."

Pryce's jaw tightened when they faced him, and he panted like a runner climbing the marble stair. He would not look at her. "Why me?" he asked. "Why not the world?" He had stood in that very room with a layer of paint under his nails.

"You meant to protect the building," she said. "You also meant to deceive. A catastrophe was coming, you say. The law does not accept that as a defence, and the precedent is clear."

The mischief of the scheme lay in its scale. The feature of the fake was its size, a full metre taller than the original study, and the collector who wanted to buy it kept a parachute in his luggage and had an unknown nationality. The size was the joke, and the error.

Barr proposed a formal test. Presumably confident, Pryce agreed to paint a stroke of Venn blue before witnesses, and the comparison of texture would be conclusive. The panel of experts convened in the grand hall.

Cordelia placed a centimetre of the sky under the lens and presented the evidence in a clear sequence: the pin, the modern line pattern, the anachronistic word, the pronunciation on the strip, the tremor, each one exemplified by a photograph blown large. The fake posed as a four-hundred-year-old truth, and every one of them had almost carried it off. The room went quiet.

"You cannot paint that blue again," she said. "The grid is baked into the varnish and it will not come out."

Barr read the proposal to charge Pryce with forgery, fraud and conspiracy. Voss offered a plea of her own. "I knew," she said. "I refused at first. Then love and debt won."

She had mocked the boy in private and lured him near the lab to make the frame easy to carry. For her part in the plot she faced charges of harassment, and her privilege as a curator protected her less than she had believed. The mistress and the director fell together.

Senator Renn, offended and embarrassed, demanded the return of the canvas and threatened a lawsuit over ownership. The museum negotiated a settlement: the fake would remain as a teaching tool, a marvelous example of skill turned to deceit, and the real Venn drawing would tour as the prize of the collection. Nobody proposed burning it, which was the only sensible thing to do with a lie.

The property question was rectified on paper, and the record was set straight. Cordelia spent the following week in retrospection, replacing the fake's frame with a plain one and hanging it beside the genuine study, labelled in honest type: A wonder of the age, and a warning.

Simple message: craft rewards the attentive and punishes the careless. The hall filled with visitors who came to see the fake more than the real; humanity, it seemed, loved a good lie almost as much as a true work. The girl at the turnstile counted her change twice and said nothing.

The reward for Tomas was modest but real: a job restoring the chapel mosaic, and a letter of apology from the official. "You saved my life," he said, "one canvas nearly ended me."

She corrected him, gentle. "I saved a story. The life was always yours." Their communication needed no longer than that.

Barr closed the case with a shrug. "The next forger will learn from this one," he said. "The methods will progress. Keep the lens, Cordelia. The truth does not need friends."

The drama of the evening had a dramatic end, but the quiet work remained. Cordelia renovated the room again, repainted the stone and polished the floor until it shone like a pond. A pigeon cooed from the roof. She knew the old staircase by heart and walked it twice a day.

A peach tree and a lemon tree grew in the courtyard beside a bench, where the staff ate mutton and melon at a picnic on warm afternoons. Two trees, one bench, and the same arrangement every summer. The site was situated for peace, and she meant to keep it that way.

One afternoon a peasant-faced man from the country arrived with a parachute he claimed had belonged to his father, a pilot in the war, and wanted it displayed in the hall as a tribute. Cordelia declined, kind but firm, and kept the story.

The chute was as real as the fake was false, an object with a true history. She learned, in the end, that forgery is commonplace only to those who stop looking. The man had carried it across three towns to stand in front of her.

"Refuse to be fooled? That is a gift. The courage to speak is another gift. With nothing but a microscope and a memory she had faced a powerful man and won without once raising her voice."

The majesty of the law, when it finally arrived, was merely the name we give to people who refuse to look away.

Winter came early to the river town, and with it a long grey quiet that suited her better than the bright noise of the gala. She walked the bridge at dusk, watching the water move under the lamps, letting her mind go soft and slow.

The work of the day was done, the papers were filed, the boy was free, and the man who had lied sat where the law could hold him. There was a peace in that plain fact, a peace that needed no speaker. The kettle in the corner was cold again, and she had not noticed.

Her friend from the café brought her a warm coat for the cold months and laughed at her for standing so long in the wind. The wind came off the water and found the gap in her coat. "You look like a cat that found a saucer," she said. "Come inside."

They spoke of small things: the price of bread, the new dog in the square, the strange habit of birds who waited at the door each morning for crumbs. None of it touched the case, and that was exactly the relief she needed.

On Sundays she visited her mother in a small house by the canal, with a garden of herbs and a cat that hunted nothing. They drank tea and looked through old photographs of a life that had nothing to do with museums.

Her mother told the same stories each time, and Cordelia listened as though hearing them fresh, because love is partly the willingness to be present for the repeated warmth of a voice. "You were always looking too closely," her mother said. "It never killed you."

She thought the habit of attention was not only for work like this. A letter arrived in spring from a school in the next town, asking if she would come and speak to the children about looking closely at the world.

"Were you afraid?" one of them asked.

"Yes," she said. "I was more afraid of saying nothing."

She said yes to the letter, though she hated speaking, and she brought the plain frame and the copy that had caused so much trouble. The children did not care about the scandal. They cared that a grown woman had trusted her own eyes.

The town, in its slow way, let the story become a normal part of its memory, the way a bruise fades to a faint mark that shows only when the light is just so. People still pointed at the building and lowered their voices, but the pointing grew rare.

Cordelia kept her small saving in the jar, kept her early hours, kept the promise to look once more before she judged. The river kept its course, the bridge kept its lamps, and the fake kept its honest place on the wall, a quiet teacher of the difference between a name and a truth.

The canvas hung still, labelled and honest, a fake that told the truth about the people who made it. Cordelia passed it each morning and nodded, the way one nods at a funny friend. It hung there under a plain strip of wood, and it did not move.

Open came the hall, and the concerts resumed, and the players played a musical piece that lifted the spirit, and a solo trumpet sounded the note of a new beginning. And in the courtyard Mara's picture remained, a small guardian of honest seeing.

In a drawer she kept the small lens she had used on the first night, and cleaned it each month with a soft cloth and a drop of oil. A drop of oil, a soft cloth, an ordinary Tuesday. An ordinary thing, no different from a thousand others, and yet it had been enough.

Rarely does the truth need a grand machine. It needs a steady hand, and someone willing to stay in the room after everyone else has gone home. The lamps in the hall were changed to a warmer light in the spring, and the copy looked almost kind under it, as though it too were sorry for the trouble it had caused.

The best forgery is a confession; it simply signs the wrong name.
chapters.translation:
"是假的。"科迪莉亚·韦恩把嗓门压得平平的，"瞧瞧那片天。四百年的天，闻着还跟新的一样。"

参议员黑尔·伦恩说到一半卡住了。那幅画那天早上装在一只木条和胶带衬垫的板条箱里运来，馆里的人已经在围着它搬椅子。九个人站在展厅里盯着看。"九个有文化的人，"她说，"只有一个人头一个瞧出来。"

科迪莉亚·韦恩是这家美术馆的首席修复师，做个艺术家在先，做个科学家在后。她对肌理和构图的那股子感觉，使她成了三个国家里公认的文恩活字典。她把画布挪到灯下，一分钟之内就找出了头一处破绽。那片天的蓝，古典时代的一双手绝调不出来。

"科西莫·文恩的《庭院中的音乐会》，"参议员说，"文艺复兴的大师，他母亲遗产里的一份馈赠。展览星期四开幕。"

伊维特·沃斯夫人笑了，笑纹一动不动。她是这城里艺术上的权威，连传单都是她自己设计的。"一部精美的归来之作，"她这样告诉报界，这话顺着附近一间间咖啡馆传开，像闲话一样。整件事都是她管着的，同一句话印成了传单，别在庭院里每一个摊子上。

哈利孔美术馆坐落在韦兰河上方的一处高地上，砖石与大理石砌出的巨宅，那硕大的圆顶俯临庭院，像第二个月亮。这是它最好的一处，也是最蠢的一个主意。冬天，河上的雾爬上山坡，把阁楼的窗子一口吞掉。

一分钱都没付。参议员是把它当赠品交出来的；市长是个乐天派，热中仪式，已经答应为首展自己剪彩。一笔来自文化部的补贴悬在那儿，全看这栋楼能不能拥有一幅文恩；楼本身就压着按揭，而市长的脾气乐观得足以系上那条彩带。只差一件够分量的盛事，也许就能把楼抬起来。

院子里搭起给乐队用的台子，另雇了个杂技演员在穹顶上方走绳。市长五月里剪了彩，说这个晚上是为艺术、也是为人类的盛举。没人留意到她脸色已经白下去。大厅的格局为了让人群走得顺重新排过，人群走得挺好，从画布边上过去，一步不停。

一位名伶和一位崭露头角的女演员接受了邀请。一位搞音乐的朋友答应在一场古典音乐会的两段之间来一段独奏小号，还有人给散场的人群排进一段说唱。乐队的鼓稳稳撑着一个节奏，把整个广场都抬了起来。科迪莉亚站在门洞里把这一场看下来，头疼得说不出口。

科迪莉亚带着侄女去排练，那是个九岁的小大人，叫玛拉。她在院子里的一个棚子边坐下，用蜡笔画了只熊猫，又用胶带把它贴到木栏杆上。这孩子脑子里还没有偏见这一样东西。"一只熊猫，"科迪莉亚低声说，"是这儿唯一诚实的评论家。"

灯下，那层旧漆讲了一个鉴定书一句也没讲的故事。天空里的颜料太干净了，不像四百年的活儿；真正的文恩之蓝，里面带着颗粒和尘土，带着四百个冬天。他们已经在传单上叫它杰作，而那行标签是用这栋楼自己的印刷机印出来的。

"纹理不对，"她说，"走向也不对。这是画上去的，不是风吹出来的。"

画布的织纹留着现代压力机的印子，一枚二十世纪钢制的别针把内框撑条钉在了一起。一枚带机制头部的钉子。一只被溶剂盖过印的盖子，年代不会比那场战争更晚。证据细微，却是肯定。

那处破绽在喊。它不问。科迪莉亚按捺住，没有立刻出声；她凭习惯专注，凭天性谨慎。这道谜题该配一套方法，不该配一场慌乱。那天晚上闭馆之后，她在展厅里独自走动，守夜人休息室那台音响发出的单调嗡声一路跟着她，像一支她怎么甩也甩不掉的曲子。

她把新画和金库里一幅真正的文恩素描摆在一起比对，一小幅农夫在井边打水的迷你习作。一个是四百年，那是说书人的说法；另一个一周就画完了。两幅在手法上太像，而这就是全部的问题。

"太像了，"她说，"太像了。造假的人把文恩的手法学得太好，好到不像会疏忽，也太好，好到不可能是真的。"

她凭直觉是有分寸的，于是她打电话给警探雨果·巴尔。他是个朴实的男人，天生会沉默，对废话又有一副好鼻子；两年前大教堂一幅马赛克失窃，就是他破的。那案子里的裂口细如发丝。这一处她能用放大镜放得更大。

"法律逼着我从最明显的地方下手，"他说，"换谁也一样。"

"那就从那儿开始，"她说，"跟我说说托马斯·奎尔。"

头号的嫌疑是那个年轻学徒画工，地下室是他扫的，箱子也是他搬进来的。他从九月起就在这儿干，睡觉在马厩上头的一间房。巴尔手里有他笔迹的一张字条，是在实验室里找到的。起先连线索都没有，只有一股松节油味儿，还有一张没人印出来的名单。

"他留了张字条，自己的笔迹，"巴尔说，"在实验室里找到的。是我跟他画的，为的是钱。"

洋泾浜式的英文，每个字后面都跟着一个孩子的慌张。科迪莉亚研究它，像研究清漆那样研究，直到一层谎话的形状从供状的形状底下透出来。"代词错了，"她说，"识字的文书会写'我和他'。"

"介词也错了，"她接着说，"整个句子压轴的那个名词——钱——含糊到了近乎滑稽。一个真造假的人会报出方法、买主、日子。这一份什么也不报，却把你愿信的每一样都证实了，而那双伪造过文恩的手在一屋子专家跟前起了关键作用。"

巴尔提出了一个反对："要是这孩子写得出来，干吗还装作不会拼？"

警方还是照旧往下推。法律的机器自顾自地转，自有它的逻辑；托马斯被控伪造与欺诈。他会作无罪答辩，他那点薄薄的希望顶着的是已经写在报纸上把他判掉的舆论。屋里没有一个人开口要给他妈妈打电话。

"他得请个律师，"巴尔说，"头版报纸正替他当律师呢。这罪名顶着几年的牢，还带了罚金。"

被告那张脸从报头回过来地看着他们，而这张脸让喜欢把事情看简单的人把案子看得更简单。科迪莉亚不肯要那个简单的版本。她盯着笔触的样子，像母亲盯着孩子的高烧。"手艺是真下过功夫，"她说，"那双伪造过的手把一群只信表面的专家全骗过去了。"

可那些高光里带着破绽：一丝极轻的颤，一种稳稳的手绝不会留下的抖。她想知道那是一只怎样的手在抖，以及为什么。那一周里冒出一份录音：一条留给伦恩参议员助手的电话留言，声音遮掩了，却遮得很不用心。"他把'文恩'念得跟'十'押韵，"她说，"没有哪个学者这么念。"

正确的念法收尾带一点轻软的辅音，几乎只剩下一个鼻音。科迪莉亚闭着眼睛也能把它念对。那个词在她牙后头，像一枚硬币。造假的人是把文恩从一本印给游客看的书里学来的，不是从一辈子跟画布打交道的日子里学来的。"他是在这栋楼里画的，"她说，"方法就在这儿。"

第二天，方法浮了上来。这赝品是在这栋楼自己的地下室里画出来的，用掉了一升合成媒介、一公斤配出来仿旧的新颜料，还有一桶松节油，桶盖搭在凳子上，凳边的长凳底下搁着一只溶剂盘。有人在这里吃过东西：一只杯子、一块面包皮、一只留在池子里的勺子。

"他投诉过维修班组，"巴尔说，"为的是动手那晚把他们支开。"

实验室里的狼藉是真的，它旁边那份不在场证明是编出来的。科迪莉亚拼出一套能自圆其说的说法，端到巴尔跟前。"那就追钱，"巴尔说，"追下去，脚印就在这栋楼里断了。"

"画它的人熟这些屋子，"她说，"熟金库，熟巡廊守卫的排班。他借这个项目弄到这块画布，又把罪名转嫁到一个自己没法替自己辩的男孩身上。他下班以后在这些厅里走动，哪儿的灯会灭，他清楚。"

巴尔慢慢点了一下头："你描的是个有钥匙、又有仇的人。""有钥匙，"她说，"还有一个理由，一个钱上的理由。"

理由很简单。这栋楼的收入连跌三年，按揭的还款一天天压到眼前，那笔补贴能保住屋顶，条件是得有一幅确凿的文恩。有人算过，一幅假货比关门倒闭便宜；报偿是接着有差事，风险是坐牢。

这笔账算得冷。下决心的那只手是热的，热手会留下痕迹。她接着把鉴定书本身翻出来，那张把画夸成真迹的纸；它把礼拜堂老马赛克里一个人物叫作"黑奴仆役"，这个字眼，十六世纪的意大利文件是绝不会用的。"它把礼拜堂马赛克里一个人叫'黑奴仆役'，"她说，"十六世纪的意大利文件不会用这个词。"

"这是英国味的年代错词，"她接着说，"抄自一本十九世纪的图录，那本图录用那个又刺耳又过时的词给同一个人贴标签。真正的文恩文件会用意大利文叫出那个人的名字。伪造年岁的时候，他抄的是后来某一双带偏见的笔，这一抄就签下了自己的无知。"

这份无知把指向了家里。当年摸过那本旧图录的，哈利孔只有寥寥数人，领头的便是这栋楼的馆长奥尔达斯·普赖斯——顺带说一句，也正是那本用过那个词的人。这东西根本不归这栋楼；它归上周把它画出来的那个人。

他受过学徒训练，是文恩讲座的忠诚接班人，也带过沃斯夫人——闲话悄悄递过来，说她是他的情妇。两人有个共有的约定：一个秘密，一笔债。"一个约定，"她说，"一笔债，还有一段长时间的来往，两个人都各有各的藏身处。"他教了十一年书，从没写过一个假的日期。

科迪莉亚要的是证据，不是猜疑。她调来画布送达那晚的安保录像带，和巴尔一起盯着看。画面里有个穿长外套的身影：高个子，用左手，右脚有点跛。

"那是普赖斯，"她说，"踝骨，两个冬天之前摔的。那次伤在他右手留下一种生理性的震颤。"

赝品的高光里有同一种震颤。物证和身体上的破绽对上了。"一只手，"她说，"一只发抖的手，还有一个极聪明的人。"她还是没有马上去当面质问；要在指控他之前先弄懂这个人，所以她花了一个星期，把他写过的每一样东西都读了一遍。

一本写学徒生涯的小说，钱是拿自家房子作抵押借来的。一部关于文恩的电影，他当过顾问。还有一位写诗赞颂这位大师的文人朋友。一个学者会变成造假的人，这念头多数人想都不想，可她一看见那震颤就想到了。

这栋楼离河上的水坝不远，坝那边立起来一栋玻璃的摩天楼，楼里装着存着普赖斯那笔债的银行。有天下午，她和巴尔一路走过去，看着水从上百米的坝面上落下来。脚下的路是用碎盘子铺的。那声音灌满她的脑袋，又同时把她脑子腾空。

"一面光秃秃的岩石墙，"巴尔说，"外加一个卖咖啡的破棚子。"一只猫睡在墙上，一只爪子搭在一片旧油漆的皮上；近旁，一个孩子剥着橘子，把籽丢进餐巾里。他们后来查明，普赖斯为让清漆"变老"申请过一份专利——一个化学与物理的小把戏，能让赝品看上去有几百岁。

专利是真的，诚实是假的。他在宣誓之下许诺要护住这批藏品，而那份誓言如今读起来像个笑话。他把那份誓言抄在一个随身带的口袋本里，画那张摹本的那一夜还揣在衣袋里。纸是真的，纸上的承诺一文不值。

消息一下就传开了。这发现把馆里的人劈成两半：有人护着普赖斯，说一幅假货总好过一栋关门的楼；有人则要他的脑袋。全镇照旧分裂，报纸往火上添柴；科迪莉亚对骄傲这东西懂得太多，早就不肯站队。她的活儿是真相，不是判决。不过一个小时，就有人把一把椅子搬到了馆长办公室门外。

"一个被逼到墙角的有势力的人，是个危险的人，"巴尔提醒她，"普赖斯有分量，上面还有人。"

被人报复、被人骚扰、被人趁着一个揭发他的证人搞一场歧视性运动——这风险都是真的，够让她夜里睡不着。她把那个造假的人向董事会直白地讲了一遍：他不是天生的罪犯，而是被害怕和欠债推着走的人，能做出极好的手艺，也能做出更蠢的蠢事。在她看来他危险，而她的眼力一直是对的。

"魔法？不，"她告诉他们，"是背叛。这赝品的魔力不在它的好看，在一门手艺掉过头来对付它嘴上要侍奉的那份传统。"

董事会静静听着，投票在诉讼进行期间暂停普赖斯的职务。"那男孩呢？"司库问，"他怎么办？"

准备这活儿从来不睡。她逼着自己把每一件事实都做得滴水不漏，几乎睡不着。几个星期过得像一整天。她呛在屋里的灰土里，每天早晨用胳膊肘从成群的记者中间挤过去。

一个古怪的收藏家上门，说愿意出有限的价钱买下那幅赝品。她谢绝了。"一分也不卖，"她说，"要是我们连自己的羞耻也卖掉，老天保佑这地方。"她话里那份责备一半是冲他，一半也是冲她自己，只是没有说出口。那人留下一张名片、一个电话号码，对那只箱子一句也没解释。

她对抗疲倦多半只是因为倔。她对运气的信仰有限，对说谎的人的耐心也有限；而检验这块画布在要求上是务实的：一双稳住的眼，一枚干净的镜头，还有一份要看清别人不肯看的东西的意志。这活儿本身从来没说过要干完。

除了科学，剩下的就是注意力，母亲守着睡熟的孩子时那种注意力。实验室里飘着洗发水的气味，让她想起头一年：她当年用温和的洗发水擦洗画框，也因此明白了颜料只把秘密交给等得起的人。

世上现存的每一幅文恩她几乎都背下来了。水坝、摩天楼、那个棚子、那只猫、整张干巴巴的名单——在唯一要紧的那个问题跟前，全淡了，她连话都不必说出口。"是格子，"她低声说，"喏，压在底下呢。"

面对质问时，普赖斯的下颌绷紧了，喘气的样子像个正往上跑大理石楼梯的赛跑者。他不肯看她。"为什么是我？"他问，"为什么不是全世界？"就在那个屋里，他站过，指甲底下嵌着一层颜料。

"你是想保住这栋楼，"她说，"可你也想骗人。你说一场灾难就在跟前。法律不接受这个当作辩解，先例清楚明白。"

这一局的所有猫腻都在它的尺寸上。这赝品有个特点就是它的尺寸——比原先那幅习作整整高一米；那个想买它的收藏家，行李里揣着一具降落伞，国籍不明。尺寸就是那个笑话，也是那个错处。

巴尔提出了一个正式的比试。普赖斯大概是心里有底，答应了在证人在场的情况下画一笔文恩的蓝；纹理一比，即可定论。专家评审团在大厅里聚齐。

科迪莉亚把一小片天空挪到镜头下，把证据按清清楚楚的次序摆出来：那枚别针、现代的线纹、那个年代错乱的词、录像带里的念法、那处震颤，每一样都配一张放大的照片。这赝品扮成了一件四百年的真迹，在座每一个几乎都快把它信了。屋里静下来。

"那片蓝你再画不出来，"她说，"格子已经烤进清漆里，出不来。"

巴尔宣读了以伪造、欺诈、共谋三项罪名指控普赖斯的提案。沃斯夫人也提了自己的一份辩解："我早知道了，"她说，"起先我拒过，后来爱情和欠债赢了。"

她私下嘲过那男孩，又把他哄到实验室附近，好让取画框这件事好办些。在这桩局里她担的那份干系，换来的是骚扰与从犯的指控；她凭策展人身价钱得的那些优待，比她相信的更少。情妇和馆长一起倒下。

伦恩参议员又恼又臊，要求把画布归还，并扬言就所有权打官司。这栋楼谈下了一个了结：那件赝品留下来当教具，一个把手艺使去骗人的绝好例子；真正的文恩素描拿去巡展，做这批收藏的压轴。没有人提议把它烧掉——对一个谎话来说，烧掉大概是唯一聪明的处置。

物权的疑问在纸面上纠正了，记录在案的东西也摆回了原样。接下来的一个星期，科迪莉亚用来回望。她把赝品的画框换成一只素白的，挂到那幅真迹习作旁边，用老老实实的印刷体标了一行：一个时代的奇观，一则警告。

意思很浅：手艺酬谢看得住的人，惩罚看不住的人。大厅里挤满了来看假的比看真的更多的访客；人这一样东西，看来对一记好谎的爱，几乎不比对一件真作品少。检票口的小姑娘把找头数了两遍，一声没吭。

给托马斯的补偿不算大，却是真的：一份修复礼拜堂马赛克的差事，还有一封信，从那位官长笔下来的道歉。"你救了我的命，"他说，"一块画布差点要了我的命。"

她温和地纠正他："我救的是一段故事。命一直是你自己的。"他们之间那份相通，不必多说一个字。

巴尔耸了耸肩，带着警告把案子合上。"下一个造假的人，"他说，"会从这一个身上学。""法子会越变越灵，"他说，"留着你的放大镜，科迪莉亚。真相不需要朋友。"

那晚的戏有个戏剧性的收场，可安静的活儿还在。科迪莉亚把这间屋子又翻修了一遍，把石头重刷一遍，把石地面擦得亮起来，像一潭水。一只鸽子从屋顶上咕咕叫。老楼梯她闭着眼也认得，一天走两趟。

院里一棵桃树和一棵柠檬树，挨着一条长凳长起来，馆里的人常在暖融融的下午聚到那儿吃羊肉和甜瓜。两棵树，一条凳，夏天的摆法年年都一样。这块地是为安宁才设在那儿的，她打算就叫它一直这么安宁。

一天下午，一张庄稼人面孔、从乡下来的男人，带着一具降落伞上门，说是他父亲——一名战时飞行员——留下的；他想把它挂在大厅里当致敬。科迪莉亚和气地谢绝了，却把这段故事留了下来。

那具伞跟那幅画一样真——一件有真实历史的实物。她最后弄明白的是：造假这件事，只有住了手不再看的人才觉得它平平无奇。那人为了站在她面前，把伞从三个镇外搬了过来。

"不肯被骗？那是天分。敢开口说，是另一份天分。她只凭一枚显微镜和一份记性，就对上了一个有势力的人，而且一次也没有提高嗓子就赢了。"

法律那副威严的样子，等它终于落到头上时，说到底只是我们给不肯把目光挪开的人起的一个名字。

冬天早早落在这座河边小镇上，随之而来的是一段又长又灰的安静，比起晚会上那种亮堂堂的喧闹，更合她的心意。她惯在黄昏上桥走走，看水在灯底下挪动，让脑子变软、变慢。

白天的活儿做完了；公文归了档；那男孩自由了；那个撒过谎的人，正落在法律够得着的地方。这件事里藏着一种平和——一种平平常常的平和，不必开口，也感觉得到。墙角那把水壶又凉了，她一点也没察觉。

咖啡馆那位朋友给她带来一件厚外套，过冬穿的，还笑她站在风里一动不动站那么久。风从河面上过来，找到她外套上那个豁口。"你看着像只找到牛奶碟的猫，"她说，"进来吧。"

她们说些小事：面包的价格，广场上新来的那条狗，一群鸟每天清早守在门口等面包屑的怪毛病。这些没有一样沾到案子上，而这恰恰是她需要的那口松快。

星期天她去看母亲，母亲住在运河边一间小屋里，屋后有个草药园，还有一只什么也不逮的猫。她们喝茶，翻看一些跟美术馆全不相干的老照片。

母亲每次都讲那几段旧故事，科迪莉亚听着，像是头一回听见——因为爱有一部分是，愿意为一份一遍遍重来的、暖烘烘的嗓音在场。"你从小就看得太细，"母亲说，"可这从没要过你的命。"

她想，注意力的习惯，并不只该用在这样的活儿上。春天里寄来一封信，是隔壁镇上一所小学写来的，问她肯不肯来给孩子们讲讲，怎么把世界看仔细。

"您怕吗？"其中一个问。

"怕，"她说，"我更怕的是什么都没说。"

那封信她答应了，虽然她讨厌当众讲话，还把那只素白的画框和那幅惹出这么多麻烦的摹本一起带了去。孩子们不在乎这桩丑闻；他们在乎的是一个大人信过了自己的眼睛。

小镇拿自己的慢法，让这件事变成了它记忆里太平常的一部分，像一块淤青淡成一道浅印，只有光刚好照到时才看得见。人们仍旧指着那栋楼、压低嗓门，可这种指指点点渐渐少了。

科迪莉亚把那点积蓄留在罐子里，守着早起的钟点，守着给自己立下的一条誓：在评判之前，永远再看一眼。河守着它的河道，桥守着它的灯，那件赝品在墙上守着它诚实的位子，一位安静的老师，教人分辨一个名字与一个真相之间的分别。

那块画布静静挂着，有标牌，坦荡荡的，一件赝品，却把造它的那些人的真相说了出来。科迪莉亚每天早上从它身边走过，点一下头，像冲一位讨喜的朋友点头那样。它就那么挂在一条素白的木条底下，一动不动。

大厅开了，音乐会照旧，乐手奏一支提神的曲子，独奏的小号吹出一个新起点的音。而院子里，玛拉那幅画还留着，一位小小的守护神，守着诚实的观看。

她书桌的抽屉里留着一枚小镜片，头一夜用过的那一枚；她每个月拿一块软布和一滴油把它擦一遍。一滴油，一块软布，一个再平常不过的星期二。平平常常的东西，跟上千枚别的镜片没两样，可当年就够用了。

真相很少需要一台大机器。它要的只是一双稳住的手，和一个等别人都回了家还肯留在屋里的人。大厅里的灯在开春换成暖一点的色，那件摹本在光底下看着几乎有点儿不好意思，仿佛也在替它招来的这场麻烦致歉。

最好的赝品是一份认罪书；它只是签错了名字。
chapters.summary: 艺术悬疑 · 本篇含 240 个目标词

chapters.title: 松鼠的证词
chapters.content:
"I am not asking for the moon," said Mrs. Quill. "I am asking for one pipe."

She had said it so often that the queue outside knew the line by heart. Behind her a squirrel came down the corridor wall, touched the floor, and climbed back up. Nobody shooed it. In Nettleford the creature kept a sort of immunity.

Sallows stacked the docket in a sensible shape. "We begin with the toilet," he said. "Then the soup. Then the pyramid. Then the squirrel. Then the puppet."

"A repertoire of small disasters," said Judge Beatrix Callow. Beatrix settled the robe on her shoulders. "Let us proceed."

Under her hand lay the questionnaire about service satisfaction. The court had mailed it to every claimant. Not one form had come back, a fact the judge regarded as the most honest verdict ever returned on paper.

On a rack by the door that questionnaire had hung since spring under a thin film of dust, waiting for one honest word.

In the hall an instrumentalist tuned a racket of loosened strings, badly, for the restless crowd. A missionary turned court-consultant hovered near the reception desk with a container of refreshments he insisted on offering to the anxious.

A superstitious old man in a sock with a hole counted the tiles aloud, certain the court would punish him for a curse. The old man counted to ninety and stopped. "Ninety-one is the dangerous one," he said, and the clerk left him be.

None of it mattered. The law mattered.

Case one. Mrs. Quill claimed that the toilet on the floor above had leaked for a month, and that the moisture had ruined her ceiling and her nerves.

The landlord, a strict man with a square jaw, refused to pay. "A toilet is a fixture," he said. "A fixture is not a fault."

Beatrix scrutinized the photographs, noted the mould, and ruled that the landlord must repair the pipe and refund half a month of rent. By lunchtime the pipe was fixed. Two months later it leaked again, and Mrs. Quill came back with the same line and a wetter ceiling.

Mrs. Quill left pleased. The landlord left muttering that the state had no business in his bathroom.

Dotty Fenn, a cook of real talent and a fierce temper, sued a blogger who had published her secret recipe for bean soup with a green sauce. "She stole my taste," Dotty said. "She posted the recipe and called it hers."

The blogger, a fashionable woman with a silver ring, laughed. "A soup cannot be stolen," she said. "A recipe is a method, and a method is free."

She had sampled Dotty's soup at the harvest fair. She recognized the flavour at once. "The theft here is of labour, not soup," she said. "You may not own a stew, but you may not pretend it fell from the sky. Pay the cook for the photograph and the postage of her letter, and henceforth credit the pot."

The blogger paid, red in the face. Dotty left with a graceful bow, and the whole front row wanted the recipe, which is how small towns work.

Wren had answered an advert for a beauty firm. She paid a fee, bought a suite of creams, and was told to recruit her friends. When the scheme collapsed, she sued for the money and for the exploitation of her trust. "They exploited my hope," she said. "They sold me a ladder with no top."

The defendant, a smooth man in a suit, argued that Wren had joined willingly. Beatrix studied the contract and found a clause that promised wealth for mere talk. "This is no business," she said. "It is a pyramid built on other people's rent. Refund the fee, and cease the recruiting, or the state will prosecute."

Prosecute. The word turned the man pale, and the clerks below stopped writing. Mr. Pell, a gardener of serious habit, sued his neighbor over a squirrel. "Her squirrel robs my feeder," he said. "It steals the seed and scares the birds. I demand damages."

The neighbor, a round woman with a kind voice, replied that the squirrel belonged to no one. "A squirrel is a creature of the wood," she said. "It does not respect a fence."

An argument was close to a riot. Beatrix tapped the desk with a ruler. "A squirrel is not property," she observed, "but a feeder filled with seed is an invitation. Split the cost of a covered feeder, and let the creature eat."

The two parties agreed, surprised into friendship. Pell went out first. The neighbor followed more slowly. At the gate they both looked up at the same roof, and neither mentioned the feeder.

Next came the razor. A barber named Hodge sued a client who claimed the razor had cut his thumb to the bone.

The client waved a towel stained red. "I beg for relief," he said. "Two weeks I have carried this." Hodge, calm as a clock, produced his register. "The razor was sharp," he said. "You twitched. The wound is a scratch."

An attendant from the clinic confirmed the injury was minor. The judge dismissed the claim and suggested a bath and a nap.

Old Mr. Ashcroft had died, and his nephew sued the estate for a coin: a gold sovereign and a silver shilling said to be hidden in a tin box behind the portrait.

The executor laughed. "There is no box," he said. "There is a skeleton in the study, a rifle above the mantel, a seal on the will, and no treasure."

Beatrix ordered a search of the house. They found the box after all, stuffed with a statute book whose pages ranged from treason to rape. At the back lay the sovereign and the shilling, warm from the wall. The treaty framed on the wall was fake, but the coins were real. The nephew grinned. The executor sighed, and said nothing at all. The box was real.

A tourist on a sightseeing tour sued a driver who had taken the long route through traffic and charged a cruel fare. "He robbed me of an hour," she said. "He showed me the same shop twice."

The driver protested that the traffic was not his fault. The judge studied the map and found the route was needlessly long. "The city provides a short way," she said. "Refund the difference, and cease the scenic detour."

Mrs. Vance bowed. The driver shrugged and kept his cap on. Nobody moved.

A writer sued a rival who had published a novel he called a satire of the writer's life. "He drew me as a spy," the writer said. "He spread a rumor that I betrayed my friend."

The rival laughed. "It is a story," he said. "A satire is a story, and a story is free speech."

Beatrix read the book and found it cruel but not libel. "Publicity is a double edge," she said. "Keep the book, but print an apology." The writer accepted. The rival grinned, and left with the book under his arm.

Mrs. Reed sued her neighbor for irrigating the wrong soil and killing her roses with too much moisture. "He flooded my bed," she said. "My flowers died."

The neighbor denied it, then stopped denying it. The judge walked to the window and looked at the garden. "The soil is wet," she said. "The roses are brown. Split the cost of new plants, and irrigate with care." Both ladies nodded, stiff but civil. Neither waved. Neither slammed a gate.

A young singer sued the organizer who had refused her a slot on the stage. "I competed and won," she said. "He gave the prize to his cousin."

The organizer, a retired referee, denied favour. The judge asked for a rehearsal tape. The singer sang, clear as a bell. The cousin croaked. "Talent is obvious," the judge said. "Give the girl her slot." The singer smiled. The referee bowed.

Then the puppet case, the afternoon's strange heart.

Two former partners in a puppet theatre stood before the bench. Marlow accused Iris of stealing his script, a play about a king, a queen, and a lost theme of love. "She took my story," he said. "She performed it as her own."

Iris, calm in blue, denied it. "The theme is old," she said. "Love is not owned."

A referee from the town talent show was summoned to testify. He swore on a book and gave his testimony: the play had won a prize, and both names were on the poster.

The judge listened, and slowly recognized the truth. Not business rivals at all, but a romance turned to quarrel. "You were spouses of a sort," she said, "partners in life before partners in art. The script is yours together. Share the prize, and settle the rest outside."

Marlow looked at Iris. Iris looked at the floor. Something soft passed between them, and the case was withdrawn.

The court rose for a break. A bee came in with the noise and went straight back out. The bee left. Beatrix walked to the window and watched the squirrel run the wall. "A strange afternoon," she murmured, "of small wrongs and small cures."

Sallows brought a cup of tea. "The questionnaire," he said, "still empty." The judge laughed. "Good," she said. "Justice is not a survey."

After the break the judge attacked the remainder of the stack. Sallows picked a case at random and read the names. A ray of late sun fell through the window and rested on the bench, and the dust in it danced.

The clerk roused a sleeping man who had come to sue his own pillow for snores. "A singular lack of proof," the judge observed, and dismissed it with a kind word.

A woman opened her purse to pay the filing fee. "What is it for?" someone asked from the corner. The tin on the desk accepted the coin. It rang twice. A talent scout sat in the corner, quietly looking for a star among the claimants, and found none worth a second look. The court kept a social page that no one followed, which the judge regarded as a small mercy.

Studies were cited like weapons. A man who slipped on a waxed floor waved a scientific study of gravity, and she skimmed it and ruled for the shop. The back page said one hundred per cent, which she did not believe for a moment. A technical fault in the sound system delayed the next hearing by ten minutes, and the judge used the time to meditate, her meditation lasting exactly as long as the hymn she hummed as a girl.

A mirror hung by the outer door, and a child peered into it, touching the glass with a clean finger. A locker in the hall held the winter coats of the staff, and the judge hung her own there too.

The mix of cases that filled the docket was, the judge had long noted, a faithful mirror of the town itself. She thought of mortality on the long nights when the gavel rested unused. Nevertheless, the small griefs outlasted the large ones. A man lost a case and smiled anyway, which the judge called the only real victory the afternoon would yield.

"To clarify," she said to a worried woman, "the fee is due today, but the court will wait." She would collect the fees at five, and the tin would fill slowly. "Concentrate," she told a nervous witness who could not remember the year; he blinked and then spoke the truth.

The court's activity slowed at four. By half past four the last strap had gone off her shoe. The judge stretched her hands and sighed. A man sued his brother over a slice of birthday cake. She ordered them to share, and they did, stiffly.

A schoolboy lost a pair of scissors and tried to sue the wind. She laughed and sent him home. A local painter drew a sketch of the bench and gifted it to the court, unsigned. It hangs there still, and somebody in the gallery keeps shading it in pencil.

From the kitchen came an offer to roast a chicken and settle a fine. The judge liked a warm kitchen and agreed. A barber offered to test the razor on a melon, and the client, wary, declined.

A member of royalty had once visited the court to pay a tax on a horse, and the tax case that followed was the dullest hour of the decade. "It is a sin to lie in here," an old man whispered to his son. The judge heard and nodded. The oath she asked them to swear was sacred and solemn, and even the liar bowed his head before it.

The law, she often said, was a shield for the weak and a net for the careless. The court would seize the goods of any man refusing to pay, and would sanction forgery by anyone who forged a receipt. Both capitulated quickly.

She looked with scorn at a cheat claiming a dog had signed a lease, and the room laughed with her. The pile of paper on her desk was a siege she endured daily. A woman alleged abuse from a neighbor who played the drum at midnight; the judge asked for proof and received a recording of a song badly sung.

The stereotype of the grumpy judge was false where she was concerned. The stereotyped view of the poor as dishonest angered her more than any lie.

She would stress the rule that all were equal before the bench. The strife between two sisters over a lamp was old and silly, and she ended it with a joke. The workers of a shop would strike at noon for better pay, and the owner capitulated before the first chant. "Strive to be honest," she told a boy who had broken a window; he promised and meant it. The struggle to keep the peace was tiring, but she drank her tea and continued.

That verdict would stun the room. A woman had just won a suit against a bank that had lost her coins. The pump in the cellar would suck the water from a flood caused by a burst pipe, and the caretaker sighed in relief. "Suppose you are wrong," she said to a man swearing on his mother; he paused, then laughed at himself. The ruling was tailored to the case, as it always was, and both sides bowed.

The brother of the defendant bore a strange resemblance to a thief she had seen years ago. She noted it only to herself, and did not mention it.

Everyone in the room knew who the target of the afternoon's last suit would be.

It was the judge. Hodge came forward with a brown package. "You examined my register," he said. "You did not touch it, but you looked at it, and looking is close enough."

Beatrix stood up. She stepped down from the bench, sat in the gallery among the bored, and folded her hands. Sallows cleared his throat and read the ruling aloud. Twice he stopped, and the judge waited for him. "The court finds for the plaintiff. The defendant is fined one shilling, payable to a barber who has waited since three." The room laughed. The judge fished a shilling from her purse and handed it over, laughing too.

A sensation of relief spread through the room as the clock neared five. The simplicity of the truth still stunned her anew each week, for most people came in wanting only to be heard. "A straightforward matter," she called a case about a lost glove, and the crowd agreed. Successive claims had wearied her, but she persevered, because the thread of every story, thin as it was, deserved a pull.

He tried to convince the court that the moon had moved his car. She declined to believe him and fined him instead. The defendant had a creative excuse for every late rent, which the judge found amusing but not legal. A dot of ink marked the corner of a page, and the clerk noted the spot. It was a small effort to be kind, and she made it whenever she could.

She pointed a finger at the map to show a man his error. The following case was the oddest of the day: a man suing a goose for his stolen lunch. "No fuss," the judge said, and the room quieted. A man in the back said he would grind his own coffee at home. "The smell is honest," he said, and it reached even the bench.

An intermediate step was needed to settle a dispute about a shared wall, and she added it to the order. "You possess the coin," she told the nephew from the sovereign case, "and the law will protect that." "You possibly mistake the date," a woman said of a ticket, and the judge checked and agreed. The reality was simple, and the woman accepted it without anger.

A man came to reclaim his hat from the lost property box, and the clerk handed it over with a bow. The state would regulate the fees that landlords could charge, and the judge welcomed the help. Her own insight, that people sue what they cannot say, had saved more cases than any statute. A remark she made about kindness was insightful enough that a lawyer in the back wrote it down. The interior of the court was plain and clean, and she liked it that way.

On the board was a boat stranded near a small island, posted but never heard; she read it and smiled at the sea logic of it. Of the two claims left, the latter was the weaker, and she dismissed it with a gentle word. The lower court in a nearby town had erred on the same point, she recalled, and she wrote a note to warn them.

A retired prosecutor sat in the gallery as a watcher of justice and nodded at her rulings. A provision of the court rule allowed a delay for the sick, and she cited it kindly. "You may pursue the matter elsewhere," she told a man whose claim fell outside her power, and he left calmly.

"Of every race and creed, this bench is open," she announced. "They try to railroad the poor through forms," she muttered to Sallows, who heard and smiled. The remainder of the filing fee was returned to a woman who had overpaid, and she bowed.

The clerk would resign at the end of the month to study the law himself; she regretted the loss but was proud of him. "Do not resort to lies," she warned a woman inventing a witness. The woman looked down and told the truth. She would revise the plain form so that a child could fill it, and the words improved. The rhythm of the gavel, steady as a heart, settled the room each time she lifted it.

A ribbon tied the bundle of files, and the draught from the window tugged it loose. The clerk's role was small but key, and she thanked him often. To his shock, a man lost a case he thought he would win, and the other side cheered softly. She took her notes in shorthand, the pen moving fast across the page. "Use your sense," she said to a woman who doubted her own eyes, and the woman blinked and agreed.

The final sentence of a letter read aloud in evidence said simply, "I am sorry," and the room softened. "Somehow we find the truth," the judge said, "even when it is dressed as a lie." Her thoughtful pause before each ruling was famous in the town, and the crowd would hush to catch it.

A title entered as proof was read aloud, and a boy in the gallery leaned in to hear it. A torch lay on the desk in case of a power cut, and she would test it once a week. "Do not touch the evidence," Sallows told a curious child, who snatched his hand back with a grin.

The old man whose voice trembled as he spoke of his late wife received the gentlest ruling of the day. Before she gave it, she would tap her pen twice on the wood, and the room counted the taps. The clerk informed the room of the rules once more, and all listened as if for the first time.

She would refine her patience as the hour lengthened, and refute with a smile any claim that the court was rude to the poor. That fine was his salvation from a worse fate, and he knew it. A sincere apology mended more than any ruling could. She would slap no one, but she once slapped a gavel so hard the room jumped. A man was said to smuggle a watch, and the claim was thrown out for lack of proof. The solution to most fights was a cup of tea and a quiet ear.

The source of the leak was found at last, and the plumber bowed, wiped his hands, and went. The spelling of a street name was wrong on a key paper, and the clerk fixed it quickly. The judge praised the cook's technique with the soup, and Dotty beamed. He paid the cost and walked out, thereby closing the matter for good. A narrow win was still a win, she said, and everyone left the building a little taller than they came in. The only obstacle to peace was pride, and pride was cheap.

It was paradoxical that the quietest mouth in the room took the most. The defendant adapted his tale to the facts at last, and the court believed him. His appearance was rough but his heart was soft. At the beginning of the year she had feared the docket; by its end she loved it.

He would quit his job at the factory after the case, he said, and she wished him well. It was the fourth place he had mentioned that year, and the fifth that afternoon. She had once written prose that no one would publish, and she knew a bad story when one was told in her defence. A member of the public paid his fee in pennies and sweated through all of it. The two sides united over a shared joke, and the suit died quietly.

"You may go," she told a man whose goose had cost him nine pounds. "Whichever side is right will find the law on its side." The cellar door needed a new pump, and the task of signing for it was hers.

When the session resumed, Beatrix addressed the room with a thought she had kept private all afternoon. "A court," she said, "is a place where strangers bring their small griefs and ask a busy woman to solve them. The law is a tool, not a salve. But now and then the truth is simple, and the rest is noise."

She paused. "Consider, for instance, the paradox of this room. We seek a fair result with a process that frustrates everyone. The logical mind wants a rule; the inner life wants a story. A subjective view is not a false one. Nonetheless, the standard of proof is objective, and the court must adhere to it, despite the tears."

A woman in the back raised her hand. "Your Honor," she said, "I came to sue my son for neglect, but now I think I came to be heard." The judge smiled. "Then you are heard," she said. "The case is dismissed by kindness."

The missionary stepped forward. "I assisted the court with a study of morality," Mr. Blythe said. "I find that people who sue their kin are lonely, not angry." Beatrix regarded him with a shrewd eye. "A missionary in a court is a rare sight," she said. "Keep your study. I suspect the truth is simpler than your theory."

A soft tune came from the instrumentalist. The squirrel sat on the sill and appeared to listen. "An audience of one," the judge remarked, "and the most honest critic in the building."

Later, when the last case was done, the judge wrote a line in her book. The law is a net; it catches the small fish and lets the large ones swim. Be glad of the small ones.

She closed the book, looked at the room, and let the quiet do the rest. "Court is adjourned," she said. "Go home. Fix the toilet. Feed the squirrel. Share the soup."

And outside, the squirrel ran along the wall, free and unsued, the only creature in Nettleford who had committed no wrong all afternoon.

The small griefs of strangers are the only cases worth the hearing.
chapters.translation:
“我不要月亮，”奎尔太太说，“我要一根管子。”

她把这话说得太多了，外头排队的都背得下来。她身后，一只松鼠顺着走廊的墙跑下来，碰了碰地，又爬回墙上去。没人赶它。在内特尔福德，这小东西有种说不清的特权。

萨洛斯把案卷摞成一个自己觉得顺手的形状。“我们从厕所开始，”他说，“然后是汤，然后是金字塔，然后是松鼠，然后是木偶。”

“一整套小灾祸的曲子，”卡洛法官说。比阿特丽斯把法袍在肩上捋平，“我们开始吧。”

她手底下压着一份服务满意度的问卷。法庭把它寄给了每一个索赔人，一张表也没回来——法官把这件事看成文书史上交回过的最诚实的一份裁决。

门边一个架子上，那份问卷从春天就一直挂在那儿，薄薄一层灰，等一个老实字。

大厅里有个乐手在调音，一把弦松松垮垮，调得很糟，调给一群坐不住的人听。一个由传教士改行来当法庭顾问的布莱特先生，端着一盒茶点守在接待台边，非要分给那些局促的人。

一个迷信的老头，袜子上破了个洞，张嘴数地砖，笃定法庭会因为他心里冒过一句咒就罚他。那老头数到九十停下来。“九十一才是要命的那个，”他说，书记员由着他。

这些都不顶事。顶事的是法律。

第一桩。奎尔太太说，楼上的厕所漏了整整一个月，潮气毁了她的天花板，也毁了她的神经。

房东是个下巴方正、一脸严丝的男人，拒绝付钱。“厕所是固定设施，”他说，“固定设施不算毛病。”

比阿特丽斯翻看那些照片，记下霉斑，裁定房东必须修管子，还得退半个月房租。不到晌午管子就修好了。两个月以后它又漏，奎尔太太照原话再来一趟，头顶也潮了新的。

奎尔太太高高兴兴地走了。房东边走边低声嘀咕，说官府管得太宽，连他浴室的门都没敲。

多蒂·芬恩，一个真有手艺、脾气也烈的厨子，告了一名博主——那人把她的秘制豆汤和青酱一并传了出去。“她偷了我的味道，”多蒂说，“她把方子贴出来，还说是她自己的。”

那博主是个戴银戒指的时髦女人，她笑了。“汤偷不走，”她说，“方子是方法，方法是白送的。”

法官曾在丰收集市上尝过多蒂的汤。她一眼就认出了那股味道。“这里被偷走的是工夫，不是汤，”她说，“你占不了这锅炖菜的便宜，可你也别说是从天上掉下来的。付给厨子照像的钱和寄一封信的邮费，往后要认那口锅。”

博主红了脸付了钱。多蒂行了个体面的礼走了，前排所有人都想要那个方子——小镇就是这么办事的。

雷恩照着一家美容公司的广告应了征。她交了费，买回一整套乳霜，又被告知要拉朋友进来。盘子塌了以后，她告他们要回钱，还要回她那份被辜负的信任。“他们利用了指望，”她说，“他们卖给我一架没有顶的梯子。”

被告是个穿得挺括的男人，辩称雷恩是自愿入伙的。比阿特丽斯细看那纸合同，找出一条只要动动嘴就能许出财富的条款。“这算不得生意，”她说，“这是一座拿别人房租垒起来的金字塔。退钱，别再拉人，不然官府就要起诉。”

起诉。这两个字把那男人的脸都吓白了，底下的书记员也停了笔。佩尔先生，一个认真到近乎刻板的园丁，为一棵松鼠告了他的邻居。“她的松鼠抢我的喂鸟器，”他说，“它把种子叼走，把鸟都吓跑了。我要赔偿。”

邻居是个圆脸、说话和气的女人，她回说松鼠不属于谁。“松鼠是林子里的东西，”她说，“它不讲篱笆。”

两边差点吵成一场乱子。比阿特丽斯拿尺子敲了敲桌子。“松鼠不是财产，”她指出，“可一只盛满种子的喂鸟器，是一道邀请。出一半钱，买个带顶的喂鸟器，让那东西吃吧。”

两边都答应了，稀里糊涂地成了朋友。佩尔先出门。邻居走得慢些。到了门口，两人都抬头看同一片瓦，谁也别提喂鸟器。

接下来是剃刀。一个叫霍奇的理发师告他的客人——那客人说剃刀把他的拇指划到了骨头。

客人挥着一条染红的毛巾。“我求法庭给个说法，”他说，“这都扛两个礼拜了。”霍奇像钟一样稳，掏出他的登记簿。“刀是锋的，”他说，“你抽了手。那伤口不过一道划痕。”

诊所来的人确认伤势轻微。法官驳回了索赔，顺口劝那位客人去洗个澡、睡一觉。

老阿什克罗夫特死了，他的侄子为一枚钱币告了遗产——一枚金索弗林和一枚据称藏在肖像背后铁盒里的银先令。

遗嘱执行人笑了。“没有盒子，”他说，“书房里有一副骷髅，壁炉架上挂着一支长枪，遗嘱上盖着印，可没有财宝。”

比阿特丽斯下令搜屋。他们到底把盒子翻了出来，里头塞的是一本法规汇编，书页从叛国一路排到强奸；盒底，是那枚索弗林和那枚先令，刚从墙边拿过来，还带着暖意。墙上挂的那幅条约图是假的，钱币却是真的。侄子咧嘴笑了；执行人叹了口气，一句话也没说。那只盒子倒是真的。

一个参加观光团的人告一名司机——司机绕远路穿城堵车，还收了一笔刻毒的车钱。“他抢走我一个钟头，”她说，“同一家店，他给我看了两遍。”

司机争辩说堵车不怪他。法官研究地图，看出那条路实在绕得没必要。“城里本有一条近路，”她说，“退差价，别再兜风景。”

万斯太太鞠了个躬。司机耸了耸肩，帽子没摘。没人动。

一位作家告他的对头——对头出了本小说，他称之为对自己生活的讽刺。“他把我画成个间谍，”作家说，“他还放话，说我出卖了自己的朋友。”

对头笑了。“那是个故事，”他说，“讽刺也是个故事，故事是言论自由。”

法官读了那本书，看它刻薄，但不算诽谤。“风声是一把双刃刀，”她说，“书可以留着，可要登一个道歉。”作家应了；对头咧嘴一笑，挟着书走了。

里德太太告邻居，说他浇错了地，用太多水把她的玫瑰浇死。“他把我的花床淹了，”她说，“我的花都死了。”

邻居先否认，后来不否定了。法官走到窗前，看看那座园子。“土是湿的，”她说，“玫瑰是褐的。新苗的钱对半分，浇水浇仔细些。”两位太太都点了头，僵着，还算客气。谁也没挥手。谁也没摔门。

一个年轻姑娘告那位不肯给她台上一个位子的主办人。“我比了，我赢了，”她说，“他把奖给了他表妹。”

主办人是个退休的裁判，否认偏袒。法官要了一盘预演的带子。姑娘一开口清亮得像铃；表妹叫得沙哑。“才艺是藏不住的，”法官说，“把这姑娘的位子给她。”姑娘笑了；裁判鞠了个躬。

接着是木偶案，是这整个下午古怪的心脏。

一家木偶戏班的两个老搭档站到了法官席前。马洛告艾瑞斯，说她偷了他的本子——一出写国王、王后，还有一段失落的爱情母题的戏。“她拿走了我的故事，”他说，“她拿去当自己的演了。”

艾瑞斯一身蓝衣，神色从容，否认。“这母题老得很了，”她说，“爱不是谁家的东西。”

镇上才艺秀请来一位裁判作证。他手按一本书发了誓，然后给了证词：这戏获过奖，海报上两个名字都在。

法官听着，慢慢认出了真相。这两人不是生意场上的对头，是一段转成了争吵的爱情。“你们在某种意义上是夫妻，”她说，“要先做人里的搭子，才做戏里的搭子。这本子是你们共有的。奖两人分，剩下的事，到外面去解决。”

马洛看着艾瑞斯；艾瑞斯看着脚下的地板。有什么软软的东西从两人之间过去了，这桩案子撤了。

法庭起立休庭。一只蜜蜂跟着喧哗飞进来，又原路飞了出去。蜜蜂走了。比阿特丽斯走到窗前，看那只松鼠沿着墙跑。“一个奇怪的下午，”她低声说，“由小小的错处和小小的补救凑成。”

萨洛斯端来一杯茶。“问卷，”他说，“还是空的。”法官笑了。“好，”她说，“正义不是一份调查表。”

休完庭，法官接着啃案卷里剩下那一摞。萨洛斯随手抽出一桩，念了名字。一缕斜阳从窗子落进来，停在法官席上，光里的浮尘跳起舞。

书记员把一个睡着的人叫醒——那人是来起诉自己的枕头打呼噜的。“证据上独缺一样东西，”法官说罢，和气地把它驳了。

一个女人打开钱包交立案费。“这是交什么的？”角落里有人问。桌上的铁罐接住了硬币，响了两声。一个星探坐在角落里，悄悄在索赔人里挑苗子，挑不出一个值得再看第二眼的。法庭自己开过一个社交页面，没人关注——法官把这件事看成一件小小的慈悲。

一叠论文像械具一样被举起来。一个在打蜡地板上滑倒的男人，挥着一份讲重力的科学研究；她扫了一眼，判那家小店胜诉。最后一页写着百分之百，她一秒也不信。音响系统出了个技术故障，把下一场庭审推迟了十分钟；法官拿这工夫静坐，静得正好和她小时候哼的一首圣诗一样长。

外门边挂着一面镜子，一个孩子凑上去照，用一只干净的手指摸了摸玻璃。门厅一只柜子收着职员的冬衣，她也在那儿挂上了自己的。

塞进案卷的这批案子，法官早看熟了，是这座小镇本身的一副如实镜子。木槌闲置的漫漫长夜里，她想过死；可不管怎样，小小的忧伤比大忧伤活得久。一个人输了官司却照样笑了——法官管这叫那个下午唯一真正的赢。

“说清楚一下，”她对一个愁眉不展的女人说，“这笔钱今天到期，不过法庭会等。”她五点收费，那只铁罐会一点点满起来。“集中精神，”她对一个想不起年份的紧张证人这么说；他眨了眨眼，然后说了实话。

四点一过，庭上的动静就慢下来。四点过半，她鞋上最后一根带子也松了。法官把手伸展开，叹了口气。一个人告了他哥哥，为的是一小块生日蛋糕。她判他们分了，他们硬邦邦地照办。

一个学生丢了把剪刀，跑来告风。她笑了笑，打发他回家。本地一位画家给法官席画了张速写，没署名，送给法庭；它还挂在那儿，旁听席上总有人拿铅笔给它补影子。

厨房那边主动提出烤一只鸡来抵罚金。法官喜欢热乎乎的厨房，就答应了。一位理发师主动要在瓜上试剃刀，那位客人存着戒心，回绝了。

从前有位王室成员来法庭交一匹马的车马税，随之而来的那桩税案，是这十年里最沉闷的一个钟头。“在这儿撒谎是罪过，”一个老头对他儿子低声说；法官听见了，点了点头。她要大家起的誓既神圣又庄重，连那骗子都在它面前低了头。

“法律，”她常说，“是弱者的盾，也是粗心人的网。”法庭会查封一个拒不付账的人的家当，也会罚任何伪造收据的人；两样都很快就服软了。

她带着轻蔑看一个骗子——那人说他的狗签过一份租约——满屋的人都跟着她笑了。桌上那一堆纸，是她天天挨的一场围困。一个女人控告邻居半夜打鼓吵人；法官要证据，收到的是一段唱得很难听的录音。

关于脾气乖戾的法官，那套成见在她身上并不成立。那些把穷人想成不老实的刻板眼光，比任何一句谎言都更叫她恼火。

她总强调一条：在法官席前，人人平等。两姐妹为一盏灯闹了很久，闹得又蠢又旧，她拿一个笑话收了场。一家铺子的工人正午罢工要加薪，主人在头一声口号之前就认了。“学着老实，”她对一个打碎窗子的男孩说；他答应了，也是当真的。维持太平的这桩累活没个完，可她喝完茶，接着做。

下一桩案子的裁决要让满屋发怔：一个女人刚告赢了一家弄丢她钱币的银行。地窖里的水泵会把爆裂水管漫出来的水抽干，管房的人宽慰地舒了口气。“假定你错了，”她对一个指着自己的母亲起誓的男人说；他停了一下，然后自己笑了起来。裁定照例是量着这桩案子做的，一向如此，两边都鞠了躬。

被告的哥哥，生得像她多年前见过的一个贼。这一点她只记在了自己心里，也没往外说。

满屋的人都知道，这个下午最后一桩官司要告谁。

是法官本人。霍奇捧着一个牛皮纸包上前。“您看过我的登记簿，”他说，“您没碰它，可您看了它；看了，也就够近了。”

比阿特丽斯站起身。她走下法官席，坐在旁听席那些无聊的人中间，双手交叠。萨洛斯清了清嗓子，把裁定念出声，念到两处停下来，法官等着他。“法庭判原告胜。被告罚一枚先令，付给一个从三点就等着的人。”满屋大笑。法官从钱包里摸出一枚先令递过去，自己也笑着。

快五点的时候，一阵如释重负的松快漫过满屋。真相的那点简单，每星期都让她重新吃一惊——大多数人也只不过想被听一听。“一件直截了当的事，”她判一桩丢了手套的案子，众人应和。一桩接一桩的索赔把她磨乏了，可她不肯松劲，因为每一根故事线，哪怕细得像根线，都值得拉它一把。

他拼命让法庭相信是月亮挪了他的车；她不肯信他，反倒罚了他一笔。被告每回迟交房租，都有一套别出心裁的说法，法官听着觉得好笑，只是不合法。一墨点的墨迹标在纸角，书记员记下了那个位子。这是想给人一点善意的小小举动，一有机会她就做。

她用手指着地图，让一个人看清自己错在哪儿。下一桩是这一天最古怪的案子：一个人告一只鹅偷了他的午饭。“别嚷，”法官说，满屋就静了。后排一个男人说，他在家自己磨咖啡。“那味儿是实在的，”他说，飘到了法官席上。

一堵共用墙的争执，需要走一步中间的路才解得开，她把这一条添进了裁定。“这枚钱币归你，”她对着那个索弗林案里的侄子说，“法律会护着这一点。”“你八成把日子记错了，”一个女人指着一张票这么说；法官一查，认了。事实很简单，那女人没带一点气就接受了。

一个男人来失物箱前领回他的帽子，书记员弯着腰递了过去。官府该管一管房东能收哪些费用，法官欢迎这种帮手。她自己那句洞见——人们告的，是些说不出口的东西——救下的案子比哪条成文法都多。她随口说的一句关于善意的话，多有见识，连后排一个律师都掏笔记了下来。法庭的里子朴素又干净，她喜欢的就是这个样。

公告板上有一桩小船搁浅在小岛附近的案子，贴了从没开庭；她读了，对着那套海的逻辑笑了。剩两桩索赔，后一桩软些，她用好话把它驳了。邻近镇子的下级法院在同一个点上判错过，她想起这个，就写了一张便条去提醒他们。

一位退休的检察官坐在旁听席上，做正义的旁观者，头点着她的每一份裁定。法庭规则里有一条，准许给病人拖一拖；她好意地引了它。“这事你可以到别处去追，”她对一个诉求落在她权限之外的男人说，他平平淡淡地走了。

“不论哪一门族、哪一种信，”她宣布，“这张席子都开着。”“他们想拿一堆表格把穷人拖死，”她低声对萨洛斯说；萨洛斯听见了，笑了。立案费多收的那部分，退给一个多付了钱的女人，她鞠了一躬。

书记员月底要辞工，自己去看法律；她为失去他惋惜，却为他骄傲。“别靠编话过日子，”她警告一个硬造证人的女人；那女人低下头，说了实话。她要把那张大白表改写得连孩子都会填，表上的字因此顺了。木槌的节奏，稳得像心跳，她每抬起来一次，满屋就落定一次。

一根丝带捆着一沓卷宗，从窗口钻进来的风把它吹松了。书记员那份活儿不大，却要紧，她常谢他。叫他吃惊的是，一个人输了本以为稳赢的官司，对面那头却轻轻欢呼。她用速记记笔记，笔在纸上走得飞快。“使你的心思明白点，”她对一个怀疑自己眼睛的女人说；那女人眨了眨眼，认了。

作为证据当庭念出来的一封信，末句只有短短一句：“对不起。”满屋的人心都软了。“我们总归找着了真相，”法官说，“哪怕它穿成谎话的模样。”她每回裁定之前的那一段沉吟，全镇都出名；一到那时候，满座会静下来等着。

一本作为证物送进来的书，书名被人念了出来，旁听席上一个男孩探着身子去听。桌上搁着一盏应急灯，防停电用的，她一星期试一回。“别碰证据，”萨洛斯对一个好奇心重的孩子说；那孩子咧嘴一笑，把手猛地缩了回去。

那个说起亡妻来声音发抖的老人，领到了这一天最温和的一份裁定。给之前，她会把笔在木头上轻敲两下，满屋就数那两声。书记员又把规矩向满屋重申了一遍，人人都在听，像头一回听见。

她随着时候往后挪，把自己的耐性一点点磨出来，也拿笑驳回那样一种说法——法庭待穷人无礼。那笔罚金是他从更坏的下场里捞回来的自救之钱，他自己心里清楚。一句真诚的道歉能补上的，多少份裁定都补不上。她不扇谁，可有那么一回，她把木槌拍得那样重，满屋子的人都跳了一下。据说有个男人走私一块表；缺了证据，这桩索赔掷了出去。多数争吵的解药是一杯茶和一只肯听的耳朵。

漏水的源头到底找着了，管道工鞠了个躬，擦擦手走了。一条街名的写法在一份要紧的文件上错了，书记员很快改好。法官夸了厨子做汤的手艺，多蒂笑开了脸。他付了自己的那份钱走出去，从此把这事了结干净。险胜也算赢，她说，于是人人走出这栋屋子时，都比进来时高了一点。通往太平唯一的障碍是自尊，而自尊并不值几个钱。

最安静的那张嘴，到手的反而最多，这道理有点怪。被告总算把他的说法摁到了事实上，法庭信了他。他的样子粗粝，心却是软的。年初她怕过这一摞案卷，到了年尾，她爱上了它。

他说打完这场官司他就把厂里的活辞了，她祝他顺当。这一年他提过四个地方，今天下午提了第五个。她早年写过一些没人肯印的字，所以一听有人在辩解里讲了个坏故事，她立刻就听得出。有个市民用一分一分凑的钱交了立案费，一路出汗到底。两边靠一个共同的笑话并到一处，这场官司悄悄了了。

“你可以走了，”她对一个被鹅赔掉九镑的人说，“哪边有理，哪边就有法律站在它那头。”地窖的门该换水泵了，签字的活儿归她。

开庭接着往下走，比阿特丽斯对满屋说了她整个下午一直捂在心里的一句念头。“法庭，”她说，“是个地方，陌生人把小小的伤心背进来，求一个忙人替他们解开。法律是件工具，不是一味膏药。可偶尔，真相是很简单的，其余的都是响动。”

她停了停。“且看这屋里的悖论吧：我们想讨一个公道的结果，用的却是一套把人人都磨垮的手续。讲逻辑的心要的是一条规矩；过日子的心要的是一个故事。主观的看法，并不就是假的。可不管怎样，证明的标准是客观的，法庭得守着它，哪怕对面淌着眼泪。”

后排一个女人举了手。“法官大人，”她说，“我是来告我儿子不尽心的，可我现在想，我是来被人听一听的。”法官笑了。“那你就被听着了，”她说，“这案子凭一份好意结了。”

那位传教士往前迈了一步。“我帮着法庭做过一份道德研究，”布莱特先生说，“我发现，跟自家骨肉打官司的人，是孤单，并不是恼火。”比阿特丽斯用一只精明的眼睛看了看他。“法庭里见着个传教士，可不多见，”她说，“你的研究留着吧。我看真相比你的学说还要简单些。”

那乐手弹了一支轻的。松鼠蹲在窗台上，像在听。“听众只有一个，”法官说，“也是这栋楼里最诚实的一位批评家。”

后来，最后一桩案子了结，法官在她的本子上写了一行：法律是一张网；它兜住小鱼，放走大鱼。为小鱼欢喜吧。

她合上本子，看了看这屋子，剩下的交给安静。“休庭，”她说，“回家去。修厕所。喂松鼠。分汤喝。”

外头，那只松鼠顺着墙跑，自在，也没人告它——整个下午，它是内特尔福德唯一没有犯过一点错的东西。

陌生人的小小忧伤，才是值得听完的那些案子。
