chapters.title: 出租车司机的十个问题
chapters.content:
"Anywhere that isn't there," the girl said. "And leave the meter off."

Cato Birch only drove. Nine years of night had left him with one habit: wait. The wind took the door off its hinge and slammed it, ice hit the glass in a shower so thick the wipers screamed, and behind the rank a shutter banged till the frame shook. Somewhere past the quay a pipe whistle held one long note.

Under the mirror, held by old silver tape, was a card. Ten lines. He had read it so often the tape had gone soft. Nine years, nine thousand fares, not one answered. "Where is the storm not?" he asked. "Behind you," she said. "That is the trick of it. It is always behind you."

Cato turned the radio down. It had six minutes of the storm left to preach, and he had heard the same six minutes every year of his life. The rain ran down the back window in ropes, and the wind had taken the last of the heat out of the engine. "Nita," she said. "That is my name. I have no plan."

Cab eighteen had worked the night streets of Marlwood for nine years. His residence was one room above a shuttered hall on Cinder Row, with a small balcony facing the northeast, and from it he could weigh the night by its scent: garlic from the corner diner, wet chalk from the builder's yard, rain on skin.

Accustomed to the ordinary noise, he drove. The siren. The electric hum of the roof sign. The soft light on his dashboard when it chose to spark. A nickname was the cheapest furniture a man could own, and the men at the garage had given it one anyway. He kept a thermos in the holder, and the thermos had gone cold.

"First question," he said. "Is it a scheme, or is everything an accident?" "Yours or the card's?" "Both. That is how questions work." She laughed, a lively sound. "Then I am already in the wrong play, and I would not have it another way."

The radio crackled. Vera, the dispatch assistant, came on with the bridge closed. "Eighteen," she said. "The bridge is down. Take the quay. Every driver is to evacuate the rank for safety." The heater banged twice under the dash and then gave up.

"Evening, Vera. Who is driving the electric fleet tonight?" "Nobody. They are charging in the yard." Cato let that sit. The new cars were electric and silent, and the last of the old ones went by a nickname: the coffin. "I am not leaving," he said. "Tonight the rank is the only place a question gets asked."

"You know the rule." "I know the rule. It has never once saved any driver who wanted to talk." "Box on your knee," Nita said. "There is a cake in it." "And why a cake at this hour?"

"My sister is spending her last night at home. I am the one leaving, so I brought the cake to the wrong house."

Cato put the car in gear. The engine complained, as it did on cold nights, and the grease and damp of the seat rose around him while her ankle boots left a splash of slush on the mat. Her coat was wet to the elbow. "Where shall I set the cake?" "Anywhere the snow is shallower."

He drove out of the rank and the city changed shape. Water reached the far quay, the smog turned to slush, and a savage wind came off the northeast to spit ice at the glass like a donkey clearing its throat. The wet road sparkled under the lamps, and an empty tram stop stood at the corner with its door hanging open.

"Second question," he said. "Can a person be free and still be told where to stand?"

"I was free an hour ago. My mother designated the flowers, the priest set the vows, and here I am in a cab at midnight with a cake for the wrong house." Her chin was sharp with decision and her cheek still glowed from the church. Her white gloves lay on the seat between them.

"Are you free now?" "Free to conform or free to run. That is the only freedom worth a name." "What is the consequence of running?" "Merely to miss the soup. That is the whole of what anyone loses." She said it the way another person says a price.

Cato evaluated her as a decisive fare and said so, noting her profile in the mirror with something like recognition. He put her down at the seaside shelter; the door snapped shut behind her, and the wind went out of the whole street.

"Choice," he wrote later, "is a door you open yourself, regardless of who built the house." The door opened for a man with a laptop and a soft accent. "A software man," he said. "I build semiconductor brains for machines that compute the weather." "Third question," Cato said. "Can a machine reason, or does it only compute?"

"A machine has no soul and no conscience. It computes. It does not reason. Reasoning needs a doubt, and a doubt needs a self, and a self is what a circuit cannot weld."

He spoke of objective observation, of software that could predict the storm to the minute, of data that proved the outcome probable to a percentage of ninety-nine. Cato, sceptical of all of it, held his own standpoint: the news was propaganda, and truth was a spectrum rather than a switch. His hands went blue inside the gloves.

"A machine that knows tomorrow and feels nothing," Cato said, "is the picture of any man who reads the news and shrugs." "And why build one?" "Because somebody must look at the sky before the sky looks at us." The man paid in exact change and left a smell of ozone. He would not name his method.

Next aboard was a gardener with a hamper of seed and a spade. The hamper smelled of wet earth, which is the honest smell of the year coming back. He carried that basket out on the first warm day of every March, when nobody yet called it weather.

"On a night like this," Cato asked, "what survives?" "Sprouts," the man said, shy as a sparrow. "You can freeze a garden and bury it in snow. A seed knows how to wait." "You sow them, then?" "Spring I sprinkle. Summer I spray. Winter I wipe the porcelain pots with a sponge. The rest is patience."

He spoke of the scenery of the eastern hills, where the bank ran steep and the shade was deep, and an old custom had gone extinct: the women who planted by the moon. The hills were only white shapes at that distance. Cato pondered it. Dead things leave seeds of meaning, the way a fire leaves ash.

The gardener paid and left a handful of grain for the balcony. Cato promised to plant them himself, and the wheel spoke cracked once and held.

By then the snowstorm had worsened and began to disrupt the traffic. The city slid toward chaos. Vera called a second time. "The bridge is still down. The size of this is beyond me, Cato. Come in at once."

"I will come in when the questions are finished." After that came a priest with wet hands. The rain had put a shine on his collar. He took no offense. He spoke of religion as a shelter, of Christ as a question more than an answer, of the spiritual life as a balance between doubt and trust.

"The soul," he said, "is the part of you that refuses to be weighed like coal. You can deprive a man of his house and his name. You cannot deprive him of his spirit without his consent." "That is worthy of thought." "Say rather that it is worth a cold night."

They parted at the chapel and Cato felt a small relief of the spirit. The priest walked back into the rain without a coat. A gambler followed, in a striped coat, smelling of brandy. His collar stood up against the cold, and the cold lost. "Is luck a thing you find," Cato asked, "or a thing you make?"

The man spat a little salt into his palm. "Luck is a percentage, driver. The probability of a good night is low and of a bad one high, and prosperity is the rare occasion when the two trade places."

"And twenty years of it have bought you?" "Poor. And happy. Which is its own kind of prosperity." He called the game a witch that blessed fools, and misfortune a debt that came due on honest men. At home he kept a dog that believed the same thing about dinner.

Cato set him down as a successful fool and said nothing more, remarking only that luck was a thing you make. "Luck," the gambler called back, "is merely fate with a smile." An old man then, with a doubting eye and a book of puzzles. A skeptic by trade, he meant to perplex Cato before dawn.

"What is truth," he asked, "when two witnesses swear the opposite?" The old man had the look of somebody paid by the hour to doubt. Cato perplexed him with a question of his own. "Is it the thing that happened, or the thing we agree upon?"

"You shift the burden," the old man said. "The trick of every preacher and every politician." "A shift in terms should end on clearer ground, provided it leads somewhere, and an impartial judge would say the same."

The man conceded and paid in coins that jingled like a spectator clapping a fight he did not follow. A whistle somewhere in the street answered the alarm, and Cato noted that skepticism was easy to say and hard to live. On his own reading the quiz of living well was optional only in theory.

A boy then, small and quiet, lost from his mother in the station hall. The boy could not have been more than six. His scarf had swallowed half his face. "Mister," he said, "are the stars real or imaginary?" "That," Cato said, "is the wisest thing said all night."

Cato drove the boy to the police hall, where a considerate employee handed him back to a weeping mother. The child left a wholesome impression, the sort that civilizes a man more than any sermon. The mother thanked him three times and he said nothing at all.

Passing the empty playground, Cato thought of what the gardener had left on his balcony and of the shallow puddle that held the ultraviolet shine of the lamp. Next came a sportsman with a ski bag and a broken shaft on his pole, down from the north slopes with the storm. The pole had snapped in half on the quay.

"Do you believe in equality," Cato asked, "on the hill and off it?" "On the slope we are equal to the mountain, and the mountain does not care who you are. Off it, equality is a word that politicians whitewash until it means nothing."

"I have seen champions treat servants like garbage, and servants behave like kings. The medal did not represent their worth. The equivalent of a medal off the hill is a kind word, and kind words are rarer."

Cato reinforced his own belief that dignity was intrinsic and not awarded. Then a woman in a grey coat, and she was crying. Her fingers were white at the knuckle. "My boy is out in this," she said. "He left the hall at six."

"Where does he go?" "The playground. He walks home by the shore." Cato switched the meter off. The wind made the cab shake, the shadow of the closed warehouse stretched along the curb, and a spine of cold ran down his back.

"Is he alive?" "Say he is alive until somebody says otherwise. That is the only rule I know." They found the boy at the lamp by the water, sitting in a shallow puddle, shaking. Cato lifted him. He was alive.

The mother wept and kept saying his name. At the hall somebody poured tea, and the relief in that room was worth a whole pulpit. Someone had turned the radio off so the boy could eat a biscuit in peace.

Last aboard was a woman carrying a collection of books under one arm. Her shoes were thin and the hem of her coat had stiffened with frost. "To the old factory," she said. "The one at the city's edge, where the looms used to weave."

"Tenth question," Cato said. "Who wrote these questions, and why leave them in my cab?" "I teach philosophy," she said. "I can answer that in one word. Vanity."

She talked her way in, through the new edition of her book, the loom yard, the rain on a tin roof, the conversion of a factory into a memory. "I came to see a city make something useful with its hands."

Cato felt the bottom drop out of his stomach. He knew her from the photograph on the back of a book he had kept on his dashboard for three years, because the hand that wrote the questions had signed the front. The back page had yellowed at the fold.

"Edith Vane," he said. "Correct." "You wrote them. I have asked them of nine thousand people and I did not know." He said her name twice, the way you try a key in a lock.

"I wrote them for me. I left them on a night like this, in a cab like yours, because I could not bear to keep them. I had preached certainty for forty years and believed none of it. The questions were my denial made plain, and I withhold the answers from myself by giving them away."

She smiled, a frail and intelligent smile. Her voice kept a kind of order inside it, and she was not an old woman so much as a tired one. "You drove them further than I ever did. You asked them of every soul in the city. That was the answer I could not reach."

Payment came in a coin older than the garage. "Now the ten answers," she said. "Sit down. They are in my head and nowhere else." "First. Accident is the mask chance wears when it wants to be taken seriously." "Second. Freedom is not the absence of rules but the presence of a choice you own."

"Third. Truth is a spectrum. The pitch of a lie is sharp. The pitch of a fact is flat." "Fourth. Rubbish and wisdom look alike until you live with them a winter." "Fifth. A stranger looks suspicious only to somebody who has never been one."

"Sixth. A machine can compute the storm and cannot fear it, and fear is the proof of a soul." "Seventh. Luck is a seed you sow on a night you will not see the flower." "Eighth. When a thing goes extinct, what survives is the question of why we noticed too late."

"Ninth. The law looks away more often than we admit, and somebody must safeguard the conscience it leaves unguarded." "Tenth. The woman who wrote the questions was merely afraid, and the driver who asked them was brave."

Cato sat with the engine off. "Professor, you preach better than you know. But you have left out the eleventh." "Which is?" "That nobody needs the answers to bring the questions home."

She laughed, a real laugh, and said he should write the appendix to her next edition. It was a historic night. They talked until the snowstorm broke and grey light leaked under the factory door.

"Perhaps the ultimate riddle is simply why we ask," she said. "The worst is always elsewhere, sneaking up the stair of the next hour, and a suspicion I could never name."

"Incidentally," he said, "the bridge is still closed." "Then sleep, or do not." At the rank before dawn the wind had gone out of it. Cato counted his fares. Nine. People with cake, with seed, with salt and saints, and the absent faces of the ones who would never ride again.

In the context of a long life, one accidental turn can carve a whole destiny, and he had weighed the significance of the coincidence that brought her back into his cab. The connotation of the word home had turned for him the night he started driving.

The phenomenon of a city that sleeps and yet hums is a delicate balance worth keeping, and he pondered the religious quiet of the empty rooms. "Somebody left these on my mirror," he told the dashboard. "Somebody always does."

Perhaps the ultimate riddle was why we ask at all, and his nightly endeavor was to keep the questions moving. The bubbles in the thermos had gone flat. "Drive, friend," he said to the empty back seat. "They are still warm."

He recalled the skillful way the gardener had tied his hamper, and the scale of the storm had shaken the cab on the bridge. That crossing had been shut since nine and would not open before dawn.

Wet earth had risen, a soluble proof of spring. His feet went numb on the floor mat. A lightning strike far off lit the sky for one sharp second, and he felt secure that the questions would outlast him, with no external cause to decide a man's peace.

The presence of a passenger was a prior event to any talk. He would rather listen than lecture, because listening built a synthesis of two lives neither could reach alone. Two lives, one cab, and a length of rubber mat between them.

In fact the cab was a sphere of temporary stability, a width of two feet. Therefore he resolved, with undoubtedly more strength than sense, to keep asking. The radio lay on the back shelf, unplugged.

Some questions transcend the men who pose them. "Ask them anyway," he said. "That is the whole trade." A unanimous nod from the regulars meant less than one honest fare, and the two of them had come to a quiet understanding that no witness needed. The regulars had long stopped asking him to stop asking.

He thought of the adverb problem. The old words hung in the air like coats on a hook. One word can distort a whole sentence, and to no avail he had tried to explain to Vera that the background noise of the city was separate music.

The connection between driver and fare was mutual, like correspondence sent by slow post. A negligent man might forbid himself joy. Cato would not. The genetic gift of curiosity is typical of children, and the minority of happy people are the few who still ask why. The excessive cold had transformed the street into a postcard.

Underneath the joke sat a real priority. Live well. He had complicated nothing, and the normalization of the strange was the work of a driver. Everybody in the rank had a story and nobody told one at the start. The kettle on his stove had whistled all week without an audience.

Nowhere did the rule book say a cab driver might not sit with the suicide of the spirit and watch wonder decompose, then choose to live. It was personal, and the prevalent belief that nonsense pays better than truth is the worst advertising.

Things grow worse before they grow strange, and the necessity of asking outweighs the comfort of silence. With sudden clarity he knew the night had changed him, and that a roughly told tale is often truer than a polished one. He owned no notebook for it and did not want one.

He embraced the lesson and, accordingly, kept the meter off. A skeptic who never arrived at a belief was only a tourist in his own head. The mirror on the back of the seat had cracked and been taped.

Cato dared to think the questions were the goal itself. A crazy idea is often the start of a discovery, and he probed the concept with Edith's patience. His behavior had surprised even him.

The necessary honesty of the bride. The impartial quiet of the chapel. The whole city rests on small kindnesses exchanged between strangers, and he would specify it to Vera in the morning. The cook had put two eggs on the counter, and a steam had come off the kettle and cleared the window a little.

A word on a page ends on a vowel more often than men admit, and the questions await anyone still open to the world who needs no further qualification than a willingness to listen.

The next morning Cato did not sleep. His coat hung on the hook and smelled of the river. He walked to the corner diner, where the cook knew his order without being told, and Vera was already on her stool with a notebook and a phone. The stool had a pale ring where a cup had stood for years.

"You look like you saw a ghost," she said. "Stranger," he said. "I saw a professor." She did not ask which one. Vera had learned that the less she asked, the more he told, and she was skeptical about most things except the people she had known for a decade.

They talked of the bridge, which had opened at dawn. The fleet was replaced the following week, the old cars were going to the yard, and the bridge would be somewhere else entirely by spring. The rain at the window had stopped being rain and turned to weather.

"Nine years, and you are only now becoming strange," she said. "The normal thing is to sleep." "I know. The silly comfort of a settled mind is the first thing a driver should distrust."

Back at the cab the seat was still wet, the oil still on the mirror, and the card still taped under the light. He read the ten lines again, and they had not shrunk. The tape at two corners had lifted and been pressed down again, and the wiper blades had gone rubbery and clicked.

Late that afternoon he passed the old factory. A woman stood at the fence looking in, and for a moment he thought it was Edith Vane. Its brick wall was the colour of a wet dog, and a gull stood on the post above her like a painted thing. The gate was locked and a chain hung across it.

He pulled to the curb. It was a younger woman, straight in the shoulders, holding her head the same way. Her coat was the same cut as the professor's. She turned, met his eye through the glass, and smiled the small smile of someone caught being tender about an empty building.

Cato lifted a hand. She lifted hers. Then she was gone down the road, and the cab was warm, and the questions seemed for the first time like something he could live with. One evening, a year after that night, a woman climbed in at the water rank. "You," she said. "The question man." Cato blinked.

"You knew my mother," she said. "Edith Vane was my mother. Before she died she told me about a cab driver who asked her questions better than she had ever answered them. She said you were the only student she ever had who did the homework." The woman's hands were folded and steady on her knee.

Cato sat with the engine running, and for a moment he could not speak. Then he laughed, the real laugh Edith had taught him, and he wrote nothing down. The mirror still carried a smear of the old oil.

"I think your mother did the teaching," he said. "I only drove." The woman reached across the seat and touched the card, soft at the corners from a year of thumbs.

"She left one more," she said, and she set a second card on the mirror beside the first. Cato read it. There was only one line.

The answers were never the point. The asking was the road.

He drove her home, charged her nothing, and watched her go up the walk to a small house with a light in the window. The plants had long since grown and died and been put in again, the way all living things do. The porch at the foot of the stair had kept one dry board.

They were still there, the questions, taped under the light, and so was he, and that, he decided, was enough.

The questions were never meant to be answered. They were meant to be driven.
chapters.translation:
"去个不是那儿的地方，"女孩说，"计程表先别打。"

卡托·伯奇只会开车。九年夜路下来，他只剩一个习惯：等。风把车门从铰链上掀下来又摔回去；冰碴像一阵骤雨砸在玻璃上，雨刮器叫得撕心裂肺；候客点后头一扇卷帘门哐哐当当，震得门框直抖。

码头那头远处，一根管子的哨音拖着长长一声。后视镜底下，用旧银胶带贴着一张卡片。十行字。他读得太多了，胶带都软了。九年，九千个客人，一道也没答上来。"暴风雪不在哪儿？"他问。"

在你后头，"她说，"就是这个门道。它永远在你后头。"卡托把收音机拧小。播报说暴风雪还剩六分钟，而他这辈子每年都听这六分钟。雨顺着后窗拉成一条条线，风把发动机里最后一点热也抽走了。"妮塔，"她说，"我叫妮塔。我没什么打算。"

十八号这辆车在玛尔伍德的夜路上跑了九年。他住在灰烬街一间拉下卷帘的礼堂楼上，朝东北开着一小截阳台；从那儿靠气味就能掂量夜色：街角小馆的蒜香、建筑场刮来的湿白垩粉、雨打在皮上的腥气。

习惯了那些平常的响动，他就这么开着。警笛。车顶招牌的电流嗡鸣。仪表盘偶尔打起火花、亮起那一片柔光。外号是一个男人能置办的最便宜的家具，修车的伙计们反正也给这辆车起了个外号。

他架上保温壶，壶里的水早就凉了。"第一个问题，"他说，"这是一场算计，还是事事都碰巧？""是你的问题，还是卡片上的？""两个都是。问题就是这么回事。"

她笑了一声，脆脆的。"那我这是错的一出戏，可我才不肯换。"收音机咔啦响。调度室的助理薇拉来了，说桥封了。"十八号，"她说，"桥断了。走码头那条路。

每个司机为了安全都得把候客点撤了。"暖风机在引擎盖底下哐了两声，然后不干了。"晚上好，薇拉。今晚是谁开那队电车？""没人。都在院子里充电。"卡托没吭声。新车子是电动的，安安静静；最后一辆老车落了个外号：棺材。"

我可不走，"他说，"今晚这候客点是全城唯一问问题的地方。""你知道规矩。""我知道规矩。它从来没有救过一个想找人说话的司机。"

"腿上放个盒子，"妮塔说，"里头有块蛋糕。""这点儿工夫要块蛋糕干什么？"

"我妹妹这最后一晚在家里待着。要走的是我，所以我把蛋糕送错了门。"卡托挂上挡。发动机跟往常的冷天一样抱怨；油污和潮气从坐垫上返上来，她那双短靴在地垫上踩出一摊泥水。她的外套湿到手肘。"

蛋糕放哪儿？""哪儿的雪薄，放哪儿。"他开出候客点，城就换了个形状。水漫到远处的码头，烟雾化成泥汤；一道野风从东北卷过来，朝玻璃啐冰，像驴子清嗓子。湿路在灯下亮闪闪，街角立着一座空电车站点，门板歪着没关。

"第二个问题，"他说，"人是自由的，还能有人来规定他站哪儿吗？"

"一个钟头前我是自由的。花是我妈指定的，誓是神父定下的，而现在半夜十二点，我坐在车里，手里是送错门的蛋糕。"她下巴尖着，一副拿定主意的样子，脸颊上还留着教堂的红光。白手套摊在两人中间那张座位上。

"那你现在自由吗？""顺从也自由，跑掉也自由。只有这一种自由配得上有个名字。""跑掉会怎么样？""无非是错过那碗汤。人能丢的就这么点儿。"她说这话的口气，跟别人报个数一样。

卡托把她归到干脆的客人那一类，说了这话，又在镜子里看她的侧脸，眉眼间有点像认出了谁。他把她在海边那座棚子里放下；门在她身后啪地关上，整条街的风一下子没了。

"选择，"他后来写道，"是一扇你自己推开的门，至于这栋房子是谁盖的，那不相干。"车门下一程客人打开了，那人抱着一台笔记本电脑，口音很轻。"做软件的，"他说，"我给那些算天气的机器造半导体脑子。""第三个问题，"卡托说，"机器能推理，还是只会算？"

"机器没有灵魂，也没有良心。它算。它不推理。推理需要怀疑，怀疑需要自我，而自我是一块线路板焊不出来的东西。"

他讲客观的观察，讲能把这个暴风雪算到每一分钟的软件，讲数据把结果证明到百分之九十九的可能。卡托对这套全持怀疑，自己有自己一套看法：新闻是宣传，真相是一片光谱，不是你随手一扳就换过来的开关。

他的手在手套里冻得发青。"一台知道明天、可什么也不感觉的机器，"卡托说，"正是那种读报然后耸肩的人的写照。""那为什么要造它？""总得有人先看天，别等天先来看我们。"那人付了刚好的零钱，身上留下一股臭氧味。问他方法，他不肯说。

再上来位是园丁，挎着装种子的藤篮，提一把铁锹。篮子里有湿泥味，那是年头回过神来最老实的味道。每年三月头一个暖和天，他就把这只篮子搬出去，那天还没人肯叫它天气。

"这样的夜晚，"卡托问，"什么能活下来？""芽，"那人说，羞得像只麻雀，"你可以把一座花园冻死、用雪埋上，可一粒种子知道怎么等。""那你播种是吧？""春天我撒，夏天我打药，冬天我用海绵擦瓷盆，剩下的是耐心。"

他讲起东边那面山坡的景致，坡陡、荫深，还有一门已经绝了的规矩：老妇人按月亮下种。那么远看，那些山只是些白影子。卡托琢磨这个。死物也留下意义的种子，就像火留下灰。

园丁付了钱，又给他的阳台留一把谷粒。卡托答应自己动手种；车轮一根辐条裂了一下，又绷住了。

这时候暴风雪更凶，开始搅乱交通；整座城往混乱里滑。薇拉又打来一次。"桥还断着。这事儿太大了，卡托。赶紧进来吧。""问题问完我就进来。"

再上来的是位神父，手是湿的。雨在他领子上打出一层亮。他不生气。他把宗教说成一间屋檐，把基督说成更像一个问题而不是一个答案，把灵性的生活说成怀疑与信任之间的一种平衡。

"灵魂，"他说，"是你身上不肯像煤一样被人称量的那一部分。你可以夺走一个人的房子、他的名字；只要他自己不点头，夺不走他的精神。""这话值得琢磨。""不如说，它值一个冷夜晚。"

他们在小礼拜堂分手，卡托心里松了一小口气。神父没披外套，走回雨里。跟着上来的是个赌徒，穿条纹外套，一身白兰地味。他的领子竖着挡冷，冷输了。"运气是碰来的，"卡托问，"还是做出来的？"

那人往手心里啐了点盐。"运气是个百分比，司机。好晚上概率低，坏晚上概率高；难得的是这两个数换了位——那就是走运。""那二十年下来呢？"

"穷。可也快活。这本身就是一种走运。"他把赌博叫作一个宠着傻子的巫婆，把厄运叫作一份连老实人也到期的债。家里养了条狗，它也认这个理：晚饭是等不来的。

卡托把他归到成功的傻子那一类，什么也没多说，只随口提了一句：运气是做出来的。"运气嘛，"赌徒在车后喊，"不过是带着笑的命。"再上来的是个老头，一只眼睛总带着疑，手里一本谜题集。他是个怀疑论者，打算在天亮以前先把卡托难住。

"两个证人赌咒发誓说相反的话，"他问，"那什么才是真？"那老头一脸拿人钱财替人怀疑的模样。卡托反问一句把他问住了："是发生过的事实，还是我们彼此认可的东西？"

"你把担子挪了，"老头说，"这一手每个说教的、搞政治的都会。""说法挪一挪，只要挪到更清楚的地界上去就该收场；一个公正的裁判也会这么看。"

老头认了，付了钱，硬币叮当响，像个看客给一场自己没看懂的架鼓掌。街上哪儿的哨音应了一声警报；卡托记下：怀疑这件事说起来容易，活起来难。按他自己的看法，活得好不好这件事，在理论上才可选。

再上来是个孩子，又小又安静，在车站大厅跟妈妈走散了。这孩子最多六岁。围巾把半张脸都吞了。"先生，"他说，"星星是真的还是画上去的？""这一句，"卡托说，"是整夜里最聪明的话。"

卡托把孩子送到警局大厅，有个热心的办事员把他领回一个正在哭的妈妈跟前。这孩子留下的是一种干净的好印象，那种比任何布道都更能把一个男人教化的印象。

妈妈说了三遍谢谢，他一句话没说。路过空荡荡的操场，卡托想起园丁留在他阳台上的那些东西，还有一洼浅水，把街灯那点紫外线的微光圈在里面。下一位是个滑雪的，背一个装雪板的袋子，手杖断成两截，从北边山坡在风雪里下来。

那根杆子在码头上就折成了两半。"你信不信平等，"卡托问，"山上信，出了山还信不信？""在坡上，我们跟山是平等的，而山不关心你是谁。出了坡，平等这个词被政客刷白了，刷到最后一文不值。"

"我见过冠军把佣人当下水的东西，也见过佣人行事像国王。奖牌并不代表他们的分量。出了坡，奖牌的等价物是一句好话——那才少见。"

卡托把自己的信条又加固了一遍：尊严是自带的，不是谁发得下来的。再上来是个穿灰大衣的女人，正在哭。她的手指在指节那儿白着。"我儿子还在外头，"她说，"他六点从礼堂出来的。"

"他去哪儿？""儿童乐园。他抄海边那条路回家。"卡托把计程表按掉了。风把车晃得直抖，那座关了门的仓库把影子在地上拉得老长，后背脊梁骨里钻过一道凉。"

他还活着吗？""你就当他活着，直到有人出来说不是。我只知道这一条规矩。"他们在水边那盏灯底下找到了孩子，坐在一洼浅水里，抖成一团。

卡托把他抱起来。人还活着。妈妈哭着一遍遍喊他的名字。礼堂里有人倒了一杯茶；那一屋子人的松快，抵得上半个布道台。

有人把收音机关了，好让孩子安安静静吃块饼干。最后上来的是个女人，一只胳膊底下夹着一摞书。她的鞋很薄，大衣下摆让霜硬住了。"去老厂子，"她说，"城边上那座，从前织布的地方。"

"第十个问题，"卡托说，"这些问题是谁写的？为什么留在我车上？""我教哲学，"她说，"一个字就能答完。虚荣。"

她一路说着话进来：自己那本新版著作，织布厂的院子，雨点敲在铁皮屋顶上，一座厂怎么变成一段记忆。"我是来看一座城市怎么用手做出过实在东西的。"

卡托觉得胃里往下一沉。他认得她——认得一本书封底上的照片；那本书他在仪表盘上搁了三年，因为写这些问题的那只手，正是签在书扉页上的那只手。书脊折过的地方，纸页已经发黄。

"伊迪丝·韦恩，"他说。"对。""是你写的。我问过九千个人，到今天才知道。"他说了两遍她的名字，像拿钥匙去试一把锁。"是写给我自己的。

这样的夜晚，在你这样的车里，我把它落下了，因为我舍不得留。我讲了一辈子确定，一句也不信。这些问题不过是我把不肯认的话摊开；我把答案给了外人，好让它们离我自己远一点。"她笑了，一个虚弱的、通透的笑。

她的声音里始终留着某种秩序；她不是老了，她是累了。"你把它们播得比我远多了。你问遍了城里每一个人。那正是我自己够不着的答案。"车钱是一枚比车行还老的银币。"现在说那十个答案，"她说，"坐下。它们在我脑子里，别处没有。"

"第一，碰巧是机会想被人认真对待时戴的一张面具。""第二，自由不是没有规矩，而是你手里真有一份选择。""第三，真相是一片光谱。撒谎的声音是尖的，真话的声音是平的。""第四，垃圾和智慧，要过了整整一个冬天才分得开。"

"第五，只有从来没当过外人的人，才觉得外人都可疑。""第六，机器能算出暴风雪，却不会怕它；怕，才是灵魂的凭据。""第七，运气是一粒你撒下的种子，撒在你永远看不见花的那个夜里。"

"第八，一样东西绝了之后，留下的是我们为什么没能早发现的问题。""第九，法律低头的日子比我们肯承认的多；总得有人替它照看不住的那点良心。""第十，写这些问题的女人无非是害怕，问这些问题的司机是勇敢的。"

卡托熄了火坐着。"教授，你讲道讲得比你自己知道的还好。可你漏了第十一样。""哪一样？""谁也不需要先把答案揣齐了，才把问题送到家。"

她笑了，是真笑，说该给她的下一版写个附录。这是个有历史的一夜。他们一直说到暴风雪散，头一线灰白的天光从厂门底下漏进来。

"也许最深的谜就是：我们为什么问，"她说，"最坏的事永远在别处，踩着下一小时的台阶悄悄摸上来，带着一种我一直叫不出名字的疑心。"

"还有一句闲话，"他说，"桥还封着。""那就睡，要不别睡。"天亮前在候客点，风已经泄了。卡托数他的客人。九个。

有带着蛋糕的、带着种子的、带着盐和圣徒的，还有那些再也上不了他车的、缺席的脸。他搁着这一辈子来看：一个碰巧的拐弯能刻出整整一段命；他也掂过这场巧合的分量——它把伊迪丝又送回了他车里。"

家"这个字的言外之意，是他开始开车的那个晚上转的。一座睡了却还在响的城，是一种极要细心的平衡，值得守着；他琢磨那些空屋子里、像祈祷一样的安静。"

有人把这些留在了我镜子上，"他对着仪表盘说，"人总是这么干。"也许最要命的谜就是这个：我们为什么问。他每晚的功课是让问题一直往前走。

保温壶里的气泡早就泄了。"走吧，朋友，"他冲空着的后座说，"它们还热着。"他想起园丁捆藤篮那手多利落，想起那场暴风雪有多大阵势，在桥上把车晃得厉害。

那道桥从九点就封了，天亮之前不会开。湿泥从地里拱起来，是春天一份会化的凭据。他的脚在脚垫上冻没了知觉。

远处一道闪电把天照亮，清清楚楚的一瞬；他心里踏实：这些问题会比他活得久；也用不上什么外头的原因，来替一个人定下他心里那点安宁。上车这件事，排在一切谈话之前。

他宁可听，也不愿教训人，因为听能把两条命合成一个两人都凑不齐的东西。两条命，一辆车，中间隔着一条橡皮脚垫。说到底，这辆车是一颗临时的稳定球，一门两英尺宽。

所以他拿定了主意，凭的多半是蛮劲而不是见识，继续问下去。收音机搁在后头架子上，没插电。有些问题比提它们的人活得久。"

接着问，"他说，"这就是全部的营生。"熟客齐齐点头，抵不上一个老实本分的客人；他们俩之间早有了一种不必请人作证的安静默契。熟客们早就不劝他别问了。他想到副词的问题。老词儿像外套挂在钩子上一样挂在空气里。

一个字就能把整句扭歪；他也试过跟薇拉说，城里那些背景响根本不是噪音，是另一门音乐，说了也是白说。司机和乘客之间是一条双向的联系，像用慢信来回寄的书信。

一个不上心的人可以把自己的高兴也禁掉；卡托不肯。好奇是一门天生的禀赋，那是孩子的专利；快活的人是少数，恰恰是那几个还问为什么的。冷得过了头，把整条街变成了一张明信片。

笑话底下压着一件正经事：好好活。他没把事情搞复杂；把怪事过成平常，才是一个司机该做的活。候客点每个人都有故事，谁也不会一上来就说。炉子上的水壶叫了一整周，连个听的人都没有。

规章里没有哪一条写着：出租车司机不许去直面精神的自杀、不许看着好奇心慢慢烂掉，然后照样选择活着。这是他自己的事；而那种"废话比真话来钱快"的普遍信条，是最坏的一种广告。

东西总要先变坏，然后才变怪；开口问的必要，压过了沉默的舒服。他忽然清清楚楚地觉得，这一夜改了他；一个讲得糙的故事，往往比打磨光了的更真。他没为此买本子，也不想买。他领了这一夜的教训，于是计程表一直没开。

一个怀疑了一辈子、始终没能走到信的人，不过是活在自己脑子里的一位游客。后座椅子上的镜子裂了一道，被人贴上了胶带。卡托敢想：问题本身就是目的地。

一个疯狂的念头常常是发现的开头；他拿伊迪丝那份耐心去探这个念头，连他自己都没料到，自己会这样行事。

新娘那种不得不如实的诚实。小礼拜堂那种不偏不倚的安静。整座城都搁在陌生人与陌生人之间那些小小的好意上；这些他要在早上跟薇拉说清楚。厨子在案头搁了两个鸡蛋，壶嘴冒起一股气，把窗户糊开一小块。

纸上的一个词收尾落在元音上的时候，比男人肯认的多；那些问题还在等着，等着任何一个还肯向这个世界敞着的人——除了肯听，别的本钱都不需要。

第二天早上卡托没睡。他的大衣挂在钩子上，一股河水的味儿。他走到街角小馆，厨子不用他开口就知道他要什么；薇拉早已坐在她那张高脚凳上，面前一本笔记本、一只电话。凳子上有一圈浅印，是多少年一只杯子搁出来的。

"你脸上像见了鬼，"她说。""外乡人，"他说，"我见了位教授。"她没问是哪一位。这些年薇拉摸出个规律：她问得越少，他讲得越多；除了一起处了十年的人，其余的事她大体都持着怀疑。

他们说起那座桥——天亮就通了。车队下周就换新车了，老车要拉回车场的院子；到了春天，那座桥会整个挪到别处去。窗外的雨已经不像雨了，成了天气。

"九年了，你到这会儿才算变成了个怪人，"她说，"正常人这会儿该睡了。""我知道。一个想通了的人给自己备下的那点舒服，是一个司机该头一个不信的东西。"

回到车上，坐垫还是湿的，镜子上旧油污还在，卡片还贴在那盏小灯底下。他又把那十行读了一遍，字没有变小。两角的胶带翘起来，又被人按了回去；雨刮片橡胶老化，一格一格地咯噔。

那天傍晚他路过老厂子。有个女人站在栅栏外往里看；有那么一瞬他以为是伊迪丝·韦恩。那墙的砖色跟一只湿狗一样，她头顶的柱子上站着一只海鸥，像画上去的。铁门锁着，一条链子横在中间。他把车靠到路缘上。

是个更年轻的女人，端着肩膀，脖子那么直的姿势一模一样；她那件大衣是和教授那一件同样的样式。她转过身，隔着玻璃跟他对上了眼，笑了，是个很小的笑，像被人撞见正对着一栋空房子软下心来。

卡托抬了抬手。她也抬了抬。然后她顺着路走了，车里还是暖的；那些问题头一回像是他可以带着过完一生的东西。那晚过了一年后的某天傍晚，水边候客点上来了个女人。"你，"她说，"问问题的那个人。"卡托眨了眨眼。

"你认识我母亲，"她说，"伊迪丝·韦恩是我妈。她临死前跟我说起过一个出租车司机，他把她的问题问出去，问得比她自己答得还好。她说，她带过的学生里，只有你是真的把功课做了的。"那女人把手叠在膝盖上，稳稳的。

卡托坐着，发动机还转着；有那么一会儿他什么也说不出来。然后他笑了，伊迪丝教给他的那种真笑。他什么也没记下来。镜子上还留着旧油污的一道印子。

"我想，"他最后说，"教你的是你母亲。我不过是开车的。"那女人把手伸过坐耦合上了那张卡片——经过一年拇指的摩挲，角都软了。

"她还留了一句，"她说，接着在镜子上、紧挨着第一张，放上了第二张卡片。卡托读了。只有一行。

答案从来不是要紧的。发问才是那条路。

他免费把她送回家，看着她沿着门前小道走进一间亮着一盏灯的小屋。那些花苗早先长了，又死了，再被换上一茬，凡是有活气的东西都这么过。楼梯底下那截门廊还留着一块干木头。

问题还在，贴在那盏灯底下；他也还在。这一点他拿定了主意，就够。

这些问题从来就不是用来回答的。它们是拿来跑的。

chapters.title: 精算师的葬礼
chapters.content:
"Forty-two," my mother said. "He ordered forty-two chairs for people who are not coming."

My father died at 3:14 in the morning, an hour he would himself have picked, so tidy was his appetite for order. My mother called it fantastic, later, for its neatness. Walter Pell, chief actuary of Northgate Assurance, stopped breathing to the minute, and the firm's computer, faithful to the last digit, had sent its condolence before my mother lifted her kettle. The note called his passing a transition. I perceive now that the company never learned a tenderer word.

"Your father left a preface to his own funeral," she said. "He paid for it in installments and dedicated the whole silly thing to me. The man quantified even his goodbye."

That was the first revelation: Walter Pell had planned his death like a quarterly report.

I flew to Cobalt Falls the next day, a town slender enough to wear its sorrow like a scarf, loosely and mostly for show. Nothing here lasts long, and nothing here is wasted, which is the two things my father would have insisted on at the very end. My mother met me at Pell's stationery, the shop she had kept thirty years, and pressed a mug of tea into my hand without a word. On the counter lay a heap of cards, a multitude of them, each identical in its printed grief.

"The floor is theirs by noon," she said, nodding at the door. "Bring a coat. The damp comes off the valley at dusk, and my father, being thorough, ordered the weather as well. He ordered the flowers, too, and that order still lies unpaid in the drawer, a debt to the only shop in town that never sent him a bill."

A troop of Northgate people arrived first, and behind them a troupe of grief consultants, led by a vice president named Croy with a trademark smile, who speculated openly that my father might have disappeared to dodge an audit.

Croy called him a giant, and then twisted the facts as easily as he tuned his tie. One consultant, who had never met my father, ventured a guess at the cause. "Loading the reports. A sector problem, and he took it with him."

"The majority of us see him as a serious man," Croy went on. "A massive mind. A gigantic error, perhaps. The firm raked in a fortune on his models."

My mother lifted her chin. "He was wealthy in the only currency that matters," she said, and the consultants took that for poetry, which it was not.

Mr. Dolloway, the funeral director, arrived with his own arithmetic. He believed a casket should match a man's magnitude and measured the height of the room with his thumbs. "We require a proportional box," he said. "A huge affair. Substantial. Out of all scale to the tiny crowd you will draw." He highlighted the figure on a sheet: a staggering sum for a vast coffin.

"A huge affair," he said again, "but the wrong proportion. Substantial, and out of all scale to the tiny crowd you will draw." A box, he explained, is the only argument a dead man has with the ground, and it should be the loudest thing he ever bought.

"I prefer the small one," my mother said with a slight laugh. "It suits a tight budget. And he remained a petty man about space."

"The overall cost will increase, increasingly so, if you reject the premium model. A permanent solution demands a lasting box."

Nobody had heard from Toby until then. Walter's partner, he was twenty-four and thin as a ruler, and he had worshipped my father.

"Mr. Pell left a preface," he said. "It begins, 'Whereas the deceased trusted numbers more than people, whoever reads this should learn the inverse.'"

A weird silence fell. The verb on the tombstone, Toby said, was to be give. Not was. Not had. But give.

The third surprise came at the wake, when my mother xeroxed the document and handed it to each participant. It was a quantitative essay dressed as a letter, in which Walter set down the exact quantity of love he owed his family and found it infinite, a number the firm's machines could not store. Toby read the page twice, then folded it into his breast pocket and said nothing further for the rest of the evening. "I underestimated you all," he had written. "The calculation of a life is not a sum. Subtract the gain, remove the loss, and what remains is not zero."

Croy paled. "This document is not advisable reading for the press. It suggests the firm's longevity model was wrong. If the death rate was underestimated, the company is insolvent by a staggering margin."

"Verify it," said Toby, and handed over a second document: Walter's final spreadsheet. It showed that he had quietly transferred his substantial wealth, accumulated over thirty years, into a fund that guaranteed every policy the firm had sold, paying the difference himself.

The majority of those policyholders would never know, and silence was the verdict of the room. My father, the numerical legend, had performed the largest act of his career on the night he died, saving the company from itself without telling a soul.

Croy recovered first. "This transaction is internal," he said. "We will handle it." He motioned to the crew, who left with the spreadsheet wrapped in a sheet of paper stamped with my mother's store emblem.

The week before the funeral the firm's auditors had already started, a grave sector of men in grey ties who treated grief as a deal to be processed. "Sorrow is merely a negative return," their leader told his team. Hollis had a slack face and held that every emotion could be reduced to a figure. Two of them took notes, and the third measured the distance between the empty chairs, as though grief were flooring to be quoted.

What he had overlooked was simple: Walter Pell had been prepared for him.

In the warehouse behind the head office, where the old records were kept, Walter had hidden a second ledger, not the spreadsheet Croy took but another, written by hand in ink that smelled of the vinegar my mother used on her counter.

Toby discovered it on the Tuesday before the service, when he went to recover a parcel of files the firm had marked confidential. The parcel needed two hands and its string had been tied twice, the way my father tied his own letters. Inside sat a note in Walter's hand: "For the boy who learned the right verb. Open this only if they lie."

The hidden list ran triple the length of any report he had ever filed. The discovery overwhelmed Toby at first, then steadied him.

Not in a court but in a meeting room on the second storey of the head office, the model had its trial. "Our predecessor," Croy said, using the polite word for my father, "made a series of irregular entries. We have corrected them."

Toby stood and read the warehouse ledger aloud, his voice out-shouting the senior vice president. The board, face to face with the truth, grew quiet. "A wise man," Toby said, quoting Walter, "knows that a model is a map, not the territory."

Croy attempted a smile. The ruling came privately: the firm agreed to honor the fund, and the press was told a version of events in which nothing unusual had happened. The public account omitted the ledger wholly, and my father's name stayed out of the paper.

We kept the family account differently, on the back of a piece of paper in the shop, beside the kettle.

Mrs. Quill, the shopkeeper on the corner, sent her condolences baked in the shape of a coin. "Your father priced my first sale," she told me. "He said the number was too low. He was right." She cried a little, then wiped her eye with the scarf at her throat. Behind her stood the old tray where he had rearranged his prices that afternoon, and she had never had it properly cleaned since.

The landlady of the little inn where Toby stayed sent a note: "He is a good boy. Quiet. Pays on time." She signed it with a single initial, as if her own name were a quantity to be spared.

A union representative came to ask whether the dead man's pension would pass to his widow. "The sector is concerned," he said. "Workers deserve clarity." My mother assured him it would. "Walter was thorough about such things. He left a plan for everything except his own heart." He wrote her answer down in a neat hand, said thank you, and went back out into the rain.

The steward of the local club, a round man in a vest, brought a book of condolence to be signed. "Your father was a member thirty years. He won acclaim for his bridge game. Few guessed he was a legend of finance." I signed with a shaky hand, beside names I did not know.

Dolloway, meanwhile, had decided to offer a package. "For the modest budget we provide a basic service," he said. "For the top, a choir, a car, and a video." He produced a chart with the options side by side. "The majority choose the middle. The rich like the top. Your father prepaid the middle and asked for the peak anyway. A contradiction, but a kind one."

The receipt was a masterpiece of numerical art. It listed, line by line, a casket medium and upgraded, flowers in plenty, a brief service, a nominal document fee, and a surplus charge for emotional oversight that no one could explain. The total was high but not enormous, and my father would have called it reasonable.

Next morning, after the wake, I went into my father's study, a mass of paper, multiple ledgers, numerous notes, a pile he had never used. The fatigue of grief sat on my shoulders like a coat. Of the valley below the window he had spoken a thousand times, yet he rarely stood in it. The sink by the window still held his mug, upside down, the enamel going faint at the rim. On the desk lay a skull from a medical class, stunning in its sheer whiteness, and a belt of coal he swore he would one day recycle into art. The perfume of his old shaving soap still hung in the air, faint and distinct.

Toby was there already, partly because he could not sleep, partly because he loved the place. "He fulfilled every promise he made me," he said. "Even the implicit ones. The ones he never uttered." He pointed at a shelf of bound reports. "That is his life's work. Vast, mainly, and largely unread." He had sat in the same chair every morning for thirty years, Toby said, and the cushion still held his shape in the mornings.

I opened the top volume. Inside, in my father's hand: "Ban the sale of policies to the sick. It is a disgrace." The firm had ignored it, and the effect was a massacre of the poor, a word he had underlined twice, as if to spur the reader to anger.

"You called it a massacre," I said.

"The audit is a massacre too," Toby said. "Hollis believes the model is robust. I believe it is broken. The two viewpoints overlap scarcely at all."

An infrared lamp glowed by the mirror, and a page in the desk was written in invisible ink to give an optical trick on wet afternoons. A perceptual error in his model was the segment the auditors missed, and he had borne their coldness with tolerance.

The turnover of clerks had been high, and the old policy yielded little, so no violence was done to the truth. He had called it his final voyage, and the firm held no warrant to search the house. The story he spent years weaving about his health was false, and he had done nothing to perfection, yet he multiplied the premiums in his head for sport. There was no doubt whatsoever in the last entry, and the clerks who signed for it were told nothing.

Then a shark entered, tight-faced and super-efficient. "Miss Pell," Hollis said, "we are here to recover company property. Kindly step aside." He had a trolley of boxes. On it sat a cup of tea and a pair of my father's trousers folded with care, a trifle he had packed by mistake, he said, though I suspected otherwise. Every box carried a label reading Pell, in the same hand that had filled these pages for forty years.

"The tariff on grief is steep," I said.

Hollis did not laugh. "The firm sponsors the funeral. In exchange we take the papers. A fair deal, versus the alternative."

"Which is?"

"Ruin. The news would ruin the company. Unless you cooperate."

A slim chance remained that he was bluffing. "You underrate my father," I said. "And you misunderstand his intelligence. He prepared for this."

Hollis pulled a file. "We find numerous errors in his final calculations. Marginal, perhaps, but sufficient to void the fund. The clause is void if the math is wrong."

"Verify it," I said, echoing Toby. "The math is correct."

He smashed a glass on the desk, not from rage but carelessness. "The reduction in cost you claim is negligible," he said. "The increase in risk is severe. The potential for loss is tremendous. We will not honor a fiction."

Outside the weather turned violent, and a severe storm broke, rain striking the window with intensity. The thunder was loud. The power was not operational for a moment, and in that dark I perceived a ghost at the curtain, a shape that turned out to be only my own reflection, pale as a shroud. The temperature had dropped, and the rain purified the air, washing the garden green by the time Toby found his voice again.

"The view from here is stunning," Toby said, slowly recovering his calm. "Alongside the hill you can see the valley. My father used to say the landscape satisfied his soul."

Hollis snorted. "Sentiment does not suffice. We need proof. Concrete proof."

"Then uncover it," I said. "Search the room. Find the second ledger, the one he hid in the warehouse." I did not tell him Toby had already found it. That was our secret.

They turned the study upside down and found nothing worthwhile, since the ledger was elsewhere. The satisfaction of watching him fail was small but real.

"We will return," Hollis said. "This is not over."

Afterward Toby sat at the desk. "He inclined to fund the numbers more than people. That was his limitation. But his heart was large. Wholly large. The opposite of selfish."

I noticed a supplement to the will, a separate page signed and dated, leaving a portion of the estate to the shopkeeper's son, who had worked for my father one summer. "A token of respect," the page read, "for a boy who learned the right word."

Such small acts revealed the type of man he had been, not in the legend sums but in the particular kindnesses. The aspect I had missed was this: he measured everything because he could not say what he felt.

"We should participate in the service together," Toby said. "As partners. He would have liked that."

I agreed. "Practically everyone cried at the wake except Hollis. He is abnormal in his lack of feeling."

Toby smiled. "The firm is a resource he protects, not a person. He hinders the truth because the truth would cost him."

In the kitchen the stove hissed, and my mother was baking. "Your father thought the world a problem to be solved," she said. "He was wrong about that. But he was super at love, in his own strange way."

She handed me a cake. "Eat. Grief is better shared. That is the one thing no spreadsheet can show."

I bit. It was good, somewhat dry, but good. The taste reminded me of childhood, and my father would have called it a transcendent moment had he known the word. "The usage of the word love in this house," my mother said, "was rare. We spoke in numbers. Two cups. Three visits. One kiss at night. That was our language."

She patted her thigh. "He was a sly old thing, utterly sly. He planned his own funeral the way a general plans a war. The utmost care. The pure detail. His surname was Pell, but we called him Wal. He hated the name Walter. Said it sounded like a warning."

Another matter, the rockets. Walter had bought a small share in a start-up building rockets for weather research, and had told his ally it was a solid venture that would soar.

"A rocket is a fine thing to own after you are dead," my mother said. "It goes up, it comes down, and none of it concerns you." The share soared for a while, then slid, and slid again until it was nothing but a line sliding toward zero as the market turned turbulent. We sold the stock at a loss and returned the money to the fund. My mother kept the little certificate in the till for a month, then let Toby destroy it in front of the whole shop, which gave him a pleased expression she described as dignity. "He would like that," Toby said. "He believed in sufficient provision. Sufficiency was his religion."

I think of that word often, enough as a number you may choose. He picked a great number for other people and a thin one for himself. The figure he left for himself was small, and he would have called that sufficient.

The shepherd on the hill returns each evening with his flock. I watch from the shop window and note the rhythm: same time, same path, same quiet. A life reduced to a loop, which my father would have called a stable frequency. This is a quiet place, radically different from the city we left.

On the morning of the burial it rained, a piece of rain the local paper would later describe as worthy of a novel. The gravediggers had cut a trench in the soft earth, and the coffin went down through a tunnel of umbrellas. My mother wore velvet and a grey jacket; the perfume of wet flowers rose around her like a fog.

Toby read the document aloud, his tone steady despite everything. "Whereas the deceased was a man of numbers, whoever mourns him should remember that a life is not a sum. Remove the gain. Remove the loss. What remains is love, and love is not numerical."

A loud clap of thunder drowned the last word. The rain hammered the umbrellas. My mother gripped my arm. "He would have loved the drama. Literally. The man plotted his own storm." The priest, a thin man with a small stoop, said a few words, blessed the ground, and stepped back. The crowd, small but sincere, sang a hymn badly. I joined, mainly for the warmth of being wrong together. The choir from the parish hall hung back under the porch and counted the mourners instead of singing. "One short of last year," somebody said, and the joke ran along the wet railings.

After the earth was thrown we walked back to the store, where the stove hissed and the mugs steamed. My mother spread the ledger open and pointed to a section marked in the margin. "Section three," she read. "In the event of my death, please feed the cat." She looked up. "We have never owned a cat."

It was the one detail he got wrong, a shortcoming, as he might say, and the only one worth laughing at.

The funeral was on Thursday, the chapel small, the crowd tiny, a handful of relations, a few colleagues, and a plentiful supply of flowers from the shop next door. Croy sent a wreath on behalf of the firm, with a card reading, in part, "Whereas loyalty is a peak virtue." My mother noted the steep price and laughed a small laugh.

Toby gave the eulogy, nervous but resolute. "Mr. Pell taught me that a number is a kind of promise. He modified the models so the sick would not be dropped. He persuaded the board by pure force of arithmetic. The board called it a shortcoming. He called it mercy." A serial number on the wreath caught my eye, serial 0001, the first of a limited edition the firm sold as an offer item. I understand now that the firm marketed even its grief.

We ate in the store afterward, the food plentiful: a turkey my mother had bought on offer, plenty of bread, and a pile of cakes a customer sent. "Your father liked turkey," my mother said, a lie we both accepted. An old customer named Vera sent her regrets on a postcard, and the postcard stayed on the counter until the day we needed the counter for trays.

Dolloway returned to measure the attendance for his records. "Forty-two souls," he announced, "against a projected maximum of three hundred. A shortage of mourners. The quota of tears was not met." He noted the deficit with the gravity of a banker. "Suffice," said my mother. "Plenty suffices."

The afternoon grew long, and I found his last note hidden in a waterproof jacket he kept for gardening. "Dear Iris. I owe you a life. I quantified everything except how to say I love you, so I wrote it as a formula: Iris equals one. Whole. No fraction. No decimal. Just one. Your father." I cried then, quietly, in the way he would have preferred, measured, partial, sincere.

That evening Croy called. The firm had reviewed the spreadsheet and found it feasible to uphold the policies. "However, given the rise in risk, we must raise premiums by twelve percent," he said. A percent here and a percent there, and a windfall reappears. The firm took in the difference it had almost lost.

Toby, promoted to chief actuary that same week, sent a note: "I will not raise your premium. That is the one number I refuse to compute." My mother smiled. "He learned the right word."

The gravestone was small, a thin slab of stone bare except for a name, a date, and one word: give. The word was carved deep, resistant to wind and to weather, and it will remain.

I left Cobalt Falls with a photograph and a question. What measure of love equals a life? My father would have said the answer is not numerical but qualitative, a truth no spreadsheet could store. He had an ambitious plan to sell the firm and a convenient lie to hide it, and the amount of paper was incredible.

The aftermath was quiet. The firm issued a statement praising his service, and the press printed a photo of the building, calling him a legend of risk. None of it mentioned the ledger, the fund, or the people he had saved, though he had an acre of land behind the house that he bought and never once stood in.

Toby messaged me a month later. "I raise premiums by two percent," he wrote. "The board called it wise. You call it what you like. The rest of his plan I keep secret."

I replied: "He would be proud."

"Prouder," Toby texted back, "that I learned the right word."

The garden behind the store is a small enclosure my father bought and never finished, and the shepherd still stops to look when he passes. That acre, green in spring, is the one part of his arithmetic that adds up. We bipedal creatures spend our short lives trying to make the world safe by counting it, and he counted better than most. Every Friday the milkman asks after him, and I give him the same answer I gave him last year, which is that the man measured everything and measured himself last of all.

He counted the world so the rest of us could stop counting, and begin to live.

“四十二。”我母亲说，“他订了四十二把椅子，给那些根本不会来的人。”

我父亲在凌晨三点十四分停止了呼吸——那正是他自己会挑的时刻，他爱一切整整齐齐的东西。北门保险公司的首席精算师沃尔特·佩尔，分秒不差地停了那口气；公司的电脑对最后一个小数都忠心耿耿，还没等我母亲端起水壶，就把吊唁信发了出去。那封信管他的死叫“过渡”。我现在才明白，这家公司一辈子也没学会更温柔的词。

“你父亲给自己那场葬礼写了篇序言。”她说，“他是一期一期分期付的款，还把整个荒唐玩意儿题献给了我。这人连告别都要量化。”

这是第一个启示：沃尔特·佩尔把自己死成了一道季度报告。

第二天我飞到钴谷市。这座城苗条得很，戴哀伤就像别的镇子戴围巾，松松垮垮，多半只为做做样子。这儿什么也不长久，也什么也不浪费，这两样是父亲临了前一定要讲明白的话。母亲在佩尔文具店门口接我，那家店她守了三十年，什么也没说，只把一杯茶塞进我手里。柜台上堆着一摞吊唁卡，多得数不清，每一张的哀伤都一模一样。

“中午之前他们就占了地。”她朝门外点点头，“带件外套。天一黑山谷里的潮气就上来了。我父亲那种人什么都安排周全，连天气也一起订了。花他也订了，那张单子还压在抽屉里没付钱，欠着镇上唯一一家从不来催账的铺子。”

北门的人先成群到了，后面跟着一队哀伤顾问，领头的是副总裁克罗伊，笑得跟招牌一样。他公然揣测，我父亲也许是装死，好躲掉一场审计。

克罗伊管我父亲叫巨人，随手把事实一扭，就像他正摆弄领带那样轻松。有个顾问压根没见过我父亲，也敢猜原因。“账做得太满。”她说，“是这一行的问题，他一个人全背走了。”

“我们大多数人把他看成一个严肃的人。”克罗伊接着说，“脑子海了去了。也许是犯了个天大的错。公司靠他的模型赚翻了。”

母亲抬起下巴。“他在唯一要紧的货币上是个富人，”她这么说，顾问们却把这话当成了诗——可它根本不是诗。

殡仪馆的多洛韦先生也来了，随身带着自己的算术。他认定棺材得配得上一个人的量级，还伸着大拇指比量房间的高度。“我们要一口成比例的盒子。”他说，“得够大，够扎实，跟你那点寒酸的人群完全不成比例。”他在纸上圈出个数字：一口大得离谱的棺材，价钱惊人。

“够大，没错，”他又说，“可比例不对。要扎实，要跟你那点少得可怜的吊客完全不成比例。棺材是一个死人跟土地唯一能争的东西，也该是他一辈子买过最响亮的一样。”

“我宁可要小的那口。”母亲略带讥笑地说，“小的小子预算也合得上。他在占地方这件事上，一向是个小气鬼。”

“你要是拒了高档方案，总费用会涨，而且越来越涨。永久的办法，得配一口永久的盒子。”

托比一直没开口。他是沃尔特的合伙人，二十四岁，瘦得像把尺子，一直崇拜我父亲。

“佩尔先生留了一份序言。”他说，“开头是这么写的：‘鉴于逝者信任数字胜过信任人，无论谁读到这页，都该懂得那个反例。’”

一阵古怪的沉默落下来。托比说，沃尔特墓碑上要刻的动词是“给”。不是“是”。不是“有”。是“给”。

第三个启示出现在守灵夜。母亲把那份文件复印了，发给每一位到场的人。那是一篇披着信笺外衣的量化文章。里头，沃尔特算出了他欠家人确切的爱之数量，发现那是无限的，一个连公司机器都存不下的数字。托比把那页读了两遍，折好塞进胸口的口袋，剩下的夜里就再没吭过一声。“我低估了你们所有人，”他写道，“人生的算法不是一道求和题。减去所得，减去所失，剩下的并不是零。”

克罗伊脸白了。“这文件给媒体看可不明智，”他说，“它暗示公司的长寿模型错了。要是死亡率被低估，公司就资不抵债了，亏空大得吓人。”

“去核实吧。”托比说着又递上第二份文件：沃尔特最后那张表格。里头显示，他悄悄把积攒了三十年的可观家财转进一个基金，用来担保公司卖出去的每一份保单，差额全由他自己补上。

大多数投保人永远不会知道，而那一屋子人的裁决就是沉默。我父亲，那位量化的巨人，在他死掉的那个夜晚，完成了职业生涯里最大的一举：他救了公司，使它免于自我毁灭，一个字也没透露。

克罗伊最先缓过来。“这笔交易是内部事务，”他说，“我们会处理。”他朝那队人一挥手，他们便带着表格走了，表格包在印着母亲店标的文具纸里。

葬礼前一周，公司的审计员早就悄悄开工了。那是一帮阴沉的男人，系着灰领带，把哀伤当成一桩待处理的买卖。“悲伤不过是一笔负收益。”头儿这么跟手下说。霍利斯一张脸松松垮垮，相信每种情绪都能化成一个数字。有两个在记笔记，第三个量起了空椅子的间距，好像哀伤也是一种能报价的地板。

他漏算的只有一件事，那就是：沃尔特·佩尔早就防着他了。

北门总部后头的仓库里，旧档案存放之处，沃尔特藏了第二本账。不是克罗伊拿走的那张表格，是另一本，手写的，墨水里带着母亲擦柜台用的那股醋味。

周二守灵前，托比去取一批标着“机密”的文件。那包裹得用两只手才拎得动，绳子系了两道，像父亲自己封信的样子。包裹里是沃尔特的手迹：“给那个学会了正确动词的男孩。他们撒谎的时候，你再打开。”

那本暗账的长度，是他这辈子报过的任何一份报告的三倍。这发现起初压垮了托比，随后又稳住了他。

模型受审，不在法庭，而在总部二楼的一间会议室。“我们的前任，”克罗伊用客气话指代我父亲，“记了一串不规范的账。我们已经更正了。”

托比站起来，大声念那本仓库账，一个二十四岁的嗓门盖过了资深副总裁。董事会面对面撞上真相，安静了。“聪明人，”托比引用沃尔特的话说，“懂得模型只是地图，不是疆土。”

克罗伊挤出一个笑。裁决下来时是私下的：公司同意履行那个基金，媒体只被告知一个版本，什么异常也没发生。公开的版本彻底略去了那本账，我父亲的名字没上报纸。

家里的版本不一样。我们把它写在文具纸背面，压在水壶旁边。

街角的店主奎尔太太，寄来一份吊唁，做成一枚硬币形状的蛋糕。“你父亲帮我定过第一次大减价的价，”她对我说，“他说数字太低。他是对的。”她轻轻哭了哭，拿围巾角擦了擦眼。她身后立着那只旧托盘，那天下午他就在那儿重新排过价，从那以后她再没好好擦过。

托比住的那家小客栈的女房东，寄来一张便条：“他是个好孩子。安静。按时付钱。”她只签了个首字母，仿佛连自己的名字都是种该省着用的东西。

一位工会代表来问，死者的养老金会不会留给遗孀。“这一行很操心，”他说，“工人该有明白话。”母亲向他保证会留。“沃尔特在这种事上向来周全，”她说，“他给一切都留了计划，唯独没给自己的心留。”他把她的答复工工整整记在本子上，说了声谢谢，又走回雨里。

本地俱乐部的管家，一个穿马甲的圆脸男人，送来一本吊唁簿签名。“你父亲入会三十年了，”他说，“他的桥牌赢过满堂彩。没几个人猜到他是金融界的传奇。”我在发抖的手旁签了名，旁边是些我不认识的名字。

多洛韦这时已打定主意搞个套餐。“预算紧的，”他说，“我们给基础服务。顶档的，有唱诗班、有车、有录像。”他摊开一张对照表。“大多数人选中间档。有钱人偏爱顶档。你父亲预付了中间档，却又开口要了顶档。矛盾，但算是种善意。”

收据送来时，堪称量化艺术的大作。它一行行列着：棺材，中号，加配升级；花，管够；仪式，简短；文书费，名义上的；外加一项“情绪监理”的盈余收费，谁也说不清是啥。总数不低，但谈不上惊人，我父亲会管这叫合理。

守灵后的第二天早上，我进了父亲的书房。屋里是一大堆纸，好几本账，无数便条，还有一堆他从没用过的。哀伤的疲惫像件外套压在我肩上。那扇窗底下就是山谷，他讲过一千遍，可他难得站进去过。窗边的水池里还搁着他的杯子，倒扣着，瓷边都磨白了。桌上摆着一颗他从医学课留下的颅骨，白得纯粹，惊心动魄；还有一条他说迟早要回收做成艺术品的煤带。他旧剃须皂的香气还挂在空气里，淡，却分明。

托比已经在那儿了，一半因为睡不着，一半因为爱这地方。“他答应我的每句话都兑现了，”他说，“连那些没说出口的、隐含的承诺也一样。就是那些他从不吐口的。”他指着一排装订好的报告。“那是他一生的活儿。大多数是庞然大物，多半没人读。”托比又说，他每天都坐在同一张椅子上，坐了三十年，早上坐下去，坐垫还留着他的形状。

我翻开最上面那卷。里头是父亲的手迹：“禁止向病人卖保单。那是耻辱。”公司没理它。后果是对穷人的一场大屠杀，这个词他划了又划，仿佛要拿它去激怒读者。

“你刚才是说大屠杀。”

“审计也是一场屠杀。”托比说，“霍利斯以为模型稳健。我以为它破了。两种看法几乎不重叠。”

角上亮着一盏红外线的灯，桌上有张纸是用隐形墨水写的，下过雨的下午能照出光学戏法。他模型里那个知觉上的错，正是审计员漏掉的那一段，而他对他们的冷，向来以容忍承受。

职员的流动率一直很高，旧保单也没什么产出，所以真相对谁都没下狠手。他说过，这是他最后的一趟航行，公司根本无权搜这屋子。他花了很多年编的那个生病的由头是假的，可他把什么事都没做到完美，却爱在脑子里把保费乘来乘去当消遣。最后那笔账里一点疑虑也没有，替他签字的人，也什么都没被告知。

于是一只鲨鱼进门了，绷着脸，效率高得过分。“佩尔小姐，”霍利斯说，“我们来收回公司财产。请让一让。”他推着辆手推车，车上放着一杯茶，还有一条父亲折得整整齐齐的裤子，他说是打包时错塞的零碎，可我疑心不是。每只箱子上都贴着一张标签，写着“佩尔”，跟他填了四十年的那笔字迹一模一样。

“哀伤的关税很贵。”我说。

霍利斯没笑。“公司赞助这场葬礼，”他说，“交换条件是拿回文件。公平交易，总好过另一种结局。”

“哪种结局？”

“破产。这消息会毁了公司。除非你配合。”

他虚张声势的可能不是没有，只是很渺茫。“你低估了我父亲，”我说，“也误解了他的才智。他早有准备。”

霍利斯抽出一份卷宗。“我们在他最后的测算里找出无数错。也许微不足道，但足够让基金作废。数学一错，条款就失效。”

“去核实。”我学托比的口气说，“数学是对的。”

他把一只杯子砸在桌上，不是发火，是毛手毛脚。“你说能减的成本可以忽略，”他说，“可风险的增加是严重的。亏损的潜力大得吓人。我们不会认一个编出来的故事。”

窗外天变得暴烈，一场严重的风暴来了，雨点带着狠劲敲窗。雷声很响。有那么一刻电都不通了；黑暗里，我看见窗帘边有东西像鬼，凑近了才明白那不过是我自己的影子，白得像块裹尸布。气温降了，雨把空气洗净，等托比重新开口，窗外的花园已经绿了一层。

“这儿的景致惊心动魄，”托比好不容易稳住神说，“顺着山坡往下，能看见山谷。我父亲总说，这风景满足了他的魂灵。”

霍利斯哼了一声。“感情顶不了数，”他说，“我们要的是证据。实打实的证据。”

“那就揭开它。”我说，“搜这屋子。找第二本账，他藏在仓库那本。”我没告诉他托比早找到了。那是我们的秘密。

他们把书房兜底翻了一遍，什么值钱的也没找着，因为账在别处。看他落空，那点满足感虽小，却是真的。

“我们会回来，”霍利斯说，“这事没完。”

他们走后，托比在桌前坐下。“他倾向于信数字胜过信人。”托比说，“那是他的局限。可他的心大。纯粹地大。跟自私正相反。”

我注意到遗嘱的一份附录，单独一页，签了名，注了日期，把一部分家产留给了店主的儿子，那孩子有一年夏天替我父亲打过工。“一份敬意，”那页上写，“给一个学会了正确动词的男孩。”

我父亲是哪种人，就在这些小事里显形。不在那些吓人的大数目里，而在那些特定的善意里。我从前漏掉的那一面是：他量尽一切，是因为他说不出心里的感受。

“咱们该一起参加仪式，”托比说，“当搭档。他准会乐意。”

我答应了。“守灵夜几乎人人都哭了，除了霍利斯。他在缺乏感情这件事上，反常得离谱。”

托比笑了。“公司是他护着的一种资源，不是人。他妨碍真相，因为真相会要他的代价。”

厨房里水壶嘶嘶响，母亲在烤东西。“你父亲以为世界是个待解的问题，”她说，“这点他错了。可他有自己的笨法子，爱得超级在行。”

她递我一块蛋糕。“吃，”她说，“哀伤分着担才轻。这是任何表格都显不出来的。”

我咬了一口。好吃，有点干，但好吃。那味道让我想起童年，父亲若懂这个词，会管它叫超凡的一刻。“这屋里‘爱’这个词的用法，”母亲说，“很稀罕。我们说的是数字。两杯。三回探望。夜里一个吻。那是我们的语言。”

她拍了拍大腿。“他是个狡猾的老东西，彻底狡猾。他把自己的葬礼排得像个将军排兵。极度的用心，纯粹的考究。他姓佩尔，可我们叫他沃尔。他恨‘沃尔特’这名字，说听着像句警告。”

还有火箭的事。沃尔特在最后一年买了家小公司的少许股份，那公司造气象研究的火箭。他跟搭档说，这是门稳当的买卖，会飙升。

“火箭是死了以后拥有的一件好东西，”母亲说，“它上去，它下来，没有一样跟你相干。”那股份确实飙升过一阵，接着滑落，再往下滑，最后只剩一条线往零里沉，市场也转入动荡。我们亏本把股票出了手，钱回到了基金。母亲把那张小凭证在柜台里搁了整整一个月，才让托比当着全店的面撕掉，他脸上那副得意的神气，母亲管它叫体面。“他本就乐意这样，”托比说，“他信的是充足的储备。充足是他的宗教。”

我常想着这个词。够，是个你可以自己选的数字。他给旁人挑了个惊人的数，给自己挑的那个薄得可怜。留下的那个数很小，他大概会管它叫足够。

山坡上的牧羊人每天黄昏赶羊群回来。我从店窗里望着，记下那节奏：同一时刻，同一条路，同一份安静。一种化进循环的生命，父亲会管这叫稳定的频率。这是个安静的地方，跟我们离开的那座城截然不同。

下葬那天下了雨。本地报纸后来写，那是一场配得上小说的雨。掘墓人在软泥里挖了道沟，棺材顺着伞搭成的隧道落下去。母亲围一条天鹅绒的披巾，穿件灰马甲；湿花的气息像雾一样绕着她升起。

托比大声读那份文件，嗓音在天气里稳稳的。“鉴于逝者是个与数字打交道的人，”他念，“无论谁哀悼他，都该记得人生不是一道求和题。减去所得。减去所失。剩下的是爱，而爱不是量化的。”

一声响雷盖过了最后那个词。雨点捶打着伞。母亲攥住我的胳膊。“他准会爱这出戏，”她小声说，“字面上。这人连风暴都给自己排好了。”牧师，一个瘦高、微微驼背的男人，说了几句，祝福了土地，退到一边。人群虽少却真心，歪歪扭扭地唱起一首圣歌。我跟着唱，多半是为了一起出错的那点暖意。教区礼堂的唱诗班缩在门廊底下，不唱，光数人。“比去年少一个，”有人说，这玩笑顺着湿漉漉的栏杆传了一圈。

土抛下去后，我们走回店里。水壶嘶嘶。杯子冒汽。母亲摊开账本，指着她标出的一段。“第三节，”她念，“我死后，请喂猫。”她抬起头。“咱们从没养过猫。”

那是他唯一算错的一笔。一个短处，照他的说法，也是唯一值得笑的那一个。

葬礼定在周四。小教堂挤，人却少得可怜，几个亲戚，几个同事，还有店旁店主供的一大堆花。克罗伊以公司名义送了花圈，卡片上写着：“鉴于忠诚是顶尖的美德。”母亲记下了这笔忠诚的昂贵价码，笑了小小一声。

托比致悼词，紧张，却果断。“佩尔先生教我，一个数字就是一种承诺，”他说，“他改了模型，好让病人不被甩掉。他用纯粹的数学之力说服了董事会。董事会管那叫短处。他管它叫慈悲。”花圈上一个序列号吸引了我的眼，零零零一号，公司当特价品卖的限量款头一件。我现在懂了，公司连自己的哀伤都拿去做买卖。

仪式后我们在店里吃。吃的管够：母亲特价买来的火鸡，足量的面包，还有客人送来的一堆蛋糕。“你父亲爱吃火鸡，”母亲说，这是我们都当假的谎，也都认了。老顾客薇拉寄了张明信片来道歉，那明信片就在柜台上搁着，一直搁到我们需要柜台摆托盘的那天。

多洛韦回来量人数，记进本子。“四十二个魂灵，”他宣布，“对比预计上限三百。吊客短缺。泪水的配额没达标。”他记下亏空，神情像银行家般庄重。“够了，”母亲说，“管够就行。”

下午拖得长。我在他种花用的防水马甲里找到了最后那张便条。“亲爱的艾莉丝。我欠你一条命。我把一切都量化了，唯独没学会怎么说我爱你。所以我把它写成一道公式：艾莉丝等于一。整的。没有分数。没有小数。只有一个。你的父亲。”我那时静静地哭了，照他大概会中意的方式，克制，不完全，却是真的。

那天晚上克罗伊打来电话。公司审过表格，觉得基金可以履行。“我们会支持这些保单，”他说，“不过，鉴于风险上升，我们得把保费提百分之十二。”这儿一个百分点，那儿一个百分点，一笔财富又冒了出来。公司把差点丢掉的差额又赚回了手。

托比在那周当上了首席精算师，寄来张便条：“你的保费我不会涨。那是唯一我拒算的数字。”母亲笑了。“他学会了正确的动词。”

墓碑很小，一块薄薄的石板，除了姓名、日期和一个孤零零的词：给。那个动词刻得深，经得住风，也经得住雨，会一直在那儿。

我离开钴谷时带了一张照片，和一个问题。多少数量的爱，才抵得上一生？父亲大概会说，答案不是量化的，是定性的，一道任何表格都存不下的真相。他有个野心勃勃的计划要卖掉公司，还编了个方便的谎来遮掩，纸多得到了难以置信的地步。

余波很静。公司发了一份声明，称赞我父亲的贡献。媒体登了张大楼照片，说明里称他是风险界的传奇。没有一字提起那本账、那个基金，或他救过的人，尽管屋后还有一英亩地，是他买下却从没踏进去过的。

一个月后托比给我发了条消息。“我把保费提了百分之二，”他写，“董事会说这叫明智。你爱怎么叫怎么叫。他计划的其余部分，我藏着。”

我回：“他准会骄傲。”

“更骄傲，”托比回，“因为我学会了正确的动词。”

店后那块地如今是个小园子，父亲买下却一直没弄完，牧羊人路过还是会停步看看。这一英亩，春天常绿，是他算术里唯一加得拢的那一笔。我们这些两足的生物，用短促的一生去把世界数安全，而他比别人数得都好。每逢周五，送奶的还问起他，我给的答案跟去年一样：那人说，什么都量过，唯独把自己留到了最后。

他数过这个世界，好让我们其余的人停下计数，开始生活。
